topics.title: mixture sweep evidence is bucket-indexed: bucket or data changes strand it
topics.body:
Our data-mixture optimization capital is **bucket-indexed**. A mixture swarm (RegMix/DSP-style) teaches "weight on bucket #7 → loss", and bucket #7 is nothing but a name: the learned surrogate has no representation of what the bucket *contains*. Any change to the bucket layer therefore strands the evidence:

- **Bucket contents drift**: dedup passes, quality relabels, source refreshes, tokenizer changes to a bucket's data all silently invalidate the coefficients learned for its name — with no signal that they did.
- **Bucketing changes**: merging, splitting, or re-partitioning the corpus (e.g. any datakit reorganization) produces buckets the sweep never named. The entire sweep becomes unusable for the new layout.
- **New data has no coordinates**: "should we add dataset X, and at what weight/schedule?" has no principled answer — the surrogate cannot price a bucket it never saw. Current fallbacks are heuristics (token-proportional share, Olmix-style reuse of old ratios) or paying for a fresh sweep.
- **Sweeps cannot be pooled**: swarms run under different bucket eras (different partitions, different quality splits) share no coordinate system, so their runs cannot serve as one training set even when the underlying corpus overlaps heavily.

The cost is recurring and large: a mixture swarm is O(hundreds) of proxy training runs (qsplit240: ~240 mixtures × 2 scales), and the bucket layer changes far more often than the corpus itself. In practice this means mixture decisions are refreshed on sweep cadence, while data curation moves on relabel/refresh cadence — and every gap between the two is bridged by heuristics.

What a solution needs to provide:

1. **Sweep reuse**: existing swarm runs remain valid evidence under bucket redefinition, re-bucketing, and corpus refresh — ideally under a representation that can be recomputed for old runs after the fact.
2. **New-data pricing**: a new dataset can be evaluated for "does it help, at what weight, in which training phase" at a cost far below a sweep (target: hours of CPU + at most a handful of validation runs), with an honest measure of how far the answer extrapolates beyond observed evidence.
3. **Pooling**: runs from different bucket eras (and, eventually, different swarms) can serve as one accumulating training set, so mixture evidence compounds rather than resets.

comments.body: @Helw150 when you have the sweep data pointers (no rush), pls share here 🙇

🤖 One potential fix, designed and validated: **mixing-via-embeddings** (#6969) — describe every bucket by a token-weighted histogram over a frozen embedding codebook and learn the mixture surrogate over the induced *content distribution* (`h = V·w`) instead of bucket names. Bucket identity is consumed in featurization, so old sweeps re-featurize under any future bucketing (reuse + pooling), and a new dataset is priced from one 20k-doc embedding pass + a CPU refit (new-data pricing), with support/novelty diagnostics quantifying extrapolation.

Validation summary (full detail on #6969 and in `.agents/logbooks/mixing-via-embeddings.md` on `rav/mixing-via-embeddings`): pre-registered retrodictive gates passed on qsplit240 (content→value LODO with shuffled/matched controls @60M; held-out-dose retrodiction @300M, beating weights-based incumbents on 32–34/36 domains), and a live pre-registered test passed — the surrogate priced a never-swept bucket (`dolma_starcoder`), proposed a mixture, and realized **0.9410** uncheatable BPB vs olmix-reuse 0.9495 / token-proportional 0.9759 / the sweep's best-ever run 0.9554 (−0.0145, ~8σ vs measured repeat noise). Cost: one embedding job + minutes of CPU + 3 validation runs. Known limits are quantified there too (within-topic quality invisible to embeddings; histogram-dispersion confound; ~0.03 argmax optimism → LCB proposer is the top follow-up).

For visibility, I pushed sweep pointers here: https://huggingface.co/datasets/marin-community/grug-moe-mix-swarm/viewer/default/train?row=0

Anyone can work on regression w/them there!
@ravwojdyla @Helw150 is there precedent for this approach? I'd be curious to read more in the research literature about these ideas...
@hammer [Domain2Vec](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.10952) is very much the inspiration here.

🤖 Reference for anyone picking this up: how to map the **Grug-MoE Fisher-DSP sweep** buckets to their underlying data.

**The sweep**: [`marin-community/grug-moe-mix-swarm`](https://huggingface.co/datasets/marin-community/grug-moe-mix-swarm) — 840 MoE runs (d512, us-central2), each a two-phase mixture over **168 buckets**, with `macro_bpb` + 52 per-task BPBs per run. Weight columns are `{bucket: weight}` dicts keyed by bucket name.

**The data**: datakit store `store_8ac06c74` — 40 lexical clusters × 5 quality tiers = 200 partitions, 10.37T tokens total:
- `gs://marin-us-east5/datakit/store_8ac06c74/` (GCS, us-east5)
- `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/datakit/store_8ac06c74/` (CoreWeave mirror)

**Mapping rule** (canonical source: `experiments/grug/moe/launch_datakit_moe_mix.py`):

1. **Direct buckets** — name arithmetic, 0-based: `cNNqQ` → `<store>/cluster=NN/quality=Q`. E.g. `c12q3` → `.../cluster=12/quality=3`. 167 buckets.
2. **`tail`** — a `ConcatDatasetComponent` over exactly the **33 below-threshold partitions** (every partition with < ~100–200M tokens; largest merged = 89M, smallest kept = 212M; separation is clean). The explicit child list is `_TAIL_BUCKETS` in the launcher: whole clusters 0, 4, 7, 9, 39 (all tiers) plus `c10q1–q4` and `c38q1–q4`. Combined: 0.42B tokens (0.004% of the store).
3. This one rule explains all bucket-list irregularities: no `c00/c04/c07/c09/c39` (whole clusters below threshold), and `c10`/`c38` appear with only `q0` (only tier above threshold).

**Format & metadata**:
- Each partition is consumed directly as a levanter cache (`flat_cache=True`, `TextLmDatasetFormat`): `part-NNNNN-of-06301/` shard dirs containing `shard_ledger.json` + `input_ids/` tensorstore arrays. No derived per-bucket caches exist.
- Per-partition `total_tokens` / `total_elements` / `n_shards`: `<store>/.artifact.json` (also records `cluster_view: 40`, quality thresholds `[0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8]`).
- Tokenizer: `marin_tokenizer`. Phase 1 starts at 0.8 of total steps (`_PHASE_1_START_FRACTION`); mixture block size 49,152. The launcher has an `enable_simulated_epoching` flag — check the swarm's launch config before interpreting high-dose runs (per-run max weight reaches 0.95, and bucket sizes span 212M→hundreds of B tokens, so epoching behavior matters for any response modeling).

**To build content features (V columns) for these buckets** with the machinery on `rav/mixing-via-embeddings`: sample per partition from the caches above (`experiments/datakit/mixture_features/build_domain_histograms.py` reads this exact format), and build `tail` as a token-count-weighted sample across its 33 children using the `.artifact.json` counts.

🤖 **Pre-registration: holdout test protocol for the grug-moe-mix-swarm** (before any model fitting on this data; the 840 runs are treated independently of qsplit240).

- **Split (locked)**: 800 train / 40 test, uniform random `numpy default_rng(seed=0)` over `experiment_index`. Test indices in `holdout_manifest.json`; test labels quarantined in a separate file whose SHA-256 is pinned in the manifest (`68a90838…`); both mirrored to `gs://marin-eu-west4/user/rav/projects/mixing_via_embeddings/v0/grug/`. Coverage checked on features only: test max-dose distribution matches train (15/40 runs above 0.4).
- **Development rules**: all featurization, variants (raw-weights ridge/LGBM incumbents; content ridge K=1000 in the frozen basis; Hellinger kernel; ± quality-tier features; ± epoch/exposure features; shuffled + matched-random controls), hyperparameters, and model selection use the 800 training runs only, via CV. Primary target: `macro_bpb`.
- **One-shot procedure**: freeze the selected model + declared baselines → write predictions for the 40 from features only → **publish the predictions file's SHA-256 here before opening labels** → open the quarantine once → compute only the pre-registered readout (anything further is labeled exploratory).
- **Readout & pass bar**: R1 predictive power (Spearman on the 40, permutation p < 0.001); R2 beats the bucket-indexed incumbent (paired ΔSpearman ≥ 0 vs best weights baseline, bootstrap CI reported); R3 no selection overfit (test Spearman ≥ train-CV − 0.15); R4 semantics-vs-shape decomposition vs matched-random control (measured, no bar). **PASS = R1 ∧ R2 ∧ R3.**

Full protocol: `test_protocol.md` at the GCS path above (sha256 `ef33dce04d156a37…`).

🤖 **Pre-registered AMENDMENT to the grug holdout protocol** (before any label opening; the quarantine file remains unopened; all evidence below is train-only CV).

**Why**: development on the 800 training runs showed the original target (`macro_bpb`) mixes an English factor with a reliable-but-mixture-orthogonal multilingual factor (33 belebele/include tasks; English↔belebele macro Spearman 0.10) over a per-run-varying task set — capping the best model at OOF Spearman 0.303 and breaking R1's power at n=40. The swarm's own registered aggregates likewise drop `macro_bpb` and use strict-common English z-means.

**Amended target** (exact formula, replaces macro_bpb): `zmacro_english_20` — for run r, y(r) = mean over observed t ∈ L of (bpb_t(r) − μ_t)/σ_t, where L = the 20 bpb tasks not matching `belebele_*`/`include_*`, and (μ_t, σ_t) are frozen train-set constants recorded in `target_candidates.json` (GCS: `gs://marin-eu-west4/user/rav/projects/mixing_via_embeddings/v0/grug/`). Lower better. Leak checks: fully-nested selection reproduces the same task list; nested vs frozen z-stats differ by 0.0002 Spearman; PC2 of the task matrix (unsupervised) recovers the same factor at 0.841.

**Selected primary model** (train-CV, frozen): Hellinger-kernel ridge, K=1000 per-phase content histograms, hyperparameters by inner CV — **train-CV OOF Spearman 0.818 ± 0.001** (≈93% of the split-half reliability bound 0.88). Declared baselines frozen alongside: train-mean, weights-ridge (0.679), weights-LGBM, DSP dose-response (best tied variant 0.643 — the qsplit240 functional form does not transfer to this 168-bucket swarm), and the primary's shuffled-columns + matched-random controls.

**Amended readout** (unchanged in structure; R1's bar now properly powered): R1 Spearman(pred, realized) on the 40, permutation p < 0.001; R2 paired ΔSpearman ≥ 0 vs the best weights baseline (bootstrap CI reported); R3 test Spearman ≥ train-CV − 0.15 (i.e. ≥ 0.668); R4 semantic-vs-matched-random decomposition (measured, no bar). PASS = R1 ∧ R2 ∧ R3. Procedure unchanged: predictions for the 40 are generated from features only, their file's SHA-256 gets published here BEFORE the quarantine is opened, labels are opened once, and only the pre-registered readout is computed (rest labeled exploratory).

🤖 **Holdout test — predictions frozen (phase 1 of the one-shot procedure).** `test_predictions.parquet` SHA-256: `0a4cc4e6430d92001e65b9ecf00873dd02b5666fb29da41c38d77d7d34c2474f` (1040 rows = 26 models × 40 runs; frozen primary Hellinger-kernel γ=1.2475/α=0.1 + declared baselines/controls; embedded provenance: git `ed7599e51a`, target formula + frozen z-stats; mirrored to `gs://marin-eu-west4/user/rav/projects/mixing_via_embeddings/v0/grug/` with `frozen_model_hyperparams.json` sha `080a504c…`). Quarantined labels accessed by checksum only so far (matches the split manifest). Opening the label file next; only the amended pre-registered readout (R1–R4) will be computed on it.

🤖 **Grug holdout test — pre-registered verdict: PASS (R1 ∧ R2 ∧ R3).** Quarantine opened exactly once, after hash verification against the published predictions SHA (`0a4cc4e6…`) and the split manifest (`68a90838…`).

| gate | result | numbers |
|---|---|---|
| R1 predictive power | **PASS** | test Spearman **0.7205**, 10k-permutation p = 1e-4 (resolution floor; max permuted ρ 0.588) |
| R2 vs bucket-indexed incumbent | **PASS** | Δ = **+0.035** vs weights-LGBM (0.6852; best baseline), paired 95% CI [−0.14, +0.21] (CI exclusion was pre-declared stretch, not required); vs weights-ridge Δ = +0.089; ΔRMSE −0.037 |
| R3 no selection overfit | **PASS** | 0.7205 ≥ 0.668 bar (train-CV 0.818 − 0.15); generalization gap −0.098 |
| R4 semantics vs shape (measured) | small | Δ vs matched-random control +0.015, 95% CI [−0.05, +0.10]; shuffled control mean-of-10 reaches 0.7212 |

**Honest headline**: the content-featurized surrogate transfers to unseen mixtures (best single model on Spearman and per-seed comparisons, 10/10 vs matched-control seeds) and beats the RegMix-style incumbent — but on this swarm most of the predictive signal is carried by histogram *shape* statistics rather than cross-bucket semantic identity (the R4 margin is CI-consistent with zero at n=40; the `_mean10` controls also enjoy an implicit 10-predictor ensembling advantage). This echoes and strengthens the qsplit240 dispersion-confound finding: for *this* store's cluster×quality buckets, "describedness" earns its keep mostly through shape+geometry, with semantics contributing a small increment.

Campaign summary on this swarm (840 runs, all development on 800 train, one-shot test on 40): target repaired from `macro_bpb` (kernel OOF 0.303 — capped by a mixture-orthogonal multilingual factor) to the pre-registered `zmacro_english_20` (0.818 train-CV, ≈93% of the split-half reliability bound); DSP functional form ported and retired for this regime (best tied variant 0.643; content-tied parameterization was its best flavor on both targets); Hellinger-kernel K=1000 per-phase selected and confirmed. Artifacts: `gs://marin-eu-west4/user/rav/projects/mixing_via_embeddings/v0/grug/` (`holdout_readout.{json,md}`, `realized_vs_predicted.parquet`, full CV/DSP/target reports); code on `rav/mixing-via-embeddings`.

🤖 Addendum refining the earlier "epoch features inert" finding (train-CV only, post-holdout, exploratory relative to the completed test): on the clean `zmacro_english_20` target, hinge exposure features give the **linear** content model a solid gain (hist-ridge 0.740 → 0.770, +0.030, 15/15 folds, p=1e-4) — `macro_bpb`'s multilingual noise had masked the repetition signal. The **kernel** does not benefit: a product hell×hinge kernel scores 0.767 vs 0.815 alone (−0.047, 0/15) — it already absorbs epoching implicitly through content-dose geometry, and explicit terms dilute its distance structure (same failure mode as kernel+quality). The frozen holdout primary stands; epoch caps at proposal time remain mandatory either way.

🤖 **Independent validation pass (Codex-collaborative): rigor vs PR #2393, epoching audit, literature review.** Two adversarial Codex CLI review rounds; its three prescribed analyses executed; corrections adopted. Full memo + artifacts: `validation_memo.md`, `codex_methodology_review.md`, `validation_checks.md`, `epoching_lit_review.md` at `gs://marin-eu-west4/user/rav/projects/mixing_via_embeddings/v0/grug/`.

**Rigor vs #2393**: exceeds on pre-registration (SHA commitment chain, quarantined holdout, amend-before-open), semantic controls (shuffled/matched-random — absent in #2393), and heterogeneous replication (two swarms + one live training test); falls short on seed-repeat noise panels, heteroskedasticity analysis, and metric-registry formality. Top data ask: a ~10-run grug seed-repeat panel (would settle the noise ceiling, bracketed at 0.837–0.923 by residual decomposition; achieved 0.8147 ≈ 97% of the pessimistic bound).

**Epoching: validated with two corrections.** Computation confirmed correct (target-budget semantics, 0.767/0.233 phase quantization). The monotone discount has the same effective-data functional form as Muennighoff 2023 (fitted δ=0.10 ⇒ R_D\*≈9 vs literature 15–31); simulated epoching at proxy scale matches what the [2026 repetition-mismatch work recommends](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.07597); keep-caps-regardless is the published recommendation. Corrections: (1) the earlier "kernel absorbs epoching" was partly an artifact of a bad product-kernel construction — **concat-ARD beats the plain kernel** (+0.0049, 12/15 folds, p=0.0015; linear models gain 6× more), so the kernel absorbs *most* of it and concat-ARD is the refit upgrade; (2) hinge knots move {1,4,8}→{1,4,16} (16 ≈ fitted half-life). Cap per phase, explicitly: `w_j ≤ 4·T_j/(f_p·target_budget)`.

**Selection integrity**: replicated-selection bootstrap (B=200) finds no selection optimism (−0.011 ± 0.002, negative); the realized holdout 0.7205 sits 1.3–1.6 SE below the de-biased train expectation (P ≈ 0.08 under sampling noise — consistent, not established; hyperparams frozen in the bootstrap, so the check is approximate). The campaign's formula-fixed target choice was more conservative than the replicated argmax rule.

**Corrected-claims register** (in the memo): semantic value is validated on qsplit240 only (grug validates *prediction*; controls match the primary there); "no replicates needed" (H3) → "not cost-effective at ~8σ on borrowed noise"; monotone discount is a literature-consistent prior, not a validated conclusion in this sweep.

🤖 **Validation campaign checkpoint: codex-collaborative loop reached its terminal state.** Four adversarial Codex CLI rounds; all its prescribed analyses executed. Round-4 verdict: *"Nothing material remains validatable without new data … rigorously bounded rather than overclaimed."*

New since the last update: **budget correction** — the 840 grug runs each trained **100.16B tokens** (verified from executor_info; not 525M as previously derived) → corrected phase fractions propagated through all epoch-sensitive analyses (all findings survive: hinge +0.0269, concat-ARD +0.0038); **robustness batch** — calibration near-affine (slope 1.020; tail rank weakness = range restriction), LODO-by-cluster median 0.682 vs 0.853 control (interpolation-dependence quantified, worst clusters named), top-1 mixture recommendation unstable (42%) vs cluster-level robust (Jaccard 0.76–0.93) → **recommend at cluster granularity**, negative control clean, heteroskedasticity clean, and the first fitted per-group repetition half-lives (code-adjacent R_D\*≈9 vs web ≈1.9; no OOF gain, informative constants). **Deliverables**: a fully self-contained HTML report (figures + four-tier claim table separating validated@100B-seed0 / unvalidated-across-seeds / unvalidated-across-budgets / not-supported) at `gs://marin-eu-west4/user/rav/projects/mixing_via_embeddings/v0/report/`, with a verification log covering 19 skeptic findings + coordinator's support-honesty fix to the dose-response demo. **In flight**: the 10-run seed-repeat panel at the exact verified swarm config (rav-approved, ~1,110 v4-8-hours; children pending us-central2 autoscale) — resolves tier B (seed variance) in ~5 days.

🤖 form-selection campaign settled — latest results

decision-focused write-up (7 figures, one per decision, each with a collapsible "what am I looking at?" explainer): https://storage.googleapis.com/marin-public/rav/mixing-via-embeddings/2026.07.21.1/index.html

**model**: `ŷ(w,B,d) = kernel(h = V·w) + Σⱼ bⱼ·max(eⱼ − τⱼ, 0)` — a bucket-independent content surrogate (Hellinger-kernel ridge over per-phase embedding histograms) + a linear-past-threshold epoch-harm term. new source = new column of `V` → priced without re-sweeping.

* **surrogate = kernel** — held-out Spearman **0.720** on the 40-run quarantined test set (p<1e-4, perm-max 0.588), ~79% of the seed-noise ceiling; beats weights-ridge / lgbm / RFF / KME / NN in the bake-off. in-regime it misses no repetition harm (0/37 tasks)
* **epoch-harm form = linear-past-threshold** — leave-one-epoch-out CV-decisive: code CV-RMSE 0.056 bpb vs quadratic 0.246 / softplus² 0.260 (curved forms over-extrapolate e32 by 10–30σ). the committed swoosh was wrong in magnitude (~119×), shape, and onset
  * threshold is **per-bucket**: τ_code≈8.85, τ_math≈11.66 (CI95 [9.9, 13.3] excludes 8.85) → needs per-bucket calibration
  * amplitude per content-type + scale-aware: `bⱼ = b₀·(B/10B)^−0.73·(d/512)^1.68`; per-epoch damage math (0.091) > code (0.052) > web (0.014)
  * generalizes across 3 independent bucket types (code / math / web)
* **★ 100B production gate — harm VANISHES** — matched-mechanism run (real `max_train_batches` subset-repeat, same mechanism as the 10B harm experiments, so only budget changed): e4→e16 rise = **−0.003 bpb** (0.4σ from zero, 9.3σ below the power-law prediction). 4-point budget-transfer curve harm(e16) {2.5,10,40,100}B = {0.688, 0.384, 0.092, −0.003}, fitted exponent **−1.15** (steeper than the −0.73 mid-range → collapses faster than the power law). agrees with the transect under a matched mechanism
  * → **at production scale (100B) the kernel alone suffices**; the harm term is a proxy-scale / extreme-repetition (≥~16–32 epoch) guardrail, not a core production requirement. the severe 10B harm (e16 +0.39, e32 +1.27 bpb) was a small-budget artifact
  * caveat: single-seed per point; a small +8.8σ residual (+0.07 bpb) survives only at e32 (extreme over-repetition), ~3.4× weaker than the 10B fit

**test-set protocol** was pre-registered before any look; the 40-run quarantine held throughout.[^1]

[^1]: remaining roadmap (refinements, not blockers): web-shape densification at 10B, combined-model held-out validation against the sacred set, codebook (K) sensitivity. artifacts under `gs://marin-eu-west4/user/rav/projects/mixing_via_embeddings/`.

topics.title: [storage] Remove legacy checkpoint discovery after the scratch TTL
topics.body:
Remove the temporary discovery of former scratch roots added by #10221 after the CoreWeave scratch cutover has drained. Normal resumes should search the run's permanent checkpoints and its configured scratch destination. Preserve explicit restore paths and the hero launcher's explicit destination.

Earliest review date: November 2, 2026. Merge only after 14 full days have elapsed since the last non-hero writer using an old scratch mapping stopped. Record that stop timestamp; a later stop moves the gate. Recheck active jobs and checkpoint expiration before merging. Removing discovery too early can prevent automatic resume from finding a checkpoint.

Done when:

- Controllers and downstream consumers use the new storage configuration, and non-hero jobs no longer write to the old scratch mappings.
- The last legacy non-hero writer stopped at least 14 days ago, lifecycle expiration has cleared its temporary checkpoints, and no non-hero resume depends on an old mapping.
- Remove `checkpoint_read_buckets` from backend configuration and parsing, and remove the migration-only `checkpoint_resume_paths` helper in favor of the trainer's checkpoint discovery.
- Update checkpoint discovery coverage for permanent plus configured scratch roots while preserving explicit restore paths and hero routing.
- Release the updated `marin-rigging` and `marin-core` packages and refresh the affected MarinSkyRL, Harbor, and Evalchemy dependency locks.

comments.body:
🤖 # Research

[PR #10221](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10221) is still open. Its [October 19 inspection](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10221#issuecomment-6271220201) found five active non-hero 02a runs with complete checkpoints under the old scratch root and no complete checkpoint metadata in their permanent roots. No last legacy non-hero writer stop time is recorded on this issue or PR, so the 14-day gate cannot be calculated yet; November 2 is only the earliest review date.

**Relevant code** (PR #10221 head):
- [`training.py#L195-L226`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/425481b1e639e942c4e3c0041c4d0af02d65e834/lib/marin/src/marin/training/training.py#L195-L226) — expands legacy resume roots.
- [`cluster_config.py#L117-L142`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/425481b1e639e942c4e3c0041c4d0af02d65e834/lib/rigging/src/rigging/filesystem/cluster_config.py#L117-L142) — defines `checkpoint_read_buckets`.
- [`cluster_config.py#L317-L338`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/425481b1e639e942c4e3c0041c4d0af02d65e834/lib/rigging/src/rigging/filesystem/cluster_config.py#L317-L338) — parses the extra buckets.
- [`coreweave.yaml#L16-L24`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/425481b1e639e942c4e3c0041c4d0af02d65e834/config/coreweave.yaml#L16-L24) — declares the old hero read bucket.
- [`launch_scaling_ladder.py#L314-L327`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/425481b1e639e942c4e3c0041c4d0af02d65e834/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/launch_scaling_ladder.py#L314-L327) — pins the hero destination.

# Proposed Fix

1. Merge and deploy #10221, release its `marin-rigging` and `marin-core` changes, and refresh the MarinSkyRL, Harbor, and Evalchemy locks. Check controller and downstream job configuration, then record the UTC stop time of the last non-hero job still writing to an old scratch mapping. A later stop resets the gate.
2. At least 14 full days after that stop time, recheck active job specifications, resume roots, and lifecycle expiration for non-hero checkpoints in the old mappings. Proceed only when no non-hero automatic resume needs an old root; preserve the hero's explicit `hero-checkpoints` destination.
3. Remove `checkpoint_read_buckets` from the YAML, `StoreConfig`, and parser, and remove the CoreWeave old-root expansion in `checkpoint_resume_paths`. Keep its permanent and configured scratch paths, explicit `temp_prefix`, and caller-supplied restore paths.
4. Replace cutover-specific discovery tests with coverage for those remaining paths and hero routing, run the affected package suites and repository lint, then open the cleanup PR. Release the updated packages and refresh affected downstream locks after it merges.

topics.title: Add structural evals for agent protocol failures
topics.body:
Add small structural evals for basic agent behavior. The [BixBench trace audit](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9258#issuecomment-6300963037) found answers left in chat instead of the required file, and simulated tool execution with no actual tool calls. The audit does not isolate model behavior from serving, tool parsing, or harness behavior.

Cover four checks:

- Required-file submission: when instructed to write an answer to a path, verify that a nonempty file exists in the actual task environment. An answer in chat or a claimed write does not pass.
- Actual tool execution: verify a real tool invocation and its execution status for tasks that need one. Tool-call markup, invented tool responses, or a narrated shell session do not pass. Distinguish missing/invalid invocations, executor failures/timeouts, and successful execution.
- Thinking disabled: verify the emitted response respects the supported `thinking=false` setting. Define the prohibited reasoning-channel output or delimiters under the pinned template; this checks observable output, not internal reasoning. Keep extraction/serving errors distinguishable from model violations.
- URL loading: when a task explicitly requires information at a supplied URL and a retrieval tool is available, verify an actual retrieval attempt. Record tool/network failures separately from failure to attempt retrieval.

Done when:

- Each check has minimal tasks and positive/negative grader fixtures, including narrated execution and missing-file cases.
- Results separate protocol compliance, submission completeness, and answer correctness. Passing the structural check alone must not imply a correct answer.
- Traces retain the request settings, raw response, parsed tool calls, execution events, and checked artifacts needed to locate failures.

Scope is evaluation additions; training interventions are separate.

Related: #10060 (output-contract validation), #10061 (tool-protocol syntax and localized supervision).

comments.body:
🤖

# Research

The [BixBench audit](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9258#issuecomment-6300963037) found 156/205 tasks without the required answer file and a trace that narrated shell execution with no tool event; the evidence does not isolate model output from parsing or execution. Harbor keeps a trajectory but maps verifier reward to one `correct` value, leaving no separate protocol, submission, and answer labels. The duplicate preflight found no PR for these four checks; [#10045](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10045) covers BFCL training and syntax diagnostics.

**Relevant code**
- [`trial_driver.py#L316-L352`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/harbor/trial_driver.py#L316-L352) — validates one Harbor dataset and agent.
- [`runner.py#L126-L145`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/harbor/runner.py#L126-L145) — reads trial result and trajectory path.
- [`runner.py#L172-L189`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/harbor/runner.py#L172-L189) — equates reward with `correct`.
- [`eval.py#L111-L141`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/finestore/src/finestore/eval.py#L111-L141) — sample and metric contract.
- [`eval.py#L288-L342`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/finestore/src/finestore/eval.py#L288-L342) — flattened trajectory fields.

# Design: agent protocol probes

Add a versioned four-task diagnostic through the evaluation launcher. Pin the model revision, chat template, tool schema/parser, agent/runtime revision, request settings, and task content. Use Harbor's existing local dataset path for sandbox checks; use a dedicated single-turn request to the same served endpoint for `thinking=false`, so the grader can inspect the exact request and response independently of an agent's final message.

1. **Required file.** Ask for a short known answer in `/workspace/answer.txt`. The verifier reads that path in the task environment after the agent stops and records existence, byte count, and content hash. Score file presence separately from matching the known answer; chat text or a claimed write cannot satisfy presence.
2. **Tool execution.** Ask the agent to obtain a per-trial nonce with an exposed shell tool. Record the raw generated response before tool parsing, parsed calls, dispatch/start/end events, and exit status. Label missing or invalid invocation, executor error/timeout, and successful execution separately. A narrated shell session, tool-call markup in ordinary text, or invented tool response must fail the execution check.
3. **Thinking disabled.** Send `enable_thinking=false` only for a pinned template that supports it. Define forbidden reasoning fields and template delimiters for that template; inspect the raw HTTP response and parsed message. An unsupported setting, server error, or extraction failure gets its own status, never a model-violation label. This measures emitted output only.
4. **URL loading.** Supply a task-local HTTP URL serving a per-trial nonce and make a retrieval tool available. Score a request observed by that endpoint or an executor-recorded retrieval attempt. Record no attempt, retrieval/network failure, and successful retrieval separately; compare the answer to the nonce independently. The local endpoint avoids public-site availability as a source of false failures.

Store one versioned evidence bundle per trial with request settings, raw response, parsed calls, execution events, URL access log, and checked file metadata. Archive it alongside the existing raw trajectory through `EvaluationStore`; link it from the sample's grading detail. Export `protocol_compliance`, `submission_completeness`, and `answer_correctness` as distinct numeric metrics; keep `not_evaluable` and its reason in grading detail when a prerequisite failed. Keep `EvalSample.correct` for answer correctness when assessed, and report each rate with its denominator; a structural pass alone cannot raise answer accuracy.

## Validation

Write grader fixtures before implementation. Include positive cases for all four checks: file submission, executed tool call, no emitted reasoning, and successful URL retrieval. Negative cases cover missing and empty files; answer only in chat; a fully narrated fake tool transcript; malformed call; dispatch failure and timeout; URL answer without retrieval and retrieval failure; reasoning-field and delimiter leaks; and a serving/extraction error. Assert both the label and the retained evidence for every fixture. Run the checked-in Harbor config through preflight and one capped end-to-end diagnostic suite covering all four checks on the pinned reference setup before using model comparisons. Keep [#10060](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10060) and [#10061](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10061) separate: they cover general output contracts and tool-call syntax/training.

## Open question

Do the pinned Pi/Harbor/vLLM versions expose the pre-parser generated text and executor lifecycle? The current archive records parsed tool calls and observations, but does not establish those boundaries. If either is unavailable, add capture there before grading that failure class, and mark earlier traces `not_evaluable`.

🤖

# Research

The [design comment](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10393#issuecomment-6302257478) covers the cause: Harbor maps verifier reward to a single `correct`, and ATIF trajectories record parsed tool calls and observations but no executor lifecycle or pre-parser text. No open PR covers these checks.

- [`runner.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/3ae74d9560/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/harbor/runner.py) — one reward per trial.
- [`trajectory.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/3ae74d9560/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/harbor/trajectory.py) — the trajectory archive the evidence bundle sits beside.
- [`eval.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/3ae74d9560/lib/finestore/src/finestore/eval.py) — `EvalSample`, `Grading.detail`, and `EvaluationStore.add_artifact`.

# Proposed Fix

This PR adds the grader layer in `marin.evaluation.protocol_probes`: a versioned evidence bundle, one typed spec and grader per check, the four minimal tasks, archiving that stores the bundle and links it from the sample, and denominator-aware rates for `protocol_compliance`, `submission_completeness`, and `answer_correctness`. Fixtures cover every positive and negative case listed in the design. When a prerequisite is missing, such as no captured executor lifecycle, the result is `not_evaluable` and never a model violation. A follow-up will connect the tasks to Harbor runs and the served endpoint once the capture question is settled.

🤖 Opened #10399 with the grader layer: evidence bundle, the four checks with separate protocol, submission, and answer results, the minimal tasks, and fixtures for every case in the design. Running the probes through Harbor waits on capturing executor lifecycle and pre-parser text, which current ATIF trajectories lack.

comments.body:
🤖 Holistic review of dae791be2e0680545087b6f8f761f4db50817837.

This change declares the provenance fields that Evalchemy's custom benchmarks now emit (`source`, `reducers`, `prompt_length`, `requires_judge`) on `BenchmarkMetadataRef`. Records that previously failed validation and were written as `artifact_failed` will now publish their scores. The fix is correct for today's Evalchemy pin. However, the same drift can reach production again because the Evalchemy pin-advance gate cannot detect it. Readers in evaldash also need a release before the backfill.

Before this change, `BenchmarkMetadataRef` (`extra="forbid"`) listed only the core protocol fields. Evalchemy's `BenchmarkMetadata.to_dict()` (`eval/contracts/benchmark_metadata.py`, pin `28631c7`) adds the four provenance keys only when `source` is set, which happens only for custom chat benchmarks. `reducers` is `asdict(ReducerSpec)`, and `source` is `asdict(SourceRef)`. The new TypedDicts match those dataclasses field for field at the pinned commit. I checked locally that pydantic applies the parent's `extra="forbid"` to the nested TypedDicts and that `total=True` requires every key. As a result, any unknown or missing nested key rejects the whole benchmark entry. The PR intends this ("other unknown fields remain rejected"). The 164 tests in `test_eval_archive.py`, `test_evaluation.py`, `tests/evals/test_records.py`, and `test_harbor_runner.py` pass locally. The parametrized `provenance` case is a real regression test: it fails at the base commit.

**Findings**

- **1. Should fix:** `lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/records.py:87` `BenchmarkReducerRef` mirrors Evalchemy's `ReducerSpec` dataclass exactly, and Evalchemy serializes that dataclass with `asdict`. Adding one field to `ReducerSpec` or `SourceRef` upstream therefore brings back this incident: scored runs become `artifact_failed`. The pin-advance gate cannot catch it. `config/external/migration.toml` `[evalchemy]` runs `gsm8k-smoke.yaml` as its e2e, and `gsm8k` takes the lm-eval route (`_lm_eval_metadata`), which never sets `source`, so the smoke never emits these keys. #10235 advanced the pin past this change with the gate green. Either make the gate cover the strict shape by switching the e2e to, or adding, a custom-route benchmark such as `MATH500` or `AIME24`, or make only the nested provenance types tolerant with `@with_config(ConfigDict(extra="allow"))` on the three TypedDicts. The second option matches the sibling `BenchmarkMetricRef`, which already uses `extra="allow"`, while the top level stays forbid.
- **2. Should fix:** `infra/marina/apps/evaldash/app.py:55` evaldash validates records with this same `BenchmarkMetadataRef` (`read_records` → `RecordParseFailure`; `results_db.py` `EvalRunRecord.model_validate`). Once this merges, newly published Evalchemy records and the planned backfill of the 117 runs carry the new keys. A deployment built before this commit drops those records as parse failures, so they will not appear on the dashboard. Release evaldash from a commit that includes this change before running the backfill, and say so in the PR body next to the backfill note.

topics.title: [harbor] Exclude inline policy references from the Tau3 prompt
topics.body:
Tau³ tasks have two blocks: `<instructions>` tells a standalone coding agent how to start, advance, and end the conversation; `<policy>` contains the customer-service rules. Our relay is meant to control the conversation itself, so it should give the Pi coding agent relay-specific conversation instructions plus only the domain policy.

The parser includes `<instructions>` in the extracted policy, giving Pi conflicting directions about who controls the conversation. In the observed run, Pi ended the conversation, then the relay tried to send another message and failed.

Extract only the policy block.

Upstream Harbor's [task template](https://github.com/harbor-framework/harbor/blob/867801035118d1e75c0996821779b59238c7fb29/adapters/tau3-bench/src/tau3_bench/task-template/instruction.md#L1-L16) has the same structure. Its [reference-agent extractor](https://github.com/harbor-framework/harbor/blob/867801035118d1e75c0996821779b59238c7fb29/adapters/tau3-bench/tau3_llm_agent.py#L28-L41) already avoids this bug by selecting the policy block immediately after `</instructions>`.

[Investigation](https://marina.oa.dev/echo/wiki/810).

topics.title: [rl] Port Pi training scenarios to vendored Harbor and SkyRL
topics.body:
Port Pi's in-memory trial capture into vendored Harbor and connect graded trials to SkyRL's shared RolloutEngine. Training uses exact served turns and preserves separate student, teacher, verifier, and tool evidence. Distribution scores each turn with a distinct row ID while group admission counts physical trials. Worker-owned Pi attempts stream bounded phase diagnostics; ordinary Pi attempts do not upload raw sandbox artifacts.

SkyRL's independent lock now installs the sibling vendored Harbor source. The Iris source bundle hashes and ships that source, so workers do not silently resolve a separate upstream Harbor revision. The port uses Marin's newer RolloutEngine harness and task spec.

The isolated Harbor runtime suite passed 973 tests plus 3 import checks. Focused SkyRL tests passed 137 cases (4 Docker-dependent cases skipped), and `scripts.skyrl_migration check-vendor` built the wheel. A bundled CPU environment installed and imported both vendored packages. A broader SkyRL sweep had 378 passes and 13 failures in tests referencing pruned baseline configs or missing test port environment; three other baseline tests could not collect because `scripts.iris` is absent. The advisory lint review could not run: available headless Codex credentials returned model-unsupported errors. No GPU job or checkpoint restart has run from this vendored revision. The earlier training gates used the standalone forks and do not qualify the vendored runtime.

topics.title: [finelog] Increase forwarding throughput for dense log backlogs
topics.body:
Increase regional Finelog → hub forwarding throughput so dense log backlogs drain faster and delayed task logs reach Iris. Forward up to four namespaces concurrently and read up to one million log rows per read-and-send cycle. Requests retain their byte limit, and chunks remain serial within the log namespace. The saved source cursor records completed progress and cannot advance past a pending or retryable request.

Encode each candidate chunk once. If its payload exceeds 150 MiB, split it in half and process each half the same way. Process the left half first to preserve source order. Source scans keep separate row-count and segment bounds, and oversized single rows retain their existing handling. Release the decoded Arrow batch before waiting for acknowledgements. Slow-cycle diagnostics separate source reads, chunk encoding, and RPC compression/transport/durable acknowledgement from cursor persistence.

During the October 17 incident, RNO2A was roughly 395 million regional sequence positions behind. Forwarding counters showed about 24,000 accepted positions/sec before deployment and 87,000–107,000/sec over successive 71- and 65-second samples after deploying namespace concurrency and larger reads. A dense source sample contained about 77,000 rows per second of event time; this measures production density. Sequence positions can include gaps and filtered rows, so those counters are not exact row counts. By 17:56 UTC, backlog was down to 91 positions and all 417 rows for the affected task were present on the hub. The chunk-splitting follow-up remains undeployed.

A local benchmark on one million synthetic NCCL-shaped rows with six log columns and 294 MB of Arrow IPC output reduced serialization attempts from seven to three compared with the deployed sizing search. Bytes serialized, including discarded attempts, fell from 1,010 to 589 MB; both versions produced two requests. With 100,000 narrow rows followed by 100,000 wide rows, halving produced nine requests against eight with the packing search. Halving accepts underfilled requests to avoid the sizing search. These measurements describe serialization work; they do not establish an end-to-end throughput improvement.

A bounded million-row regional read took 1.32 seconds initially and 0.19 seconds on repeat. Later live scans took 5.4–8.2 seconds in 12–16-second cycles, including a 128-segment window returning only 424,000 rows. Read cost varies with segment geometry and cache state. An isolated local server capped at four CPUs acknowledged compressed 500,000-row writes in 0.70–0.78 seconds. Live hub samples showed about three active cores on a four-core VM, compaction/index work, and near-zero disk I/O wait. The largest resolved perf symbols involved copying, comparisons, and page faults; stripped Rust symbols limited attribution. These probes do not fully apportion live cycle time; the added stage timings expose the remaining waits.

[Incident record](https://marina.oa.dev/echo/wiki/780).

topics.title: [taskforge] Add triage: structural checks and a surface for expansion
topics.body:
Add triage as a deterministic preflight. `stage20_triage.checks` holds the structural proposal checks, each reporting PASS, FAIL or SKIP; `stage20_triage.preflight.preflight` runs them and rejects a FATAL failure or a null proposal with the failing check as the reason, accepts anything else, and makes no model call. The machine-kind rule is one of the checks: `solver_machine_fits` applies stage10's `solver_machine_violation`, the rule `parse` enforces. Whether the host can provide the machine is the build's check. `verdict.py` holds the `Verdict` record and `TriageDecision`.

The preflight is the default, and the package has no model review: the README describes a panel with repair and a bounded review with obligations as designs a consumer could add, which experiments found not to be meaningful predictors of downstream quality. `StageCoordinator` still triages with `verdict.accept` here; #10298 moves it onto the preflight's verdict.

Builds on #10295; #10297 builds on it.

```mermaid
  end
  parse -->|"TaskProposal"| preflight
  checks -.->|"solver_machine_violation"| parse
  verdict -->|"decision, reasons"| coord["StageCoordinator (#10298)"]
  verdict -->|"to_json"| file["slot-NN.verdict.json (#10301)"]
  coord -->|"REPAIR: repaired/k.md, read back with parse"| parse
  coord -->|"ACCEPT, author_state"| author["Author"]
  classDef changed fill:#fde7c8,stroke:#e8710a,stroke-width:2px
  classDef added fill:#d7f0dd,stroke:#1e8e3e,stroke-width:2px
```

Green boxes are new in this PR, and the orange box changes. A PR number marks where a later PR in the stack uses the triage. At this head the coordinator still triages with `accept`.

Before this change, `stage20_triage.verdict.accept` admitted every proposal. The coordinator still uses `accept` at this head; #10298 switches it to `preflight`. The #10301 driver (`propose_tasks.py`) calls `preflight` and writes each verdict, advisory results included, to `slot-NN.verdict.json`. Every proposal that reaches triage in the stack has passed `parse`: `CapabilitySource` parses each reply (`proposal_source.py:405` and `:436` in #10301), and the coordinator reads a repaired proposal back with `parse` before triage judges it (`coordinator.py:217` in #10298). The PR also deletes `llm.store.CallStore`, which only the removed model review used.

The 82 tests in `tests/stage20_triage` and `tests/stage10_proposal` pass locally at this head.

**Findings**

- **1. Should fix:** `lib/taskforge/src/taskforge/stage20_triage/checks.py:139` `header_schema_valid` and `checks.py:174` `solver_machine_fits` cannot fail for a proposal that came from `parse`. Their own comments say so, and every proposal that reaches triage came from `parse`. They contain two new rules: resource paths stay inside the build root, and build names are unique. Enforce those in `stage10_proposal.model._header`, so every reader of a proposal gets them, and move their tests to the stage10 tests. A proposal that breaks them then gets the one repair request `CapabilitySource` makes for a parse failure, where today triage rejects it. Delete both checks and revert the `solver_machine_violation` split in `model.py:372-401`.

- **2. Should fix:** `checks.py:86` `CheckContext` holds only `allowed_combinations`, and no caller narrows it. `preflight` defaults to `EVERY_COMBINATION`, and both the coordinator and the #10301 driver call it with the proposal alone, so `combination_allowed` cannot fail outside tests. Delete `CheckContext`, `ALL_COMBINATIONS`, `EVERY_COMBINATION`, `combination_allowed` and the `ctx` argument on `preflight` and on every rule. The `Check` protocol (`checks.py:96`) then has one implementation; type `CHECKS` as `tuple[RuleCheck, ...]` and delete the protocol. Tests can call the rule functions directly, which removes `CHECKS_BY_NAME`. With findings 1 to 3 applied, the table is:

  ```python
  # lib/taskforge/src/taskforge/stage20_triage/checks.py
  CHECKS: tuple[RuleCheck, ...] = (
      RuleCheck("required_sections", Severity.FATAL, required_sections),
      RuleCheck("grader_matches_verification", Severity.ADVISORY, grader_matches_verification),
      RuleCheck("research_has_purpose", Severity.ADVISORY, research_has_purpose),
      RuleCheck("resources_in_build_plan", Severity.ADVISORY, resources_in_build_plan),
  )
  ```

- **3. Should fix:** `checks.py:293` `null_reason_only` is fatal, but `preflight.py:28` rejects every null proposal anyway. The check changes only the text of the reason. If a null proposal must declare empty `research`, `build` and `resources` lists, enforce that in `parse`. Otherwise delete the check.

- **4. Should fix:** `verdict.py:27` `REPAIR` and `verdict.py:47` `author_state` have no producer in the stack. At this head, `TRIAGE_EXITS` (`stage_coordinator/coordinator.py:109`) has no `REPAIR` entry, so a triage that returns it raises `KeyError` at `coordinator.py:258`. The owner chose the repair edge in the review thread, and #10298 adds it. No triage returns `REPAIR`, and every `StageFunctions` caller passes a placeholder `repair` (`no_call`, `no_repair`). #10298 also adds `author_state` as a third argument of the `Author` protocol. `glm_author` ignores it, and the coordinator docstring says nothing in the package writes one. Add `REPAIR` in #10298 together with the edge that handles it. Drop `author_state` and its `Author` argument until a triage writes one.

- **5. Related PR:** `lib/taskforge/src/taskforge/llm/store.py` (`CallStore`) and `tests/llm/test_store.py` come from #10291, and this PR deletes them. No PR between the two uses them. Remove both files and the README paragraph from #10291, so the stack does not add and then delete 231 lines. This PR then changes nothing under `llm/` except the docstring in `test_live.py`.

- **6. Should fix:** `lib/taskforge/README.md:80-89` describes two triage designs that the package does not implement. It says experiments found that neither predicts downstream quality, and it links no experiment. Commit `40a489966e` states the result more precisely: no review feature predicted build defects better than the base rate. Link the experiment in one sentence or delete the subsection.

topics.title: [data] Sequence-level shuffled v16384 cache removes 128-step loss sawtooth and improves eval
topics.body:
Sequence shuffling reduces the 128-step train-loss sawtooth seen with flat-cache training on `hero_tok/v16384_shuf` at batch 1024. In a single-seed S7 d512 comparison, it improves Paloma macro loss by 0.0135 and reduces train-loss autocorrelation at lag 128 from 0.226 to 0.026. A second seed and a batch-256 rung are still needed to confirm the gain size.

The default block shuffle (`BlockShuffleConfig(io_block_size=256, window_blocks=512)`, [datasets.py:574](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/data/text/datasets.py#L574)) gives a 128-step train-loss sawtooth on [s7l-d1280L16](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/s7l-d1280L16), for example +0.11 at step 5504 = 43×128. A window contains 131,072 sequences. Long documents (56.5% of tokens are in documents >4096 tokens, 16.3% in >256k, up to 1.6M) occupy consecutive sequences inside one 256-sequence block. Every slice of a document therefore lands in the same window, and the model sees the same file for 128 steps.

The old cache, `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/datakit/hero_tok/v16384_shuf/train`, contains 124,408,413,939 tokens. Hero store `store_4d2e363d` was decoded to text and sampled by `harrier_mix_2026_08_18.json` (`hero_text`), documents were capped (`hero_text_capped`), tokenized with `hero-bpe-v16384` (`v16384_617680a7`), then shuffled at the document level by `experiments/grug/fast_track/shuffle_cache.py`.

The sequence-shuffled cache, `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/datakit/hero_tok/v16384_seqshuf/train`, packs the old cache into 4096-token sequences exactly as `TokenSeqDataset` reads it, then permutes them with `numpy.random.default_rng(20261020).permutation(30373147)`, one sequence per row ([seq_shuffle_cache.py](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/marin_belay_v1_fp8quality/experiments/grug/fast_track/seq_shuffle_cache.py), e53d6b0620). Sequence contents are unchanged; only their order changes. Validation found the same sequence and token counts, with 514 sampled sequences byte-identical.

S7 d512, batch 1024, 1346 steps, seed 0, and the default block shuffle were held fixed; only `--train-cache` differs (a5a8647840). [saw5-ctl](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/saw5-ctl) uses the old cache; [saw5-seq](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/saw5-seq) uses the sequence-shuffled cache:

- Paloma macro loss: 2.9322 → 2.9187 (−0.0135)
- Paloma micro loss: 2.6586 → 2.6460 (−0.0126)
- Uncheatable macro loss: 2.3959 → 2.3817 (−0.0142)
- Eval loss: 2.6232 → 2.6103 (−0.0128)
- Paloma macro BPB: 1.2139 → 1.2077 (−0.0062)
- Uncheatable macro BPB: 0.9136 → 0.9075 (−0.0061)
- Eval BPB: 1.0429 → 1.0378 (−0.0051)
- Train-loss autocorrelation at lag 128: 0.226 → 0.026

d512 seed noise is ~0.007 in macro loss. BPB uses the current token-weighted levanter computation, which has a known batching dependence; losses are the primary metric.

Done when ladder and large-batch fast_track runs default to `v16384_seqshuf`, and a second seed and batch-256 rung confirm the gain size.

---

🤖
# Research

The default 256 × 512 block shuffle keeps consecutive 4096-token slices of a long document in one 131,072-sequence window. Current `main` still selects `v16384_shuf`; the experimental branch has the sequence-shuffled cache builder and a `--train-cache` override, but the second-seed and batch-256 comparisons in the definition of done have not been reported.

**Relevant code**
- [`datasets.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/data/text/datasets.py#L599-L611) — block-shuffle default
- [`launch.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/df2a8d9883ba5c2b6b9b35ce5c127d763706ebb2/experiments/grug/fast_track/launch.py#L107-L108) — current training-cache default
- [`launch.py` on the experimental branch](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/marin_belay_v1_fp8quality/experiments/grug/fast_track/launch.py#L1084-L1088) — cache override
- [`seq_shuffle_cache.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/e53d6b0620/experiments/grug/fast_track/seq_shuffle_cache.py) — cache permutation and validation

# Proposed Fix

1. Reuse the `saw5-ctl` / `saw5-seq` recipe for a matched seed-1 pair at batch 1024 and 1346 steps. Change only `--train-cache` within each pair; retain the same model, data seed, evaluation sets, and block shuffle. Publish both run links, cache paths, code revision, Paloma and Uncheatable macro losses, eval loss, and train-loss autocorrelation at lag 128.
2. Run a matched batch-256 pair at seed 0 for 5384 steps, holding the 4096-token sequence length and total training tokens equal to the batch-1024 comparison. Report the same held-out losses and autocorrelation at lag 512, the window period at batch 256.
3. Compare paired loss deltas across the existing and new runs. If Paloma, Uncheatable, and eval losses improve consistently, change the fast_track and large-batch defaults to `v16384_seqshuf`; if deltas are near the reported ~0.007 seed noise or losses regress, add matched seeds before changing the default. Keep an explicit old-cache override for reproducing prior runs, update the fast_track README with the cache identity, and check the constructed training data config in a local test.
4. Coordinate the launcher edit with [#10108](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10108) and [#9371](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9371), which both change `fast_track/launch.py`, then use the normal lint, test, PR, and CI workflow. No open PR covers the sequence-shuffled default.
Purpose of this issue is just to log the experiment showing the impact. Closing.

topics.title: [levanter] Add plateau dropping as a train_lm option
topics.body:
Add plateau_dropping to train_lm. With it set, a supervised token leaves the
loss once its loss has stopped changing: from its third visit on, a token is
dropped when both visit-to-visit relative changes, including the current
visit, are below 10% (each relative to the earlier loss, floored at 0.05 nats).
The token stays in the input, its loss is still measured, and it is trained
again as soon as its loss moves. The loss is the mean over kept tokens, and
each step logs kept and dropped token counts and loss sums. The rule follows
the write-up in #10028; the defaults are configurable.

History is kept per row on the host, keyed by a hash of input_ids and
loss_weights, so it does not depend on loader order and survives per-epoch
permutations. It is written beside every checkpoint as
plateau-updates-<N>.npz, and a resumed run refuses to start without the file
for its restored update count. A resume reproduces the uninterrupted run's
training metrics and history bit for bit, and on a 2-way context, 4-way expert
CPU mesh the per-epoch dropped counts equal a mesh without context
parallelism. PlateauTrainer plugs into two new Trainer.train_step overrides,
one adding per-step inputs and one consuming metrics before the step's hooks
run.

Microbatching and z-loss are rejected with plateau dropping. Multi-host
gathering of the per-token losses and host memory (about 16 bytes per
supervised token) are untested at scale.

Part of #10213

topics.title: [datakit] Truncate Harrier documents at read time
topics.body:
Harrier's embed step now keeps the first `HARRIER_MAX_RAW_TEXT_CHARS` (100,000) characters of each document while it reads the normalized parquet. Before, `load_file` turned whole row groups into Python dicts and the cut happened in `_embed_shard`, after `window(4096)`. A window could hold 4,096 untruncated documents, so worker memory grew with the largest documents in a source.

The new reader takes each row group from `load_parquet_batch`, converts it to Python dicts in slices of about 64 MiB of Arrow data, and cuts the text before it yields a record. It returns a Zephyr `Reader`, so input progress and `zephyr/records_in` still work. `embed/bytes_in` still counts UTF-8 bytes of the truncated text, as before, and the other `embed/*` counters are unchanged. A row with null text still raises `TypeError`, now from the reader; normalize drops such rows, so normalized input never reaches it. The step hash, `EMBEDDING_ATTR_DATA_VERSION` and output paths do not change. The slice sizing, `rows_per_chunk`, moves from the luxical pipeline to `marin.processing.embeddings.read_chunks` so both pipelines import it from the library; luxical reads with the same target as before.

TEI receives the same texts in the same order as on main, so the embeddings do not change. The test source had 4 shards and 342 documents: lengths from 0 to 10x the cap, multi-byte and astral-plane characters at the cut, and one 186 MB row group. It ran with and without dedup attrs, whose `sorted_merge_join` depends on the reader's record order, on 1 and 8 workers. With a hash-based fake TEI, the texts it received and the written parquet files were byte-identical to main.

Memory was measured in one local process with a fake embedder. On 2.1 GB of 2-20 MB documents (4 shards, 264 MB row groups, with dedup), median peak RSS over 3 runs fell from 6,676 MB (runs 6,638-6,685) to 5,298 MB (runs 4,824-5,651). The largest window, as Python object size, fell from 418-543 MB to 3.7-4.6 MB. The remaining peak is about 650 MB of imports plus Zephyr's whole-row-group Arrow read, which costs 4-5x the row-group size for each shard being read; main pays it too. With 2 shards of 10 MB documents in 200 MB row groups, growing each shard from 200 MB to 1.2 GB (one run per size) raised peak RSS on main from 2.5 GB to 4.8 GB; on this branch it stayed between 2.5 and 3.0 GB. On 8 shards of 25,000 short documents, median wall time over 6 runs was 13.13 s on main and 13.03 s here. We have not run this on real normalized data or against a live TEI server.

Harrier does not reuse luxical's `_load_records_bounded`. That loader emits its own `embed/bytes_in` in raw characters next to Harrier's byte count, maps null text to an empty string, and returns a plain generator, which Zephyr does not count in `zephyr/records_in`.

topics.title: Experiment: Sanity-check MXFP8 training on Blackwell
topics.body:
<!-- experiment-tldr:start -->
## Summary

The full hybrid MXFP8 quality gate is complete. BF16 and MXFP8 each trained a d2560/L26/E128/top-4 Grug MoE for 31,474 optimizer steps / 66.006B tokens with the same data order, seed, schedule, optimizer, and 32xGB200 topology. Both arms finished with 8/8 task exits, zero failures or preemptions, final W&B evaluation rows, and audited non-temporary `step-31474` checkpoints.

MXFP8 increased mean non-compile throughput from 788,954 to 845,920 tok/s (+7.220%) and reduced measured runtime to the terminal evaluation by 5,460.6 seconds (91.0 minutes, 6.092%). It also produced slightly higher final losses than BF16: +0.001301 aggregate eval (+0.0562%), +0.002885 Paloma (+0.1105%), and +0.004287 uncheatable (+0.2088%). Aggregate eval favored BF16 at all 32 paired evaluations, and MXFP8 did not reach BF16's final held-out targets within the fixed schedule.

The tested hybrid recipe is therefore a speed-quality tradeoff, not quality-neutral. #7282 subsequently attempted uniform MXFP8 for grouped and dense GEMMs, but the available distributed path aborts before execution at EP2 and EP4. Its training-quality result remains unmeasured.

### Helpful links

- [Final W&B comparison, tables, trajectory chart, and CSV artifact](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/MXFP8Q-007-full-comparison)
- [Detailed experiment logbook](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/c189a6a31/.agents/logbooks/mxfp8-quality-7271.md)
- [BF16 full-run W&B](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/MXFP8Q-007-full-bf16-s31474)
- [MXFP8 full-run W&B](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/MXFP8Q-007-full-mxfp8-s31474)
- [Uniform MXFP8 feasibility result in #7282](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7282#issuecomment-5028942402)
<!-- experiment-tldr:end -->

## Description

Work stream from #6998 ("Sanity Check FP8 training on Blackwell"). Get MXFP8 working for both GMM (MoE expert/ragged matmuls) and dense GEMM on B200, then train a small ~A2B MoE model to compute-optimal and compare against a BF16 baseline on a wall-time-matched basis.

Builds on the prior FP8 work on Hopper (per-token-scaled fp8 ragged dot, #6880) and the B200 MFU work in #7012; Blackwell adds native MXFP8 (block-scaled) tensor-core support, which has not yet been validated in our training stack.

## Hypothesis or Goal

MXFP8 GMM+GEMM training on Blackwell is quality-neutral: a small ~A2B model trained to compute-optimal shows no regression against BF16 when matched on wall time.

## Status

The hybrid quality gate is complete. Both 31,474-step arms succeeded and their terminal W&B histories and S3 checkpoint metadata were verified. MXFP8 delivered a 7.220% throughput gain with a small persistent fixed-token quality cost. It did not reach BF16's final aggregate eval, Paloma, or uncheatable target within the schedule. Uniform grouped+dense MXFP8 quality remains unmeasured because the current distributed implementation aborts before execution; see #7282.

## Links

* Logbook: [mxfp8-quality-7271.md at `c189a6a31`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/c189a6a31/.agents/logbooks/mxfp8-quality-7271.md)
* W&B comparison: [MXFP8Q-007 final BF16 vs MXFP8](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/MXFP8Q-007-full-comparison)
* W&B group: [MXFP8 quality group](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/groups/mxfp8-quality-7271)
* Source runs: [BF16](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/MXFP8Q-007-full-bf16-s31474), [MXFP8](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/MXFP8Q-007-full-mxfp8-s31474)
* Implementation: [quality launcher snapshot](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/485e23f7f4d89d1d2f218c777766497d6a8d7ae4), [stabilized smoke implementation](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/f8be94f87), [final logbook](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/c189a6a31)

## Decision Log

* Keep stochastic rounding and Hadamard rotation as reserve numerics levers if loss degradation can be attributed to quantization.
* Treat the first smoke's data-loader failure as a shortened-run configuration bug, not a quality result.
* Fix evaluation casting so tagged eval reuses the training cast for ordinary weights while preserving FP8 state.
* Treat the initial hybrid MXFP8 NaN as a w2 weight-gradient issue; stabilize by consuming the fused w2 gradient and recomputing only invalid w2 gradients from BF16 saved operands.
* Launch the full matched 31,474-step pair only after finite 20-step smoke training, forced final evaluation, and checkpointing succeeded.
* Do not classify the tested hybrid recipe as quality-neutral. Its 7.220% throughput gain comes with a small persistent fixed-token quality cost.
* Resume uniform MXFP8 grouped+dense quality work when the distributed backend can execute it; the current EP2 and EP4 paths abort before training (#7282).

## Conclusion

The quality-neutral hypothesis is not supported for the tested hybrid recipe. MXFP8 increased throughput by 7.220% and saved 91.0 minutes, but final aggregate eval / Paloma / uncheatable losses were 0.0562% / 0.1105% / 0.2088% higher than BF16. Aggregate eval favored BF16 at all 32 paired evaluations. MXFP8 finished before BF16 reached step 30,000 and was better than BF16 at that earlier equal-wall-time boundary, but it never matched BF16's terminal held-out targets. Strict time-to-BF16-final-loss is censored rather than improved.

comments.body:
🤖 Note for the quality-gate design: two standard numerics levers to keep in reserve if the fp8 arms show loss degradation attributable to quantization. Neither is implemented in our stack today; both are cheap to add and should be tried *before* concluding a recipe is numerically insufficient (or switching the dense recipe wholesale).

1. **Stochastic rounding on cotangents.** Round-to-nearest on quantized gradients introduces a small per-step bias that accumulates over long trainings (loss drift, dead-weight subspaces); stochastic rounding makes the quantization unbiased in expectation, at the cost of an RNG threaded into the gradient quantizers. Standard practice for gradient quantization — qwix exposes per-leg stochastic-rounding hooks (dlhs/drhs noise fns), and NVIDIA's NVFP4 training recipe has SR on by default. Only relevant to the backward; pointless for forward activations.

2. **Hadamard rotation before quantization.** Shared-scale formats (per-tensor fp8, and to a lesser degree 32-block MXFP8) waste resolution when one outlier channel forces a large scale — and LLM activations grow outlier channels as training progresses, especially at the attention projections. Rotating by a Hadamard matrix (orthogonal ±1, O(n log n), exactly invertible through the matmul by folding Hᵀ into the weights) smears outliers across all channels so a shared scale fits well. This is the QuaRot/SpinQuant/Quartet idea; NVIDIA's NVFP4 recipe includes a random Hadamard transform, and qwix ships it as a fused kernel + jax impl. Most valuable as a fix for the *per-tensor dense* legs (attn q/k/v/o, shared expert) — likely cheaper than switching dense to mxfp8, which measured ~2x slower fwd+bwd at our shapes (see #7282, MXFP8-001b).

Suggested gate protocol addition: if an fp8 arm fails the loss bar, attribute first (which legs — dense vs grouped, fwd vs bwd — via selective bf16 fallback), then apply the matching lever (SR for bwd-attributed drift, Hadamard for dense-activation outlier clipping) before rejecting the recipe.

| Terminal metric | BF16 | MXFP8 | MXFP8 − BF16 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Train loss | 1.554700 | 1.557329 | +0.002629 |
| Trailing-100 train loss | 1.581135 | 1.584242 | +0.003107 |
| Trailing-1,000 train loss | 1.594350 | 1.597402 | +0.003052 |

The quality difference is small but persistent. MXFP8 aggregate eval is higher at all 32 paired evaluations (mean delta +0.002098, range +0.000314 to +0.003768). The speedup does improve quality at earlier equal-wall-time boundaries: MXFP8 finished before BF16 reached step 30,000, and its final aggregate eval / Paloma / uncheatable losses were better than BF16-at-30k by 0.011187 / 0.012284 / 0.009287. However, within this fixed schedule MXFP8 never reaches BF16's exact final aggregate eval, Paloma, or uncheatable target. Strict time-to-BF16-final-loss is therefore censored, not improved.

Conclusion: this recipe gives a stable 1.0722x throughput gain and saves about 91 minutes, but it is not exactly quality-neutral at fixed tokens. The observed cost is +0.056% aggregate eval, +0.110% Paloma, and +0.209% uncheatable at the endpoint.

topics.title: [mlx] Add a pipeline for MLX builds of Grug MoE models
topics.body:
Add Grug MoE conversion to 8-bit and mixed 4-bit MLX builds for Apple Silicon, with thinking and tool calls. An artifact graph binds the pinned source revision, prompt fixture, vLLM reference, converted model, logprob dump, and parity report. Conversion uses a fresh source directory; model file hashes and source/recipe metadata prevent a stale dump from qualifying a different build.

The Mac stages use a separate frozen environment pinned to mlx-lm 0.32.2. The reference stage submits an H100 job through Iris and waits for its output. Short prompts and long-prompt positions beyond the sliding window have separate parity gates. The mixed recipe keeps non-expert weights at 8 bits because the earlier uniform 4-bit Snowball build failed the short-case probability-error gate (0.193 against 0.15).

The artifact graph, provenance checks, and updated prompt fixture have not completed a full model conversion and GPU parity run. Historical Snowball measurements predate these workflow changes and do not qualify a new build.

topics.title: [grug] Add the H100 pipeline foundation
topics.body:
Add a stage-local JAXPP pipeline for the full MoE model blocks, including latent/shared experts, SConv, attention positions and QB routing. Standard 1F1B remains the default. The synthetic runner supports the main recipe with FP32 parameters, BF16 compute and compute-scaled MuonH; the historical BF16 capacity recipe remains available.

Each routed expert parameter bank now shares one Frobenius norm across its experts, matching the stacked EP model. `--expert-normalization per_expert` provides an explicit comparison mode. `--qb-bias-mode frozen` retains the current pending QB bias while expert and router weights continue updating; adaptive QB remains the default. Numerical CPU regressions cover stacked-versus-stage-local updates and both QB state transitions.

The historical 48-layer, 65K synthetic diagnostic ran on 192 H100s with BF16-stored parameters and per-expert normalization. Its PP24/EP8/CP1 layout placed two layers in each stage and kept expert traffic within eight-GPU workers. It was chosen to establish capacity; no matched PP8/EP32/CP4 Megatron comparison was performed. The README records the later CP2 result and the differences in batch size and attention helpers. Historical hardware results do not validate the new normalization or frozen-QB option, and no SFT/RL quality comparison has been run.

The affected safe suite passed 2,391 tests with four skips and five expected failures. Focused CPU checks passed 86 tests with one skip; required lint, full type checking, strict docs and source links passed.

#9662 is stacked above this foundation and adds checkpoint/data support, the GB200 launcher, tracked runtime setup and bounded main-recipe hardware validation. Before merge, this foundation still owns replacing the positional result from `initialize_stage_local_pipeline_state`, centralizing the repeated backend/rematerialization identifiers, and separating the synthetic runner lifecycle in `pipeline_smoke.main`. These deferred changes require compiled-startup transport and optimizer-parking/warmup cleanup validation; #9662 then owns adapting its added checkpoint/data lifecycle.
