Please verify my answer, and tell me if I am correct. ## Answer 1 If $ T(n) = T(n-2) + \frac{1}{\log(n)} $, then $$ T(n)=\left\{\begin{array}{}T(0)+\sum_{k=1}^{n/2}\frac{1}{\log(2k)}&\text{if }n\text{ is even}\\T(1)+\sum_{k=1}^{(n-1)/2}\frac{1}{\log(2k+1)}&\text{if }n\text{ is odd}\end{array}\right.\tag{1} $$ Note that $$ \begin{align} \sum_{k=1}^{(n-1)/2}\frac{1}{\log(2k+1)} &\le\frac{1}{\log(3)}+\int_1^{(n-1)/2}\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\log(2x+1)}\\ &=\color{#C00000}{\frac{1}{\log(3)}+\frac12\int_3^8\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\log(x)}}+\frac12\int_8^n\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\log(x)}\tag{2} \end{align} $$ and $$ \begin{align} \sum_{k=1}^{n/2}\frac{1}{\log(2k)} &\le\frac{1}{\log(2)}+\int_1^{n/2}\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\log(2x)}\\ &=\color{#C00000}{\frac{1}{\log(2)}+\frac12\int_2^8\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\log(x)}}+\frac12\int_8^n\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\log(x)}\tag{3} \end{align} $$ For $ n\ge8 $, we have that $ \log(x) \le 2(\log(x)-1) $, thus $$ \begin{align} \frac12\int_8^n\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\log(x)} &\le\int_8^n\frac{(\log(x)-1)\mathrm{d}x}{\log(x)^2}\\ &=\frac{n}{\log(n)}\color{#C00000}{-\frac{8}{\log(8)}}\tag{4} \end{align} $$ Combining (1) through (4), we get that $$ T(n)\le\color{#C00000}{C}+\frac{n}{\log(n)}=O\left(\frac{n}{\log(n)}\right)\tag{5} $$ ## Answer 2 $$T(n)=T(n-2)+1/\mbox{log }n=T(n-4)+1/\mbox{log }(n-2)+1/\mbox{log }n=\cdots $$ So $$T(n)=a+\sum_{i=1}^{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}\frac{1}{\mbox{log}(n-2i)}\leq a+\sum_{i=1}^{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}\frac{1}{b}=a+bn/2=O(n) $$ Where $ a=T(0),T(1) $ and $ b=\mbox{log }2,\mbox{log }3 $ depending on even or odd $ n $. This shows that $ O(n) $ is an upper bound. ## Answer 3 $ T(n) = T(n-2) + \frac{1}{\log(n)} $ $ \implies T(n-2) = T(n-4) + \frac{1}{\log(n)} + \frac{1}{\log(n-2)} $ So, $ T(n) = T(n-2r) + \sum_{0 ≤ 2s < 2r} \frac{1}{\log(n-2s)} $ If $ n $ is even, $ 2r \leq n-2 $, $ T(n) = T(2) + \sum_{0 ≤ 2s < n-2} \frac{1}{\log(n-2s)} $ If $ n $ is even, $ 2r \leq n-1 $, $ T(n) = T(1) + \sum_{0 ≤ 2s < n-1} \frac{1}{\log(n-2s)} $ In either case, $ O(n) = \frac{n}{\log(n)} $. ``` **Good extraction — forum Q&A (sprinklertalk)** ``` # Richdel 500 PRI controller error **Question (jrebcarlson, Monday, June 11th 2012, 5:40 pm):** When a particular station is ready to turn on (7), the controller displays and blinks a FU 5 error. Inference on TPU/marin Did a deep audit of marin's current inference stack (`lib/marin/src/marin/generation/`) and researched modern vLLM + Ray Data patterns. The current system has several architectural problems that compound on our highly preemptible TPU cluster. Summary of findings and improvements: | Problem | What's Happening | v2 Improvement | |---|---|---| | **TPU sits idle during preprocessing** | Template formatting, tokenization, and truncation all run *inside* the vLLM actor on the TPU node. TPU waits for CPU work to finish before each `generate()` call. | Separate CPU preprocessing stage from TPU inference stage (a la `ray.data.llm.build_processor`). Each scales independently via backpressure. | | **Scaling stuck at 1 replica** | Ray requests a custom resource name (`TPU-v5p-8-head`) — if the cluster doesn't register that exact string, scheduling silently fails. Zero logging of how many replicas are actually running vs. pending. No way to tell "Ray chose 1" from "Ray can't find the resource." | Validate resource names at startup (fail fast). Log replica counts periodically. Explicit `min_replicas`/`max_replicas` config. | | **Head node is the bottleneck** | The entire `run_inference` function runs on the head node — including GCS glob resolution, checkpoint scanning (batches of 20 files, 120s timeout), and write orchestration. With 10k+ output files the checkpoint scan alone takes 20+ minutes and saturates head node I/O, which also kills other people's jobs. | Head node only partitions work and writes a lightweight shard manifest. All heavy I/O (reads, writes, checkpoint tracking) moves to CPU workers. | | **10+ min recompilation on every preemption** | JAX compilation cache lives in `/tmp` — wiped on every preemption. Each restart triggers full XLA recompilation. | Cache XLA compilations to GCS (`gs://marin-{region}/compilation-cache/{model_hash}/`). After first compile, restarts take seconds. | | **Checkpoint resume is O(millions)** | On restart, every output file is scanned to extract processed row IDs into a Python set, then the entire input dataset is filtered row-by-row against that set. Stragglers that time out at 120s are silently dropped, causing those rows to be reprocessed. | Shard-based checkpointing: partition input into small shards (~5-10 min each), track completed shards in a manifest. Resume = skip completed shards. Bounded data loss on preemption. | | **Confusing config API** | Single `filetype` field means both input and output format; `output_filetype_override` bolted on separately. Resolution logic copy-pasted in 3+ places. Checkpoint glob can use the wrong filetype and silently miss old outputs. | Clean config with separate `input_format` and `output_format` fields. Each used exactly once. No override, no ambiguity. | A big part was moving to **Zephyr**. On a single v5p8 node I got from 400 tokens per second to close to 1k!!!

# Cooldown data "midtrain" experiment ## Baseline run we’re pulling from (Nemotron 1.3B) - We are evaluating cooldown variants starting from the same Nemotron 1.3B training run / checkpoint lineage. - W&B link: https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin/runs/exp2166-scaling-ladder-nemotron-validation-optimal-1e+20-9563f0?nw=nwuserheld ## What this experiment is We start from a **pre-cooldown checkpoint** (step 35000) and run cooldown training with different data mixtures. The main question: - does replacing part of the standard **Nemotron cooldown data** with **DCLM** or **Rephraser** data improve downstream benchmark performance? - More fundamentally to us: Does our **Rephraser** beat **DCLM**? ## Headline result **Nemotron-only is the best aggregate condition** in these runs. In aggregate our rephraser might beat DCLM but individually DCLM outperforms our rephraser.

Solve the first order differential equation $$ \frac{dy}{dx} - xy = x $$ ## Reasoning **First equation** The equation is separable: $$ \frac{1}{1 + y^2}\,dy = \frac{1}{1 + x^2}\,dx $$ Integrating both sides: $$ \int \frac{1}{1 + y^2}\,dy = \int \frac{1}{1 + x^2}\,dx $$ Which gives: $$ \arctan y + C_1 = \arctan x + C_2 $$ Simplify to: $$ \arctan y = \arctan x + C $$ Thus the solution is: $$ y = \tan(\arctan x + C) $$ **Second equation** Rewrite the equation: $$ \frac{dy}{dx} = x(y + 1) \quad \Rightarrow \quad \frac{1}{y + 1}\,dy = x\,dx $$ Integrate both sides: $$ \int \frac{1}{y + 1}\,dy = \int x\,dx $$ Which yields: $$ \ln|y + 1| + C_1 = \frac{1}{2}x^2 + C_2 $$ Simplify to: $$ \ln|y + 1| = \frac{1}{2}x^2 + C $$ Exponentiate both sides: $$ |y + 1| = e^{\frac{1}{2}x^2 + C} = e^C e^{\frac{1}{2}x²} $$ Thus: $$ y + 1 = \pm e^C e^{\frac{1}{2}x²} $$ Let $ A = \pm e^C $, so: $$ y = A e^{\frac{1}{2}x^2} - 1 $$ ## Answer 1. $ y = \tan(\arctan x + C) $ 2. $ y = A e^{\frac{1}{2}x^2} - 1 $ [[ ## completed ## ]] ```

Obtain the solution to the differential equation $$ \frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{1 + y^2}{1 + x²} $$ 2. The first order differential equation $$ \frac{dy}{dx} - xy = x $$ has the solution $ y = ? $ These are both separable. A: **First equation:** We separate variables: $$ \frac{1}{1 + y^2}\,dy = \frac{1}{1 + x^2}\,dx $$ Integrating both sides: $$ \int \frac{1}{1 + y^2}\,dy = \int \frac{1}{1 + x^2}\,dx $$ The integrals yield: $$ \arctan{y} + C_1 = \arctan{x} + C_2 $$ Combining constants: $$ \arctan{y} = \arctan{x} + C $$ Thus the solution is: $$ y = \tan(\arctan{x} + C) $$ **Second equation:** Rewrite the equation: $$ \frac{dy}{dx} = x(y + 1) $$ Separate variables: $$ \frac{1}{y + 1}\,dy = x\,dx $$ Integrate both sides: $$ \int \frac{1}{y + 1}\,dy = \int x\,dx $$ The integrals give: $$ \ln|y + 1| + C_1 = \frac{1}{2}x^2 + C_2 $$ Combine constants: $$ \ln|y + 1| = \frac{1}{2}x^2 + C $$ Exponentiate both sides: $$ |y + 1| = e^{\frac{1}{2}x^2 + C} = e^C e^{\frac{1}{2}x²} $$ Thus: $$ y + 1 = \pm e^C e^{\frac{1}{2}x²} $$ Let $ A = \pm e^C $, so: $$ y = A e^{\frac{1}{2}x^2} - 1 $$ The answer is 1. $ y = \tan(\arctan{x} + C) $. ```

# Results of the Code Experiment

**Experiment**: Fine-tune Qwen3-0.6B on code-heavy web content (47 URL patterns across Stack Exchange, language docs, tutorials, and framework docs; 10 CC crawls) and evaluate on HumanEval pass@1. Compare standard HTML extraction (resiliparse) vs LLM-based extraction (Qwen3-8B reformats HTML into structured code files with `/* */` comments and code fences).

| Model | HumanEval pass@1 | vs. Baseline | Training tokens |
|-------|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| **Baseline** (Qwen3-0.6B, no SFT) | 19.5% | — | — |
| **Resiliparse SFT** | **24.4%** | **+4.9pp** | 792.5M |
| **Extraction SFT** | 12.2% | -7.3pp | 177.5M |

**Resiliparse wins.** Plain text extraction with no LLM involvement improves HumanEval by +4.9pp. LLM extraction *hurts* by -7.3pp.

## Why extraction hurts

Two problems, both visible in the eval traces:

1. **Format contamination** — The extraction prompt trains the model on `/* */` comment blocks and ` ``` ` code fences. At eval time, the model generates correct code but appends these artifacts, causing syntax errors. Several problems (HumanEval/4, /13, /14) have *correct implementations* that fail solely due to trailing ` ``` ` markers.

2. **4.5x less data** — The extraction prompt aggressively filters pages without code blocks (`[NO_USEFUL_CONTENT]`), leaving only 177.5M tokens vs 792.5M for resiliparse. For code, volume of exposure matters more than reformatting.

## Analysis

### Resiliparse wins (+4.9pp)

Continued pretraining on 792.5M tokens of raw code-heavy web text improved HumanEval by 4.9 percentage points (19.5% -> 24.4%). This is a meaningful gain from a simple pipeline: standard HTML extraction, no LLM involvement, just exposure to more code.

### LLM extraction hurts (-7.3pp)

The 8B extraction branch significantly degraded performance (19.5% -> 12.2%). Several factors likely contribute:

1. **Much less data**: The extraction branch has only 177.5M tokens vs 792.5M for resiliparse (4.5x less). The LLM filters aggressively — pages without code blocks are mapped to `[NO_USEFUL_CONTENT]` and discarded. This may filter too much useful context.

2. **Format mismatch**: The extraction prompt reformats code into a `/* comment */ + code fence` structure. HumanEval expects raw Python function completions. Training on commented/fenced code may teach the model a completion style that doesn't match the eval format.

3. **Fewer training steps**: Only 677 steps vs 3,023 for resiliparse. With a single epoch, the smaller dataset means fewer gradient updates.

### Takeaways

- **Raw text wins for code**: Unlike the math domain where structured extraction might help with reasoning chains, code generation benefits more from volume of raw code exposure.
- **Aggressive filtering can backfire**: The extraction prompt's `[NO_USEFUL_CONTENT]` filter removed ~77% of the data. For a domain where the model needs broad code exposure, this is too aggressive.
- **Format matters**: Training data format should match evaluation format. Reformatting code into `/* */` comment blocks doesn't align with HumanEval's raw function completion format.

### The Takeaway

A lot of the gains we were seeing was from the instruction model having lower scores on these tasks in part because the prompting-style of these tasks is not suited for instruction tuned models.  I want to keep iterating on top of the base models to get better performance on these tasks.  It seems that the gains we were seeing are in part due to this error, although the gains on MATH seem more real.

**Why?** I think that the Question/Reasoning/Answer format really does matter, but the data source is a better match for the MATH dataset than GSM8k.  The types of content covered on that forum are just more related to the MATH dataset than GSM8k.  For Code I think we aren't seeing serious improvements yet, so I think I need to keep iterating on the prompt.  I also might try updating the MATH prompt to encourage showing more arithmetic steps which will probably boost GSM8k performance but could lead to a "distillation effect" where a bigger rephraser imparts some capabilities to smaller models.

## What the SFT Actually Teaches

Analysis of all 164 HumanEval problems for 14B:

| Category | Count | % of fixes |
|---|---|---|
| Format/stopping fixes (correct code + trailing markdown junk) | 35 | 78% |
| Genuine algorithm improvements (wrong code → correct code) | 10 | 22% |
| Regressions (baseline passes, SFT fails) | 7 | — |

The base model already solves most problems but appends markdown fences that break the test harness. Stripping the format effect, real coding improvement is +6pp. The remaining +17pp is output formatting.

MBPP isn't affected because 3-shot prompting already teaches the base model correct output format, eliminating the SFT's formatting advantage.

#### Example 2: Genuine Algorithm Improvement (HumanEval/1)

```python
from typing import List

def separate_paren_groups(paren_string: str) -> List[str]:
    """ Input to this function is a string containing multiple groups of nested parentheses. Your goal is to
    separate those group into separate strings and return the list of those.
    Separate groups are balanced (each open brace is properly closed) and not nested within each other
    Ignore any spaces in the input string.
    >>> separate_paren_groups('( ) (( )) (( )( ))')
    ['()', '(())', '(()())']
    """
```

**Baseline (FAIL):** Uses a stack but doesn't track the actual characters — returns empty strings:
```python
    for char in paren_string:
        if char == '(':
            stack.append(char)
        elif char == ')':
            if len(stack) == 0:
                result.append('')     # always appends empty string
            else:
                stack.pop()
                if len(stack) == 0:
                    result.append('')  # never captures the group content
    return result
```

**V3 SFT (PASS):** Tracks `current_group` to build up each parenthesis group:
```python
    for char in paren_string:
        if char == "(":
            stack.append(char)
            current_group += char
        elif char == ")":
            if stack:
                stack.pop()
                current_group += char
                if not stack:
                    result.append(current_group)
                    current_group = ""
    return result
```

<details>
<summary>Potential Framings/Regimes</summary>

I would like to think more about how this project is impactful both in encouraging the wider community to use the tool we've built and also how this is directly useful to the Marin project.

One thing that is clear: the place this wins is infinite compute world because it is very compute-intensive.

**Framing 1:** By prompt engineering the extractor model we can get purpose built datasets for downstream domains.  This data can be useful for midtraining or mixing into pretraining (see https://arxiv.org/pdf/2603.16177)

<img width="702" height="389" alt="Image" src="https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/0d0b5ba7-a89c-4687-8eb6-c779cb5261e6" />

They mix in about 300M tokens of domain specific data during pretraining and it makes these domains easier to learn during SFT.  My code dataset is 262M tokens and Math + Medical are shaping up to be slightly larger so maybe there is potential for this to be the regime we are targeting.

**Framing 2:** Intelligent Pretraining Data selection for infinite compute.  Try to run the pipeline at pretraining scale with a few prompts and see if we get better performance.  Forget about filtering and try to extract as much data as possible from the internet.  Perhaps compare a training run versus other pipelines on the same amount of data.  E.G. maybe we take 3000 WARC files which is about 8B tokens and train a 400M parameter model on this, versus same 3000 WARC files and train on DCLM filtered data which would yield 120M tokens.  This is somewhat ridiculous but it would showcase how we can extract way more juice from the internet.

**Framing 3:** Controllable Pretraining.  Now that we have a model that can rewrite the web content we can steer pretraining in interesting directions.  For instance we can tag data with toxicity tags, or rewrite documents to change the outcomes.  Maybe this is the most interesting part of this tool, so I can select some ways that people would meaningfully want to improve models at the pretraining stage (value alignment, personality, etc.) and see if we can bake any of this into the pretraining.

</details>

Flop Accounting We compute inference FLOPs per document by decomposing each forward pass into position-independent (MLP, projections, LM head) and position-dependent (attention) terms. For a request with $P$ input tokens and $O$ output tokens: $$\text{FLOPs} = \underset{\text{prefill}}{\left(C_{\text{non-attn}} \cdot P + C_{\text{attn}} \cdot P^2\right)} + \underset{\text{decode}}{\left(C_{\text{non-attn}} \cdot O + C_{\text{attn}}\left(O \cdot P + \frac{O(O-1)}{2}\right)\right)}$$ where $C_{\text{non-attn}}$ and $C_{\text{attn}}$ are constants derived from the model architecture (Qwen3-8B, 36 layers, $d=4096$, GQA with 32/8 heads). **Projection**: $6.60 \times 10^{22}$ total inference FLOPs (95% CI: $\pm 2.0%$). ---
Derivation ### Derivation of Inference FLOP Accounting **Starting point.** Levanter's `lm_flops_per_token` ([`flop_utils.py`](lib/levanter/src/levanter/utils/flop_utils.py)) computes FLOPs per token for a forward pass at a given sequence length $S$. We decompose it into position-independent and position-dependent terms for inference. **Step 1: Identify per-token components.** Each forward pass through one layer computes: | Component | FLOPs per token | Source | |---|---|---| | MLP (SwiGLU: gate, up, down) | $2 \cdot 3 \cdot h \cdot d_{\text{ff}}$ | `2 * 3 * hidden_dim * intermediate_dim` | | QKV projection (GQA) | $2h(n_h d_h + 2 n_{kv} d_h)$ | `2 * hidden_dim * (num_heads * head_dim + 2 * num_kv_heads * head_dim)` | | Output projection | $2h^2$ | `2 * hidden_dim * hidden_dim` | where $h$ is hidden dim, $d_{\text{ff}}$ is intermediate dim, $n_h$ is query heads, $n_{kv}$ is KV heads, and $d_h = h / n_h$ is head dim. These are **constant per token** regardless of position. The LM head adds $2hV$ FLOPs per token (applied once, not per-layer). Combining, the **position-independent cost** per token is: $$C_{\text{non-attn}} = L \cdot (6 h \cdot d_{\text{ff}} + 2h(n_h d_h + 2 n_{kv} d_h) + 2h^2) + 2hV$$ where $L$ is the number of layers. **Step 2: Identify the attention term.** The function computes attention FLOPs over the full sequence then divides by $S$: $$F_{\text{seq}} = S^2 (2 n_h d_h + 3 n_h + 2 d_h n_h) = S^2 (4 n_h d_h + 3 n_h)$$ This accounts for: - Key-query logits: $2 S^2 n_h d_h$ (matmul of $[S, d_h]$ queries against $[d_h, S]$ keys, per head) - Masking + softmax: $3 S^2 n_h$ (comparison, subtract max, exponentiate — 3 ops per element) - Value aggregation: $2 S^2 d_h n_h$ (matmul of $[S, S]$ attention weights against $[S, d_h]$ values) Per token (dividing by $S$), per layer: $$\text{attn per token} = S \cdot (4 n_h d_h + 3 n_h)$$ Defining the **attention cost per unit of context length**, per layer: $$c_{\text{attn}} = 4 n_h d_h + 3 n_h$$ The full attention constant across all layers: $$C_{\text{attn}} = L \cdot c_{\text{attn}}$$ **Step 3: Verify decomposition.** The original function returns: $$f(S) = C_{\text{non-attn}} + C_{\text{attn}} \cdot S$$ which is **affine in $S$** — this is the key structural property. **Step 4: Apply to inference.** Inference has two phases: *Prefill* ($P$ prompt tokens processed in parallel): Each token attends to all $P$ tokens (full-attention assumption from the original function). Total prefill FLOPs: $$\text{FLOPs}\_{\text{prefill}} = P \cdot f(P) = C_{\text{non-attn}} \cdot P + C_{\text{attn}} \cdot P^2$$ *Decode* ($O$ output tokens generated sequentially): At decode step $i$ $(i = 0, \ldots, O-1)$, one token attends to a context of length $P + i$. Its FLOPs are $f(P + i) = C_{\text{non-attn}} + C_{\text{attn}} \cdot (P + i)$. Summing: $$\text{FLOPs}\_{\text{decode}} = \sum_{i=0}^{O-1} f(P+i) = C_{\text{non-attn}} \cdot O + C_{\text{attn}} \sum_{i=0}^{O-1}(P+i)$$ The sum is an arithmetic series: $$\sum_{i=0}^{O-1}(P+i) = O \cdot P + \frac{O(O-1)}{2}$$ **Step 5: Combine.** $$\text{FLOPs}\_{\text{total}} = C_{\text{non-attn}} \cdot (P + O) + C_{\text{attn}} \cdot P^2 + C_{\text{attn}} (O \cdot P + \frac{O(O-1)}{2})$$ **Step 6: Plug in Qwen3-8B values.** With $h=4096$, $d_{\text{ff}}=12288$, $L=36$, $n_h=32$, $n_{kv}=8$, $d_h=128$, $V=151936$: $$C_{\text{non-attn}} = 36 \cdot (6 \cdot 4096 \cdot 12288 + 2 \cdot 4096 \cdot (32 \cdot 128 + 2 \cdot 8 \cdot 128) + 2 \cdot 4096^2) + 2 \cdot 4096 \cdot 151936$$ $$C_{\text{attn}} = 36 \cdot (4 \cdot 32 \cdot 128 + 3 \cdot 32) = 36 \cdot 16480 = 593280$$ This closed-form runs in $O(1)$ per document. We evaluate it for each record using exact token counts ($P$ from prompt reconstruction, $O$ = thinking + response tokens from `generated_text`), then sum across all records per batch and project via bootstrap.

Math Behind Projection Based Simulated Epochs ## Setup We sample 3,000 of ~7.9M Common Crawl WARCs and run each curation method on them: - **D_obs**: tokens in our sample (e.g. 2.66B for DCLM) - **s** = total_warcs / sampled_warcs ≈ 2,642 - **D_proj** = D_obs × s (projected full-CC token count, e.g. ~7.0T) ## Experiment B (simulated full-scale) Simulate training on D_proj tokens at target compute T_target by matching the **epoch count** of the full-scale regime. At full scale, epoch count = `T_target / D_proj`. We match this by training T_exp tokens on a slice: ``` slice = T_exp × D_proj / T_target ``` Verify: `T_exp / slice = T_target / D_proj` ✓ **Ceiling**: slice can't exceed D_obs, so: ``` T_exp ≤ T_target / s ``` Candidates above this ceiling are excluded from Experiment B. ## Example (DCLM, T_target = 20T, budget 3e18, d512 model) ``` slice = 4.3B × 7.0T / 20T ≈ 1.5B unique tokens epochs = 4.3B / 1.5B ≈ 2.87 (matches 20T / 7.0T ≈ 2.86 ✓) ```

**THE PROBLEM:** The token cliff Sampling 3,000 of 7.9M WARCs gives a scale factor s ≈ 2,642, which caps Experiment B at T_exp ≤ T_target / s ≈ 7.6B tokens — excluding our largest compute candidates regardless of curation method. ### Solution 1: Increase Target Token Budget
Solution 1 This solution is to tackle the `T_target` part of the hard cap. We could raise to 200T tokens instead of 20T. **Pros:** Super simple. Probably also makes our method look insanely good because DCLM has to epoch 28x and we only need to epoch 1.2x **Cons:** Somewhat "sci-fi" and not as directly applicable to marin. Also epoxying some datasets 20-90x might ruin the scaling curves anyway.
### Solution 2: Increase Number of WARC files (with clever hack)
Solution 2 This solution is to tackle the `s` part of the hard cap. We could raise to 1000 WARC files instead of 3000. **Pros:** This is easier to justify and probably a more fair comparison. 10k WARCs is the minimum size DCLM releases for comparison. It also allows us to stay within the realm of "useful to marin". More extraction is free from all sources besides LLM extraction because I am just mapping from the data releases. **Cons:** LLM extraction is really expensive. This involves 3x scale up.... except there is a hack. **The Hack:**. Since we are simulated epoching at 0.13 epochs we actually only use a fraction of the data we extracted. We extracted ~60B tokens, and the hard cap would become 25.2B tokens. We can pretend we got these from 10k WARCs when we really got them from 3k. In fact we could push this as far as 20k WARCs, although at some point it really feels like we are punishing our method for over-extracting data.

If any matches, output [NO_USEFUL_CONTENT] and do not extract.    Categories that typically qualify (still subject to all criteria above):    - Long-form journalism with original reporting and analysis — including editorial tech journalism or product reporting that includes quotes, context, history, or analysis (even when the subject is a company's product launch)    - Educational or explanatory articles (science, math, history, engineering, medicine, philosophy, economics, etc.)    - Tutorials, how-tos, and documentation with real teaching — instructions plus the reasoning behind them    - Encyclopedia and reference entries written with substantive prose    - **Substantive technical forum, mailing-list, or Q&A threads** — e.g., a Stack Overflow question with a thorough accepted answer, a numpy/scipy mailing-list discussion working through a real problem, a developer forum thread that reaches a meaningful technical conclusion. The "casual forum threads" FAILS bullet does NOT apply when the discussion is technical and develops the topic.    - Research papers, white papers, technical writeups    - Essays and analyses that develop an argument with evidence — including substantive opinion or commentary on a personal blog or social platform like Tumblr/Medium/Substack    - Code accompanied by genuine teaching, not just a snippet    - Technical blogs sharing real domain expertise    - Institutional or organizational descriptions with substantive prose (academic program pages with curriculum and outcomes, organizational reports, conference or event summaries with real narrative)    - Religious or scriptural texts presenting substantive narrative or doctrine (e.g., a Bible chapter, Quran sura, philosophical canon — numbered-verse format is fine)    Categories that FAIL — filter even if the writing is fine:    - **News briefs, sports recaps, and transaction roundups** — "X happened, said Y" reporting without analysis, depth, or context. Includes local sports recaps ("West Side beat Cumberland 14-4"), team transaction logs ("Signed pitcher X to a minor-league contract"), and short news items even when several are stitched together on one page.    - **Personal lifestyle or diary blogging** — daily-life updates, travelogues, opinion pieces without intellectual substance. (A personal blog with substantive analysis or argument is fine — judge by content, not platform.)    - **Light reviews — including aggregator pages of light reviews** — "I tried it, it's good" without genuine analysis or comparison. A page that strings together several short product blurbs is still light reviews, not substantive content.    - **Reference stubs and structured-data dumps** — one-paragraph wiki entries, definitions, factoid lists, player stat cards, whois/BGP/DNS records, raw lookup results, single-formula pages. If the page is mostly a table, a record, or one isolated fact, it fails — fastText-style classifiers may rate this content highly because it "looks structured," but it is not teaching prose.    - **Casual forum threads** — chit-chat, brief Q&A without resolution, social exchanges that don't reach a meaningful conclusion. Technical mailing-list or Q&A threads that DO develop the topic are covered by the qualifying bullet above and are NOT this.    - **Vendor sales copy or purely promotional material** — product descriptions, ad copy, "buy now" pages. (Institutional descriptions of academic programs, mission statements with real content, organizational reports, or editorial journalism about a product launch are NOT this; judge by whether the page sells a product or describes/teaches.)    - **Mostly un-decoded HTML / escape soup** — pages where the visible text is dominated by raw HTML entities (` `, `<`, `&`, `&#NNN;`), escape sequences, or malformed markup that survived the page render. Even if the underlying content might be code or text, a page presented this way is junk for training.    - **"No results" / search-empty pages** — "your search returned no results", "no items match", "0 records found" — even when they list related links or alternative searches alongside.    - **Anything that fails a normal quality filter** — commerce pages, navigation or aggregation surfaces, login walls or other site machinery, fragments and microposts, wrappers around non-textual media, raw data dumps, empty placeholders, incoherent text    **When in doubt, output [NO_USEFUL_CONTENT].** Reject borderline pages aggressively; only clear winners pass. First determine if the page clears the EXTREME quality bar. If it does, follow the following rules to extract the content. 2. **Extract the full page content in reading order**. Keep explanatory text, discussion, and comments that add substantive information. Begin your output directly with the page content. 3. **Remove boilerplate**: navigation, footers, sidebars, ads, share buttons, related links, breadcrumbs, cookie banners, and UI elements. Do not output framework markers or metadata tags. 4. **Preserve all technical content** exactly as written: code, math, formulas, tables, and data. Preserve original line breaks and the structure of code blocks. 5. Decode HTML entities to plain characters (e.g. & → &, ’ → '). Remove raw HTML tags. 6. **Do not add, invent, or embellish content.** Every sentence must come from the source page. 7. For pages with multiple authors or speakers (forums, reviews, comments), preserve who said what — include usernames or speaker labels. 8. If the page contains content spinner templates like {word1|word2|word3}, pick the first option. If most of the page is spinners, output [NO_USEFUL_CONTENT]. ```

Rule Based Heuristics Expressed each DCLM and custom HTML rule as a tunable threshold on a single feature, then greedily assembled them under a hard recall ≥ 0.99 constraint: at each step we add the threshold that discards the most no_useful documents per unit of useful lost, stopping once the ~1% recall budget is spent.

FastText + ModernBERT Usefulness Classifier Cascade **fastText (stage 1)**: Trained as a binary "useful vs [NO_USEFUL_CONTENT]" classifier on ~2.46M raw body_strip HTML docs (189k useful + 2.27M non-useful, the 12:1 deployment ratio) from 80 WARCs across 24 CC snapshots, using the hand-set DCLM bigram recipe (epoch 5, lr 0.1, dim 100, wordNgrams 2, softmax). Pruning with --min count 500 shrank it to a sub-GB model (0.96 GB) at full quality (F1 0.594). **ModernBERT (stage 2)**: Fine-tuned answerdotai/ModernBERT-base (8192 ctx) on the same target but over 1M docs sampled only from the fastText survivor pool, on TPU v6e-4 with PyTorch + torch_xla in bf16 (effective batch 256, lr 5e-5, 1 epoch). Training on the survivor residual specialized it for exactly the deployment distribution, lifting standalone F1 to 0.705 and giving the best high-recall operating point in the cascade.

FastText Router The jusText-extractability router is a fastText classifier that predicts, from a raw doc, whether a cheap jusText extraction will land within 0.85 normalized Levenshtein similarity of the gold LLM extraction (i.e. ≥85% character-identical) — labeling such docs "extractable" (→ jusText) and everything else, including all [NO_USEFUL_CONTENT] abstentions, as "needs LLM" (→ 1.7B/gpt-oss-120b). Because only ~5.5% of docs naturally clear that strict bar, at its F1-optimal threshold the router sends just ~8% of survivors (3,381 of 41,245 ≈ 1.9% of all raw docs) to jusText and leaves the remaining ~92% (37,864 docs) on the expensive model path, offloading less than a tenth of the extraction workload.

New Devset (and ways of measuring spec quality) **Labelled a Devset of 935 docs so far (999 to go, but seeing if claude can help)** Labelled it for keep, weak keep, weak drop, or drop. Also marked some for top quality (we really MUST keep), and some that are tricky edge cases to test the extraction. ---
How the docs were selected **Document selection.** The core of the dev set is a *disagreement-and-topicality* sample from a 10,000-WARC CommonCrawl pool: for each held-out eval example that `high_quality` scored worse on than DCLM/Nemotron, we built a keyword fingerprint and selected corpus documents containing ≥3 and ≥80% of that example's keywords, then joined each to a membership table recording every pipeline's keep/drop decision (hq, DCLM, Nemotron-CC, FineWeb-Edu, FineWeb-CC) and stratified the draw by (register × cross-pipeline agreement × hq's own decision) so both kept and dropped documents appear in every register. We then supplemented this with an unbiased uniform sample from a 2013–2026 CommonCrawl timeline, targeted raw-HTML scans that recover code/table pages (via `
`/``/`` and
syntax-highlighter signatures that extraction destroys), diverse general-forum threads, mined
hard-negatives, and the highest-confidence documents DCLM keeps but hq drops.

**Register identification.** Registers were first assigned by domain — each URL reduced to its
registered domain (eTLD+1) and matched against a hand-curated, priority-ordered list of
domain-substring patterns per register — but because that mis-binned platform domains (e.g. a
chemistry article on `geeksforgeeks`, a novel e-text on `gradesaver`), every document was subsequently
re-classified by *content*, with an LLM reading the extracted text and assigning the register it
actually belongs to.

How we defined knowledge-dense

How the `hq_dense` reweight bucket was defined in the Phase-2 dilution ablation
(`experiments/baseline_collection/build_hq_variants.py`).

A doc was counted as **dense** iff its **registered domain** contained one of the substring
patterns below — i.e. `categorize(url) in {reference_wiki, academic, blog, news, qa_help}`.
This is a **domain-only heuristic** (never reads page text); patterns are **priority-ordered**,
first match wins, else `other`. Source of truth: `CATEGORY_PATTERNS` in
`experiments/baseline_collection/provenance_audit_10k.py`.

The five "fact-bearing expository" registers were chosen to mirror what DCLM over-represents
(knowledge-gap decomposition: reference_wiki 2.4×, blog 2.6×, academic 1.7× char-share vs hq).
This subset was ~12% of hq tokens; mixed back at weight 0.144 it lifted the dense char-share
~12% → 25% (matching DCLM) at a fixed token budget.

## reference_wiki (11 patterns)

```
wikipedia, wikia, fandom, wiktionary, wikihow, wikimedia, wikinews, wikibooks, britannica, wikidot, wikispaces
```

## academic (22 patterns)

arxiv, biorxiv, ssrn, researchgate, academia.edu, jstor, sciencedirect, springer, ncbi.nlm.nih, plos, pubmed, semanticscholar, citeseerx, iopscience, ieee, acm.org, aps.org, mdpi, tandfonline, wiley, oup.com, sagepub
```

## blog (12 patterns)

## news (29 patterns)

bbc., cnn., nytimes, theguardian, reuters, washingtonpost, forbes, bloomberg, huffpost, huffingtonpost, npr.org, apnews, aljazeera, telegraph, dailymail, foxnews, nbcnews, cbsnews, usatoday, wsj., economist, theatlantic, politico, news, tribune, gazette, herald, chron., latimes

## Caveats

- **Plain substring match on the domain** — over- and under-catches. Generic `news` grabs any
  domain containing "news"; `faq` / `howto` are bare substrings that can match mid-domain;
  `blog` is really the *platform* (blogspot/wordpress), whose content is heterogeneous.
- **Domain-only, no text** — "academic" is genuinely journal/preprint domains, but expository
  *quality* within blog/news is unresolved. So the reweight concentrated these **registers by
  domain**, not fact-dense text — a coarse proxy, and part of why the reweight moved nothing.

Custom Metrics

Three numbers for "did the extraction keep the page's content, and nothing else."
Everything is computed on **normalized** text, so markdown, emphasis, quotes,
dashes, whitespace and rendered-vs-LaTeX math (`κ` = `\kappa`) never count as a
difference.

Let $G$ be the gold text and $P$ the prediction.

- $S(x)$ = the **set of 5-grams** of $\text{normalize}(x)$
- $U(G)$ = the **sentences of $G$** with at least 8 words

## KEPT — recall

Fraction of gold's sentences that survive. A sentence counts as kept if at least
half of its 5-grams appear anywhere in the prediction:

$$\text{KEPT} = \frac{1}{|U(G)|}\sum_{u \in U(G)} \mathbb{1}\!\left[\frac{|S(u) \cap S(P)|}{|S(u)|} \ge 0.5\right]$$

Sentences shorter than 5 words can't form a 5-gram, so they're matched by direct
substring containment instead.

## CLEAN — precision

Fraction of what we emitted that actually exists in gold:

$$\text{CLEAN} = \frac{|S(P) \cap S(G)|}{|S(P)|}$$

## FIDELITY — the headline

F-score of the two, with **recall weighted twice as heavily** as precision
($\beta^2 = 2$), because dropping content is worse than keeping extra:

$$\text{FIDELITY} = \frac{(1+\beta^2)\cdot \text{CLEAN} \cdot \text{KEPT}}{\beta^2 \cdot \text{CLEAN} + \text{KEPT}} = \frac{3\cdot \text{CLEAN}\cdot \text{KEPT}}{2\cdot \text{CLEAN} + \text{KEPT}}$$

The same construction gives **CODE**, **MATH**, **TABLE** and **WHO** — identical
to KEPT, but with $U(G)$ replaced by gold's code lines, math expressions, table
cells, or speaker names.

More principled FLOP estimation ## Inference FLOPs of the fast curation cascade **Estimate: 1.3e10 to 1.7e10 FLOPs per extracted document, 5.1e14 to 6.7e14 per WARC, and 4.0e21 to 5.3e21 for the 8M-WARC run (7,925,398 WARCs).** The low end charges each document its real token count; the high end charges the padded length the chip actually runs. ettin68 accounts for 98% of the total. | | Actual lengths | Padded lengths | |---|---|---| | Per extracted doc | 1.3e10 | 1.7e10 | | Per kept doc | 6.9e10 | 9.0e10 | | Per WARC | 5.1e14 | 6.7e14 | | Per kept token (ModernBERT tokens) | 5.1e7 | 6.7e7 | | 8M run total | 4.0e21 | 5.3e21 | The rest of this note explains how the numbers are produced. The deployed pipeline (`lpv11_fastpipe_v2_1_fused`) scores every extracted document with three classifiers in sequence: fastText, a pooled super-token transformer, and ettin68. Each stage only sees the documents the previous stage passed on, so the cost per document is an expectation over the stages a document reaches. ### Stages and reach rates | Stage | Model | Context | Condition to run | Share of extracted docs | |---|---|---|---|---| | 1 | fastText w640 | full doc | always | 100% | | 2 | pooled transformer (90M-doc ckpt) | 8192 | fastText prob ≥ 0.0048 | 58.2% | | 3 | ettin68 | 2048 | pooled prob in [0.079, 0.8883) | 20.1% | Of the documents the pooled model scores, 18.3% are accepted outright, 47.2% are dropped, and 34.6% go to ettin68. Overall, 19.2% of extracted documents are kept. Rates are measured from production catalogs (52 shards, 12,824 WARCs). Per WARC: 39,464 records, 38,560 extracted docs, 22,423 fastText survivors, 7,749 band docs, 7,413 kept docs. ## Expected cost per document ``` E[FLOPs per extracted doc] = c_ft + p_ft * E[ c_pool(min(L, 8192)) | passed fastText ] + p_ft * p_band * E[ c_ettin(min(L, 2048)) | in band ] p_ft = 0.5815 p_band = 0.3456 ``` Each stage's cost is averaged over the token-length distribution of the documents that actually reach it. Those distributions come from the 100k comparison sample, which stores every stage's score per document: we tokenize its deployment text with the ModernBERT tokenizer and apply the production thresholds. The sample's reach rates match production within two points. **How padding works.** Within a WARC, the scorer sorts a stage's documents by length, takes batches of 32, and pads each batch to the smallest bucket in (128, 256, ..., context) that fits the longest document in that batch. The last batch is filled to 32 rows with empty rows. Because batches are length-sorted, all 32 documents in a batch are close in length, so the padded cost is well approximated by charging each document its own bucket; simulating the real per-batch procedure on the sample gives the same mean within 1%. Padding raises the mean charged length by 1.37x for the pooled stage and 1.30x for ettin68, which is the gap between the two columns below and in the headline table. | Stage | Reach rate | Mean tokens, actual (capped at context) | Mean tokens, padded | Cost per doc, actual | Cost per doc, padded | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | fastText | 100% | 1,318 (no cap) | n/a | 2.0e5 | 2.0e5 | | pooled | 58.2% | 1,010 | 1,380 | 4.1e8 | 5.7e8 | | ettin68 | 20.1% | 608 | 792 | 6.5e10 | 8.5e10 | ## 8M run document counts (7,925,398 WARCs) | | Count | |---|---| | Docs scored by fastText | 3.1e11 | | Docs scored by pooled | 1.8e11 | | Docs scored by ettin68 | 6.1e10 | | Kept docs | 5.9e10 | For reference, 4.0e21 to 5.3e21 FLOPs is the 6ND training cost of a 1B model on 700B to 900B tokens. ## Caveats - FLOPs and chip time diverge. Measured chip time from the catalogs implies MFU of 0.1 to 0.4% for the pooled stage and 1.4 to 5.7% for ettin68. All-in, the run is 26.2 v6e-8 slice-seconds per WARC (about 58k slice-hours for 8M WARCs), which is 0.35% MFU against the FLOP total. - fastText FLOPs count arithmetic only. Its measured cost is 0.55 CPU-ms per document, mostly hashing and table lookups. - Token counts use the ModernBERT tokenizer, not the training tokenizer. - Reach rates are from the current ladder's crawl mix.
Conventions - Forward pass only; a multiply-add counts as 2 FLOPs. - Embedding lookups, layer norms, softmax, activations, and the pooling reduction count as zero. - Length `L` includes the two special tokens and is capped at the stage context. The padded variant rounds `L` up to the next bucket in (128, 256, 512, 1024, 2048, 4096, 8192). - Empty tail rows in a WARC's last batch are included in the per-batch simulation and add under 1%.
fastText formula dim 100, word bigrams, no character n-grams (read from the model header). Features are words plus bigrams, about twice the word count; words are taken as 0.75 of ModernBERT tokens. One add per dimension per feature, then a 100 x 2 output layer. ``` F = 2 * 0.75 * T c_ft = 100 * F + 2 * 100 * 2 ≈ 150 T + 400 ``` At T = 1,318 this is 2.0e5.
Pooled transformer formula Levanter's `PooledTransformerConfig.flops_per_token`, called directly. `L` padded tokens, `S = L / 64` super-tokens, hidden `D = 512`, pooled input width 768 (mean, max, min of 256-dim embeddings), feed-forward 2048, 4 layers, 2 labels. ``` proj = 2 * 768 * D * S layer = 2 * 4 * D^2 * S # q, k, v, o projections + 2 * 2 * S^2 * D # QK^T and AV + 2 * 2 * D * 2048 * S # MLP head = 2 * D * 2 c_pool(L) = proj + 4 * layer + head ``` About 4.1e5 FLOPs per input token, nearly flat in `L`.
ettin68 formula Hand-derived (Levanter's generic helper adds a vocabulary-head term a classifier does not have). Hidden `D = 512`, GeGLU feed-forward 768, 19 layers, 8 heads, global attention on every third layer starting at layer 0 (7 layers), sliding window 128 on the other 12. ``` linear_per_token_per_layer = 2 * 4 * D^2 # q, k, v, o + 2 * D * 2 * 768 # GeGLU up and gate + 2 * 768 * D # down attn_per_token_per_layer = 4 * span * D # span = L (global), min(L, 128) (local) c_ettin(L) = L * sum over 19 layers of (linear + attn) ``` Linear term 8.5e7 per token (two times the 42M non-embedding parameters); attention 3.2e7 at L = 2048; total 1.17e8 per token.
Data sources - Reach rates and per-WARC counts: fused catalogs, 52 random shards of the 404 to 8079 ladder. - Per-stage length distributions: 100k comparison sample (`extractor_compare/high_quality_200warc`), deployment text tokenized with `answerdotai/ModernBERT-base`, production thresholds applied to stored scores. - Model shapes: checkpoint `config.json` for pooled 90M and ettin68; fastText hyperparameters from the model binary header. - Chip time: catalog columns `pooled_s` and `score_s` times device count, per device type.

Why do TPU and GPU differ? RoPE bug in vllm-tpu version :( Our TPU inference stack (vLLM + Google's `tpu-inference`) has two ways to run a model: a JAX re-implementation of each architecture (the default for dense Qwen3, Qwen2, Llama) and a path that runs vLLM's PyTorch model definition through torchax. The JAX Qwen3 implementation reads the model's RoPE settings from the Hugging Face config like this: ```python self.rope_scaling = getattr(config, "rope_scaling", None) ... if rope_scaling: # truthy dict -> apply Llama-3 long-context scaling timescale = apply_rope_scaling(timescale, rope_scaling) ``` With transformers 4.x, a model that uses no RoPE scaling (Qwen3's `config.json` says `"rope_scaling": null`) returned `None` here, and nothing happened. transformers 5 changed the API: `config.rope_scaling` is now an alias of `rope_parameters` and returns `{"rope_type": "default", "rope_theta": 1000000}`. That dict is truthy, so the JAX port started applying `apply_rope_scaling`, which never checks `rope_type` and uses hard-coded Llama-3 defaults (scale 8, cutoffs at 2k and 8k tokens). Result: 37 of Qwen3's 64 RoPE frequency bands were rewritten, the lowest divided by 8. The model's sense of position was wrong at every token, and worse the farther apart two tokens were, so long documents suffered most. ### Timeline - **2026-06-12** tpu-inference cuts `releases/v0.23.0`; the bug is latent (it needs transformers 5). - **2026-06-26** Google fixes it on `main` (PR #2838, "Get the right rope_scaling values from config"); the fix ships in v0.24.0 and later, never in v0.23.0. - **2026-06-29** Marin `main` migrates to transformers 5 (#6735) while every tpu-inference pin from 06-17 to 08-13 is v0.23.0-based, so `main` is broken for every dense model on the default JAX path. - **2026-08-13 11:39 PT** `main` auto-refreshes the stack to v0.26.0 (#8207) and is fixed, by accident. - **My checkout** tracked `main` as of 05-06 (transformers 4.57.5, tpu-inference 0.18.0 fork) until the parity sync on **2026-08-13 13:54 ET**, which landed 11 commits before #8207. With transformers 4 the config reports `rope_scaling = None` and the scaling branch never runs, so the lpv11 10k extraction (late July to ~Aug 20), the 3,000-WARC llm_pipeline_v1 run and all distillation data gathered by Aug 12 were produced on a correct model. Being behind `main` skipped the broken window entirely. - **after the sync, from the same checkout** (transformers 5.12.1 + the v0.23.0-based `e8809d49` pin): the lpv11 gap-fill (12 re-extracted WARCs, 09-01 to 09-04), WebMainBench 7,809 (09-19), the devset "lpv11 direct" reruns, classifier logprob scoring, and all ReScraper TPU runs (late Sept to 10-12): broken port. Any 10k-extraction worker relaunched after 08-13 13:54 ET would also have picked up the new lock; the tail of that run (~Aug 13-20) should be checked against the job logs. - **2026-10-13** root-caused and confirmed. Reruns on the correct path are in progress. ### Something nice we know (more easily) because of this GitHub issue log **FROM AUGUST 12th THE DAY BEFORE** So 7k WARC files were processed properly. The last 3k may be corrupted by this. All of our distillation data for the cascade came from an uncorrupted version. **I AM RUNNING SOME EXPERIMENTS NOW AND TRYING TO DETERMINE HOW SERIOUSLY THIS IMPACTS RESULTS**
> [!TIP] > A bug impacted RoPE embeddings on vllm-tpu. This only impacted us after August 13th so the damage is somewhat contained. Doing a deeper analysis of what this fully impacts. ---
Updated Ablation Plots
> [!TIP] > Better presentation of our filter and extractor ablations. ---
Investigating Filter Disagreements Artifact: https://claude.ai/artifact/6dJ1HuoXNyofFeJhbXwdbM My general sense: Although I prompted the LLM against keeping docs like this (and on average it drops them) there are edge cases where long lists make it through, and these are not high quality training docs: **ONLY LLM KEEPS** **ONLY CASCADE KEEPS** The cascade has a few of these too: Clear that the LLM noise drops some good docs that the cascade keeps: === Extraction Differences === Less clear why the rule based is better for extraction... If anything I like a lot of the LLM extractions better. Might be the hallucination problem especially for the last 3000 WARC files with the tpu-inference bug. Extractions Viewer: https://claude.ai/artifact/DvebZUJJy3w3647QzArytD
> [!TIP] > Investigated qualitatively why the cascade is better. Some clear cut cases for the filtering, but the LLM extraction really does seem better, so it is a bit odd that the cascade extraction seems so much better on downstream benchmarks after you train the model. ---

## Weekly Sync 10/19 - 10/23 **Agenda:** - Investigation of how RoPE impacted the LLM Data - Deduplication details - Decontamination plan - Release Plan ---
Investigation of how RoPE impacted the LLM Data Last week's worry: the last ~3k WARCs of the lpv11 10k extraction might have run with the vllm-tpu RoPE bug. **They did not. No LLM data we use was affected.** **Why:** the bug lives in tpu-inference's JAX re-implementation of Qwen3. Our Qwen3-8B extractor loads from a `gs://` checkpoint through the runai streamer, and the JAX Qwen3 port has no streaming weight loader, so vLLM's `auto` setting resolves to the PyTorch-via-torchax path, which is correct. **Only models loaded from the HF cache or local disk took the JAX path. In our work that was only ReScraper.** **Verified three ways:** - Code path and old job logs: every Qwen3-8B run used the torchax path (lpv11 10k extraction, gap-fill, WebMainBench 7,809, devset, classifier scoring). - Reruns with the implementation pinned to torchax: devset 99.8% decision agreement; WebMainBench shard 00 F1 .6400 vs .6422; 1k lpv11 pages 626/975 byte-identical, median similarity 0.994 on the rest. - Quality unchanged on the 1k rerun: major hallucinations 1.1% vs 1.6%, within judge noise (51 vs 52 flagged on identical pages); SRS 2.64 vs 2.66. **The 8M hero data runs no LLM at inference time:** it is resiliparse-rs extraction, then a fastText gate, then a ModernBERT classifier. The LLM only produced the distillation labels, and those came from the correct path.
> [!TIP] > False alarm for our data: only ReScraper (loaded from local disk) hit the bug. Every Qwen3-8B extraction ran on the correct path, which logs and reruns confirm. ---
Deduplication details | Stage | Docs | Characters | Tokens (llama3) | |---|---:|---:|---:| | Extracted (8,582,115 WARCs) | 61.21B | 341.8T | ≈80.6T | | After exact dedup | 21.84B | 133.9T | ≈31.6T | | After fuzzy dedup (hero cluster method, c075) | **9.95B** | **72.7T** | **17.15T** | Characters are exact at every stage. The final token count is measured; the first two use the final corpus's 4.239 chars/token. - **17.15T llama3 tokens** (72.7T chars, 26.5 TB). The refit after the 2M run projected 16.9T (15.7–18.9T); the projections made at 500k (21.8–25.0T) were too high. - 64% of extracted records were exact duplicates, confirmed to be the same pages recrawled across crawls. - By source: **CC-MAIN 16.68T**, **CC-NEWS 0.21T** (tagged `CC-NEWS-YYYY-MM`, so it can be mixed separately), **CC-SUPPLEMENTAL 7.8B**. - Random-sample viewer: https://claude.ai/artifact/9Wp8sdhFwC7xmRqz74ddpx
> [!TIP] > Dedup is done: **17.15T tokens** from 8.58M WARCs, in line with the post-2M projection. The hero run used ~25T. ---
Decontamination plan Full walkthrough with examples: https://claude.ai/artifact/FPrunN93nfrApC6j4hcgSN **How Marin's decon works.** Take the test questions and answers from every benchmark we report (the 9 Artificial Analysis benchmarks plus the lm-eval tasks in Marin's eval suite). Split each training doc into paragraphs. If at least half of a paragraph's 13-word runs also appear in the eval text, the doc is removed. Phrases that are common all over the web are ignored, so boilerplate can't trigger a removal. The version the hero run used (v3) adds one more check for short paragraphs (3–12 words), which are too short to contain a 13-word run: a short paragraph that exactly matches a short line from the evals also removes the doc. That check is meant to catch short eval answers, but it also matches ordinary lines like "2 years ago" or "Lana Del Rey". Marin changed this after the hero run (v4, PR #8327, Sept 24): a paragraph now needs at least two different eval phrases in it to count, so a single short line can't remove a doc by itself. **Where we are.** Every doc in the pool has been checked. Picking a rule now just means one ~3 h filter run, then an ~18 h re-tokenize. **Tokens each rule would remove** (estimated from a 24k-doc audit sample): | Rule | Eval set | Docs removed | Tokens removed | |---|---|---:|---:| | v3 (hero run's rule) | hero's + 118 tasks the hero failed to load | ~11M | ~87B (0.5%) | | v3 (hero run's rule) | hero's | ~5M | ~40B (0.23%) | | v4 (Marin `main` today) | hero's + 118 tasks | ~0.46M | ~8B (0.05%) | The two v3 numbers will drop somewhat: I'm re-running the boilerplate count with the hero's sample size (1M docs per crawl; my first pass used ~80k). **Problems with the hero run's decon:** 1. **gsm8k was probably never checked.** 118 of the lm-eval tasks, including gsm8k, truthfulqa, winogrande, boolq and triviaqa, failed to load in the hero's eval set because their old dataset names break with the `datasets` version the hero branch uses. The pipeline skips tasks that fail to load instead of stopping. This is based on the eval set's manifest in us-central2. **Not yet checked against the CoreWeave copy that production actually used.** 2. **The short-line check mostly removes harmless pages.** On our data, ~95% of v3 removals come from a single short line like "2 years ago" or "Mechanism of Action", and none of the 40 I read by hand were contamination. Our extracted text has lots of standalone short lines (96% of docs have one, against 25–77% in Nemotron-CC), so this hits us harder than it hit the hero data. v4 fixes the second problem. On the audit sample it still caught every real overlap we found (SQuAD passages, wikiHow/HellaSwag, MATH problems, paper abstracts) and only let through stray short phrases and two generic LSAT question stems. **Decisions:** 1. **Eval set:** add the 118 tasks the hero missed? 2. **Rule:** v3 (~87B tokens, mostly harmless pages) or v4 (~8B tokens, same real catches)? 3. **ACTION ITEM:** Check with Will about the potential GSM8K gap in decontamination
> [!TIP] > Every doc has been checked against the evals. The hero run's rule (v3) would remove ~87B tokens, mostly harmless pages; Marin's current rule (v4) removes ~8B with the same real catches. The hero run also perhaps checked 117 fewer tasks. ---
Release Plan **Need to run the embedding and scaling ladder**: Reached out to Will to discuss this. I have all my data in `us-central2` ready to run a scaling ladder! Just want to figure out pointers on what to run and if I need to do control against Nemotron or if that has already been run somewhere. **Otherwise after decontamination the data is ready to go!**
> [!TIP] > After decontamination we are ready to release! ---

topics.title: Agent MoE Experiment: Over-Encoding scaling ladder
topics.body:
<!-- experiment-tldr:start -->
## Summary

This issue evaluates Over-Encoding (OE) for the Grug MoE July Baseline: hierarchical 2-gram/3-gram input embedding tables with row-wise tensor-parallel lookup. The first Gate 1 run proved the implementation was feasible on v5p-8 but did not improve d512 or d768; it finished effectively tied/slightly worse than same-runtime controls, and the d768 OE run was about 13% slower. A clean checkout then reproduced the canonical July Baseline exactly at d512 and d768, showing that the same-runtime `oe=0` controls were not equivalent to the historical baseline despite matching serialized hyperparameters. Follow-up canonical-July OE work is therefore using the exact reproduced baseline, lower OE-table learning rates, full-rank SparseCore gradients, and `(RMSNorm(token) + RMSNorm(OE)) / sqrt(2)`. As of July 19, 2026, that Gate 2 variant is still in progress: d768 is ahead of canonical July through step 15,000, and d1024 is healthy with an early step-1,000 lead, but terminal matched metrics and final checkpoint verification are still pending. Do not promote or extend the original Gate 1 formulation; judge the approach from the canonical-July Gate 2 terminal results.

### Helpful links
- Gate 1 terminal negative result: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7368#issuecomment-5011757700
- Canonical July Baseline exact reproduction: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7368#issuecomment-5013108535
- Latest Gate 2 status in this scrub window: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7368#issuecomment-5016726810
- W&B runs: https://wandb.ai/marin-community/dial_moe/runs/MOE-OE-001-d512, https://wandb.ai/marin-community/dial_moe/runs/MOE-OE-002-d768
<!-- experiment-tldr:end -->

## Description

OE preserves the base tokenizer, sequence length, and output vocabulary while adding hashed hierarchical multi-token input embeddings. The paper reports consistent loss improvements for MoE models but warns that naive FSDP communication causes substantial slowdown and OOM at large vocabulary sizes.

The Marin variant uses four slices for each of the 2-gram and 3-gram tables. Each table is row-sharded across all data-parallel ranks. Token IDs are routed to the owning rank, looked up locally, and the resulting vectors are routed back, matching the paper's two forward all-to-all exchanges and one backward all-to-all exchange. Packed-document boundaries must zero preceding-token contributions.

The initial HBM-safe ladder targeted roughly 6.4M OE rows at width 1280 on v5p-8, corresponding to `C ~= 139.75`, subject to a compile/HBM smoke before Gate 1. Gate 1 ran d512 and d768 against the July Baseline; later Gate 2 work keeps the canonical-July comparison baseline and adjusts OE-specific optimization/formulation details before considering larger promotion.

Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.16975

## Hypothesis or Goal

OE should improve effective wall-clock convergence after accounting for row-wise lookup communication, and the `width^1.5` vocabulary schedule should fit v5p-8 HBM with adequate training headroom. The current unresolved question is whether the canonical-July Gate 2 formulation's promising intermediate d768/d1024 signals persist to terminal matched evaluation.

## Status

Gate 1 is complete and negative/neutral: d512 and d768 finished successfully but did not beat controls, and d768 was slower. Canonical July Baseline reproduction is complete and exact at both widths. Gate 2 is active as of July 19, 2026: d768 is ahead of canonical July through step 15,000, while the sole required d1024 run is healthy and still early. d1280 was intentionally retired from Gate 2 scope.

## Links

* Experiment branch: [codex/oe-sparsecore-throughput-7368](https://github.com/WhenWen/marin/tree/codex/oe-sparsecore-throughput-7368)
* Logbook: `.agents/logbooks/over-encoding-gate1.md`
* W&B Report: pending
* Important updates: July Baseline #6882; parent research issue #4281; SiTU negative gate #7255

## Decision Log

* 2026-07-17: pivot from SiTU to OE after both SiTU Gate 1 cells failed effective-speed thresholds.
* 2026-07-17: require row-wise tensor-parallel OE lookup with explicit all-to-all routing; reject the existing FSDP-style embedding layout.
* 2026-07-17: use hierarchical 1+2+3-gram encoding with four low-rank slices per added gram order.
* 2026-07-17: scale `m` approximately as `C * width^1.5`; calibrate `C` with a v5p-8 compile/HBM smoke before full training.
* 2026-07-18: Gate 1 completed without an OE benefit at d512 or d768; revisit formulation/optimization before extending the original ladder.
* 2026-07-18: clean-checkout canonical July Baseline reproduced exactly at d512 and d768, so later comparisons use canonical July rather than the newer same-runtime `oe=0` controls.
* 2026-07-19: Gate 2 keeps d768 and d1024, uses lower OE-table LR plus norm-summed/full-rank SparseCore formulation, and intentionally drops d1280 from required scope.

## Conclusion

Original Gate 1 OE should not be promoted. The active question is whether the canonical-July Gate 2 formulation converts its intermediate d768/d1024 gains into terminal matched improvements; wait for those final metrics and checkpoint verification before deciding on promotion or further scaling.

topics.title: Acquire pinned Harbor Hub releases through the curation cache
topics.body:
Acquire pinned Harbor Hub releases through the existing cached source-download stage. Preserve each task's original archive bytes, verify its extracted contents with Harbor's native content hash, and record the resolved task references in a release manifest.

The Hub client is bundled with the Harbor evaluation framework. This implementation reuses Marin's pinned, isolated Harbor environment and command builder. Acquisition itself does not run agents or graders.

Like HF acquisition, download the complete release before curation sampling and retain native files for dataset-specific parsing. HarborHubSource uses the existing read(StoragePath, ConversionContext) callback, download cache, and local-input overrides. Retries reuse completed archives. Cache identity includes the release, acquisition code, and pinned Harbor commit. Harbor resolves release membership; per-task content verification is independent of that resolution. Dataset-level scoring files remain unsupported.

Seven focused cases pass locally. Pipeline tests run in ordinary CI; the three SDK-dependent acquisition cases run manually in the pinned Harbor environment and skip in ordinary CI. A live smoke test downloaded the pinned Skill2Env task task_api-design-reviewer_jdkbai64, verified its native content hash, and read the resulting archive through the existing pipeline custom-reader interface, producing one row with the task prompt. This validates acquisition and reading for one task; full-release acquisition, remote-storage acquisition, runnable conversion, and grading were not exercised by this smoke test.

Part of #9630.

topics.title: [eval] Mirror model weights in a CPU job before reserving GPUs
topics.body:
When an evaluation serves a model from Hugging Face, the model weights are downloaded by the GPU serving job itself, as the first thing it does before starting vLLM. The evaluation orchestrator waits at most 2400 seconds (`ENDPOINT_READY_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` in `lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/serving_config.py`) for the endpoint to come up, and that budget has to cover both the download and vLLM startup. For large checkpoints the download alone takes longer than the budget, so the orchestrator times out and terminates the serving job. Two problems follow: the GPUs sit idle for the whole download, and the timeout kills the download partway through.

Observed with GLM-5.2 (`cyankiwi/GLM-5.2-AWQ-INT4`, 474 GB in 83 weight shards). Job `/karan/eval-20260916-190154-glm-5.2-awq-int4-pp2-1m-3ac6` started mirroring at 19:04 UTC on 2026-09-16 at roughly 106 MB/s and timed out at 19:42 UTC with about 295 GB uploaded. Sixteen H100s were reserved for the full 38 minutes and did no inference. A retry on 2026-09-17 hit the same deadline, so the weights were finally mirrored by a hand-submitted CPU-only job, which took about 70 minutes. Incident record: https://marina.oa.dev/echo/wiki/468.

How the jobs fit together today. The eval CLI submits one CPU orchestrator job (`run_evaluation_batch` in `lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/runner.py`). The orchestrator submits a GPU child job for inference (`_start_direct_inference` in `lib/marin/src/marin/inference/iris.py`). Inside that GPU job, `resolve_model_path` mirrors the Hugging Face repo into the region bucket under a lock and writes a completion marker, and only then does vLLM start. Iris has no job dependency primitive, so ordering between jobs is done by the orchestrator waiting on children.

Proposal: prepare the weights in a separate CPU job before the GPU job is submitted.

- Before submitting the inference job, the orchestrator checks whether the pinned checkpoint already has a completion marker in the region cache.
- On a miss, it submits a small CPU child job (for example `prepare-<run_id>`) that calls the existing mirror function, and waits for it with its own timeout sized for the download rather than for vLLM startup. The job needs enough disk for one shard at a time (about 30 GB for GLM-5.2) and the same region constraint as the GPU job, so the mirror stays in-region.
- The GPU job is submitted only after the prepare job succeeds. Its own `resolve_model_path` call then finds the marker and returns immediately, so nothing in the serving path changes.
- The 2400-second readiness deadline then covers only vLLM startup, which is what it was sized for.

Expected: launching an evaluation against a large uncached checkpoint reserves GPUs only once the weights are in the region cache, and a slow download fails the cheap prepare job instead of the GPU job.

Related: #9230 covers reusing shards that were already uploaded before a mirror was interrupted. That makes an interrupted prepare job resumable, and is independent of this change. #8215 is the pipeline-parallel serving work that first hit this on GLM-5.2. Setting `HF_TOKEN` on the prepare job may raise the download rate, since the current mirror runs unauthenticated and Hugging Face rate-limits anonymous requests.

Done when: an evaluation launch against an uncached large checkpoint runs a CPU prepare job first, the GPU inference job starts with a cache hit, and a test with a fake Iris client covers the miss, hit, and prepare-failure paths.

topics.title: [inference] Add matched native and vLLM checkpoint fixtures
topics.body:
Export small Snowball and Hero BF16 checkpoints and benchmark the same weights and token workload in Levanter and the promoted Marin vLLM fork. Verify every exported tensor through native loading. Retain checkpoint identity, configuration, runtime topology, effective execution modes, and generated-token hashes. A separate non-unit normalization fixture changes only norm weights and records its seed and affected tensors.

Use packed expert banks, isolate Triton caches, and bound Ninja/nvcc concurrency. Expose expert parallelism, bounded KV memory, and eager or compiled execution. An optional hashed FlashInfer cache wheel loads and hashes precompiled MoE libraries with JIT disabled, preserving backend selection and autotuning. Setup and warmup remain outside measured samples.

The compare command verifies checkpoint, architecture, dtype, exact workload, and accelerator allocation, including native EP versus vLLM DP/EP or TPU SPMD data parallelism. Validate Grug aliases and derived defaults while retaining raw configuration differences. An untimed validation batch identifies the first divergent token; mismatched outputs suppress throughput ratios.

Bounded Snowball diagnostics compare shared-prefix logits, router precision, actual layer activations, and independent FP64 head reprojections. Native tracing records its effect on logits; named worker RPC captures every vLLM DP rank. Ordinary-engine generation independently varies embedding-gate SiLU and sigmoid precision without activation tracing. On H100, sigmoid-only FP32 matches all 32 vLLM tokens for both all-one and non-unit norm fixtures; promoting both functions still fails the non-unit fixture. Shared training and serving defaults are unchanged. An exhaustive standalone diagnostic evaluates all 65,280 finite BF16 sigmoid inputs against an independent FP64 reference, separating normal, subnormal, and saturated outputs. Both CPU runtimes execute successfully; fourteen focused tests and the delta affected-test run pass. Accelerator unary validation remains pending.

H100 EP2 tiny eager Hero produces identical 32 tokens using marin-community/vllm#83. On v5p, the combined short-convolution/cache stack passes twelve cases, then both runtimes produce identical 32 tokens for the same tiny Hero checkpoint with data parallelism four and tensor/expert parallelism one. Native measures 790.72 output tokens/second and eager vLLM 358.54 (2.205× for this workload only). The two-layer fixture exercises local and global attention because the final layer is always global. The measured pins, workload, and production Hero memory accounting are in the inference design docs.

GB200 Snowball starts with precompiled FlashInfer kernels and JIT disabled: 54.64 seconds of model/cache setup and a 12.01 GiB sampled cgroup peak under the unchanged 48 GiB limit. Unmodified Snowball outputs still disagree across runtimes, so its ratios remain withheld. Production checkpoints and Hero CUDA graphs remain unvalidated. Stacked on #9661. Part of #7219.

topics.title: levanter: bound native tokenizer batches, add tokenizer_content_hash
topics.body:
`HfMarinTokenizer.encode_batch` now flushes a native `encode_batch` call after 64 parts or 400,000 characters, instead of one native call for every part of every text. It uses the same canonical parts, so token IDs do not change. Padding and BPE dropout still use one native call because padding applies across the batch and dropout draws depend on batch order. In a local 32 MiB probe, all 19,532,169 token IDs were retained while peak RSS fell from 4.60 GiB to 2.85 GiB. `encode` also uses `encode_batch` when a text has more than one part.

`tokenizer_content_hash(name_or_path)` returns the SHA-256 hash of the tokenizer files that `load_tokenizer` reads, allowing consumers to record which files produced their tokens. It includes only the top-level files that match `_TOKENIZER_ALLOW_PATTERNS`, through a new `include` filter on rigging's `directory_content_hash`, so model weights in a checkpoint directory do not change it. This work was split from #10108, which uses `tokenizer_content_hash` and tokenizes raw-corpus documents up to 64 MiB.

topics.title: [finelog] Provision and rotate forwarding signing keys
topics.body:
[#7091](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/7091) moved cross-cluster forwarding from Iris controllers into the per-cluster Finelog servers. Each sender now signs `aud="finelog"` tokens with a distinct Ed25519 private key in Secret Manager, and the hub trusts the matching public key in `lib/finelog/config/marin.yaml`. [#7690](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/7690) moves sender deployment to Pulumi but deliberately references and syncs an existing pinned secret version. Initial provisioning and rotation remain manual in [`lib/finelog/OPS.md`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/finelog/OPS.md).

Add a Finelog key-lifecycle command that provisions or reuses a sender signing key, emits the pinned secret reference and public trust configuration, validates that the two halves match, and supports overlap-safe rotation. The generic key mechanics should not be duplicated under Iris and Finelog. Extract reusable generation, Secret Manager storage, inspection, and explicit rotation behavior from [`iris cluster init-keys`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cli/cluster.py) into a neutral Rigging or Marin admin surface. Keep Finelog-specific sender and hub configuration sequencing in the Finelog command.

Do not generate private key payloads or Secret Manager versions through Pulumi. That would copy the private PEM into Pulumi state and make identity rotation an incidental deployment diff. Rotation must publish the new public key on the hub before switching the sender to the new pinned version, then verify forwarding before retiring the old public key. Pulumi remains responsible for stable IAM grants and may own secret-container metadata; it must not own private key payloads or `SecretVersion` resources.

Done when:
- Neutral key-lifecycle functions generate, inspect, reuse, and explicitly rotate Ed25519 keys in Secret Manager without service-specific naming.
- The Iris and Finelog entry points use the shared functions rather than carrying separate Secret Manager and key-generation implementations.
- A Finelog operator command provisions or reuses a sender key and returns its pinned `gcp-secret://` reference, public PEM, and `kid`; replacing an existing identity requires an explicit rotation option.
- Finelog provisioning validates that the configured private key matches the public key trusted for that sender.
- Rotation keeps old and new public keys trusted during the sender transition and provides a verifiable point before retiring the old key.
- Private key material never enters Git, logs, rendered deployment manifests, Pulumi configuration, or Pulumi state.
- Tests cover initial provisioning, idempotent reuse, explicit rotation, mismatched trust configuration, and the public-key overlap.

topics.title: [rolloutengine] Run managed agents on chat endpoints
topics.body:
👨 "Managed Agent" is an instance of Rollout Engine with an agentic harness and LLM endpoint.

```py
engine = RolloutEngine({}, {"agent": ShellHarness(tools=...)})
spec = TaskRolloutSpec(task=task, harness="agent", trace=TraceMode.MESSAGES, ...)

async with openai.AsyncOpenAI(base_url=base_url, api_key=api_key) as client:
    result = await engine.run_task(spec, ChatModel(client, "glm-5.3", ...))
```

Managed Agent can be used for an arbitrary task, including data analysis, cleaning or synthesis.

<hr>

🤖  Managed agents can now run on chat endpoints through one `run_task` call. A registered harness is the agent program, the model is its endpoint, and a task with `NoGrader` holds open-ended work. This is part of #10165.

`ChatModel` in `rolloutengine.chat` uses `TraceMode.MESSAGES` with an OpenAI-compatible chat endpoint, such as vLLM, SGLang, or GLM. Prompt options replace its `max_tokens` and `extra_body` keys. The `model`, `messages`, `stream`, and `n` fields are reserved, including within `extra_body`. A response without `usage` fails one model attempt instead of raising a `RolloutContractError` that stops the caller. The next request sends back only `role`, `content`, `tool_calls`, and `reasoning_content`; a refusal goes into `ModelTurn.metadata`.

`HarnessContext` now holds `limits` so an `AgentHarness` program can read them without a `ModelSession`. Three failure paths are corrected: `check` rejects `output_paths` without a task machine, which previously produced `outputs={}` without an error; an agent that ends with a `CancelledError` before the engine stops it, for example from a cancelled child task or a cancel of its own task, fails its attempt instead of making `run_task` raise `CancelledError` (in #10203, a cancel of the agent task by another task propagated); and `RolloutInterrupted` and `GradedRolloutInterrupted` survive pickling with their rollout, operation, and grade. `RolloutFailure.diagnostics` also retains the error message and notes that pickle drops. Previously, Zephyr replaced the exception with a `ZephyrWorkerError` retaining only its type and message.

`docs/references/task-rollouts.md` now has a short “Run an agent” section.

---
