topics.title: Experiment: MXFP8 block-scaled GEMMs for grug MoE on Blackwell
topics.body:
<!-- experiment-tldr:start -->
## Summary

MXFP8 on Blackwell is viable for Grug MoE expert GEMMs, but only when the block-scaled quantization producer is fused into the expert-MLP path. Dense matmuls should stay on the delayed per-tensor FP8 path: native dense MXFP8 lowered and produced reasonable numerics, but standalone block quantization erased the GEMM win. The best supported direction is the hybrid recipe now encoded behind `GrugFp8Config(recipe="mxfp8")`: delayed per-tensor FP8 for dense attention/shared MLP matmuls, fused MXFP8 grouped kernels for ragged experts, and `recompute_all` as the production remat mode. The latest EP1 apples-to-apples D6144 run is an important caveat: with FP8 wire communication disabled, MXFP8 was 0.749x BF16 end-to-end on that topology, so the production recommendation still depends on profiling, communication settings, and the #7271 quality/perf gate rather than the early grouped-GEMM microbench alone.

### Helpful links
- Latest EP1 apples-to-apples result: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7282#issuecomment-5037422197
- Uniform MXFP8 feasibility decision: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7282#issuecomment-5028942402
- Research branch: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/research/mcwitt/7282-mxfp8-blackwell
<!-- experiment-tldr:end -->

## Description

Implement and tune a Blackwell-native FP8 path for grug MoE training on B200/GB200, using the hardware's MXFP8 (block-scaled, 32-element blocks with E8M0 scales) tensor-core support instead of the Hopper delayed per-tensor-scaling recipe:

- **Dense GEMMs** (attention q/k/v/o, shared-expert MLP): `jax.nn.scaled_dot_general` / cuDNN-cuBLASLt block-scaled matmuls, replacing `Fp8DotGeneralOp`'s per-tensor path where profitable.
- **Grouped expert GEMMs** (`w13`/`w2` ragged dots): an SM100 block-scaled grouped kernel -- CUTLASS via `cutlass_call` or a Mosaic-GPU tcgen05 port of the Hopper kernels.
- MXFP8 scaling is computed per-block on the fly (stateless -- no amax history), which should simplify the train-step state handling that per-tensor delayed scaling required.

Base: PR #7079 (FP8 end-to-end wiring: #6880 `Fp8RaggedDotOp` expert GMMs, #6660 `Fp8DotGeneralOp` dense GEMMs, FP8 wire collectives, `GrugModelConfig.fp8` + train-step state). The FP8 wire (per-token scaling) is hardware-agnostic and expected to carry over unchanged.

Part of the #6998 "Sanity Check FP8 training on Blackwell" work stream. This issue tracks the implementation and kernel/perf tuning; the compute-optimal training quality check (MXFP8 vs BF16, wall-time matched) is #7271 and consumes this work.

## Hypothesis or Goal

MXFP8 on B200 matches or beats the Hopper per-tensor FP8 speedups at the canonical grug shape (d2560/F1280/E256/K4): grouped GEMMs >=1.3x vs bf16 at the layer level, dense GEMMs >=1.2x isolated, with a simpler stateless recipe and numerics adequate for #7271's regression gate.

## Status

E2E goal met for the early d2560/L26/B64 GB200x4 configuration (MXFP8-005, 2026-07-17): mxfp8 beat bf16 and per-tensor fp8 under `recompute_all`, with loss parity near 4e-4/step. Later production-shape checks added caveats: uniform dense MXFP8 is not ready in the current distributed stack, and the latest EP1 D6144 same-config pair showed MXFP8 slower than BF16 when FP8 wire communication was disabled. Treat the hybrid path as promising but still gated on topology-specific profiling and #7271.

## Links

* Logbook: `.agents/logbooks/mxfp8-blackwell.md` (on the research branch)
* Branch: [`research/mcwitt/7282-mxfp8-blackwell`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/research/mcwitt/7282-mxfp8-blackwell)
* W&B Report:
* Important updates:
  * Latest EP1 apples-to-apples result: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7282#issuecomment-5037422197
  * Uniform MXFP8 feasibility decision: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7282#issuecomment-5028942402

## Decision Log

- 2026-07-16 (mcwitt): stay on MXFP8 for its numerics upside; push perf to per-tensor class rather than falling back to a per-tensor grouped kernel. (Logbook: "Direction decision", MXFP8-002c.)
- 2026-07-16: dense GEMMs stay on per-tensor `Fp8DotGeneralOp`; dense mxfp8 shelved unless #7271 shows per-tensor numerics insufficient. (MXFP8-001b.)
- 2026-07-17 (mcwitt): benchmark only production-viable configs (>120B total / >15B active). The #7012 slim-vjp/`all_but_moe` port is dropped -- those modes OOM 3-12x at the d5120/L48/b1024 64-GPU reference config (#7012 branch logbook, B200MFU-032), leaving `recompute_all` (already our benchmark mode) as the production mode. New top item: MXFP8-006 production-shape ladder. (Logbook: "production-viability filter" entry.)
- 2026-07-21 (mcwitt): same-source, same-config EP1 D6144 pair found MXFP8 at 0.749x BF16 with FP8 wire disabled; do not use the earlier EP-confounded comparisons as isolated MXFP8 effects.

## Conclusion

comments.body:
🤖 Update: background research brief (MXFP8-000b) — foraging done, vehicles chosen

- Change: four-track prior-work pass (pinned-JAX source probe, NVIDIA MXFP8 recipe, SM100 grouped-GEMM survey, internal corpus). Full brief with evidence map and source ledger in the logbook (`.agents/logbooks/mxfp8-blackwell.md` @ 61aa41d0f).
- Key findings:
  - Our jax 0.10.1 pin already has the complete dense MXFP8 path: `jax.nn.scaled_dot_general` with a real custom_vjp (dgrad and wgrad both run as block-scaled matmuls), custom_partitioning, and ceil-rounded E8M0 scales; gpu-extra lockfile ships cuDNN 9.19 (floor 9.7.1). Footguns: `configs=None` silently falls back to bf16; residuals are stored full-precision.
  - Correct recipe (NVIDIA arXiv 2506.08027, matches TE and the jax defaults): E4M3 for everything including gradients (E5M2 grads degrade MXFP8 — opposite of our Hopper per-tensor finding), round-UP E8M0 scales, dual rowwise+columnwise quantized copies from the high-precision original.
  - Grouped vehicle: pinned nvidia-cutlass-dsl 4.5.2 ships an MXFP8 MoE scaled-grouped-GEMM kernel (`CuTeDSL .../moe/torch_scaled_grouped_mm.py`) — offs-ragged 2Dx3D fwd + 2Dx2D wgrad, shape-for-shape our ragged_dot decomposition; NVIDIA measured 1.29-1.41x vs the cuBLAS grouped path on B200. Plan: vendor it behind the existing `cutlass_call` FFI adapter from the fp8-ragged-cute branch (sm_100a). Mosaic tcgen05 (fully plumbed in our jaxlib, incl. block-scaled MMA) is the bake-off second entrant.
  - Expectation bound from #7012's step anatomy: MoE GEMMs are ~24% of the single-node step, so the e2e MXFP8 ceiling is ~1.1x there; layer-level targets (grouped >=1.3x, dense >=1.2x) remain the gate. Grouped bf16 baseline on B200 is QuACK/Triton (XLA ragged_dot has no SM100 path).
  - FP8 wire stays bf16 during the MXFP8 phase (NVIDIA EP quantizes after dispatch); re-test later.
- Confidence: recipe/API claims high (installed source + paper + TE agree); grouped-kernel perf is NVIDIA's own table, unreplicated here.
- Links:
  - Commit: 61aa41d0f (logbook brief), branch `research/mcwitt/7282-mxfp8-blackwell`
  - Related: #7012 (baselines), #5816 (older B200 FP8 issue), PR #7079 (base)
- Next: MXFP8-001 — B200 env probe + dense microbench (`scaled_dot_general` vs bf16 vs per-tensor `Fp8DotGeneralOp` at grug dense shapes, plus numerics check vs bf16 reference).

🤖 Update: MXFP8-001 (dense microbench, 1x GB200) — surprising first result

- Change: ran the dense GEMM microbench (bf16 vs per-tensor fp8 vs native mxfp8 `jax.nn.scaled_dot_general`) at row-13 dense shapes (T=65536; qkvo 2560x2560, shared-expert 2560<->1280) on cw-us-east-08a GB200, jax 0.10.1 / cuDNN 9.19.
- Result delta:
  - Native mxfp8 WORKS (lowers to `__cudnn$blockScaledDot`; rel-err ~3.7e-2, slightly better than per-tensor fp8) but is SLOWER than bf16: 0.82-1.00x fwd, 0.64-0.81x fwd+bwd. The compiled HLO shows XLA materializing the quantized block tensors with standalone kernels around the cuDNN GEMM — quantize overhead is the prime suspect, especially on bwd (cotangent re-quantized for both grad legs).
  - Per-tensor `Fp8DotGeneralOp` — the dense path PR #7079 already wired — is excellent on sm100: 1.35x fwd / 1.61x fwd+bwd at qkvo (1990 / 2363 TF/s vs bf16's 1471). Better than its H100 showing. For dense GEMMs the merged per-tensor path is the incumbent on Blackwell.
- Confidence: exploratory (single GPU, single run; GB200 not B200, same sm100 compute die).
- Links:
  - Commit: 6d3cf1a02 (harness `experiments/grug/moe/standalone/bench_mxfp8_dense.py`), logbook entry MXFP8-001 @ 91b0a1973
  - Job: /mwittmann/mxfp8-001-dense-r3 on cw-us-east-08a
- Next: MXFP8-001b — isolate GEMM-only throughput via `jax.nn.scaled_matmul` with precomputed quantized operands+scales. If the bare blockScaledDot beats bf16, mxfp8 dense is rescuable with a fused quantizer; if not, dense stays per-tensor fp8 and MXFP8 effort concentrates on the grouped expert GEMMs (CUTLASS DSL kernel).

🤖 Update: MXFP8-001b — GEMM-only isolate; dense decision made

- Change: added a `scaled_matmul` arm with operands quantized outside the timed region (job /mwittmann/mxfp8-001b-dense-r2, 1x GB200), isolating the `__cudnn$blockScaledDot` GEMM from XLA's quantize kernels.
- Result delta:
  - GEMM-only mxfp8 is healthy: 1.33x vs bf16 at qkvo 2560x2560, 1.11-1.14x at the narrow shared-expert shapes.
  - The culprit is quantization: XLA's emitted block-quantize kernel costs 0.26-0.36 ms per operand (~a full GEMM's worth, roughly 1 TB/s effective on ~8 TB/s HBM). On the backward pass the cotangent is quantized twice, hence MXFP8-001's 0.65-0.79x e2e.
  - Even with a free quantizer, mxfp8 GEMM-only merely ties per-tensor fp8 (1.33 vs 1.35 at qkvo; loses at narrow shapes). Per-tensor delayed scaling is structurally cheaper: no amax reduction in the hot path, and its scalar multiply+cast fuses into neighboring ops.
- Decision: dense GEMMs on Blackwell stay on the per-tensor `Fp8DotGeneralOp` path that PR #7079 already wired (1.35x fwd / 1.5-1.6x fwd+bwd measured here). Native-mxfp8 dense is shelved unless #7271's quality gate later shows per-tensor numerics are insufficient (mxfp8's error is only marginally better: 3.7e-2 vs 4.3e-2 rel-Frobenius). MXFP8 effort now concentrates on the grouped expert GEMMs, where sm100 has no working fp8 path at all.
- Confidence: exploratory (single GPU, single run each), but the quantize-overhead decomposition is internally consistent across all three shapes.
- Links: logbook entries MXFP8-001b + hypothesis queue @ branch `research/mcwitt/7282-mxfp8-blackwell`.
- Next: MXFP8-002 — vendor the CuTeDSL MoE scaled-grouped-GEMM kernel (pinned cutlass-dsl 4.5.2) behind the fp8-ragged-cute `cutlass_call` adapter; correctness vs emulated reference, then bench vs QuACK bf16 at row-13 expert shapes.

🤖 Update: MXFP8-002 — MXFP8 grouped GEMM working from JAX on GB200 at 2.2 PF/s

- Change: vendored the cutlass v4.5.2 CuTeDSL MoE scaled-grouped-GEMM kernel (tcgen05 block-scaled MMA, e4m3 + e8m0 block-32 scales) and drove it from JAX via `cutlass.jax.cutlass_call` on stock jaxlib + the stock aarch64 cutlass-dsl wheel — no fork, no torch. Code: `experiments/grug/moe/standalone/mxfp8_grouped/` + `bench_mxfp8_grouped.py` @ 42f7d9fa2.
- Result delta (1x GB200, M=262144 tokens, E=64, row-13 expert shapes, median of 50):
  - w13 (K2560,N1280): 0.781 ms = 2,200 TF/s. w2 (K1280,N2560): 0.838 ms = 2,050 TF/s.
  - 1.32-1.42x vs an equal-FLOPs dense bf16 cuBLAS yardstick, and ~1.4-1.5x vs the tuned bf16 grouped baselines from the B200 MFU thread (QuACK 1,449-1,560 TF/s at these shapes). ~49% of dense-FP8 peak on a ragged problem.
  - Correctness: 3e-06..1e-05 rel-Frobenius vs a dequantized-same-operands reference; skewed (Dirichlet-0.5) routing incl. zero-token experts costs ~1%.
  - Forward gate (>=1.3x) met. Not yet covered: dgrad/wgrad products and the quantize+swizzle producer — the bench builds scale factors with a slow gather; MXFP8-001b showed naive quantization can eat the entire win, so a fused quantize+swizzle kernel is the critical path to a layer-level fwd+bwd claim.
- Confidence: exploratory (single GPU; kernel numbers replicated across uniform/skewed and a tile ablation — (128,256,128) beats (128,128,128) by ~8%).
- Links: jobs /mwittmann/mxfp8-002-g1..g9 on cw-us-east-08a; logbook entry MXFP8-002 (incl. 5 new integration gotchas, notably: the cu13 cutlass-dsl wheel delivers cutlass_call tensors in GENERIC address space, unlike the base wheel the Hopper notes were written against — fixed at the launcher boundary via integer-value make_ptr).
- Next: dgrad/wgrad via the same kernel's 2Dx2D scenario, fused quantize+swizzle kernel, then layer-level fwd+bwd bench (MXFP8-004).

🤖 Update: MXFP8-002b — all three GEMM products green; the quantizer now decides everything

- Change: extended the grouped-kernel port with dgrad (2Dx3D, transposed-weight view via TensorSpec — no materialized transpose) and wgrad (the kernel's 2Dx2D scenario, natural layouts, TMA-aligned for any group sizes), plus a fused dual-orientation quantize+swizzle producer in pure XLA. Commits 92f7af921, b6fa1f9de; job /mwittmann/mxfp8-002b-g1 (single job, first-attempt green).
- Result delta (M=262144, E=64, GB200, errors all 3e-6..1e-5 vs dequantized ref):
  - fwd 2130/2027 TF/s (w13/w2), dgrad 2041/2112, wgrad 2209/2214 — every product ~1.4-1.5x over the bf16 dense yardstick. wgrad is the fastest product.
  - Honest layer-quad (fwd+dgrad+wgrad for w13+w2 vs 3x bf16 dense = 6.95 ms): GEMMs alone 4.86 ms = 1.43x; adding the XLA quantize producers (7.06 ms for 4 activation + 2 weight tensors) drops it to 0.58x — a net loss. XLA quantization runs at ~1.6-2.2 TB/s and cannot get near the 2.09 ms break-even.
  - Producer budget math: an HBM-ideal standalone dual-write quantizer (~1.4 ms) yields only ~1.11x; a fusion-grade producer (quantize folded into ops that already touch the tensors, ~0.7 ms marginal) yields ~1.25x. Same conclusion as the Hopper thread, where the dual-write cast-transpose kernels were what made FP8 pay.
- Confidence: exploratory but internally consistent (independent quantize measurements in MXFP8-001b and 002b agree).
- Links: logbook entry MXFP8-002b (incl. gotchas: 2Dx2D SF atom-block permutation, zero-token-expert epilogue semantics), branch `research/mcwitt/7282-mxfp8-blackwell`.
- Next: MXFP8-002c — prototype the fused dual-write MXFP8 quantizer (CuTe/Mosaic, Hopper cast-transpose analog) targeting <=0.7 ms marginal for the activation tensors. This is the 0.58x-vs-1.25x decision point; op wiring (MXFP8-004) follows the verdict.

🤖 Update: MXFP8-002c — CuTe dual-write quantizer lands the layer at break-even; decision point

- Change: implemented and validated a CuTe DSL dual-orientation MXFP8 quantizer (one bf16 read -> rowwise+columnwise e4m3 copies + e8m0 scales; integer-only round-up exhaustively validated; no transpose stage needed since wgrad consumes natural-layout columns). Jobs /mwittmann/mxfp8-002c-g1..g11; commits 68bbe7d5a..189c3faf0.
- Result delta:
  - Bit-exact vs the corrected reference on all outputs including adversarial blocks. Along the way it exposed a real bug in the XLA reference: GPU `jnp.exp2` is inexact on 217/256 e8m0 exponent bytes — the reference had been quantizing with wrong scales at extreme exponents (fixed in adapter.py; never decode e8m0 via exp2).
  - Producer cost for the 4 activation tensors: 2.074 ms vs 5.19 ms XLA (2.5x), effective ~4.8 TB/s. Layer-quad: 0.58x -> **1.00x** (weights amortized; 0.80x if XLA weight producers run every microbatch).
  - The <=0.7 ms fusion-grade target (=> ~1.25x) is out of reach for any standalone kernel: this design is instruction-issue bound with a ~1.4 ms ceiling. Epilogue-fusion probe says SwiGLU+dual-quantize fusion into the grouped GEMM's epilogue is feasible but a targeted rewrite (~1-2 weeks; single elementwise hook exists, no multi-output mechanism, needs w13 column interleave + SIMT side-stores).
- Where this leaves the thread — three options, ranked by expected value:
  1. **Per-tensor-scaled fp8 grouped kernel on sm100** (new hypothesis MXFP8-H7): the recurring lesson (dense MXFP8-001b, grouped 002c) is that block scaling pays a producer tax per-tensor scaling doesn't — per-tensor quantize fuses into XLA for free, so the ~1.4x GEMM-level win should survive at layer level. tcgen05 also supports mixed e5m2xe4m3 natively (no wgmma same-dtype restriction), enabling the numerically-correct backward the Hopper path had to approximate. Moderate port (same vendoring pattern as 002, which went smoothly).
  2. Epilogue fusion for mxfp8 (~1.25x, 1-2 weeks of kernel work).
  3. Wire MXFP8-004 with the break-even producer now (removes producers as dominant cost; useful if mxfp8's numerics are the priority for #7271 regardless of speed).
- Ops notes: GB200 nodes are heterogeneous for libNVVM (`nvvm.cvt.packfloat` fails on most nodes, passes on some — inline PTX bypasses); CPU-only sm_100a compile does not exercise the pod's libNVVM stage.
- Confidence: exploratory; producer/GEMM numbers each replicated within-job across shapes and routing distributions.
- Links: logbook entries MXFP8-002c + hypothesis queue, branch `research/mcwitt/7282-mxfp8-blackwell`.
- Next: awaiting direction on the 3-way choice above; H7 is the recommended default.

🤖 Update: direction — pushing MXFP8 to per-tensor-class perf; kernel survey finds the fusion upstream (MIT)

- Change: per owner direction, staying on MXFP8 (numerics rationale) and pushing performance; ran a third-party-kernel survey (tokamax source deep-dive + TE/QuACK/CUTLASS/triton/DeepGEMM/fal.ai web track). Full brief in the logbook (MXFP8-000c).
- Key findings:
  - **cudnn-frontend >=1.21 ships MIT-licensed CuTeDSL fused MoE grouped kernels** — `grouped_gemm_swiglu_quant` (grouped GEMM -> SwiGLU -> dual-orientation MXFP8 quantize with swizzled SFs + per-expert amax), plus dSwiGLU+quant, plain quant-epilogue, and wgrad variants. Same file lineage as the kernel we vendored in MXFP8-002. This is exactly the epilogue fusion MXFP8-002c estimated at 1-2 weeks, already written and maintained by NVIDIA (their blog: 1.3x fwd / 2.1x bwd kernel-level on GB200).
  - Standalone-quantizer path formally closed: even a perfect 6.2 TB/s dual-orientation quantizer leaves producers at ~1.6 ms vs the 0.7 ms fusion-grade target. Every credible implementation gets there via epilogue fusion.
  - tokamax (user question): no MXFP8 on any arch, in any version — sm90 quantized ragged_dot is weight-only dequant-to-bf16 (no fp8 tensor cores on Hopper at all), sm100 kernels are W4A8 inference with float subchannel-128 scales, and there is no sm100 wgrad kernel. MXFP8-on-Hopper generally: no prior art anywhere, and the wgmma arithmetic caps it at ~bf16 throughput — recorded as a dead end.
  - Ceiling check: measured cuBLAS mxfp8 dense tops out at ~2.5-2.7 PF/s (not the 4.5 spec number); our 2.0-2.2 PF/s grouped is ~80% of the honest ceiling. The remaining headroom is in fused epilogues + scheduler, not the mainloop.
- Next (in flight):
  - MXFP8-004a: vendor the cudnn-frontend fused kernels behind our proven cutlass_call adapter (prerequisite: bump nvidia-cutlass-dsl past <4.6 and re-run the 002c bit-exactness suite). Gate: layer-quad >=1.2x vs bf16.
  - MXFP8-004b (time-boxed): bench TE 2.15+ te.jax `grouped_dense` MXFP8 at our shapes — the NVIDIA-tuned narrow-N reference datapoint.
- Links: logbook MXFP8-000c + hypothesis queue (new H8; H5 resolved; Hopper dead-end), branch `research/mcwitt/7282-mxfp8-blackwell`.

🤖 Update: MXFP8-004a/b — fused kernels land the layer at 1.39x vs bf16; gate met

- Change: two parallel results. (a) MXFP8-004a: vendored NVIDIA's MIT-licensed cudnn-frontend fused MoE grouped kernels (SwiGLU+dual-MXFP8-quant fwd, dSwiGLU+quant bwd, quantizing-epilogue GEMM, wgrad; upstream 3041f3e88) into `experiments/grug/moe/standalone/mxfp8_fused/`, driven from JAX via the same cutlass_call adapter pattern — no cutlass-dsl pin bump needed (a 6-site compat shim runs them on stock 4.5.2). (b) MXFP8-004b: TransformerEngine 2.16 grouped_dense MXFP8 benchmarked on the same pod as the NVIDIA-tuned reference.
- Result delta (1x GB200, M=262144, E=64, real gated shapes D2560/F1280):
  - Correctness: swiglu_quant and dswiglu_quant outputs (data + both scale-factor orientations) are BIT-EXACT vs our validated reference; the other legs are at 6e-6..3.6e-5 rel-Frobenius. The fused column-SF layout is byte-identical to what our wgrad kernel consumes — zero glue.
  - Fused layer pipeline (6 GEMM legs + the two remaining x/g2 producers): 8.777 ms vs 12.220 ms for the full bf16 layer (GEMMs + XLA SwiGLU/dSwiGLU) = **1.39x**; 1.13x against a strict 6-GEMM-only yardstick; 1.35x gemm-only. The >=1.2x gate is met on the honest full-layer accounting: the h and dc quantize producers are gone (fused into epilogues), which is what turned MXFP8-002c's 0.58x into a real win. Note the baseline is now the real gated w13 width (2F=2560); earlier half-width numbers aren't comparable.
  - TE reference: cuBLAS grouped MXFP8 GEMM-only 2085/1950 TF/s at our shapes — parity to ~4-12% behind our CuTeDSL kernels; TE's own e2e mxfp8 fwd+bwd is 1.28-1.32x its bf16 and visibly quantize-bound, independently confirming the fusion thesis. (TE V2 MXFP8 grouped also requires every group size %128 — real routing violates this; our kernels don't care.)
  - Remaining headroom, ranked: the dswiglu leg (1244 TF/s; C-read + dual-store epilogue) and folding the x/g2 dual-quant upstream into attention/dgrad epilogues (1.43 ms).
- Confidence: exploratory (single GPU; tiler ablations replicated across nodes; in-sequence timings reported — same-kernel-after-idle measures ~25% faster, a new benchmarking gotcha).

🤖 Update: production-shape OOM root-caused — MoE dispatch/combine buffers across the 48 *unrolled* layers; scan-over-blocks port in validation

- Change: diagnosed the 851 GiB step-0 OOM from the first production-shape ladder attempt with compile-only AOT probes on 2-node gangs (XLA memory analysis + buffer-assignment census; the probes never execute, so they measure the arena without holding 32 GPUs).
- Findings, in falsification order:
  - `eqx.error_if` callbacks: falsified (`EQX_ON_ERROR=nan` rerun — arena identical; those checks don't even trace in this config).
  - FA4 per-layer metadata on device 0 (the poison documented in the mcwitt/moe-standalone-ep bench): the fix ports cleanly and is kept, but the arena was unchanged — not the dominant term here.
  - Instruction-keyed census (cache-off dump): the 792 GiB temp arena at d5120/L48/B128 ring-EP8 is the **ring-MoE dispatch/combine buffers of all 48 layers held concurrently live** — full-global-batch combine scatters (`bf16[524288,5120]`, 2/layer) and top4-expanded dispatch buffers (`bf16[262144,5120]`, 5/layer), across the unrolled per-layer subgraphs. Attention and MuonH are not drivers.
  - Scaling: arena is ~linear in global batch (B64 → 340 GiB), so no batch retreat fits the 138 GiB pool; it persists under pure DP (EP1 → 581 GiB).
  - fp8 memory: **mxfp8's arena is 37% smaller than bf16's** (500.82 vs 792.47 GiB, same config) — fp8 is the memory-friendlier arm, not a regression risk.
- Fix in flight: ported the scan-over-stacked-blocks model path (`use_array_stacked_blocks`, from the moe-standalone-ep bench: Bool[num_layers] mask schedule + precomputed FA4 bounds selected by `jnp.where`, traced per-layer rope disable, 4D expert stacks routed through distributed Newton-Schulz). A `lax.scan` bounds the live set to one layer's buffers and should also collapse the 13–40 min lowering times (one traced body instead of 48).
- Confidence: high on the attribution (census names the ops); scan-mode memory number pending the current probe.

🤖 Update: CuTe DSL compile flakiness root-caused — dependency packaging conflict, not node heterogeneity

- Change: the long-standing "compiles on some nodes, fails on others" NVVM errors (the MXFP8-002c gotcha, and the reason the mxfp8 producer compile-probe subprocess existed — including its multi-node startup wedge from MXFP8-007c) are root-caused. `nvidia-cutlass-dsl` installs both `-libs-base` and (via the `cu13` extra) `-libs-cu13`; the two wheels ship 99 overlapping files with different CUDA-12/CUDA-13 builds of the DSL frontend and its MLIR compiler, and whichever wheel wins the install silently decides whether any CuTe kernel compiles — re-rolled on every environment sync, so it presented as random node heterogeneity. Fix: exclude `libs-base` via a uv dependency override. The producer probe is deleted; `mxfp8_producer="auto"` now selects the CuTe quantizer directly.
- Result delta: on the fixed lock, repeated multi-pod compile surveys went from ~coin-flip-per-pod to 100% green, and the GPU op ladder passes with the CuTe producer (dequant refs at the 1e-5 class; blackbox vs bf16 unchanged). The native fp8-convert intrinsic also compiles on a clean cu13 install — the 002c inline-PTX bypass is kept only for its validated numerics.
- Confidence: replicated (two failing-lock survey draws, one fixed-lock draw, plus the op ladder).
- Links: commits d064dc173 (lockfile fix), f4cac5066 (probe removal), 166696dfb (survey tool); logbook MXFP8-009.

- Available Marin implementation: the correct CuTe producer is 1.2125x delayed per-tensor time on the production-weighted dense mix. Projection fusion improves this to 1.1345-1.1426x, which projects to 98.56-98.66% of hybrid throughput and misses the 99% gate in both replications.

The minimum valid EP2 graph uses d5120, seq4096, 65,536 tokens/device, 16 experts/device, and `recompute_all`.

  | arm | outcome |
  |---|---|
  | hybrid EP2 | succeeded: 48,157 tok/s, 2.7221 s/step, finite loss through step 14 |
  | uniform EP2 | deterministic XLA GPU backend abort before execution: `AllReduceThunk::CheckImplementable(): reduction_kind.has_value()` |
  | uniform EP4 | same backend abort before execution |

- Confidence: high that no implementation currently available to Marin meets the uniform distributed gate. The in-repo path is measurably too slow; the faster TE path aborts at both EP2 and EP4 and is not a Marin dependency. This does not prove that a future fused producer or corrected TE partitioner cannot pass.

- Links: [research log at `f487d4a76`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/f487d4a76/.agents/logbooks/mxfp8-blackwell.md), [uniform integration](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/5a4e285bc), [mesh-context fix](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/5c782b91c). Iris jobs: `/mwittmann/mxfp8-{uniform,hybrid}-fullstep-two-r1`.

🤖 Correction and apples-to-apples EP1 result (2026-07-21)

The earlier 108.4K MXFP8 result should not be compared with the published EP1 BF16 result: those runs differed in expert parallelism and backend/config details. I have caveated the earlier comments.

I reran a same-source, same-config pair on 64 GB200 GPUs. Both arms used d6144/L48/E128/top4, EP1 (FSDP only), the same batch/data/optimizer, FA4 attention, ring/current scatter MoE dispatch, scan, Liger CE, rematerialization, and the branch's current fixes/optimizations. The only treatment change was `SCALE_FP8=mxfp8` with the XLA producer. MXFP8 wire communication remained disabled (`wire: null`).

Median rank-0 throughput over steps 2–29 (28 samples per arm):

| Compute path | Median tok/s | Relative to BF16 |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| BF16 | 187,502 | 1.000× |
| MXFP8 | 140,351 | 0.749× |

On this EP1 implementation, enabling MXFP8 reduced end-to-end throughput by 25.15% (BF16 was 1.336× faster). This result does **not** show that MXFP8 tensor-core arithmetic itself is 25% slower: it includes quantization/cast/lowering and kernel-path overheads. It also does not include reduced wire communication, so communication savings are not masking the result here.

Both runs completed all 30 training steps with finite, decreasing loss, then failed while writing the disposable local final checkpoint. That post-training failure did not affect the measured window. This is one run per arm, so treat the size of the gap as exploratory pending profiling or replication.

topics.body:
`TrainingProgressStalled` and `TrainingLossSpike` enroll hero roots from `iris.task_state`. GCE controllers do not publish that rollup, so these rules cannot evaluate a hero run on GCE. The [stall runbook](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/docs/ops/training-stall-alert-contract.md) records this limit; the [jobs dashboard](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/infra/grafana/dashboards/jobs.json) already queries GCE controllers live for job state.

topics.title: [rl] Raise SkyRL rollout concurrency to the inference GPU capacity
topics.body:
SkyRL rollout workers each run up to 1,024 tasks at once (four workers by default), so rollout concurrency is set by vLLM's KV cache and `max_num_seqs` (1,024 per engine rank) rather than by a fixed task count. The Snowball MOPD Ultra 32k config inherits that `max_num_seqs` and allows 512 Harbor trials.

At 32 tasks per worker, runs hold 128 requests in flight in total (2.6–4 per inference GPU on 32–48 GPUs, with an empty vLLM queue), while Snowball decode rises from about 1,100 tokens/s per GPU at 12–16 running requests to about 3,200 at 48–64. Watch `num_preemptions_total` and `kv_cache_usage_perc` on long-context runs; a per-config `max_num_seqs` at the KV-limited depth is the remedy if preemptions rise.

topics.title: Reject matrix roots in exact scalar grading
topics.body:
Reject matrix-valued expressions before asking SymPy whether an exact scalar answer is finite. A matrix square root can currently raise `TypeError` and abort AIME grading. Unsupported candidates earn zero; invalid references still raise `InvalidTask`. Ordinary scalar comparisons retain their existing behavior.

The repair and regression cases are identical to the [qualified Verifyit tree](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/5ef1e703d3bae94d510d8cf3f50d902958e10d20). All 192 [retained fixed-reply grades](https://github.com/yonromai/marin/blob/3b9f0183badb2c20d4c9bd4468489a442f9222e2/experiments/post_training/score_centering_integration/evidence/grader-repair-task-parity.json) remain unchanged. In a fresh replay of 145 constructed matrix-root candidates, the published grader raises `TypeError` in 124 cases; the fixed source grades all 145 incorrect. The complete Verifyit suite passes 1,482 tests with two Go-toolchain skips.

MarinSkyRL [#968](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/pull/968) needs a matching published release of Verifyit, TaskCompendium, RolloutEngine and Shellbox containing this fix. Published TaskCompendium requires an exact Verifyit version, so the existing Git repair at version `0.1.0` cannot replace the selected published Verifyit package alone. That integration stays blocked until the public dependency floors, exact Rigging pin, root `uv.lock` and standalone `skyrl-gym/uv.lock` consistently select a repaired release.

topics.title: [grug] Run the production hero with a PGLE latency profile
topics.body:
The hero's step is about 1.5-1.9% shorter with a PGLE (profile-guided latency estimation) profile, and production does not use one yet. The hero schedules with one collective in flight, and XLA's default latency estimator gives every collective the same small latency, so the scheduler treats a multi-millisecond ragged transport as hidden under a single GEMM. A profile built from the program's own trace replaces those estimates with measured costs.

All four runs below are on the same 64-GPU rack (restore step-180000, seed 0, 100 steps); the same code ran 0.8% faster on another rack, so only same-rack comparisons count.

| Program | No profile | Own profile |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Stack #9830-#9836 with #9835, plus #9829 | 12.695 s | 12.506 s (+1.51%) |
| The same without #9835 | 12.763 s | 12.522 s (+1.92%) |

With a profile, #9835's hand-placed transport ordering was worth 0.13% (12.506 against 12.522 s), so #9835 was closed and its scheduling left to PGLE. Without a profile it was worth 0.54%, which production gives up until it runs with one.

`experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/pgle_profile.py` (#9831) builds a profile from one XProf trace, and the hero README describes the trace, build and rerun loop. Automatic PGLE (`JAX_ENABLE_PGLE`) cannot profile with one process per GPU. A profile matches instructions by name, so it applies only to the program it was traced from: production needs a profile traced on its own 11-rack mesh, rebuilt after any change to the model, mesh or XLA flags. A stale profile loses the gain without an error.

Done when: the production hero runs with a profile built from its own program, the launcher warns or fails when the profile does not match the compiled program, and the production step-time change is recorded here.

Part of #9636.

comments.body:
🤖 Two ways a profile can break a hero run, both found on one rack while testing the stack (#9830-#9834). A production rollout needs a guard for each.

**1. XLA compile abort (fixed in a candidate plugin, not yet promoted).** With `--xla_gpu_enable_host_memory_offloading` (#9831), rematerialization may offload values to host when its estimate of the step exceeds its budget. One profiled schedule overshot the budget (124.77 GiB against 114.09 GiB inside the layer loop), and remat picked an f32[] operand of an all-reduce whose start was scheduled before the loop and whose done came after it. `GetCostOfHostOffload` counts users reached through the all-reduce's alias; `OffloadInstruction` places the reload before direct users only, found none unplaced, and failed `CHECK(!place_before_list.empty())` at hlo_rematerialization.cc:2118 on every rank. The bug is unchanged on openxla/xla main and has no upstream report.
- Fix: skip candidates whose buffer `has_indirect_uses` in `GetCostOfHostOffload`, as recomputation already does. Branch `marin/remat-offload-indirect-uses` (0f6dc61dee) on marin-community/xla. A plugin built from it on Iris (`0.11.1+marin.0f6dc61dee6d`, 15 minutes) compiles the case that aborted.
- A second branch, `marin/remat-no-offload-strategy` (ff858b5447), also keeps the flag's host accounting but turns the offload strategy off. Its cost model prices host copies at HBM bandwidth. It is built but untested on the rack.

**2. Out of memory at runtime.** With the fix, the same program compiled and then failed to allocate its 143.75 GiB pool on the first step. Remat estimated the profiled schedule about 26 GiB above the unprofiled one. A near-identical program (the shared expert as two custom VJPs instead of one) trained with its own profile at 119.5 GiB peak, so this depends on the schedule. I have not traced which buffers grow.

What this adds to the done criteria: before a long run, a preflight that compiles the profiled program and runs a few steps, with a fallback to no profile when either fails. Both failures appear within minutes of start.

🤖
# Research

This is a gated two-domain experiment: the canonical MMLU-Pro data is prepared, but E₂ training awaits approval, and all four transfer arms need the resulting checkpoint. [#9920](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9920) supplies the B/E baseline and single-expert recipes; [#9974](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9974) already implements the checkpoint-merging tools and remains under review. The repository's named evaluation suite does not include working MMLU-Pro or CruxEval tasks, so the frozen Evalchemy configuration from #9920 must be used for comparable scores.

**Relevant code**
- [`SFTSpec`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/experiments/sft/launcher.py#L494) — shared SFT recipe and checkpoint source
- [`SkyRLSpec`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/marin/src/marin/rl/skyrl.py#L150) — versioned rollout and model inputs
- [`evaluation/cli.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/experiments/evaluation/cli.py#L147) — explicit Evalchemy config launch
- [`evaluation/evals.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/experiments/evaluation/evals.py#L297) — named-suite task limitation

# Proposed Fix

1. After approval, train E₂ on the pinned canonical subset with E's #9920 recipe. Export it, evaluate B/E/E₂ on both target domains and the collapse checks, and apply the stated MMLU-Pro paired-gain and GSM8K gates. Stop the transfer arms if E₂ fails.
2. If E₂ passes, pin its k=8 demo collection and construct the two mixed SFT datasets from the same 3,206 prompts. Record rejection-sampling coverage and supervised token counts. Smoke the domain-routed MOPD setup, including teacher score alignment, one update, and HF export, before the four-epoch run.
3. Run MOPD, mixed SFT, and mixed SFT-RS from B with the issue's fixed optimizer and epoch budget. Use #9974 for the B/E/E₂ coefficient sweep and TIES/DARE-TIES after its tools are ready; verify checkpoint tensor alignment and complete exports.
4. Score each selected arm on CruxEval, MMLU-Pro (full set, training subset, held-out groups), GSM8K, GPQA-D, and MATH500 with the frozen evaluator. Report paired intervals, the issue's checkpoint-selection rule, verifier access for SFT-RS, and H100-hours in one final issue update. The trained MMLU-Pro and CruxEval prompts must be labeled as seen-prompt results.

🤖 **Final report: two experts into one student (MOPD, mixed SFT, mixed SFT-RS, merging)**

## Summary

E_2 reached 66.4% on the MMLU-Pro subset used for its fine-tuning (B 44.5%) and 64.0% on the remaining docs (B 44.1%). Its CruxEval output score was 4.9 percentage points below B in one pass. Its IFEval instruction-strict point estimate was also below B (80.2% versus 81.1%), with an interval spanning zero; the other reported probe point estimates were above B. At the selected finals, mixed SFT-RS step-727 exceeds MOPD step-100 on the MMLU-Pro subset by 4.0 pp [1.6, 6.3]; the held-out difference is unresolved (+0.4 [−0.5, 1.4]). MOPD exceeds RS on CruxEval input by 4.9 pp [1.6, 8.1]; the output difference is unresolved. RS-727 and MOPD-100 are the selected finals of their arms (RS-727 similar to 546, MOPD-100 similar to 50 on every target). They use unequal compute, token budgets and verifier access. Mixed SFT = one demo per prompt (E's and E_2's sample 0 from k=8 pools). Mixed SFT-RS = the first sample per prompt in index order that is execution-correct (CruxEval) or accepted by the implemented answer selector (MMLU-Pro) from the same k=8 pools (1,503 + 1,400 covered prompts; uncovered prompts stay in every denominator). MMLU-Pro runs score all 12,032 docs; subset and held-out numbers are sliced from the record's active FineStore snapshot against the canonical gold; intervals resample question-text groups for MMLU-Pro (subset 1,589, held-out 10,212) and problems within each CruxEval direction (800), conditional on the observed sampled completions; they do not estimate generation or training run-to-run variability. At ae362881, MMLU-Pro extraction uses final content when available, falls back to reasoning for REASONING_ONLY responses, and returns no answer for truncated reasoning-only responses; it applies `final_response_text`, then the three answer-letter regexes, and uppercases the result. Exact replay reproduced native predictions on all 12,032 rows of each of B-220c, E_2-254, RS-727 and MOPD-100. The broader matrix has uniform runtime-revision metadata; it was not replayed in full. The stored normalized output is not always the scorer input (the scorer saw the parser-split final content), so re-grading must start from the native completions. All comparisons are paired on the same docs.

## Reading the result

(1) At RS-727 and MOPD-100, both domains improve over B. Relative to the specialists, MOPD's MMLU-Pro subset difference from E_2 is −2.24 pp [−4.47, +0.06], while RS's is +1.74 pp with an interval spanning zero. Intervals spanning zero do not establish preservation or equivalence. Both checkpoints have higher CruxEval output scores than E's first pass; their input differences from E are unresolved. Paired changes versus B on each split: MOPD-100 +19.7 pp on the subset and +20.3 on the held-out docs; RS-727 +23.7 and +20.7. (2) RS-SFT and MOPD differ by domain: RS higher on the MMLU-Pro subset, MOPD higher on CruxEval input, output unresolved. RS-SFT had ground-truth verifier access, 8 teacher samples per prompt and an unequal token budget; MOPD had on-policy samples scored by the teachers. Neither is a matched control for the other. (3) Plain mixed SFT recovers less than either (MMLU-Pro −5.8 pp vs RS; CruxEval below E on input). (4) Merging recovers CruxEval input (76.5 at a = b = 0.5) and most of MMLU-Pro (63.2) with no training, but its CruxEval output (67.6) is 2.6 pp below E's first pass (70.25), 3.8 below E's two-pass mean (71.4), 8.8 below MOPD-100 (76.4), 9.65 below RS-727 (77.25) and 3.9 below plain-803's first pass (71.5); TIES output (68.1) sits 0.5 pp above TA-0.5 on each of those comparisons; at full strength (a = b = 1.0) the merge shows a large regression on valid GSM8K (50.0) and GPQA-D (30.0) evaluations with unusually long outputs (median 85–95k characters), so it was withheld from the rest of the matrix. (5) Probes on the two finals (single pass each; 0 infrastructure-error rows; MATH500 median output 2,496 and 1,525 characters): RS-727 MATH500 92.4, GPQA-D 57.6, IFEval instruction-strict 78.3 (below B with the interval excluding 0: −2.76 [−5.21, −0.24]; loose −0.36 [−2.66, +2.03]); MOPD-100 MATH500 90.0, GPQA-D 47.5, IFEval 80.0 (−1.08 [−3.59, +1.21] vs B). RS-727's GPQA-D score is above every other model in this matrix (B 41.9, E 44.8, E_2 47.6, MOPD-100 47.5, merges 47.1–47.3); it is one evaluation with three generations for each of 198 questions and is reported with its paired interval, not interpreted.

## Caveats

One pass per checkpoint except the explicitly reported repeats; plain 603/803 selection uses per-item two-pass means. Intervals are unadjusted for multiple comparisons and checkpoint selection; additional-probe findings are exploratory. Targets are 800 problems per CruxEval direction and 1,606 docs; intervals resample question-text groups for MMLU-Pro and problems within each CruxEval direction, conditional on the observed sampled completions, and do not estimate generation or training run-to-run variability (E's two CruxEval passes differed by 0.1 / 2.25 pp in #9920). The MMLU-Pro subset was the fine-tuning set for E_2 and the training prompt set for every arm; the 10,426 held-out docs are an additional probe, reported and never used for selection. RS demo selector mismatch: the k=8 demo grader implemented the older first-match-anywhere extractor on the whole text, while the evaluator grades the final answer after the think block; under the evaluator's rule 14 of the 1,400 selected RS MMLU-Pro demos (1.0%) are wrong, 15 more prompts would have been covered and 1 lost, and 45 prompts would have used a different sample. The RS arm is reported as trained; no corrected run was made. Record provenance: two records (B MMLU-Pro and MOPD-100 MMLU-Pro) had a retried eval attempt that left a second full sample stream; all numbers here come from each record's pinned active FineStore manifest (HEAD), with the native writer taken from the active source-blob provenance (normalized sample rows can carry null correctness); superseded attempts are kept as overhead and evidence, not as independent repeats (an earlier reading of the first stream gave B 43.90 and MOPD-100 65.32 on the subset and has been superseded). Three merge MATH500 records from 2026-10-10 are invalid (Evalchemy `AgentTimeoutError` in 500/500, 455/500 and 300/500 rows) and were rerun for TA-0.5 and TIES; TA-1.0 was not rerun.

**Costs (H100-hours = GPUs × Iris task or attempt duration; method: https://gist.github.com/karansag/500604143668730f8e79277b43f39298; every figure labelled by what it includes).** Training-gang allocations (image pull, load, steps, in-gang checkpoint/HF export and teardown; queue time excluded): E_2 60.6 (3 epochs, 32 H100). Mixed SFT-RS 93.57 (728 updates, 32 H100). Mixed SFT 107.83, plus 14.21 for a first attempt evicted by Kueue after 16 updates and relaunched from B. MOPD 557.9 for the 2-epoch run (100 optimizer updates, 7 × H100x8; the launch plan said ≈102, the sampler yielded 50 full windows per epoch; the W&B run `skyrl/snowball-mopd2-cruxeval-mmlupro-2ep` logged 99 steps and is marked `crashed`; coordinator logs record 100 updates and the terminal export at global_step 100 succeeded), plus 28.3 in two separate export-only jobs (step-50 13.8, step-100 14.5), which the SFT figures include in-gang; allocation to the step-50 checkpoint ≈ 317 and to step-100 ≈ 531 from timestamps (full run, not pro-rated). E_2 k=8 demo pool 8.91 (counted once, shared by both SFT arms; #9920's CruxEval pool is reused and its cost stays in #9920). Merges: CPU only (33, 28 and 68 min). Excluded from every total: GLM trace generation, E's construction (#9920), CPU preparation and audit jobs, the MOPD smoke run (≈60.6, reported in the design ledger). Evaluation serve allocation (serve attempt `started_at`→`finished_at` × 8 H100; queue time and CPU eval tasks excluded; two sweeps, 2026-10-13 05:20 and 11:40 UTC, 82 groups): 1,752.6 H100-h. Of this, 858.2 belongs to 51 groups with at least one successful eval child, including groups with invalid or superseded records; 894.5 belongs to 31 groups with no successful eval child. Per evaluated model (record / no-record): B 121.7 / 0; E 46.2 / 0; E_2 167.5 / 284.9; mixed plain 111.7 / 0; mixed RS 73.3 / 13.6; MOPD 112.0 / 0 (the step-50 retry alone 72.4: its MMLU-Pro eval ran 8 h 41 min without errors); merge TA-0.5 94.4 / 231.6; merge TA-1.0 79.9 / 241.6; merge TIES 51.6 / 122.7. Eight serves ran 13.8–14.6 h (110–117 H100-h each): six in the no-record bucket (`20261010-043736` E_2-85 MMLU-Pro, `20261010-030122` and `…030230` TA-1.0, `20261010-042000` and `…042104` TA-0.5, `20261010-042136` TIES; 689.4 together) and two in the record bucket (B's MMLU-Pro group `20261007-172014-…-9225`, 116.9, whose MMLU-Pro eval ran two attempts while its GPQA-D eval failed; E_2-85's `20261010-003548`, 110.3). Several of these groups have documented stale-endpoint failures after a serve preemption (#10030; its fix #10033 was not applied to this frozen evaluator), and B's group is documented as an eval retry after `PodDeleted`; the totals include all serve allocation regardless of cause, and the per-group attribution is only as complete as the overhead ledger's entries. These are infrastructure allocation costs, not inference-compute estimates. For scale, the #9984 training-gang allocations listed above sum to 834.1 H100-h (E_2 60.6 + RS 93.57 + plain 122.04 + MOPD 557.9), plus 28.3 of MOPD export-only jobs and 8.91 for the demo pool.

</details>

🤖

## Weight deltas against the student

A reader asked what the weight changes behind these transfers look like. Table and method below; numbers are percentages; cosines are given against E and against E₂.

| Model (vs student B) | ‖Δ‖/‖B‖ all, % | attention % | expert MLPs % | shared expert % | router % | LM head % | weights changed, % | cos(Δ, Δ_expert) all | attention | expert MLPs | LM head |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Expert E (CruxEval) | 0.036 | 0.65 | 0.047 | 0.069 | 0.17 | 0.13 | 13.7 | — | — | — | — |
| Expert E₂ (MMLU-Pro) | 0.035 | 0.64 | 0.043 | 0.067 | 0.15 | 0.11 | 12.9 | 0.21 vs E | 0.37 | 0.06 | 0.38 |
| Mixed plain SFT step 803 | 0.180 | 0.40 | 0.40 | 0.42 | 0.033 | 0.53 | 56.3 | 0.02 / 0.02 | 0.06 / 0.06 | 0.02 / 0.02 | 0.40 / 0.50 |
| Mixed RS-SFT step 727 | 0.171 | 0.38 | 0.38 | 0.40 | 0.030 | 0.49 | 54.7 | 0.02 / 0.02 | 0.06 / 0.06 | 0.02 / 0.02 | 0.42 / 0.51 |
| MOPD update 100 | 0.045 | 0.13 | 0.099 | 0.12 | 0.008 | 0.084 | 25.2 | 0.05 / 0.05 | 0.11 / 0.13 | 0.07 / 0.07 | −0.14 / −0.15 |
| Merge TA a = b = 0.5 | 0.031 | 0.53 | 0.041 | 0.064 | 0.13 | 0.11 | 12.1 | 0.71 / 0.69 | 0.82 / 0.82 | 0.60 / 0.56 | 0.78 / 0.71 |
| Merge TIES d = 0.5 | 0.043 | 0.73 | 0.057 | 0.084 | 0.19 | 0.14 | 17.2 | 0.73 / 0.69 | 0.75 / 0.73 | 0.73 / 0.65 | 0.84 / 0.69 |

Reading:
- The two experts are built the same way and look the same: 0.035–0.036% of B's norm overall, change concentrated in attention (0.65%), router (0.15–0.17%) and LM head, expert MLPs nearly untouched, 13% of weights changed. Their deltas share a direction (cosine 0.21 overall, 0.37 in attention, 0.38 at the LM head) while their expert-MLP changes are nearly independent (0.06), consistent with a common change in how the model answers (both experts start using their reasoning block on far more prompts) on top of domain-specific MLP changes.
- The mixed SFT arms move the weights most (0.17–0.18% overall, 55–56% of weights changed, expert MLPs 0.38–0.40%), 5× more than the experts whose text they train on, and in a direction almost orthogonal to both experts' deltas (cosine ≈0.02 overall and in the expert MLPs; 0.06 in attention). Only the LM head aligns (0.40–0.51).
- MOPD moves the weights a quarter as much as the SFT arms (0.045% overall, 25% of weights changed), again nearly orthogonal to the experts (0.05–0.13), with the LM head moving against both experts (−0.14 / −0.15). It recovers both experts' scores anyway.
- The merges are, by construction, the experts' deltas: TA 0.5 is their average (cosine 0.69–0.71 with each, magnitude 0.031%), TIES keeps the larger of the two per weight (0.043%, attention 0.73%). They sit far from where the trained arms end up (cosine between merge and arm deltas not computed here).
- Net: four different weight changes, differing in size by 5× and nearly orthogonal in direction, all land within a few points of the experts on both domains. The transfer is not a recovery of the expert's parameters; it is a re-learning of the behaviour from a different starting direction, which is also why the arms' off-domain scores (GSM8K, MATH500, GPQA-D, IFEval) do not simply track the experts'.

Method: every tensor of each checkpoint was compared with the student B (open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-10T-Mixed-RLVR-Sync-Step92 @ fdc3c3c5) in float32 after widening the bf16 exports; ‖Δ‖/‖B‖ is the relative Frobenius norm over all 67.1 B weights or over one component (attention q/k/v/o and attention gates; the 26 layers' fused MoE expert MLPs, 65.4 B weights; shared experts; router weights and biases; embeddings; LM head), 'weights changed' is the share of scalars whose bf16 value differs from B's, and cos(Δ, Δ_expert) is the cosine between the checkpoint's delta and the expert's delta over the same weights (two values = vs E / vs E₂). Embeddings and norms are omitted from the table (relative change ≤ 0.01% everywhere). Caveat: the exports are bf16, so training-time changes below half a bf16 ulp of a weight are invisible; magnitudes and 'weights changed' are lower bounds, and the cosines are computed only on what survived rounding. Script `experiments/tutorials/weight_delta_stats.py` (eval worktree); per-tensor results at `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/scratch/karan/mopd2/review/wdelta-<model>.json`, all summaries in `wdelta-all-summaries.json`.

🤖 Follow-up on the delta-direction question: is the MOPD update "nearly orthogonal" to the expert update, or aligned beyond chance?

## Method

Deltas against the student B (`Snowball-67B-A2B-10T-Mixed-RLVR-Sync-Step92` @ fdc3c3c5) for expert E (CruxEval, step 272), expert E₂ (MMLU-Pro, step 254), the MOPD update (step 100) and the two mixed SFT arms (plain step 803, RS step 727). Three measures per component: cosine, sign agreement on weights changed in both, and subspace overlap, the share of a delta's energy inside the reference delta's top-k singular directions per matrix (k holding 50% of the reference energy), against two nulls: a random k-dim subspace and the reference delta with entries permuted within each matrix. The run reproduces the cosines posted above exactly. Script: `experiments/tutorials/weight_delta_subspace.py` on branch `task/239` (4c99d4d9a4).

## Result

Overlap with E's half-energy subspace, as a multiple of the random null:

| Component | E₂ (peer expert) | MOPD | plain SFT | RS-SFT |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Attention | 3.4× | 3.5× | 2.4× | 2.4× |
| Expert MLPs | 1.5× | 1.6× | 1.3× | 1.3× |
| Shared experts | 3.9× | 3.4× | 1.7× | 1.8× |
| Router | 2.0× | 2.8× | 1.7× | 1.6× |
| LM head | 295× | 198× | 397× | 407× |

Cosine and sign agreement with E, all weights: E₂ 0.21 / 0.55; MOPD 0.049 / 0.56; plain SFT 0.021 / 0.53; RS-SFT 0.023 / 0.53. In attention MOPD reaches 0.10 / 0.68 against E₂'s 0.38 / 0.71.

## Reading

- Cosine 0.05 over 6.7e10 weights is about 12,000 chance SDs (1/√n = 3.9e-6), so "beyond chance" is a weak bar. The informative controls are the SFT arms (same student, same prompts, same expert texts) and the peer expert.
- Against those controls, MOPD shares direction with the experts more than the SFT arms do, in every component except the LM head, and relative to the random null it sits close to the peer expert in attention and expert MLPs. The permuted null equals the random null everywhere, so the excess comes from the experts' dominant singular directions, not from their entry distribution.
- The shared part is small in energy: 0.24% of MOPD's update lies along E's delta, and 16% inside E's half-energy subspace against 10% for a random subspace. The posted conclusion stands: the transfer is mostly a different weight change that reaches the same behaviour.
- The LM head reverses the pattern: the SFT arms align strongly with the experts there (cos 0.40 to 0.51), while MOPD moves inside the same narrow top directions with the opposite sign (cos −0.14, sign agreement 0.39).
- None of the deltas is rank-1: participation ratios are 20 to 90 directions per matrix. The experts' attention deltas are the most concentrated (top-10 directions hold 80% of their energy); MOPD's is more spread (39%), the SFT arms' more still (24%).

## Limits

Correlational geometry only; no ablation, so no causal claim about the recovered scores. Cross-step self-consistency of the MOPD direction could not be measured because only step 100 exists. The bf16 exports hide changes below half an ulp, so every measure covers only what survived rounding.

The agent above put some numbers together for "how orthogonal" the task vectors really are for each experiment arm. This is related to @penfever 's [comment](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9920#issuecomment-6201304545) about how the Frobenius norm of the task vector for MOPD is significantly smaller than SFT's.

However, I realized something else that I put in the experiment setup but forgot about: **The MOPD arm's batch size was effectively 16x higher than the SFT arm's with the same LR and fewer steps** . This might explain the whole difference. Specifically, they were "prompt matched", with each epoch seeing 3200 unique prompts / epoch. Specifically:

* SFT had 16 demonstration rows / step
  *  x 200 steps / epoch x 4 epochs = 12800 rollouts
  *  LR 1e-6
* MOPD had 64 prompts x 4 student rollouts / step x 50 steps / epoch x 2 epochs = 3200 prompts
  * x 50 steps / epoch x 2 epochs = 25600 rollouts 
  * LR 1e-6

As for why, at the time:
* We had known SFT runs on Snowball that used a 1e-6 LR, and I think even after doing sweeps in #10213 , that seems to be a good LR for this class of experiments
* We had existing M/OPD experiments under the proof-of-life experiments that used the 256 rollouts + 1e-6 LR
* MOPD needed more rollouts / batch to keep it from being as rollout-constrained
* MOPD by construction would see more unique sequences / epoch anyways if they started with the same dataset. 

Either way, we can do an experiment increasing MOPD LR to 4e-6, computed by sqrt(MOPD batch  / SFT batch) ( 1e-6) = 4 * 1e-6.

We'll also run for 4 epochs. This will give us a better sense of whether MOPD was under-stepped. 

Another difference I should note that won't change: MOPD is running using Megatron (our SkyRL setup), SFT is using Levanter

🤖 Efficiency view: target scores against GPU-hours and trained tokens, per checkpoint.

| Arm, checkpoint (updates) | H100-h | trained tokens | MMLU-Pro subset | CruxEval in / out |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| B (start) | 0 | 0 | 44.5 | 55.4 / 57.75 |
| Mixed plain SFT 201 / 402 / 603 / 804 | 50.5 / 77.4 / 104.4 / 131.4 | 2.8 / 5.7 / 8.5 / 11.3M | 61.0 / 62.8 / 60.9 / 62.4 | 69.5 / 66.75; 71.1 / 71.5; 79.25 / 73.4; 75.4 / 71.5 |
| Mixed RS-SFT 182 / 364 / 546 / 728 | 46.9 / 70.3 / 93.7 / 117.1 | 2.1 / 4.2 / 6.3 / 8.4M | 61.7 / 61.8 / 67.2 / 68.2 | 76.25 / 74.6; 75.1 / 74.6; 78.75 / 76.0; 77.25 / 77.25 |
| MOPD 50 / 100 | 292.8 / 572.4 | 56.7 / 77.8M | 65.0 / 64.2 | 80.5 / 76.0; 82.1 / 76.4 |
| E₂ (MMLU-Pro expert) / E (CruxEval expert) | 60.6 / 35.9 | 2.2 / 1.8M | 66.4 / – | – / 79.4, 71.4 |

How the numbers are built:
- **H100-hours.** Each arm's measured training-gang allocation, pro-rated by updates.
- **SFT arms.** Each carries both demo pools from step 0: E's (14.6 H100-h, reused from #9920) and E₂'s (8.9).
- **MOPD.** Each checkpoint carries its export job (about 14 H100-h). Measured allocation-to-checkpoint for MOPD, as a cross-check: ≈317 / ≈531 H100-h.
- **Trained tokens.** As in #9920: SFT from the row manifests × epochs, MOPD from per-update scored tokens.
- **Excluded.** Evaluations, building the experts, and the evicted plain attempt (14.2 H100-h).

Reading:
- **The arms reach different targets.** RS-SFT reaches E₂'s MMLU-Pro subset level at update 546 (93.7 H100-h); MOPD never does (best 65.0). MOPD reaches E's CruxEval input level at update 50 (292.8 H100-h); neither SFT arm does (best 78.75 / 79.25).
- **Matched GPU-hours.** Both SFT runs ended (117 and 131 H100-h) before MOPD's first checkpoint (292.8). At the SFT arms' final cost, a straight line from B to MOPD update 50 puts MOPD at about 53 MMLU-Pro and 65–67 / 65–66 CruxEval. That is an interpolation, not a measurement.
- **Trained tokens.** MOPD trains on 7–9× more tokens than the SFT arms; most of them (56.7M) come in its first epoch.

Caveats:
- This is not a matched-compute experiment; the arms differ in optimizer, batch geometry and verifier access.
- Single passes unless marked.
- MOPD's W&B history logged 99 of 100 updates.
- The RS demo selector used a different MMLU-Pro answer rule from the evaluator, which affects 1% of its demos.

topics.title: [shellbox] Run local commands below their host process's CPU priority
topics.body:
Local sandbox commands now start at niceness 10 above the host process, so
CPU-bound commands compete less with the process that drives their machines.
With the local backend, solver and grader commands run in the coordinator's
own pod. In a Taskforge validation run on cw-rno2a, sandbox and ShellSim starts
in a 4-CPU coordinator grew to 5-32 s while long CPU-bound solver commands
ran. With 16 busy-loop commands pinned to two CPUs, creating and running a new
machine took 484 ms at p50 and 916 ms at p99 at equal priority, and 360 ms and
383 ms with this change. Sizing the coordinator's CPU request stays the main
remedy.

The local-machine suite passes as root on cw-rno2a under the PRIVILEGED profile (35 passed, 2 skipped after merging main), except `test_a_python_environment_runs_its_own_interpreter_and_locked_packages`, which also fails on main there (offline resolution with a fresh uv cache). Part of #10119.

topics.title: Experiment: Hero throughput and expert drops at 8K and 16K context
topics.body:
Agent-driven experiment issue: the runs and this record were produced by a Claude agent, supervised by @mcwitt.

## TL;DR

On one GB200 NVL72 rack, restoring the hero's step-180000 checkpoint at a fixed 4.19M tokens per step, 8K context trains at 297.0k tokens/s, 1.6% below 4K, and 16K at 292.5k tokens/s, 3.1% below 4K. The fraction of expert assignments dropped rises from 1.9e-4 at 4K to 8.3e-4 at 8K (4.5×) and 2.9e-3 at 16K (16×). The drops come from the receiving shard's per-chunk capacity; the ragged transport counts all of them as `sender_dropped` (see the correction comment). Each arm has three seeds; the seed-to-seed standard deviation is at most 0.03 MFU points and 4% to 7% of the drop fraction.

## Description

The hero plan in #8435 moves from 4K to 8K sequences at 50% of training (step ~195k) and to 65K at ~95%. These runs measure what the 8K switch costs in throughput and expert-capacity drops before it happens, with 16K as the next point and a 4K control from the same checkpoint.

Setup:

* Source: `main` at f38da1173de79f1eacd5f54bcfb88db6cb0a9f6e with no code changes. Launcher: `experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/launch_diagnostics.py`.
* Checkpoint: `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/grug/hero-fa4sm100-nomask-step146k/2026.08.19.2/checkpoints/step-180000`, the newest permanent hero checkpoint on 2026-09-30. The current hero run id records that it started from step 146k.
* Hardware and parallelism: one rack (16 nodes × 4 GB200), EP64, the hero's ragged all-to-all transport and capacity factor 1.15.
* Every arm keeps 4,194,304 tokens per step (65,536 per GPU), so the learning rate from the hero's heuristic (`MoeHeuristic` in `experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/heuristic.py`, which scales with tokens per step and total tokens) is the same in all arms. `--schedule-steps 390251` is the hero's full schedule length, so the restored step sits at the hero's position in the learning-rate schedule.
* `qk_mult`, the multiplier on the query-key attention scale, follows the #8435 extension rule `1.3 × (0.1 × ln(seq / 4096) + 1)`.
* Each run trains steps 180000 to 180099 with the production watch interval (10) and coordinated GC interval (100). There is no eval and no checkpoint write.
* The trainer seed sets the data shuffle, so seeds 0, 1, and 2 train on different batches.
* Statistics cover steps 180010 to 180099 (90 steps). Each run contributes its median MFU, median tokens/s, and mean drop fraction; the tables report mean ± standard deviation across the three seeds. Starting the window at step 180030 instead moves no run's median MFU by more than 0.03 points.

| Arm | `--seq-len` | `--batch-size` | `--qk-mult` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 4K control | 4096 | 1024 | 1.3 |
| 8K | 8192 | 512 | 1.39 |
| 16K | 16384 | 256 | 1.48 |

Command for one run (8K, seed 0):

```bash
python -m experiments.grug.moe_hero_ep.launch_diagnostics \
  --run-id mhep-ctx8k-s0-20260930 --seed 0 \
  --num-steps 180100 --schedule-steps 390251 \
  --batch-size 512 --seq-len 8192 --qk-mult 1.39 --gc-interval 100 \
  --restore-from s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/grug/hero-fa4sm100-nomask-step146k/2026.08.19.2/checkpoints/step-180000 \
  --version dev --run
```

## Results

| Arm | tokens/s | vs 4K | step time | MFU | drop fraction | vs 4K |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 4K | 301.9k ± 0.2k | | 13.89 s | 28.25 ± 0.02% | 1.86e-4 ± 0.08e-4 | 1× |
| 8K | 297.0k ± 0.2k | −1.6% | 14.12 s | 28.47 ± 0.02% | 8.29e-4 ± 0.39e-4 | 4.5× |
| 16K | 292.5k ± 0.3k | −3.1% | 14.34 s | 29.37 ± 0.03% | 2.94e-3 ± 0.20e-3 | 16× |

The logged `moe/receiver_drop_fraction` is zero in every run because the ragged transport hard-codes it to zero and counts receiver-capacity clipping as `sender_dropped`. Peak HBM was 103.1 GiB per GPU in every run. In every run, including the 4K control, the mean drop fraction over steps 180055 to 180099 was 0.75 to 1.00 times the mean over steps 180010 to 180054, so part of the measured drop fraction may be a transient after restore.

The live hero (11 racks, 4K) measured over steps 183310 to 183710 on 2026-09-30 had a median MFU of 26.47% and a mean drop fraction of 9.1e-5.

Caveats:

* MFU uses the analytic FLOP count, which charges more attention FLOPs per token at longer sequences (full causal attention on every fourth layer, a 2048-token window elsewhere). MFU therefore rises with sequence length while tokens/s falls. Compare arms by tokens/s.
* The one-rack 4K drop fraction is about 2× the 11-rack hero's. We have not tested the cause. The ratios between arms are the quantity to carry to the hero; an 8K hero drop fraction near 4e-4 is an extrapolation from that ratio, not a measurement.
* Each run covers 100 steps after the switch. Routing over thousands of steps at the new length is untested.
* The 8K and 16K arms change `qk_mult` together with sequence length.
* The diagnostic's peak learning rate comes from a one-rack token budget and is 0.69× the hero's. The diagnostic also leaves the attn_gate/router weight decay at 0 (the hero uses 0.02). Loss values are not comparable with the hero's.
* At 8K and 16K, XLA logged at compile time that rematerialization could only reduce its memory estimate to 193 GiB against a 161 GiB limit. The warning does not stop compilation. The runs trained normally with a runtime peak HBM of 103.1 GiB, the same as 4K, so the estimate overstated actual use.

## Links

* W&B runs (project `marin_moe`, group `moe-hero-ep`): 4K [s0](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/mhep-ctx4k-s0-20260930), [s1](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/mhep-ctx4k-s1-20260930), [s2](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/mhep-ctx4k-s2-20260930); 8K [s0](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/mhep-ctx8k-s0-20260930), [s1](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/mhep-ctx8k-s1-20260930), [s2](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/mhep-ctx8k-s2-20260930); 16K [s0](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/mhep-ctx16k-s0-20260930), [s1](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/mhep-ctx16k-s1-20260930), [s2](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/mhep-ctx16k-s2-20260930)
* Hero plan: #8435. 262K context-parallel probe on the same hardware: #8754.

## Conclusion

At the planned 4K to 8K switch, expect about 1.6% fewer tokens per second and about 4.5× the 4K drop fraction, still below 0.1% of assignments on one rack. At 16K the costs are 3.1% and 16×.

@ClassicLarry I've been looking into this, and it seems pretty tricky to resume with a different context length without repeating or dropping tokens. It seems like there are at least 4 independent sources of potential misalignment:

1. Levanter currently splits sources into "shuffle blocks" of 256 sequences and then the blocks are permuted. When we change the sequence length, the block sizes also change and the permuted sequence differs. So even if we restart the run at a shuffle block boundary, we'll inevitably drop and repeat tokens. #9689 fixes this by setting the tokens per shuffle block to ~1M (the current value, with 4k context), independently of the context size.
2. In addition to the block-level permutation above, we also permute _sequences_ within 512-block windows. When we change the sequence length, we change the result of permutation. (Note, we can't just work around this by doing the handoff at a step divisible by some number, since each source is at a different point in its window, and the rate at which tokens are consumed from a source is determined by its mixture weight). This seems like the largest effect after (1) and also the hardest to work around.
3. The token stream is divided into "mixture blocks" of 49152 sequences. To avoid dropping/repeating tokens, we need to hand off at a mixture block boundary. For a given batch size, mixture block boundaries coincide with steps every `49152 / gcd(49152, B)` steps. At C=16k, B=2816, this is 192 steps.
4. The data mix has a stage start at 108k. But mixture stages must fall on steps that are also mixture block boundaries, which are multiples of 192 steps at batch size 2816 (what we'd use with 16k context). We could either move the stage start to 108096 or 107904; the former skips some tokens from sources whose weight decreased at the switch and repeats some tokens from sources whose weight increased; the latter vice-versa.

One option is to merge #9689 to fix (1), hand off at the 216k permanent checkpoint to avoid (3), and accept the drops/repeats due to (2) and (4). I'm a bit hesitant, though - it seems like this has the potential to drop/repeat 10s of billions of tokens.

Wondering if we should instead look into an adhoc patch, something like finishing each source's current window in the order the 4k run was using before switching to 16k? This seems like it could get quite messy, though, and I'm hesitant to pursue it unless we think it's really necessary.

@ravwojdyla @Helw150 curious for your thoughts here as well. How did we manage this for the 67B run?

🤖 **Proposal: a clean context-length handoff** (replying to @mcwitt's four misalignment points above)

1. Fix shuffle blocks at ~1M tokens, so the level-1 block permutation is the same at every seq_len (#9689).
2. Give each data-mix stage its own `seq_len` and `batch_size`, e.g. `(216000, mix2, seq_len=16384, B=2816)`. A stage then only has to land on a mixture-block boundary in its own units, which fixes points 3 and 4.
3. Track each source's read position in **tokens** carried across stages, instead of in sequences of a single length.
4. On a `seq_len` change, advance each source to its next shuffle-window boundary (skip-to-window). Nothing repeats; only the unread rest of each source's current window is skipped, which fixes point 2. Using `harrier_mix_2026_08_18` at a 216k handoff, that is about **52B unseen tokens** across 200 sources, ≈0.26B each and ~0.6% of the remaining run.
5. Inside a stage, mixing, batching and BOS/EOS/segment handling are unchanged.

Finishing the partially read windows instead would serve leftover 4k slices glued into 16k sequences. Those need segment and loss masking at the joins, carry only 4k of context, and low-weight sources would keep serving them for thousands of steps after the switch. So skip-to-window looks like the better trade-off.

@mcwitt @ClassicLarry Short version: the qk arms will probably tie, so it may help to write down a tie rule before the 11-rack runs. The rule: keep the formula value (1.48 at 16K) unless another arm beats it, on both Uncheatable and the Paloma macro without PTB and WikiText, by more than the noise the rehearsal measures. The details below build on Larry's 100-step test and the agent's one-rack rehearsal plan (2–3 seeds × 200 steps per arm).

**1. On the 67B, the qk arms were nearly tied, and the two metrics disagreed.**
- In the [67B qk test](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/moe_67b_a2b_d2560_ep1_rep8_bs1024_seq65536_sw2k_v4_2048_muon_cooldown_step39k_yarn_mscale01_test20) (five arms, 20 steps from step 39k at 65K packing), the arms spanned 0.009 on Paloma and 0.003 on Uncheatable at the last eval. The best two were 0.0002 apart on Paloma and 0.00002 on Uncheatable.
- All-layer 1.570, which the 67B cooldown then used, was first on Paloma and fourth of five on Uncheatable.
- The arms were still converging. Over the 19 steps after the first eval, their spread shrank from 0.013 to 0.009 on Paloma and from 0.015 to 0.003 on Uncheatable.

**2. PTB and WikiText make the full Paloma macro a noisy judge for this trial.**
- On the hero, the two carry 77% of the 16-subset macro's eval-to-eval variance. Over the last 30 evals, the SD of the change is 0.0049 for the full macro, 0.0026 for the other 14 subsets and 0.0012 for Uncheatable.
- Both look like exposures to copies in the training data (#9874). Over those evals, PTB or WikiText moved by up to 0.2 between consecutive evals, which is up to 0.012 on the macro.
- Arms that share batches see the same exposures, but they need not memorize them equally, and any difference lands in the comparison.
- In Belay, where paired arms also share batches, PTB's differences between configs barely reproduce across seeds (r = 0.10 near the frontier). Dropping PTB and WikiText there cuts the noise SD by about 20% ([analysis](https://github.com/bethehand/marin-hero-forecast/tree/main/belay-noise)).
- On the 67B test, dropping them didn't change the ranking; the disagreement there was between Paloma and Uncheatable.

**3. The rehearsal can set the bar.**
- Its seeds give the seed-to-seed SD of each arm's difference from the 1.48 arm on these two metrics. With 2–3 seeds per arm, pool that SD across arms.
- The pooled SD will be rough, and probably conservative for 11 racks, since one rack runs 11× fewer tokens per step. Matching the trial's length helps.
- A rule written down in advance could be: keep 1.48 unless another arm beats it on both metrics by more than twice that SD. If the metrics disagree, it's a tie.
- Applied to the 67B test, this rule keeps the formula arm, which is what the 67B used.
- For selection, score the arms on the 16K-packed evals that the agent's plan adds, and use the 4K-packed evals as a retention check. qk_mult changes the model at every length, so a 4K score alone could favour a smaller qk for reasons unrelated to 16K quality.
