topics.title: [snowball] Antidoom-lineage checkpoints emit stacked think blocks into replies
topics.body: Snowball checkpoints from the Antidoom RLVR1 lineage onward often write several consecutive think blocks in one assistant message. The blocks are near-duplicates with nothing between them, for example: ``` <|start_think|>We need to see the files first. Let's list them and examine content.<|end_think|><|start_think|>We need to inspect the files to understand the corrections. Let's list and view them.<|end_think|><|start_think|>We need to see the content. Let's run ls to see files.<|end_think|><|start_think|>I'll list the files in the workspace.<|end_think|> ``` The `grug` reasoning parser moves only the first block into `reasoning`. It splits at the first `<|start_think|>` and the first `<|end_think|>` ([`basic_parsers.py:157`](https://github.com/marin-community/vllm/blob/3a054c458ca8a32609ba2bc578c4d9b93eabb395/vllm/reasoning/basic_parsers.py#L157), inherited by [`grug_reasoning_parser.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/vllm/blob/3a054c458ca8a32609ba2bc578c4d9b93eabb395/vllm/reasoning/grug_reasoning_parser.py)). Later blocks stay in `content` with raw think tags, so users and LLM judges see them. Tool calls after the blocks still parse. The same conversations also show long thinking-only loops that hit the token limit with an empty reply, for example `\n\nNow.` repeated 7,986 times. Reproduce: 1. Open case `108de5fc` in the [Smartie step 14 vs Qwen 3.6 comparison](https://applets.marina.oa.dev/a/25f504c6-c6fb-4e14-8401-07dd8e6fbfba/v/28/?run=smartie-rl-step14-vs-qwen36-20261019-v3-final4#108de5fc029a4b65adb39205bdae818e). 2. Round 0, first assistant message: the reply text contains four stacked think blocks before the `ls` tool call. 3. Rounds 2 and 3: the turns end at `finish_reason=length` with no reply. Expected: at most one think block per assistant message, as rendered by `MARIN_CHAT_TEMPLATE` (`lib/marin/src/marin/datakit/chat_template.py:108`). Rate by checkpoint: 150 random completed ShellSim cases per run from the same comparison applet, counting Snowball assistant messages whose `content` or `reasoning` still contains a think tag after parsing. | Checkpoint | Parser | Cases with leftover tags | Messages with leftover tags | |---|---|---:|---:| | Grug-67B-A2B-Datakit-SFT-262K-2026.09.21-dr-doom | grug_optional | 0/150 | 0/4,859 | | Grug-67B-A2B-Antidoom-RLVR1-Step12-2026.10.02 | grug_optional | 32/150 | 40/2,148 | | Grug-67B-A2B-Antidoom-RLVR1-Step12-2026.10.02 | grug | 47/150 | 94/2,688 | | Grug-67B-A2B-Merge-NUPA-BFCL-Shared100-2026.10.09 | grug | 146/150 | 294/1,757 | | Grug-67B-A2B-Merge-Campaign3-DARE-Linear-02-2026.10.12 | grug | 42/150 | 63/2,699 | | Snowball-Smartie-RL-2026.10.15.32-step14 | grug | 127/150 | 410/2,666 | | Qwen3.6-35B-A3B (reference) | qwen3 | 0/150 | 0/2,742 | Observations: - The behavior first appears at Antidoom RLVR1 step 12. Antidoom RLVR1 started from an Antidoom FTPO/DAPO step-45 export, which has no run in the applet and was not measured. The plain 09.21 SFT checkpoint and Smartie's initializer (Merge-Campaign2-DARE-TIES-02) also have no runs. - SFT data: a sample of 7 rendered SFT sources on `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/rendered/sft/` (nemotron-terminal, agenttrove, openthoughts-agent-sft-100k, gpt-oss-rollouts, glm-5.2-kernelgym-rollouts, coderforge, massive_function_calling; 178k assistant turns) has no turn with more than one think block. These sources are about 10% of the 09.21 SFT tokens. `nemotron_sft_v3`, `open_swe_traces`, and `penfever-traces` were not checked. - `grug_optional` does not hide the pattern: the same Antidoom checkpoint shows leftover tags under both parsers. - Hypothesis, not tested: FTPO de-looping penalizes exact repeated token spans. A policy can avoid that penalty by closing and reopening thinking with paraphrased text, which matches the near-duplicate blocks. Related: #10305 (Smartie RLVR), #9691 (Dr. Doom de-looping). ￼ ￼￼ ￼ ￼ ￼

comments.body:
🤖

# Research

The reported raw generations contain consecutive think blocks; the Smartie step-14 sample has leftover tags in 127/150 cases, versus 0/150 for the Dr. Doom SFT control. The Marin template renders at most one think block per assistant message, while the pinned vLLM parser extracts only the first block, exposing later blocks in `content`. The exact-periodic-suffix loop detector cannot establish whether paraphrased blocks were penalized; the first bad training stage and the proposed FTPO cause remain unverified.

**Relevant code**
- [`chat_template.py#L105-L114`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/036702ca09e1498893582ce1ec6e8e2f04c1bcff/lib/marin/src/marin/datakit/chat_template.py#L105-L114) — renders one reasoning span.
- [`basic_parsers.py#L157`](https://github.com/marin-community/vllm/blob/3a054c458ca8a32609ba2bc578c4d9b93eabb395/vllm/reasoning/basic_parsers.py#L157) — extracts the first span.
- [`trajectory_reward_shaping.py#L262-L294`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/036702ca09e1498893582ce1ec6e8e2f04c1bcff/vendor/skyrl/skyrl-train/skyrl_train/trajectory_runners/trajectory_reward_shaping.py#L262-L294) — detects exact periodic tails.
- [`ftpo.py#L190-L205`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/036702ca09e1498893582ce1ec6e8e2f04c1bcff/vendor/skyrl/skyrl-train/skyrl_train/ftpo.py#L190-L205) — selects that boundary for FTPO.

# Proposed Fix

1. Run the same fixed ShellSim prompts and generation settings on the Dr. Doom SFT control, the Antidoom step-45 parent if retained, RLVR1 step 12, the Campaign-2 initializer, and Smartie step 14. Save raw token output and parsed messages; report repeated-block, leaked-tag, empty `finish_reason=length`, and task-success rates per checkpoint to locate the first regression.
2. In `marin-community/vllm`, make the Grug reasoning parser consume adjacent balanced think blocks into `reasoning` while preserving reply text and tool calls. Cover full and streaming responses, including incomplete blocks, with parser regression tests; release that serving fix separately.
3. Once the onset is known, inspect the unsampled SFT sources and the responsible training stage, then test a structural training signal for one reasoning span and a completed reply. Re-run the matched cohort before selecting a checkpoint: target 0/150 cases with repeated raw blocks or leaked tags, zero empty length-truncated replies, and no regression in task success. A parser fix alone cannot repair the thinking-only loops.

No open Marin PR matched #10400 or this parser symptom during the duplicate-work check.

topics.title: [taskcompendium] Tell a failed grading preparation from a failed grader
topics.body:
A grading that fails while the verifier machine is being prepared, unpacking the staged archive, removing it, making the workspace, or making the reward files' directories, was recorded with the same kinds as a grader command that failed or timed out, `EXECUTION` or `TIMEOUT`, with only the message to tell them apart. A verifier deadline that expired before the grader's command ever ran was recorded as the grader timing out. A caller deciding whether a failure is the task's or the host's had nothing typed to go on. In a Taskforge generation run under a saturated cluster controller, 235 of 279 program revisions were spent on host-caused grading failures of this shape (269 deadline expiries during staging commands among them).

Two additions make the distinction typed:

- `GradingFailure.STAGING` for the runtime's own preparation commands, among them the protected directory an artifact is archived into. Commands the task's author chose, the grader's own command, its environment's setup commands and its collect commands, keep `EXECUTION` and `TIMEOUT`, and so does collecting an artifact, which reads what the candidate wrote; a missing, linked or wrong-kind artifact stays a submission failure. The reward files' preparation moves out of the script grader's run into the staging block it belongs to, ahead of the setup commands.
- `GradingProgress`, which the sandbox grading path moves to `STAGING` before it captures the agent's output files and to `GRADER` around the commands the author chose and the artifact collection: the collect commands and the artifacts, then the setup commands and the grader's own. The rollout engine, whose verifier deadline covers the preparation as well as the grader, now reports an expiry outside the author's commands as `STAGING` with the error "Verifier deadline expired while preparing the verifier machine", and as `TIMEOUT` with the unchanged message otherwise. A session that grades without the sandbox path leaves the phase at `GRADER`, so nothing changes for it.

Downstream, Taskforge's validation classifier and its build-time grading will map `STAGING` to a host cause instead of a task one; that lands on its own once this is in.

🤖 Removed the test-inventory paragraph from the body.

🤖 Holistic review of e690c61e14a8fa1ddc95b694a69640538637309b.

This change adds a typed `GradingFailure.STAGING` for failures in the runtime's own grading preparation, and a mutable `GradingProgress` that lets `RolloutEngine` report a verifier deadline that expired before the author's commands as `STAGING`. The split is sound and the tests cover tar, output capture, and the grader. One gap remains: the task author's `collect` commands still run under `STAGING`, which goes against the rule the body states. It should be fixed before Taskforge starts treating `STAGING` as a host cause.

**Before.** Every failed grading command became `EXECUTION` or `TIMEOUT`, whether it was `tar -xf` of the staged archive or the grader's own script. When `verifier_timeout` in `RolloutEngine._run_session` ran out, the result was always `TIMEOUT`, even if the grader never started. **After.** `_run_staging` labels the unpack, archive removal, workspace, and reward-file preparation as `STAGING`. Reward-file preparation moves out of `_script_reward` into `_grade_on`. `grade_in_sandbox` sets the phase to `STAGING` on entry, and `_grade_on` switches it to `GRADER` just before the environment's setup commands. The engine sets `STAGING` around output capture, and `_expired_verifier_grade` maps the phase to the deadline's failure kind.

**Evidence.** I ran the changed tests locally and they pass: `test_a_verifier_deadline_names_the_phase_it_expired_in` (3 cases) and `test_deadline_during_grading_keeps_captured_outputs` in rolloutengine, plus `test_grading_progress_is_staging_until_the_authors_commands` (2 cases) in taskcompendium. The 235/279 revision figure from Taskforge is the PR's own claim. No artifact in the PR backs it, and it is not a merge criterion. No test covers a grader with `collect` or `artifacts`.

**Findings**

- **1. Blocker:** `lib/taskcompendium/src/taskcompendium/runtime/grading.py:542`. The `grading.collect` loop runs inside `_grade_staged`, after `grade_in_sandbox` has set `STAGING` at line 469 and before `_grade_on` switches to `GRADER` at line 628. These are the author's commands, and the body says collect commands keep `EXECUTION`/`TIMEOUT`. Each one runs with `timeout=grading.limit`, which is `min(verifier_timeout, grader.timeout)`. The engine's verifier deadline started earlier, before output capture, so the outer deadline always fires before the command's own timeout. As a result, any task whose collect command hangs gets `STAGING` with "Verifier deadline expired while preparing the verifier machine". This is the same misclassification Codex found for setup commands, which 2be6f617a8 fixed only there. Taskforge's planned mapping would then retry a broken task as a host failure. Fix: set `progress.phase = GradingPhase.GRADER` around the collect loop and restore `STAGING` before the artifact downloads and machine creation that follow. Add a `test_a_verifier_deadline_names_the_phase_it_expired_in` case with a `ScriptGrader(collect=...)` whose collect command stalls and expects `TIMEOUT`.
- **2. Should fix:** `lib/taskcompendium/src/taskcompendium/runtime/grading.py:133`. `_download_artifact` runs only runtime-generated commands: the `artifact-kind` probe, the protected-directory `mkdir`, and the archive `tar` (via `_run_checked` at lines 184/200/224). It still reports their failures as `TIMEOUT`/`EXECUTION`, which the new `GradingFailure` docstring reserves for the author's commands. Meanwhile, a verifier deadline that expires during the same download is reported as `STAGING`. So one host-side stall gets two different kinds depending on which timer fires first. Fix: use `_run_staging` for those commands and `GradingFailure.STAGING` in the probe's two explicit `_infra_error` calls. Keep `SubmissionFailure` for missing, linked, and wrong-kind artifacts, which are the agent's fault.
- **3. Should fix:** `lib/taskcompendium/README.md:314` still documents `grade_in_sandbox(task, attempt, factory, machine_spec, *, task_machine=None, timeout=None)` without `progress`. The `verifier_timeout` row at `docs/references/task-rollouts.md:345` does not say that an expiry before the author's commands is reported as `staging`. Add the parameter and the `STAGING`/`TIMEOUT` split to both, so downstream classifiers can find the contract without reading `engine.py`.
- **4. Related PR:** #10203 (`[rolloutengine] Replace task sessions with registered harnesses`) rewrites the same verifier-deadline block (`engine.py:420-436`) and the `_grade_rollout` call path. It still builds the literal `GradeResult(..., "Verifier deadline expired", failure=GradingFailure.TIMEOUT)`. Land this PR first. #10203 then needs to pass `GradingProgress` through its new `_grade_rollout` call and use `_expired_verifier_grade`. Otherwise the rebase silently restores the old `TIMEOUT` mapping, and the 3-case deadline test is the only thing that would catch it.

topics.title: [inference] remote_inference keeps a stale address after the served task is rescheduled
topics.body:
`remote_inference` resolves the served endpoint's address once (`lib/marin/src/marin/inference/iris.py:682`) and keeps using it for the life of the client. When the inference task is preempted and Iris reschedules it on another host, every later request goes to the dead address and fails with `httpx.ConnectError: All connection attempts failed` until the client process restarts.

Observed on 2026-10-17 in the SFT-shootout relay collection (#10213): the v0 student server for TMax relay shard-02 round 1 (`inference-7998e252`) shows `preemptions=1` and its log stops at 14:35:18 UTC; from then on the relay proxy logged thousands of `ConnectError`s, 198 of 200 trials in that round raised `InternalServerError` between 14:33 and 15:13 UTC, and the driver still wrote `_SUCCESS` because Harbor exited 0. SWE-smith relay shard-00 round 3 failed the same way earlier that morning (85 of 97 trials raised; both student children of that job show `preemptions=1`).

Reproduce: serve a model through `remote_inference`, start a long-lived client, preempt (or cancel and let Iris reschedule) the inference task, send a request after the task is running again on a different host.

Expected: the client re-resolves the endpoint through Iris when a connection error occurs (bounded retry), so a rescheduled server is picked up without restarting the client; callers that cannot recover should fail loudly rather than report success.

Done when: `remote_inference` (or its client wrapper) re-resolves on connection failure with a bounded retry, a test covers a rescheduled endpoint, and callers that batch many requests (relay collection, eval launchers) surface a failed run instead of a success marker when the server is unreachable. The relay collector's own copy of this fix (re-resolve on `ConnectError`, retry up to 20 minutes, then fail the run when over 20% of trials raise) is on branch `task/212` at `174906474a` and can serve as a reference.

- [`runner.py#L460-L472`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/2f3897ebfdbdbc2246bbe0a3bf6bca91a89b6f9d/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/runner.py#L460-L472) — failed record returns as step success

# Proposed Fix

`remote_inference` → `_local_endpoint_session` → lm-eval retains the old URL after Iris moves the serving task. This needs changes at the session, evaluator route, and run-status boundaries:

1. Route Evalchemy model requests through the existing Iris capability URL, which resolves the current endpoint per request; retain the direct URL for metrics. Verify long-request timeouts and measure a representative evaluation's throughput before landing.
2. Add a session-owned direct endpoint resolver and use it in direct HTTP callers on `ConnectError`, with a monotonic deadline, bounded poll interval, and terminal-job check. Make `wait_until_ready()` probe the newly resolved address after rescheduling; propagate failure when the deadline expires.
3. After persisting a non-success evaluation record, raise from `run_evaluation_step` so the enclosing step cannot write a success marker. Reuse the existing Evalchemy/Harbor coverage checks and integrate the relay branch's unserved-trial gate without duplicating it.
4. Test a request across two local serving addresses, a permanently unavailable endpoint, Evalchemy's selected route, and failure propagation through the evaluation step. Run the touched package tests and repository lint before opening a PR.

topics.title: Add a fixed-batch Belay+CPLM TPU baseline
topics.body:
Add a native d512 Belay+CPLM baseline on TPU v4-32 with fixed logical batch 16×8192, EP1 dropless routing and the frozen 10980-update optimizer schedule. The entry point retains Belay's copy head, runs a finite-gradient preflight, initializes online W&B before updates, and preserves separate logs and checkpoint paths for every fresh distributed execution. A 400-update calibration mode measures a drained 300-update window without changing the learning-rate schedule.

The TPU path supports ungated ReLU² experts in local scatter, enables exact QB histogram counting at the 8192×512 local shape, and includes the qualified KDA, Inkling attention, projection, embedding and Muon execution paths. The portable CPLM loss is also proposed separately in #10230. This PR targets `ladderclimb_v1_batch14`, the original Belay development branch; that architecture is not yet in `main`.

The native entry point completed 400 TPU updates at commit `1c4e1b334`: **417400 sustained tokens/s, 5.7162% useful MFU and zero drops**. All 400 losses exactly match the optimized harness, ending at NLL 4.25661278. The drained 300-update window took 94.2059 seconds. The preceding harness measured 416823 and 418299 tokens/s in independent runs, versus 230953 for unoptimized EP1, with the same losses. Every run uses seed 0 and unchanged B16×8192. See the [native W&B curve](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/auto-understanding-arch/runs/upstream-native-v2-fcda5d913e534635a7e99856da23cea1) and [frozen evidence](https://github.com/WhenWen/astra-d8-research/blob/4792fab7/research/belay-mfu-native-ep-result.md). Full-run quality, evaluation/checkpoint endpoints and checkpoint restore remain unvalidated for this port.

Remote non-training numerical checks passed for copy loss, ungated/gated scatter, histograms and blocked attention (32 tests). Required lint/type checks and the advisory lint review passed. Reproduction commands, tokenizer hashes, frozen data identities and evidence links are in `experiments/grug/moe_cplm/README.md`; the complete run record is [research issue #236](https://github.com/WhenWen/astra-d8-research/issues/236).

Preserve the science SFT generation and training recipes used in September and October 2026. The branch includes the three Step38 physical-mix builders and trainers, their checkpoint exporter, the 17-source MiniMax conversion pipeline, and the frozen-snapshot Dr Doom trainer and exporter. topics.title: [taskforge] Add the agentic author that builds through the program build
topics.body:
Add `stage40_build_with_agent`, the agentic author. `author_round` runs one agent session per program round in a workspace that starts with the standard template, the proposal, the SDK reference and an empty notes file. Its tools read, write and edit workspace files, run the loader in a child process, build the program with the caller's own build stage on the same step store, grade a candidate against the last draft, and search and fetch the web when the proposal lists research; `submit` hands the program in. A host failure or an expired clock never reaches the model: the tool retries a `BuildInfrastructureFailure` with backoff and then ends the round without a record, and re-raises a `BuildExpired` at once, so neither spends a revision.

The agent build is a second package at stage 40. It drives the program build through its `run_build` tool, so `test_imports` gains `BUILDS_ON`: `stage40_build_with_agent` may import `stage40_build_with_program` and never the reverse.

Builds on #10298; #10300 builds on it. The taskforge suite passes 591 tests here (24 more than #10298).

comments.body:
🤖 Branch: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/june_10T_run

Contains the launch script (`experiments/grug/moe/moe_may_d2560_10T.py`) and job summary (`experiments/grug/moe/job_summary_d2560_10T.md`) for the d=2560 / 10T-token run on v4-1024 us-central2.

# Job Summary: d=2560 MoE on 10T tokens

Big-batch d=2560 MoE training run on ~10T tokens (~1.2e23 FLOPs), with the May Recipe baked in. Below are sections on model, optimizer, training, scaling principles, and outputs.

## 1. Model

### Hyperparameters

- **hidden_dim**: 2560
- **num_layers**: 26 (heuristic-derived: `round(2560 / (64 + 4·log2(2560) − 9))`)
- **num_heads**: 20 (`hidden_dim / 128`)
- **num_kv_heads**: 5 (GQA 4:1; largest divisor of 20 ≤ 5)
- **head_dim**: 128
- **intermediate_dim**: 1280 (`ceil(d/2/128)·128`)
- **shared_expert_intermediate_dim**: 2560 (= d)
- **num_experts**: 256
- **num_experts_per_token**: 4
- **vocab_size**: 128,256
- **max_seq_len**: 4096
- **sliding_window**: 4096
- **active_params**: 2.34B (2.01B core + 0.33B lm_head; excludes embed per guidelines)
- **total_params**: 67.1B (66.4B core + 0.33B embed + 0.33B lm_head)

### Features

- **GQA**: 4:1 ratio (20 Q heads, 5 KV heads).
- **QB Routing**: stop-gradient bias updated each step from previous step's QB-β statistics (applied inside JIT).
- **Sigmoid Combine Weights**: sigmoid on unbiased router logits for selected experts.
- **GatedNorm**: rank-128 low-rank gating after RMSNorm, pre-attention and pre-MLP.
- **XSA**: subtracts V-parallel component from attention output per head.
- **Attention Gate**: learned per-head sigmoid gate on attention output, initialized to zero.
- **Shared Expert**: dense FFN (d=2560) in parallel with routed experts per layer.
- **Sliding Window**: every 4th layer (plus last) uses full window (4096); others use half (2048).
- **Half-RoPE on every layer**: RoPE applied only to the first half of Q/K per head (`q[..., :head_dim/2]`, `k[..., :head_dim/2]`). The second half is rope-free on every layer.
- **PKO (Partial Key Offset)**: on every-4th + last layer (7 of 26 layers here), the rope-free second half of K is additionally shifted by 1 position with doc-start zeroing.
- **QK Gain**: `qk_mult = 1.3`.
- **Split w_gate / w_up**: separate weight matrices for SwiGLU gate and up projections (`split_w_gate_up=True`).
- **Routing renorm sum**: 2.5 (combined-feature baseline).
- **Router z-loss**: disabled (`router_z_loss_coef = 0`).
- **Expert dispatch**: ring (May Recipe default; `moe_implementation` not exposed in current model config).

## 2. Optimizer

### Hyperparameters

(Using the refit `MoeAdamHHeuristic` from #5951.)

- **adam_lr**: 0.000432  (= `0.06602 · 1e13^-0.395 · 2560^-0.150 · √(2048·4096)`)
- **muonh_lr (= adamh_lr)**: 0.001870  (= adam_lr · 13/3)
- **beta1**: 0.9062
- **beta2**: 0.95 (clamped; `0.999^(2048/32) = 0.938` → clipped up to 0.95)
- **epsilon**: 1.06e−14  (= `1e-15 · √((32·1e13)/(2048·1.4e9))`)
- **weight_decay**: 0
- **max_grad_norm**: None (1pct-noclip schedule)
- **warmup**: 1% (= 11,921 steps)
- **decay**: None (linear schedule decays to 0 over full run)
- **min_lr_ratio**: 0.0
- **lr_schedule**: linear
- **z_loss_weight**: 0.0

### Features

- **MuonH** (`GrugMoeMuonHConfig`): scale-invariant Newton-Schulz updates on the `muonh` group (matmuls + GatedNorms), Frobenius hyperball step on top. Used in place of AdamH on weight matrices.
- **Multi-group optimizer**: 3 groups —
  - `muonh`: attn matmuls, MoE expert matmuls (gate/up/down), shared expert, GatedNorms.
  - `adamh`: lm_head / output_proj (LR = `muonh_lr`).
  - `adam`: token_embed, router weight + bias, attn_gate, 1-D norm weights (LR = `adam_lr`).

## 3. Training

- **hardware**: v4-1024 us-central2 (= 512 chips).
- **num_train_steps**: 1,192,093  (= `1e13 / (2048 · 4096)`)
- **batch_size**: 2,048 sequences
- **seq_len**: 4,096
- **tokens_per_batch**: 8.39M (= `2048 · 4096`)
- **total_tokens**: 1.00e13 (= 10T)
- **compute_budget**: ~1.21e23 FLOPs (= `6 · 2.01e9 · 1e13`)
- **mixed_precision**: `params=float32, compute=bfloat16, output=bfloat16`
- **expert_parallelism**: 4
- **data**: Nemotron mix (block-shuffled) with default validation sets
- **checkpoints**: every 10 minutes (rolling temporary), permanent every 5,000 steps

## 4. Scaling Principles

All optimizer hyperparameters derived from the refit MuonH May Recipe heuristic (issue #5951, R² = 0.996 on 17 cells).

### Learning rates (current heuristic)

- **adam_lr** = `0.06602 · tokens^-0.395 · dim^-0.150 · √(B·seq_len)`, capped at 0.05.
- **muonh_lr** = `(13/3) · adam_lr`.

### Momentum and precision

- **beta1** = 0.9062 (fixed)
- **beta2** = `clip(0.999^(B/32), 0.95, 0.9999)` → 0.95 at B=2048
- **epsilon** = `1e-15 · √((32·T) / (B·1.4e9))`

### Architecture scaling

- **num_layers** = `round(hidden_dim / (64 + 4·log2(hidden_dim) − 9))` → 26 for d=2560
- **num_heads** = `hidden_dim / 128`
- **num_kv_heads** = 4:1 GQA, largest divisor of num_heads ≤ num_heads/4
- **intermediate_dim** = `ceil(hidden_dim / 2 / 128) · 128`
- **shared_expert_intermediate_dim** = hidden_dim
- **initializer_std** = `0.5 / sqrt(hidden_dim)` ≈ 0.00988
- **num_experts** = 256, **num_experts_per_token** = 4 (fixed for May Recipe; differs from the 64-expert v16 baseline used in the 1e23 summary)

### Schedule

- **warmup** = 1% of training (1pct-noclip baseline)
- **decay** = linear all the way to 0 (no separate decay phase)
- **max_grad_norm** = None (no clipping)

## 5. Outputs

- **GCS checkpoint path**: `gs://marin-us-central2/grug/moe_may_d2560_10T/marin-big-run-moe_may_d2560_10T-XXXXXX/checkpoints` (pending — actual hash assigned at submission)
- **WandB run link**: `https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/marin-big-run-moe_may_d2560_10T` (pending)
- **Final eval metrics**: pending (run not submitted yet)
  - eval/paloma/c4_en/bpb
  - eval/paloma/macro_loss
  - eval/uncheatable_eval/macro_loss
- **Throughput** (mean over last 100 logged steps): pending

Many works calculate critical batch size as a function of the token budget. 22.91 · T^0.47 for 10 trillion tokens gives 29.5 million tokens, fit on AdamW. https://arxiv.org/pdf/2505.13738. Specifically, we use an initial batch size of 4M tokens and sequences of length 4,096, and double these values to a batch size of 8M sequences of 8,192 tokens after pre-training 252M tokens. We double the batch size again to 16M after pre-training on 2.87T tokens. We found this training recipe to be very stable: we observed few loss spikes and did not require interventions to correct for model training divergence. The key line here is "We use a lower batch size early in training to improve training stability". The root cause of the issue is that the sharded NS calc in Muon was silently dropping when num_matrices didn't evenly divide into num_chips. This was originally written on v4-1024 where 256*26 is divisible by 512 chips. However it isn't divisible by 1024 chips. The fix was to explicitly replicate the NS calc over the same size as the replica axis, and also patch the silent failure. After doing this, we get stable replication of the v5p-8 d512 200 step run: Increasing precision to fp32 was helping the non orthogonalized approach not diverge, but not addressing the root cause. # Job Summary: 67B / 2B-active MoE 10T pretrain (d=2560, MuonH, v4-2048)

~10.07T-token MuonH MoE pretrain at d=2560 / 67B total params / 2.01B active per token (run_id `moe_67b_a2b_d2560_ep1_rep16_bs4096_seq8192_sw2k_v4_2048_muon_10T`; batch ramp from 4,096 → 8,192 at step 15,000, with total steps reduced so total tokens stay near 10T). Below are sections on model, optimizer, training, and scaling principles.

## 1. Model

### Hyperparameters

- **hidden_dim**: 2560
- **num_layers**: 26
- **num_heads**: 20
- **num_kv_heads**: 5 (GQA 4:1)
- **head_dim**: 128
- **intermediate_dim**: 1280 (MoE expert FFN; `ceil(hidden_dim / 2 / 128) * 128`)
- **shared_expert_intermediate_dim**: 2560 (= hidden_dim)
- **num_experts**: 256
- **num_experts_per_token**: 4
- **vocab_size**: 128,256
- **max_seq_len**: 8,192
- **sliding_window**: 2,048
- **total_params**: 67.1B
- **active_params**: 2.01B per token (2.34B w/ lm_head)

### Features

- **GQA**: 4:1 ratio (20 Q heads, 5 KV heads, head_dim 128)
- **QB Routing**: stop-gradient bias updated each step from previous step's QB-β statistics (applied inside JIT)
- **Sigmoid Combine Weights**: sigmoid on unbiased router logits for the K=4 selected experts (not softmax). Combine weights are then renormalized to sum to **2.5** across the K selected experts (`_ROUTING_RENORM_SUM = 2.5` in `model.py:51`), which effectively rescales the routed-expert contribution per token by 2.5× compared to a standard sum-to-1 (softmax-style) normalization.
- **GatedNorm**: rank-128 low-rank gating after RMSNorm, pre-attention and pre-MLP
- **Shared Expert**: dense FFN (d=2560) in parallel with routed experts per layer
- **Sliding Window**: every 4th layer + final layer uses full window (8,192); the other 19 layers use the short window (2,048). Layout: 7 long / 19 short (`i % 4 == 3 or i == num_layers - 1`).
- **disable_long_rope**: long (full-attention) layers skip rotary embedding entirely. Short (windowed) layers still apply half-RoPE.
- **disable_pko**: no per-key offset on long layers. Plain attention only.
- **RoPE**: partial rotary — only half of `head_dim` is rotated (the leading 64 of 128 dims), the rest is passed through unchanged. Applied on short (windowed) layers only; long (full-attention) layers skip RoPE entirely per `disable_long_rope`.
- **ArrayStacked + scan**: all 26 blocks stacked via `jax.lax.scan` (`use_array_stacked_blocks=True`) for reduced compile time and HBM footprint

## 2. Optimizer

### Hyperparameters

- **muonh_lr**: 0.003733 → **0.005279** at step 15,000 (×√2 with the BS doubling)
- **adam_lr**: 0.000861 → **0.001218** at step 15,000 (= muonh_lr / (13/3); also ×√2)
- **beta1**: 0.9062 (unchanged across the BS ramp)
- **beta2**: 0.95 — clamped both before and after the ramp (raw formula 0.999^(B*S/131072) gives 0.774 pre-ramp and 0.599 post-ramp; both clamp to 0.95)
- **epsilon**: ~8.01 × 10⁻¹⁹ → **~5.66 × 10⁻¹⁹** at step 15,000 (÷√2 with the BS doubling)
- **weight_decay**: 0
- **max_grad_norm**: None (no clipping in MuonH 1pct-noclip schedule)
- **warmup**: 0.01 (1% of training; ~3,000 steps)
- **decay**: None (linear decay over the whole post-warmup period)
- **min_lr_ratio**: 0.05 (decay to 5% of peak by end-of-training)
- **lr_schedule**: linear
- **z_loss_weight**: 1e-4 (logit z-loss; router z-loss = 0)

### Features

- **MuonH (Muon + Frobenius hyperball)**: Newton-Schulz orthogonalization on weight matrices followed by a scale-invariant Frobenius-hyperball projection. Three LR groups:
  - **muonh** — 2D weight matrices and stacked MoE expert weights (NS + hyperball)
  - **adamh** — `lm_head` / `output_proj`. AdamH = Adam moments + Frobenius hyperball (`scale_by_adamh`); no Newton-Schulz. Uses the same LR schedule as muonh.
  - **adam** — biases, RMSNorm scales, router weights, gated-norm scales, and (via `rmsnorm_to_adam=True`) stacked RMSNorm scales
- **Multi-group optimizer**: separate optax chains per group routed by parameter path (see `experiments/grug/moe/optimizer.py:create_mask`).
- **Logit Z-Loss**: penalizes large output-logit norm to stabilize training (no router z-loss in this run).

## 3. Training

- **hardware**: v4-2048 (1,024 chips), us-central2, production priority, --no-preemptible
- **num_train_steps**: 157,500 (reduced from 300,000 to absorb the batch-size doubling and hold total tokens ~constant)
- **batch_size**: 4,096 → 8,192 sequences (step change at step 15,000 ≈ 5% of training)
- **seq_len**: 8,192
- **tokens_per_step**: 33,554,432 (~33.5M) for steps 0–14,999; 67,108,864 (~67.1M) for steps 15,000–157,499
- **total_tokens**: ~1.007 × 10¹³ (~10.07T) — 5.03 × 10¹¹ from the BS=4,096 phase (15,000 steps) + 9.56 × 10¹² from the BS=8,192 phase (142,500 steps)
- **compute_budget**: ~1.69 × 10²³ FLOPs (SWA-aware, with lm_head)
- **mixed_precision**: `params=float32,compute=bfloat16,output=bfloat16`
- **mesh**: `(replica_dcn=16, data=64, expert=1, model=1)`. EP=1, `replica_axis_size=16`. Batch is sharded across (replica_dcn, data, expert) → 1,024 shards.
- **expert_parallelism**: 1 (no expert sharding; routed experts replicated across the expert axis)
- **data**: datakit MoE mixture (`_datakit_data_config`, simulated epoching disabled) with default paloma validation sets
- **eval cadence**: every 3,000 steps; `eval_batch_size=1024`, `max_eval_batches=1` (8.39M tokens per eval)
- **checkpoints**: permanent every 3,000 steps; temp save every 60 minutes; auto-resume on preemption

## 4. Scaling Principles

All optimizer hyperparameters derived from the MuonH May Recipe refit (issue #5951, 17 finished cells across d ∈ {512, 768, 1024, 1280} × R ∈ {4, 10, 20, 60, 120, 240} × lr_mult ∈ {0.4, 0.7, 1.0, 1.3, 1.6}, R² = 0.996). Reference seq_len = 4096; conversions assume `tokens_per_batch = batch_size * seq_len`.

### Learning rates

- **muonh_lr** = `18.31 · T^(-0.395) · d^(-0.150) · sqrt(B)`, capped at 0.05
  - Equivalent to `lr_coeff · T^(-0.395) · d^(-0.150) · sqrt(tokens_per_batch)` with `lr_coeff = 0.06602` (= 18.31 / ((13/3) · 64))
  - At T = 1.007e13, d = 2560, B*S = 33.55M → **muonh_lr ≈ 0.003733**
- **adam_lr** = muonh_lr / (13/3) ≈ **0.000861**
- **adamh_lr** = muonh_lr ≈ **0.003733** (the `adamh` group — `lm_head` / `output_proj` — uses the same LR schedule as muonh, via `scale_by_adamh`: Adam moments + Frobenius hyperball, no Newton-Schulz)

### Momentum and precision

- **beta1** = 0.9062 (fixed)
- **beta2** = `clip(0.999^(tokens_per_batch / 131072), 0.95, 0.9999)`
  - At B*S = 33.55M → raw 0.999^256 ≈ 0.774 → clamped to **0.95**
- **epsilon** = `9.676e-18 · sqrt((B0 · T) / (tokens_per_batch · T0))` with B0=32, T0=1.4e9
  - At T = 1.007e13, tokens_per_batch = 33.55M → **epsilon ≈ 8.01e-19**

### Architecture scaling

- **num_layers** = `round(hidden_dim / (64 + 4·log2(hidden_dim) - 9))` = 26 for d=2560
- **num_heads** = `hidden_dim / 128` = 20
- **num_kv_heads** = largest divisor of num_heads ≤ num_heads // 4 = 5 (GQA 4:1)
- **intermediate_dim** = `ceil(hidden_dim / 2 / 128) · 128` = 1280
- **shared_expert_intermediate_dim** = hidden_dim = 2560
- **initializer_std** ≈ `0.5 / sqrt(2560)` ≈ 0.00988
- **num_experts** = 256, **num_experts_per_token** = 4 (fixed; differs from the 1e23 d=5120 run which used 64 experts)

### Schedule

- **warmup** = 1% of training (~3,000 steps)
- **decay** = none (linear schedule decays over the whole post-warmup period)
- **min_lr_ratio** = 0.05 (decay to 5% of peak)
- **lr_schedule** = linear

Notable updates to architecture:
1. Since we are planning to extend context out to 262k, there will likely be several iterations on datamix and attention scaling to enable this. To minimize possible confounders during this process, PKO has been disabled, along with RoPE on the global layers. This puts our architecture close to published literature on effective long context extension. Once we have successfully extended context using textbook approaches, then we can consider adding back partial rope and PKO. We may be incurring a 10-20% efficiency hit from this, but the risk/reward tradeoff here of taking a controlled approach seems worthwhile to maximize learnings and our later models.
2. Re-adding final logit z loss. At compute optimal scale, z loss had a neglible impact. However on the new data mix and extreme overtrain, we see meaningful gains from including z loss, both on the train loss and evals. https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/reports/Z-Loss-Under-OverTrain-650B-tokens---VmlldzoxNzMyODk1NQ.
3. Batch size schedule. The hardware profile is heavily encouraging us to run at extremely large batch sizes to achieve acceptable MFU. Instead of performing the full run at 67 million tokens per batch, we are running the first 5 pct at half that. Which is the window when smaller batch sizes have the biggest impact.
4. LR decay to 0.05 instead of 0. This is because we will extend out from 64k->262k, and do subsequent posttrain. decay to zero is only optimal if we have no subsequent weight updates.

### Data-position continuation (new mechanism)

Prior cooldowns (step-39k, step-102k) used a fresh mix-2 shuffle from position 0. This one continues main run's mix-2 stream *exactly*:

- Main run consumed **905.97 B mix-2 tokens** between steps 127,500 → 141,000 (13,500 steps × 8,192 seq × 8,192 BS).
- Cooldown at seq=65,536 wants to start at the same underlying token offset → sample-index **13,824,000**.
- New `resume_data_offset` field on `GrugMoeLaunchConfig2xBS` builds a 3-stage BatchSchedule `[(0, 98), (135000, 99), (141000, 1024)]` that lands `cumulative_size(141000)` at exactly 13,824,000 samples. Zero re-consumption of main run's exposure, zero skip past it.
- Per-bucket read positions in each of the 168 mix-2 buckets exactly continue where main run left off; the mixture-shuffle order differs (unavoidable: mixture-shuffle indexes are in cooldown's seq_len enumeration, which is 8× the main run's).
- 12 small-weight buckets will epoch during the 1 T cooldown budget (aggregate ~1.3% extra re-exposure; largest is `c34q4` at 2.88×).

## Design spec

- **seq_len**: 65,536 → **262,144** (4× extension).
- **BS**: 1024 → **256** sequences → tokens/step stays at 256 · 262,144 = 67.1 M (matches the step-141k cooldown's per-step token budget).
- **Steps**: 1,000 (step 156,000 → 157,000) → **67.1 B tokens** total.
- **LR**: linear decay from 5 % of source peak (0.000264, matches cooldown exit LR) → 1 % of source peak (0.0000528), no ramp. Implementation pins the resume schedule's abstract "peak" to 0.000264 with `min_lr_ratio=0.2` so the floor lands at exactly `0.000264 · 0.2 = 0.0000528`.
- **qk_mult**: 1.75 (`1.3 · (0.1·ln(32) + 1) = 1.7506`, rounded) vs. 1.57 (held from the step-141k cooldown, which used `1.3 · (0.1·ln(8) + 1) = 1.5703`). Both applied Q-only as a single logit multiplier (one-sided YaRN; note this delivers `mscale` on logits, not the paper's `mscale²`).
- **Data continuation**: exact per-token — `resume_data_offset = (13,500·8,192·8,192 + 15,000·1,024·65,536) / 262,144 = 7,296,000` samples. The launcher builds a 3-stage BS schedule `[(0, 46), (36000, 47), (156000, 256)]` that hits exactly 7,296,000 cumulative samples at step 156,000 (zero re-consumption AND zero skip). Post-run cumulative mix-2 consumption = **1.980 T tokens** (98.99% of the 2 T mix-2 design budget).
- **Checkpoints / evals**: every 250 steps (4 total: 156,250 / 156,500 / 156,750 / 157,000).
- **Mesh** on v4-2048 (1024 chips): `(replica_dcn=1, data=256, context=4, expert=1, model=1)`. `batch_shards = replica · data · expert = 256`, `per_device_parallelism = 1`. `context_axis_size = 4` shards the seq axis → `seq_per_device = 65,536` (identical chip-local seq to the step-141k cooldown, our known-good memory point).

## Context-parallel implementation

Landed on this branch as a self-contained addition; `context_axis_size = 1` is a no-op vs. the pre-CP code path.

- **Mesh axis** (`lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/sharding.py`): added `"context"` to `_GRUG_MESH_AXIS_NAMES`; `compact_grug_mesh` now takes `context_axis_size`. `_batch_axes()` returns the full flat-token axes and now includes `"context"` when present so MoE psums / shard_maps reduce over the correct set.
- **Grug MoE model** (`experiments/grug/moe/model.py`): seq axis on Q / residual stream / MLP / embed / output_proj sharded on `"context"` via helpers `_seq_spec_3d` / `_seq_spec_4d` / `_token_spec`. K/V explicitly resharded to seq=`None` before splash (splash's TPU entry refuses `kv_seq_shards > 1`), i.e. the **all-gather-KV** flavor of CP.
- **RoPE cache**: `_apply_half_rope` reshards its precomputed cos/sin to `P(None, "context", None, None)` so the per-shard broadcast against context-sharded Q/K lines up.
- **Segment IDs**: `Transformer.__call__` reshards q_seg to `P(_BATCH_AXES, "context")` and kv_seg to `P(_BATCH_AXES, None)` before passing the mask to splash, so splash's per-shard segment-id shape check matches.
- **Router / QB shard_map**: uses `_token_axes()` (batch + context) for the shard_map in_specs and `pmean` so the QB threshold pmean reduces across both data and context shards.
- **Splash kernel wrapping** (`lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/attention/_core.py`): the splash kernel is now passed as an input to `shard_map` with its own `manual_sharding_spec` (mirroring the classical levanter path). Prior closure-capture would leave `fwd_mask_info.q_sequence` at global shape, and splash's forward broadcast would fail against the local `q_seq_len`. Each mask_info leaf is `jax.reshard`ed to the manual spec before the shard_map, since shard_map now rejects mismatched in_specs.
- **(B,S)↔(B*S) reshapes**: `_flatten_bs` / `_unflatten_bs` helpers wrap `jnp.reshape` with explicit `out_sharding` (`_token_spec()` and `_seq_spec_3d()` respectively). einops's `rearrange` goes through `array.reshape()` with no sharding hint, which JAX can't lower when two sharded axes fuse into one.
- **Trainer mesh** (`experiments/grug/moe/launch_2x_bs.py`): passes `"context": context_axis_size` into the TrainerConfig's `MeshConfig` so `data_axis_size` (used for the BS-divisibility check) reflects only the actual batch shards.
- **Loss parity** verified at `context = {1, 2, 4}` for a small config: identical loss at c=2, bf16-precision noise (~1e-6) at c=4.

- Known artifact: `wikitext_103` and `ptb` paloma tags read `0.0` in both runs. Root cause: `TokenSeqDataset.async_len = total_tokens // seq_len` uses integer division, so any val cache smaller than one 262k window (wikitext_103 ~247k tokens, ptb ~86k tokens) yields **0** eval sequences. Not a training bug; only affects small paloma tags at long seq_len.

Recommendation:
Run multiple experiments, varying the following factors:
- qk_mult. This specifies the attention 'sharpness' (how strongly can it natively pick out a single target). It started at 1.3 during 8k seqlen, then was bumped to 1.57 during 65k seqlen. This is a softer version of yarn mscale. For 262k, could hold at 1.57, or bump to ~1.75 or 2. Increasing may help on longer documents and slightly hurt on shorter documents. Previously tried an experiment bumping it only on global layers, didn't help. (However may be worth it on this 65k->262k extension)
- number of steps. Defaulting to 1k. 67B tokens. Can be varied.
- LR schedule. Defaulting to linear decay from 5 pct peak to 1 pct peak.
- Checkpoint averaging. Am saving checkpoints every 250 steps during this cooldown. EMA over these may give stronger final model.
- Data. First two experiments were on the exact same mix2 from this run, continuing off from where last step was. Alternatively, can upweight long context data (data over 65k seqlen). Or, swap to datamix we are using on the 535B hero run.

Checkpoints exist for the two tests above, both they don't have a long context eval in wandb. This will be good to be comparing against. Need to debug and fix the 0 eval score for the evals with under 262k context length.

topics.title: [storage] Route shared CoreWeave scratch to US-EAST-08A
topics.body:
Route temporary writes from every CoreWeave cluster to the separate `s3://marin-us-east-08a` scratch bucket. Keep permanent output roots in `marin-us-east-02a` and `marin-us-west-04a`. The d6144 hero explicitly keeps rolling checkpoint writes and resume searches in `hero-checkpoints`.

Resolve scratch storage by backend on launch hosts and workers, preserving explicit per-job overrides. CoreWeave resume searches include permanent storage, the new scratch destination, and former scratch roots in the output bucket and `hero-checkpoints`, so resubmitted runs can find their newest complete checkpoint. Explicit restore paths remain authoritative.

Remove R2 from shared job storage configuration, CoreWeave CI fixtures, and Datakit sync routing. Use the bucket registry for Datakit sync credentials, endpoint, and signing region. Keep the existing R2 bucket and lifecycle resources declared independently in the bucket stack. Finelog archive and Ducky query configuration are outside this change.

Manage the scratch bucket's nine TTL prefixes (1–7, 14, and 30 days) and seven-day multipart cleanup through `marin-buckets`. The live bucket, lifecycle configuration, and organization access policy are adopted with deletion protection. Existing jobs retain their launch environment; controller defaults take effect after deployment. After releases of `marin-rigging` and `marin-core` containing the routing, configuration, and checkpoint discovery changes, update the affected dependency locks in MarinSkyRL, Harbor, and Evalchemy.

topics.title: [grug] Add the quality-classifier fast track
topics.body:
* add the quality-classifier fast track: for each rung budget `B`, score the first `10·B` tokens of a fixed raw pool, keep the top whole documents until they fill `B`, and train the fast-track ladder on them
  * this PR holds only the quality track from #9371 [^1]
* `corpus_sample_cli` builds a `RawCorpusPool` from the registered DataKit sources in proportion to corpus size with `corpus-id-interval-v1`: one seeded cyclic interval in the 128-bit document-ID space for each source. it skips a row group only when its ID statistics show no overlap
  * `--label-exclusion-manifest` is required, so the pool contains no labelled duplicate group
  * one map task reads 64 normalized shards, with 128 workers. a 291-source pool has 149,717 shards. one task for each shard with 8 workers did about 100 shards a minute, and each reducer had to merge one scatter output per shard. the 10.7B-token pool now takes 25 min
* `quality_labels_cli` freezes the GLM-5.2 labels and fits a ridge head on cached Harrier features (target `(quality - 1) / 4`, 80/10/10 split by duplicate group)
* `quality_cli --stage features|score|select|train` scores the pool one time at the largest rung, then selects and trains each rung from the same `ScoredPool`
  * `--selection-method candidate|incumbent|random`. `random` ranks the same `10·B` prefix by a seeded hash and is the matched control
  * a custom scorer is a `module:factory` that returns a `DocumentQualityScorer`, with a JSON `--classifier-identity`
  * the selected documents keep the raw-pool order, so scores do not change the training order
  * the feature stage joins the complete Harrier pins (`hero_data.pinned_map("harrier")`, not the `hero_data.harrier` `StepSpec`) and converts only the selected rows of each row group [^2]
* gate the quality track on downstream capability, not on Paloma macro loss [^4]
  * `downstream_eval` scores a saved dense checkpoint on one H100: 13 OLMES-style cloze tasks (per-choice log-likelihood, acc, acc_norm, correct-answer BPB), gold-answer BPB on GSM8K, MATH-500, HumanEval, and MBPP, and Paloma/Uncheatable loss by token class, by context length, and on fixed targets at 128–3968 tokens of context. the tasks are a frozen copy (`downstream-cloze-v3`, 20,472 cloze examples)
  * the code and math gold answers have no format tokens: MBPP code has `\n` line ends and no spaces at line ends (same Python AST for 500 of 500), and GSM8K has no `<<48/2=24>>` calculator annotations [^5]
  * `quality_judge` compares a candidate with its matched random control on English knowledge, English commonsense, code, math, and long context, with Welch t intervals: the seed variance of the per-run gains of each arm plus a bootstrap over paired examples [^6]. better = weighted gain of English, code, math above 0 at the lower bound and no group below its harm limit (1% per English group, 2% for the others)
  * `quality_cli --save-checkpoints` keeps the final checkpoint for the scorer. the model ladder keeps Paloma macro
* loss-validity study: 99 dense runs, 14 probe selections (`probe_scorers.py` plus a local production fusion-score probe), d512/d768 with 3 seeds, d1280 with random ×3 and four selections ×2, judge frozen on d512 before d768/d1280 ([report](https://claude.ai/artifact/46KvN5W9qp7rMnMPCdcNc9)). all numbers use the v3 tasks
  * Paloma macro ordered selection pairs like the capability target on 32% (d512), 40% (d768), and 11% (d1280) of pairs, 23% and 32% at d512/d768 without the longest-documents probe. Uncheatable macro: 84%, 76%, 44%. no single held-out loss passed at every rung
  * with all 138 runs, the positive controls included: Paloma macro 28%, 35%, 16% (25 pairs at d1280), Uncheatable macro 84%, 78%, 68%
  * dirty web (Nemotron-CC medium tiers + HPLT) at d1280: Paloma −1.5%, c4_en −6.2%, but cloze BPB +2.5%, acc_norm −0.6 pt, code gold BPB +181%
  * shortest documents at d1280: acc_norm +2.0 pt, but Paloma +10.9%, because on fixed targets its loss at 3968 tokens of context is 58% worse than random
  * quality classifiers (GLM ridge head, production fusion score) trade commonsense for knowledge: fusion within source quotas at d1280 gains 2.0% on knowledge BPB but loses 8.9% on commonsense and 4.7% on math; ridge at d1280 gains ARC-Easy +2.0 pt and loses HellaSwag −2.4 pt and LAMBADA −11.4 pt. no probe beat random
  * whitespace-heavy selection lowers the whitespace part of the Paloma loss, but not Paloma macro, so format gives no false gain when the track only filters documents
  * held-out losses have 0.2–0.3% seed SD (d512/d768), cloze BPB 1.2–1.5%. the decisions transfer: the three d1280 selections get the d512 and d768 decision
* positive control: `probe_scorers:dclm_fasttext_web` ranks the raw web documents by the public DCLM fastText classifier and takes 60% of the web tokens, against a random 60% (`web_only`)
  * 12 seeds per arm at d512: `better`, G +2.2% [+1.7, +2.7], knowledge, commonsense, code, and math up. Paloma macro is 0.2% worse and c4_en 1.1% worse, so a Paloma gate rejects a published good classifier
  * 3 seeds: G +2.0% (d512), +4.0% [+2.6, +5.4] (d768), +4.1% (d1280), all `inconclusive`, because a knowledge or commonsense interval is wider than its 1% harm limit
  * a local FineWeb-Edu classifier probe with 12 seeds at d512 gives G +1.5% [+0.9, +2.1] but commonsense −2.1% [−3.0, −1.2], so the judge says `worse`, and a rule on G alone accepts it. SmolLM2 also reports this commonsense loss. with 3 seeds at d768: G +3.4%, commonsense −1.0% [−1.7, −0.3], Paloma macro 1.4% worse
  * in the full pool web is 17% of the tokens, and the same classifier on the web sources gives G +0.3% (d512), +0.4% (d768), and +0.4% [−0.9, +1.8] (d1280), which three seeds cannot resolve
* seed test, planned before the runs: 9 more seeds (27 runs) for `web_only`, `dclm_web`, and `fineweb_edu_web` at d512, so 12 per arm
  * A/A on the 12 `web_only` runs: the percentile bootstrap that the judge used before said `better` for 5.5% of 3-seed pairs, and each bound missed 0 in about 10% (target 2.5%). the Welch t judge: 0.6% `better` at 3 seeds, 1.4% at 6, bounds miss 0.4–3.2%. a 10,000-experiment simulation agrees
  * the knowledge seed SD of one run is 2.3%, against a 1% harm limit, so knowledge sets the seed count. the README gives `16 s² / (g + h)²` seeds per arm for 80% power: 24 for a 0.9% knowledge gain, 86 for none. use 3 seeds only to rank search candidates. the count is fixed before the runs, and `inconclusive` does not accept
  * with the Welch t judge, 4 of 38 decisions against random move from `worse` to `inconclusive`: a harm near its limit, or 2 seeds at d1280. the large harms stay `worse`
* add `fast-track-long-string-v1` for raw-corpus tokenization: split at the first whitespace at or after 10,000 characters, and reject a document above 64 MiB with its source and ID
  * bound native tokenizer batches by bytes, from #10419. a local 32 MiB probe kept all 19,532,169 token IDs, and peak RSS went from 4.60 GiB to 2.85 GiB
* `launch.py` resolves the rung budget in `resolve_h100_ladder_budget` and takes a `TrainingSource`, so the quality track uses the same training wiring as `fast-track`
  * add `--seed` and `--data-seed`. `--submit` forwards `WANDB_MODE` and accepts `WANDB_MODE=disabled` without `WANDB_API_KEY`
  * the quality CLIs default to MoE and `d512`, and derive `--data-seed` from `--seed`
* the library fixes of the validation runs are in their own PRs: #10416 (fray actor concurrency), #10417 (levanter eval telemetry), #10418 (artifact load paths), #10419 (tokenizer batches and `tokenizer_content_hash`), #10420 (iris CUDA files and coordinator names), #10421 (datakit CPU group)
  * this PR keeps the #10418 and #10419 changes until they merge, because the quality track loads nested artifacts and imports `tokenizer_content_hash`. the files are the same as in those PRs
  * grug dispatch forwards `WANDB_MODE`
* validation on `cw-us-east-02a`: one 10,695,475,362-token pool from the 291 sources other than `stack-v3`, scored one time at d768, dense models, final eval loss from the training logs [^3]

  | run | selection | Paloma macro | Uncheatable macro |
  |---|---|---:|---:|
  | d512 control, tie seed 0 / tie seed 1 / model seed 1 | random | 3.704 / 3.699 / 3.682 | 3.264 / 3.264 / 3.245 |
  | d512 ridge head | top `B` | 4.017 (+8.7%) | 3.353 (+2.9%) |
  | d512 inverted ridge head | top `B` of `-score` | 3.706 (+0.3%) | 3.513 (+7.8%) |
  | d512 longest documents | top `B` by UTF-8 bytes | 4.262 (+15.3%) | 3.871 (+18.8%) |
  | d512 shortest documents | bottom `B` by UTF-8 bytes | 3.781 (+2.3%) | 3.248 (−0.3%) |
  | d768 control | random | 3.296 | 2.791 |
  | d768 ridge head | top `B` | 3.597 (+9.1%) | 2.868 (+2.8%) |

  * changes are against the mean of the three d512 controls, or against the d768 control. a new random selection moved Paloma loss by 0.005, and a new model seed by 0.022. the d512 control is near the Hero-cache baseline (3.676)
  * each rung prefix is 10.00·B, each selection is at most one document above `B`, and the random selections have the source mix and mean ridge score of their prefix (0.6097 against 0.6095)
  * the ridge head is a domain filter: its selection has a mean score of 0.818, moves tokens from `finetranslations` and medium-quality web to PDFs, books, and synthetic QA, and improves s2orc (−7.0%) and arXiv physics (−7.6%) but not social text (Twitter +19.0%). the inverted head gives the opposite change on each of these datasets
  * the longest selection is 862 documents (mean 420k tokens, SEC filings, books, PDFs). the shortest selection is 1,223,195 documents (mean 296 tokens)
* known limits
  * `stack-v3` has documents of 79–213 MB, above the 64 MiB limit, so a pool from all 292 sources stops with an error. select the other sources with `--source` until a policy exists
  * the feature stage reads almost all Harrier data, because one Harrier row group holds about 127k rows and a pool samples each one
  * the pool excludes only the candidate's labels, not the training labels of an incumbent scorer

[^1]: #9371 keeps the Hero-mix track and the `max_train_sequences` rename. it can rebase on this PR after merge.
[^2]: the complete pins from #8270 agree with the normalized shards in shard names, row counts, and ID order. the join compares each ID and stops on a difference.
[^3]: the inverted-head and length probes in this table are in `probe_scorers.py`. W&B ran offline.
[^4]: a selection moves the training mix, and Paloma has its own fixed mix (web-heavy, long documents), so a selection can move Paloma without moving downstream capability. the GLM ridge head and the fusion score are still worse than random or inconclusive under the judge at every rung.
[^5]: 499 of 500 MBPP gold solutions use `\r\n`. in web-only models `\r` tokens carried 25–56% of the MBPP bits, and at d1280 they made the DCLM selection look 22% worse on code and gave `worse` (G −5.8%), while HumanEval had DCLM 7% better. MBPP and GSM8K were scored again on 133 checkpoints with the judge and its limits unchanged: one of 18 judge decisions changed, the d1280 pair above. one merged checkpoint matched a fresh full evaluation exactly.
[^6]: with three runs per arm, the percentile bootstrap over runs and examples covered about 80% at a nominal 95%. the Welch degrees of freedom come from the seed part only.

🤖 Thank you. The two concerns had different results:

- `hero_data.harrier` returns a `StepSpec`: this is correct, and it is a real bug on current main. Commit 7b3728aa2 joins the relative path from `hero_data.pinned_map("harrier")` to `hero_data.MANIFEST_PREFIX`, the same rule that the raw pool uses for normalized paths. A new test checks the resolved paths. Commit db6cb6e18 corrects the scoring test, because it replaced `hero_data.harrier` with a string path and hid the bug.
- Row offsets after a dedup filter: this does not apply to the pinned features. The pins point to the complete `datakit/embed/harrier-all/...` outputs from #8270, not to the deduplicated `datakit/embed/harrier/...` outputs. #8270 records that the complete outputs agree with the normalized shards in shard names, row counts, and sampled ID order. The join also compares each Harrier ID with the normalized ID and raises an error if they differ, so a different pin stops the run before it can select wrong data.

🤖 Holistic review of 1b566cc4a80a8ed63ab995cdf68777c59d286284.

> **In short:** The diff adds a quality-classifier track to fast-track: it samples a raw pool, scores it, selects the top `B` tokens, and trains a rung. It also carries seven independent fixes in iris, fray, levanter, and marin. Item 1 recommends moving those fixes to their own PRs. The track works as stated, but its pool skips decontamination and dedup (item 3).

### System
```mermaid
flowchart TB
  subgraph dk["DataKit pins"]
    N["normalized shards (hero_data_paths.json)"]
    HR["Harrier embeddings (pinned_map)"]
  end
  subgraph ft["experiments/grug/fast_track"]
    CS["corpus_sample_cli → RawCorpusPool"]:::added
    QL["quality_labels_cli → ridge head + label_exclusion"]:::added
    QF["quality_features"]:::added
    QP["quality_pipeline: score → select → token cache"]:::added
    L["launch.py: TrainingSource"]:::changed
  end
  subgraph libs["shared libraries"]
    TK["levanter.tokenizers"]:::changed
    FR["fray / iris actor server"]:::changed
    JX["iris.jax.init"]:::changed
  end
  N -->|"ID-interval sample"| CS
  QL -->|"exclusion manifest"| CS
  CS -->|"10·B prefix"| QP
  HR --> QF --> QP
  QP -->|"QualityTrainingSource"| L
  CS --> TK
  classDef changed fill:#fde7c8,stroke:#e8710a,stroke-width:2px
  classDef added fill:#d7f0dd,stroke:#1e8e3e,stroke-width:2px
```

### Why
The fast-track ladder could only measure model changes on a frozen Hero cache. This PR adds a track that holds the model fixed and changes the document scorer, so a classifier is judged by final Paloma macro loss. It splits the quality half out of #9371, and it builds on the complete Harrier pins from #8270.

### Current state
Before the change, `launch.py` was the only entry point. It trained a dense or MoE H100 rung (d512 to d1280) on one frozen Hero v16384 flat cache through `_flat_cache_data_config`. `--match data|compute` set the budget, the seed was fixed at 0, and `--submit` re-ran the command as an Iris job with `--reserve H100`. Nothing in fast-track selected data. DataKit already pins per-source `decontam`, `exact_dups`, `verified_fuzzy_dups`, and `fusion_scores` attributes (`experiments/datakit/hero_data.py:70-75,136-141`), and the DataKit store removes the flagged documents. Iris actor servers always ran 32 method threads, whatever `ActorConfig.max_concurrency` said.

### How
**The pool is a seeded interval of the 128-bit document-ID space, per source, so source shares follow token mass without a full scan.** Row groups are skipped only when their ID statistics exclude the interval (`corpus_sample.py:187-196`). Each map task reads 64 shards.

**Each rung scores the first `10·B` raw tokens and keeps whole documents up to `B`, in raw-pool order.** `random` ranks the same prefix by a seeded hash, so it is the matched control. A selection holds at most one document above `B` (`ranked_pool.py:142-150`).

**A scorer is a worker-loaded `module:factory` with a JSON identity, and one `ScoredPool` at the largest rung serves every rung.**
```python
# experiments/grug/fast_track/quality_pipeline.py
identity = {
    "raw_pool": raw_pool.name,
    "classifier_identity": candidate.identity,
    "label_exclusion": label_exclusion.identity(),
    "token_budget": token_budget,
    ...
}
step_name = content_step_name("scored-pool", identity, version)
```

**Labels are frozen, and a ridge head is fit on cached Harrier features with an 80/10/10 split by duplicate group.** The pool build requires the label-exclusion manifest at the CLI.

The fixes that ride along: actor concurrency passthrough, JAX coordinator names, CUDA `ptxas` repair, tokenizer batch limits and a content hash, eval-metric sampling in telemetry, `raw_load` context, and the DataKit CPU group. The fast-track tests (54) and the affected iris, fray, levanter, and dispatch unit tests pass locally at head. The PR states the validation table from runs on `cw-us-east-02a`.

### Limitations
- **`stack-v3`:** its 79–213 MB documents exceed the 64 MiB limit, so a pool from all 292 sources fails. Each run must list the other sources with `--source`.
- **Validation evidence:** the probe scorers and the selection report are scratch code, and W&B ran offline, so nothing in the repository reproduces the table.
- **Domain, not quality:** the PR states that the ridge head acts as a domain filter (PDFs and books up, social text down). A Paloma gain can therefore come from domain shift.
- **Incumbent labels:** the pool excludes only the candidate's labels, not the training labels of an incumbent scorer.
- **Harrier reads:** the feature stage reads almost all Harrier data, because one row group holds about 127k rows.

### Review

**Should fix**
1. `lib/fray/src/fray/iris_backend.py:333` The diff carries seven library fixes that do not depend on the quality track: actor concurrency (fray/iris), `iris/jax/init.py:275` coordinator names, `iris/cluster/setup_scripts.py:173-188` CUDA repair, `levanter/tokenizers.py:644-681` batch limits, `levanter/tracker/telemetry.py:199-206`, `marin/execution/artifact.py:148`, and `marin/datakit/__init__.py:12`. Their owners cannot review them inside a 6k-line experiments PR, and #9371 carries byte-identical copies. Move each fix to its own PR, and keep only the fast-track code here.
2. `lib/fray/src/fray/iris_backend.py:333,742` `ActorConfig.max_concurrency` defaults to 1 (`fray/types.py:578`). Iris used to ignore it, so every actor that uses the default config goes from 32 threads to 1, which can deadlock an actor that calls itself. `LocalClient` still ignores the value, so the two backends now differ. The in-repo callers (Zephyr 100, inference broker 32) set it explicitly. Change the `ActorConfig` default to the old 32, or pass it through only when the caller sets it. Add a fray test that checks the value reaches `ActorServer`. The current test stubs the server with `lambda **_kwargs`.
3. `experiments/grug/fast_track/corpus_sample.py:349-353` The pool globs the normalized shards with no `decontam`, `exact_dups`, or `verified_fuzzy_dups` filter, while the Hero cache it is compared against applies them. A scorer can then select Paloma-overlapping documents, or many copies of one high-scoring document, at a different rate than the random control. Filter `_sample_records` with the pinned attributes from `hero_data`, and add those pins to `_spec_identity`.
4. `experiments/grug/fast_track/quality_pipeline.py:778-790` The scored-pool identity hashes the user-supplied `--classifier-identity` but not the `--scorer-factory` path. Two different factories with the same identity JSON silently share one cached `ScoredPool`. Put the factory path into `ScorerSpec` and into the identity.
5. `experiments/grug/fast_track/ranked_pool.py:49-64` `write_parquet_tables` duplicates `zephyr.writers.write_parquet_file` (`lib/zephyr/src/zephyr/writers.py:378`) through a Python `StoragePath.open("wb")` sink. The zephyr writer's own comment (`writers.py:338-346`) says this sink copies whole pages and has pushed workers over their memory limit. The token cache rows here carry `input_ids` for documents of up to 64 MiB. Use `write_parquet_file` at the five call sites.
6. `experiments/grug/fast_track/quality_pipeline.py:483-648` Rank keys are unique (source and ID), so "top `B` whole documents" is "every row with key ≤ k\*", where k\* is the key at which the cumulative tokens first reach `B`. Sort the `(key, token_count)` pairs, find k\*, and filter the raw prefix in one pass in raw order. This deletes `_summarize_scores`, `_score_range`/`_random_range`, and the second group-by.
7. `experiments/grug/fast_track/corpus_sample.py:272` The normalized ID is `xxh3_128(text)` (`marin/datakit/normalize.py:125`), so the `sha256(text)` `duplicate_group` marks the same documents as the ID, and the ID check at `corpus_sample.py:268` already excludes them. Key the exclusion and `label_split` on the normalized ID, and drop the column and the per-document SHA-256 (`label_exclusion.py:21`, `quality_labels.py:207`).
8. `lib/levanter/src/levanter/tokenizers.py:781` `tokenizer_content_hash` hashes the whole staged directory. A leftover `.tmp`, or a mirror staging that copies more files than the HF allow-patterns, changes the hash, and `require_tokenizer_content` (`contracts.py:76`) then fails the run. An HF cache snapshot with symlinks raises. Its only callers are in fast-track. Move it to `experiments/grug/fast_track/contracts.py`, and hash only the `tokenizer*.json` files.
9. `experiments/grug/fast_track/quality_labels.py:34-37` The default label inputs are in personal scratch prefixes (`marin/user/rav/...`, `marin/user/muchanem/...`). The frozen-label artifact then depends on files that their owners can delete. Copy them under `datakit/`, and pin that path.
10. `experiments/grug/fast_track/corpus_sample_cli.py:25` `--max-training-tokens` defaults to 17,478,713,344, which requests a 175B-token raw pool. That is 16× the 10.7B pool that was validated, which took 25 minutes. Also, `CorpusSampleSpec.label_exclusion` defaults to `None` (`corpus_sample.py:77`), so the exclusion is required only at the CLI. Make both explicit.

**Tests to drop**
11. `test_pinned_feature_sources_resolve_complete_harrier_paths` (`test_quality_features.py:123`): it rebuilds the path with `pinned_map` in the expectation, which copies the implementation.
12. `test_corpus_sample_low_probability_preserves_global_rank_order_and_prefix` and `test_corpus_sample_grows_integer_cutoff_until_pool_is_large_enough` (`test_corpus_sample.py:207,362`): they recompute the expectation with the private `_sampling_cutoff` and `_rank_salt`, which copies the implementation.
13. The asserts on `num_train_steps == 16669` and `training_tokens == 17478713344` in `test_quality_cli_reuses_scored_pool_for_moe_rung` (`test_quality_pipeline.py:261-262`): they project the ladder table, not quality-track behavior.
14. `test_text_scorer_selects_only_after_the_deterministic_raw_prefix`, `test_larger_training_budget_expands_the_raw_candidate_prefix`, and `test_max_scored_pool_matches_exact_rung_pools_through_raw_cache` (`test_quality_scoring.py:63,249,292`) all check prefix-then-select, and `:209` and `:389` both check the constant-score error. Replace them with two parametrized tests.

**Related PRs**
15. #9371: it has byte-identical copies of 30 of these files, including every library fix, and differs only by its Hero-mix track and older versions of four pool files. Merge this PR first, then rebase #9371 to keep only the Hero-mix files, as its footnote says. If item 1 moves the library fixes out, remove them from #9371 too.
16. #9718 (draft) conflicts in `experiments/grug/dispatch.py` in either merge order. The other overlapping PRs (#10074, #9863, #10067, #9495, #9706, #9799, #9502, #10169, #8567) merge without a conflict.

Since the earlier review at `1b566cc4`, the PR also changes how the track decides whether a selection is better. It no longer uses Paloma macro loss. It scores saved dense checkpoints on downstream tasks (`downstream_eval`) and compares candidate and control runs by capability group with a bootstrap (`quality_judge`). The track hangs together, but two of its inputs need attention before it serves as a decision gate. The pool skips the DataKit decontamination and dedup attributes, which matters more now that GSM8K, HumanEval, MBPP and MMLU decide the outcome. The judge also turns a missing or mismatched input into `inconclusive` instead of an error.

```mermaid
    CS["corpus_sample_cli → RawCorpusPool"]:::added
    QP["quality_cli: features → score → select → train"]:::added

  classDef added fill:#d7f0dd,stroke:#1e8e3e,stroke-width:2px
```

**Before.** `launch.py` trained an H100 dense or MoE rung on one frozen Hero v16384 cache, and nothing in fast-track selected data. **Design.** For each source, the pool takes a seeded interval of the 128-bit document-ID space. Each rung ranks the first `10·B` raw tokens and keeps whole documents up to `B`, in raw order. `random` ranks the same prefix by hash and serves as the matched control. The judge reads `downstream_records.parquet` and the `text` block of `metrics.json`. It takes the correct-choice BPB for English cloze, gold-solution BPB for code and math, and the fixed-target loss at 3968 tokens of context. It draws one paired example index per task and resamples the runs. A candidate is `better` when the 95% lower bound of the E/C/M mean is above zero and no group passes its harm limit.

**Evidence and limits.** The fast-track tests and `tests/test_grug_dispatch.py` pass locally at head (63 passed). Everything else comes from the PR body: the validation table, the 85-run loss-validity study (an external artifact; W&B ran offline), and the `cw-us-east-02a` runs. A scorer that prefers documents containing benchmark text, or many copies of one high-scoring document, therefore gets a gain that the random control receives at a lower rate. A checkpoint scored with `downstream_eval --skip-text` writes `"text": {}`, so `np.mean([])` makes `L` NaN. Every comparison involving `L` is then false, and the judge prints `inconclusive` instead of failing. It also ignores the `tasks_version` and `scorer_version` that `metrics.json` records (`downstream_eval.py:379-380`; the scorer is already at `v4`). It takes `example_counts` from `control[0]` alone, so runs from different task copies are paired by position or raise an `IndexError`. topics.title: Harbor eval record fails as infra_failed when one trial raises unclassified DaytonaError
topics.body:
A single plain `DaytonaError` causes a Harbor eval record to be marked `infra_failed` with empty `metrics`. Harbor's error taxonomy (`harbor_config/errors.py`) lists `DaytonaProcessError`, `DaytonaDockerSetupError`, and `DaytonaSandboxStopError`, but omits the base `DaytonaError` raised by the Daytona SDK when session creation fails. The runner records the trial as `unknown:DaytonaError`, so `_evaluation_outcome` (`lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/harbor/runner.py`) rejects the whole run as taxonomy drift.

The affected TBLite-100 run used Harbor 38742b0f. Its [record](s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/evals/20261020-233725-v7-plain-low-v01-20261020-openthoughts-tblite-100-66da/record.json) reports `EvaluationError: Harbor eval encountered error names absent from its taxonomy under '…/results': unknown:DaytonaError=1`. Trial `harbor_openthoughts-tblite_8b8e96c3cc54/cpp-daemon-sighup-segfault__2uaQ4iL/attempts/000` has `exception_type: DaytonaError` and message `Failed to create session:` with empty detail. The same run's `results/harbor_result.json` already contains a complete aggregate: 100 attempted, 93 scored, 12 solved, mean reward 0.146, and errors `AgentTimeoutError 42, ModelInitiatedTmuxFailure 4, TmuxBatchProtocolError 3, TmuxSessionEndedError 2, TmuxCommandError 1, unknown:DaytonaError 1`.

About 2 h of an 8×H100 serve produced a usable score that the record discards. The same error can affect any Daytona-backed Harbor eval.

A session-create failure should count as an infrastructure error because the model never ran. For this run, the record should report 12 solved of 93 scored, mean reward 0.146, and completion 93/100 = 0.93, above the default 0.9 gate (`DEFAULT_MIN_COMPLETION_RATE`). It should list these seven unscored trials and their error types:

| Task | Error |
|---|---|
| basic-message-queue | TmuxBatchProtocolError |
| grid-pathfinding | TmuxBatchProtocolError |
| iot-device-registration-server | TmuxBatchProtocolError |
| maven-slf4j-conflict | TmuxSessionEndedError |
| sign-vector-game | TmuxSessionEndedError |
| image-tile-identification | TmuxCommandError |
| cpp-daemon-sighup-segfault | DaytonaError |

Classify `DaytonaError` as `ErrorCategory.INFRASTRUCTURE` in `src/harbor_config/errors.py` in marin-community/harbor (missing at 38742b0f and on main), then bump the Harbor pin. The drift check works as designed; the missing name causes the rejection.

---

```markdown
## Summary

A Harbor eval record is marked `infra_failed`, and its `metrics` are empty, when a single trial raises a plain `DaytonaError`. Harbor's error taxonomy (`harbor_config/errors.py`) lists `DaytonaProcessError`, `DaytonaDockerSetupError` and `DaytonaSandboxStopError`, but not the base `DaytonaError`. The base class is what the Daytona SDK raises for a failed session create. The runner records the trial as `unknown:DaytonaError`, and `_evaluation_outcome` (`lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/harbor/runner.py`) rejects the whole run as taxonomy drift.

## Example

- Record: `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/evals/20261020-233725-v7-plain-low-v01-20261020-openthoughts-tblite-100-66da/record.json` (TBLite-100, Harbor 38742b0f)

About 2 h of an 8×H100 serve produced a usable score that the record discards. The same error can hit any Daytona-backed Harbor eval.

## Expected behaviour

A session-create failure is an infrastructure error: the model never ran. For this run the record should:

- report 12 solved of 93 scored (mean reward 0.146), with completion 93/100 = 0.93, above the default 0.9 gate (`DEFAULT_MIN_COMPLETION_RATE`);
- list the 7 unscored trials and their error types:

| sign-vector-game | TmuxSessionEndedError |
```

# Research

Harbor's creation subprocess rethrows Daytona SDK exceptions. The vendored taxonomy omits the base `DaytonaError`, so Marin records `unknown:DaytonaError` and rejects the aggregate before applying its completion gate.

topics.title: [levanter] Repair DPO exports and explicit-mesh sharding
topics.body:
Repair full-model DPO exports so periodic saves follow completed optimizer updates and the final save occurs once. Export only the policy subtree, support output dtype and pinned tokenizer revisions, and preserve trained weights when copying reference code from URL checkpoints.

Preserve explicit-mesh sharding during microbatch and Snowball reshapes for context-parallel training, and select an explicit CPU mesh when exporting models that require one. Correct repeated row-zero reads in the jagged store.

Part of #10040.

comments.body:
🤖 Archived the description before automated prose cleanup.

<details><summary>Original description</summary>

```markdown
Full-model DPO on current main has three handling gaps. First, the HF export cadence is wrong: the separate-reference export hook fires on the legacy step counter, so exports land on the wrong updates and the final update can be missed or saved twice. This registers the hook on completed optimizer updates and makes the forced final save idempotent, with the interval-final naming semantics documented.

Second, the export path cannot produce serving-ready DPO artifacts: no dtype control, no tokenizer revision pinning, an always-Auto CPU mesh that breaks explicit-mesh Snowball and MoE models, and reference-code copying that breaks on URL-like checkpoints while risking trained-weight overwrite. This adds export_dtype (bfloat16 halves artifact size), name@revision tokenizers, explicit CPU meshes for explicit-mesh models, and URL-aware code copying with unconditional weight protection; the DPO save path exports only the policy subtree since the reference copy is frozen scaffolding.

Third, explicit-mesh sharding is dropped by reshapes: the Haliax unflatten_axis, the grad-accum microbatch split, and the Snowball MLP flatten/restore all lose sharding, breaking context-parallel training, and the jagged store returns stale slices for repeated row-0 batches. This threads out_sharding through each reshape and fixes the row-0 offsets.

Includes the one-line Haliax companion the grad-accum fix depends on. Coverage is a DPO cadence test with a no-double-write tripwire, bf16-subtree plus pinned-tokenizer plus URL code-copy export tests, numerical parity tests on explicit meshes, and row-0 regression tests: 101 passed with 1 device-gated skip, plus both 8-device Snowball tests. Lint review reports no findings.

Part of #10040.

```

</details>

topics.title: [grug] Flatten MLP tokens locally under context parallelism
topics.body:
The shared and routed MLPs now flatten `[B, S, D]` into tokens inside a `shard_map`. Each device flattens its own block of rows and sequence shard, so no data moves between devices. `_unflatten_tokens` reverses the flatten and restores the residual layout.

The old flatten used a global `(b s)` rearrange. Under context parallelism with more than one row per batch shard, it needed an all-to-all each way in every layer. Without context sharding, the token order does not change. With it, each expert-parallel group gets one sequence slice of each row instead of whole rows. This changes which tokens a full expert drops.

A CPU test checks that CP2 logits equal CP1 logits when no token drops. The compiled CP2 forward has 4 all-to-alls instead of 8.

On one GB200 rack at 65K context on CP4/EP16, restored from hero step 240000 (106 steps per arm):

| | main | this PR |
|---|---|---|
| step time | 15.938 s | 15.586 s (+2.26% tokens/s) |
| drop fraction | 1.17% | 0.23% |
| loss | | −2.3e-3 |

With #10121, CP4 takes 14.626 s per step against 15.137 s and 1.94% drops on CP1. At 262K on CP4/EP16, each device holds one row, so the compiled program does not change.
