🤖 **KITE ([arXiv 2609.27294](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.27294), StepFun, Sep 2026): read it. My take is that it doesn't fit the d512 objective; details below in case you still want it run.**

**What it is:** a *mid-training depth expansion*.
- A trained model (33.8B-A1.1B MoE, 512 experts, top-8) is copied into two towers of equal depth. The **Prefiller** (the original) computes K/V at every layer. The **Decoder** (a copy, run after it) has its own queries but no K/V projections: decoder layer *l* attends to prefiller layer *l*'s K/V.
- Decoder input is `RMS(e_t) + RMS(h^P_L,t)`. The embedding and head are shared, and gradients flow back through the reused KV.
- "KV-invariant": the model gains depth, but prefill cost and the KV-cache size stay those of the small model.

**Results:**
- One seed, ≈ 5e21 FLOPs, grown after 168B tokens then trained 222B more.
- Training loss at equal FLOPs vs a same-cost deeper dense-depth baseline: −0.011 (vs 47B) and −0.002 (vs 63B, about noise).
- The headline win is an *analytical* inference-cost saving at a fixed prefill/KV budget (6.7–31.6%).
- There are no ablations: no from-scratch variant, no growth-time sweep, no loss at the growth point.

**Mapping here:**
- **Closest thing already tested:** batch 9's looped / grown models. That's the *tied* version of the same move: run the 6-layer stack a second time from 70% of training. Result: +0.021 at best, and the doubled stack runs at 0.51× throughput.
- **KITE's other piece**, reusing K/V across layers, is close to batch 15's `mla_share_kv_latent` (+0.0056).
- **Porting it** would mean duplicating all 6 layers including the 512-expert MoE (2× parameters and EP all-to-all), a decoder KDA that reruns the recurrence with its own queries, and swapping the parameter tree and optimizer state mid-run. That's ≈ 400–550 LOC, medium-high risk. The d1024 two-tower version may not fit 8×H100.
- **Step time after growth ≈ 1.9×.** Our objective is training loss at fixed time; KV-cache invariance doesn't enter it.

**Recommendation:** skip at d512. The paper's gain is inference cost at fixed KV, which the d512 loss objective doesn't measure; its training-loss edge over a same-cost deeper model is ≈ 0; and both of its pieces have already lost here (tied growth +0.021, KV reuse +0.006).

**If you want it tested anyway:** untied KITE growth at 70% and 85% of an 8-minute fixed-time run, 2 seeds each, vs candidate 9. My expectation is +0.01 to +0.03. It is also a mid-run growth, so it needs your ruling under the schedule rules.

  - MLA layers compute the KV latent from `RMSNorm(s_l)`. Their main-stream `w_dkv` is removed. `kv_latent_norm`, `w_uk`, `w_uv` and the key norm / offset stay as they are.
- **The main stream keeps queries, the KDA gates (g, β, erase / write) and everything downstream,** so "who comes next" gates and queries, while "what am I" supplies the keys and values.

- **Main layers:** layer *l* reads a learned RMSNorm of the side state leaving side block *l*. KDA `w_k` / `w_v` and MLA `w_dkv` now read only the side stream; the main stream produces no K/V.

- **The side stream is numerically healthy** (per-layer RMS 0.95–1.39, rising with depth), so this is not a numerics failure.
- **My reading: it is a transport bottleneck.** Attention is the only way information moves between positions. With K/V taken only from the side stream, a later position can retrieve only what the *side stream* computed at earlier positions: its embedding plus 1–2 small attention heads and a narrow MLP. Everything the main stream builds at earlier positions (MoE outputs, multi-layer context) never becomes retrievable. The main stream can only query and gate.
  - Doubling *w* recovers only 0.012 of the 0.077, so width isn't the limit; the cut is structural.
  - The KDA layers are hit hardest: their recurrent state *is* the K/V sum, so the whole local-mixing memory becomes side-stream-only.
- **A "some sharing" variant that keeps the idea without the bottleneck,** if you want to pursue it: K from the side stream (identity, "what am I"), V from the main stream (content, "what I carry"). Or K = main + side, so the side stream adds a clean identity signal to keys rather than replacing them. Both keep full-rank content transport, so they test whether a *separate identity source for keys* helps. I'd expect at most a small effect; it's cheap to try if you want it.

🤖 **Batch 115: why candidate 9 OOMs at d1024 — the bigram table is all-gathered and all-reduced at full size every step**

**The failure:** all three d1024 runs died on the same `cuMemAllocAsync` of **48.04 GiB** inside `jit_train_step`: at step 435 (remat, 0.75), at step 7 (remat + 0.9), and at step 4348 (no remat + 0.9, a coordination shutdown after another rank failed). That is XLA's single temp buffer for the whole train step, not one tensor. It sits on top of ≈ 21.5 GiB of resident params, optimizer state and EMA copy (21.5 + 48 = the 69.5 GiB peak W&B reported), and the remat + 0.9 runs failed below the 71 GiB limit because the allocator couldn't find one contiguous 48 GiB block.

**Attribution probes** (candidate 9 at d1024, attention remat, 0.9 fraction, 20 steps, no eval / EMA; memory in GiB):

| probe | in use | peak | Δ peak |
|---|---|---|---|
| A, unchanged | 17.9 | 65.0 | — |
| B, no value embeds | 17.9 | 65.1 | +0.1 |
| **C, no bigram table** | **13.9** | **55.2** | **−9.8** |
| D, shared expert 1024 | 17.8 | 64.6 | −0.4 |
| F, 256 experts | 12.2 | 59.2 | −5.8 (all resident expert state) |

The bigram table is the outlier.
- Its ≈ 4 GiB resident share is expected: 2M × 1024 in fp32 plus two Adam moments, row-sharded over 8 GPUs.
- It also adds **≈ 6 GiB of temporaries**. With `embed2_fsdp=true` the model does `reshard(token_embed2, P(None, None))`, so every step:
  - the forward **all-gathers the whole table** (≈ 4.3 GB bf16 at d1024);
  - `_embedding_gather`'s backward builds a **dense full-size fp32 gradient** (8.6 GB) on every GPU and **all-reduces** it, although each GPU keeps only its 1/8 of the rows.
- That is also ≈ 8.6 GB of all-reduce traffic per step. At d512 it is ≈ 1 GB per step, which is likely a good part of the table's known step-time cost.

**Fix being implemented:** a row-sharded lookup that moves ids and activations instead of the table.
- Forward: all-gather the batch's hashed ids (a few MB); each GPU looks up only rows it owns; a reduce-scatter hands each GPU its own tokens' embeddings.
- Backward: all-gather the per-token cotangents; each GPU scatter-adds into its own shard only, with **no all-reduce and no full-size accumulator**.
- The token axis is chunked to cap the temporaries at ≈ 0.5 GB.
- Same math (fp32 gradient accumulation), checked against the current path on a multi-device CPU mesh.
- Expected at d1024: ≈ 6+ GiB less peak, and the table's comm drops from ≈ 8.6 GB all-reduce to ≈ 2 × 2 GB gathers per step. At d512 it should recover some of the table's speed cost.

Candidate 9's d1024 run relaunches on the fix.

🤖 **Embedding ideas from the new modded-nanogpt record** ([#360, ANVIL2](https://github.com/KellerJordan/modded-nanogpt/pull/360), merged today: 39.9 s from 73.9 s), per your comment.

Its biggest non-CE change is one **84.6M-row hashed bigram + trigram table** (× 768, row-sharded 1/8 per GPU), worth **35.8 millinats / 7 s** of the gain at only **+1.2 s** of wall time. Their row-count grid: 377k → 21M → 84.6M rows gives 3.315 → 3.284 → 3.279 val loss for +0.5 s total, because nothing in the step scales with table size. How:

1. **Sign trick** (from [#299](https://github.com/KellerJordan/modded-nanogpt/pull/299)): each n-gram's row is multiplied by a ±1 vector chosen by an *independent* hash from a pool of 8192 sign rows, so n-grams colliding on a row roughly cancel (count-sketch). ≈ −0.5 s in #299. **We don't have it.** It's free and composes with our `embed2_norm`.
2. **Sparse row exchange:** only the unique rows a step touches are fetched from their owners (all-to-all of ids, then rows), and gradients go back the same way. No dense gradient, no all-reduce, no all-gather of the table.
3. **Row-sparse Adam:** β1 = 0 and one fp32 second moment *per row*, so a row with no gradient has an exactly zero update. The update can therefore be gathered, applied and scattered for only the touched rows, and optimizer state is 4 bytes per row. Plus a period-4 update cadence.
4. The **same sparse treatment for value embeddings** (−1.1 s).

**What maps onto us:**
- The row-sharded gather already being built for the d1024 OOM (batch 115) is step toward (2).
- **(3) is the gate for everything else.** Our table uses Adam with momentum and AdEMAMix, which keeps every row moving and so forbids a sparse update.

🤖 **Batch 123: semi-orthogonal LatentMoE projections, frozen or updated on the Stiefel manifold** (intake suggestion from RavnaBergsndot; d512 candidate 9, equal steps, 2 seeds, paired vs 2.9750 / 2.9791; [`583d97d120`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/583d97d120))

**The idea:** `w_latent_down` / `w_latent_up` are small and shared by every expert in a layer, so they may work as information-preserving maps rather than doing computation. If so, keeping them semi-orthogonal should cost nothing. Freezing them (option B) should then be about as good as updating them with an orthogonality-preserving optimizer (option A).

**Implementation:**
- **Init** (`latent_orthogonal_init`): a Haar-random semi-orthogonal matrix, with orthonormal columns for down and orthonormal rows for up. Every singular value is `std · √d`, which gives the same Frobenius norm as the current normal init, so only the spectrum changes.
- **Option B** (`latent_proj_update=frozen`): both projections stay at their init.
- **Option A** (`latent_proj_update=stiefel`): Skewon from [arXiv 2608.06218](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06218), Muon on the Stiefel manifold.
  - With Nesterov momentum M (MuonH's 0.95) and normalized weight Xn, take `N = skew(M Xnᵀ)` and step along `B = −msign(N) Xn`. That's the exact closed-form solution of Muon's subproblem restricted to the tangent space.
  - Then retract with `Xn ← polar(Xn + ηB)`, using cubic Newton-Schulz.
  - `‖ηB‖_F = lr · ‖Xn‖_F`: the same relative step as MuonH's hyperball, at the MuonH LR, so there's no new hyperparameter.
  - CPU tests check three things. The singular values stay at the init value to 1e-4 over 300 steps. On `max ⟨T, X⟩` it reaches 99.96% of the optimum `c‖T‖_*`. Tall and wide matrices both work.
- The paper's own experiments are synthetic (solver accuracy and speed), so this is its first test inside a network.

| arm | what it isolates |
|---|---|
| `ortho` | orthogonal init only, still trained by MuonH |
| `orthofrz` | option B: orthogonal init, both projections frozen |
| `skewon` | option A: orthogonal init, updated with Skewon |

**How to read it:**
- If `orthofrz` ≈ `skewon` ≈ baseline, the projections really are just information-preserving maps.
- If `skewon` beats `orthofrz`, rotating the subspace matters but reshaping its spectrum doesn't.
- If both lose to the baseline, the trained projections do more than preserve information. I'll check that directly against their spectra in the gradient-capture diagnostics, which record the weights of layers 0 and 5.

🤖 **OKLS deep dive, part 1: what the optimizer assumes, measured on candidate 9's real gradients** (per [your comment](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9451#issuecomment-5885091228))

**Setup.** Batch 120 captured every step's raw gradient and applied update for 46 matrices over four 48-step windows (starting at steps 100, 700, 1700 and 2760). That covers every family: KDA and MLA projections, the shared expert, the LatentMoE projections, the router, and 4 routed experts in layers 0 and 5.
- Two runs: candidate 9 under MuonH (2.9777), and with OKLS on attention (2.9780, 7% slower). So OKLS gives no gain at equal steps on candidate 9, down from −0.0057 on the old base.
- The analysis ran next to the data ([`analyze_grad_capture.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/ladderclimb_v1_batch14/experiments/grug/fast_track/analyze_grad_capture.py)). Charts and a data table are on a separate page (private until shared): https://claude.ai/artifact/BSgehVG6J8rfvFegH6ewra

| OKLS assumption | measurement | result |
|---|---|---|
| The Kronecker factors are anisotropic, so whitening changes the step | effective rank and condition number of the row (input-side) factor A and the column (output-side) factor B | **Holds, strongly, on the input side.** A's effective rank is 0.8–17% of the dimension at step 100. Condition numbers (top 90% of eigenvalues) reach 10³–10⁷. B is much flatter (19–81%). |
| The covariance is close to Kronecker | fit A, B on even steps, whiten the odd steps, compare the leftover anisotropy with a Gaussian that has exactly that covariance | **Holds late.** Whitening removes 2–5 decades. At step 2760 the residual is 0.28–0.50 (log₁₀ max/median) against a 0.17 floor. Earlier windows keep 0.5–1.5. Shampoo's factors are within 0.11 of the KL factors. |
| The preconditioner must be fresh | overlap of A's top-10% eigenspace within a window and between windows | **Mixed.** It's stable within 48 steps (0.72–0.94). Between windows it turns over early (0.30–0.58, step 100 → 700) and settles late (0.80–0.92). |
| High-variance directions are mostly noise | signal-to-noise of the window-mean gradient, by A's eigen-rank | **Holds, weakly.** The largest-variance directions have the lowest SNR (log₁₀ −0.7 to −0.15 at step 100). Nothing rises much above batch noise, though. |
| A better-conditioned step makes more progress | overshoot of each applied update along its own line, and each direction's stable rank | **Not here.** See the next point. |

**New finding: every dense step overshoots.**
- For each applied update I measure r = ⟨g_{t+1}, U_t⟩ / ⟨g_t, U_t⟩. On a quadratic, r = 0 means the step landed on the line minimum and r = −1 means it went twice that far.
- Under MuonH, **100% of dense-matrix steps through step 1700 overshoot**. The median r is −0.2 to −0.6 at step 100, meaning steps go 1.2–1.6× past the line optimum. That's the edge-of-stability pattern, and it matches lag-1 gradient autocorrelations of −0.25 to −0.86 at step 100.
- **OKLS on attention cuts the overshoot about in half** (−0.13 to −0.39), but loss is no better.
- By step 2760, with the LR decayed, r is ≈ 0.
- Routed experts sit near 0 throughout. Their per-step gradients are noise-dominated.

**Why OKLS stopped paying on candidate 9, as far as this shows:**
- The inputs to our matrices are dominated by a few directions: effective rank 2–12% for the value, output, KV-latent and shared-down projections at step 2760. So whitening does most of its work boosting weak input directions by orders of magnitude.
- The resulting direction keeps only **14–33% of Muon's stable rank**, and the step overshoots less.
- Muon's flat-spectrum step ignores the input covariance and makes the same progress per step, more cheaply.
- Weight stable rank under OKLS rises for queries and keys (MLA `w_uk` 70 → 106) and falls for output and down-projections (KDA `w_o` 93 → 70). The blog's "higher stable rank" claim holds only for some of our families.

**One correction to my own method.** My first pass also scored each candidate direction (Muon, OKLS, Shampoo, one-sided, SGD) by its first-order gain on the next batches. That's confounded: those gradients come after the run already stepped along roughly the Muon direction. Every gain came out negative, which is how the overshoot showed up. Those scores aren't reported, and the overshoot ratio replaces them.

**What would make OKLS worth another look.** Each item comes from a measurement above:
1. **Output-side-only whitening.** B is well-conditioned, and whitening only that side avoids amplifying near-dead input directions.
2. **A damped input factor** (A + λ·tr(A)/m·I), sweeping λ rather than LR.
3. **Targeting overshoot directly.** Overshoot is uniform across families early on, so a per-matrix step cap during the first third of training is a cheaper test than any preconditioner.

🤖 **Plan for your router comment ([5905815824](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9451#issuecomment-5905815824)): two arms, implementing now**

**A. A tiny-MLP router, as a residual on the linear one:** `logits = x W_r + W_b · silu(W_a x)`, with 32 hidden neurons and `W_b` zero-initialized.
- It starts exactly as candidate 9, so the MLP only has to learn what a linear router can't express.
- This differs from the low-rank routers that lost earlier: those *replaced* the linear router with a rank-r bottleneck.

**B. Removing the router-aligned component before the expert sees the token.**
- Every token routed to expert e has a large component along the router column r_e. Removing it lets the expert's neurons spend their capacity on how the arriving tokens differ.
- **Handling the LatentMoE:** the router and the latent projection read the same normed input x, and the expert reads `latent = RMSNorm(x W_down)`. The router direction's image in latent space is `u_e = r_e W_down`. RMS scaling doesn't change direction, so projecting `û_e` out of the latent input removes exactly the router-aligned part.
- **As a weight transform:** that projection equals constraining expert e's up-projection to ignore `û_e`: `W_up,e ← (I − û_e û_eᵀ) W_up,e`. It's applied each forward on the weights (E × 256 × 384 multiply-adds, negligible), so the dispatch and expert kernels don't change.
- **Decoupling:** with a stop-gradient on `û_e`, growing the router's alignment no longer raises that expert's neuron activations for the token, which is the separation you describe. The combine weight still carries the router's contribution to the output.

Lets do a deepdive on how Muon is behaving. Train for half the duration. Then lets take one step and compute the gradient. For each matrix, make a plot showing the singular values of the gradient, and then after applying NS. 

The opinionated part of Muon is choosing to upweight the low singular values. We want to see where this decision is accurate. We can view each singular value as being connected to a direction in the input space which activates it, which produces a direction in the output space. Boosting a singular value means we really care about strengthing that relationship. More in input X produces more in output Y. 

There are two ways to evaluate if that signal is accurate: 
-does the gradient hold up locally when we sample new data. We can measure SNR via mean(behavior)/square(behavior)
-is the gradient useful beyond nonzero step-size (something can accurately estimate the global gradient, but its not stable for a real step-size change in weights)

Taking an actual step may be too computationally heavy. What we can do to estimate 2 is to repeat the process for n steps in the same local neighborhood. If a gradient aligns across those points, it indicates the direction is consistently downhill in that whole neighborhood, and is likely robust to a step-size update.

Think through this carefully before executing, using clean math and awareness of how much compute it will cost.

**Results:**
1. **On new data, a direction's reliability falls steadily with its singular value.**
   - Attention and router matrices: held-out consistency (mean / RMS of `s_i = u_iᵀ G_b v_i` over 64 unseen batches) is ≈ 0.95 in the top quarter of directions and ≈ 0.2 in the bottom quarter. The last eighth is essentially noise (0.07–0.12).
   - **Exceptions:** the LatentMoE and shared-expert matrices stay reliable deep into the spectrum (0.40–0.67 even in the last eighth). Routed experts are weak throughout: 0.5 at the top, 0.06 at the bottom.
2. **Newton-Schulz already soft-truncates the noisy tail.**
   - Five quintic steps can't lift singular values below ≈ 10⁻³ of the top one. So for the attention, router and value matrices, Muon's output falls off over the last 20–50% of directions, which is where reliability is lowest.
   - What Muon boosts 10–100× is the **middle** of the spectrum, which is still reliable on data (0.5–0.8). **On the question you asked:** boosting the mid-σ directions is accurate, and the truly unreliable tail mostly isn't boosted.
3. **The expected payoff scales with σ, but that's consistent with Muon's choice.**
   - `E[s_i]` tracks σ_i closely (cosine 0.83–1.00, vs 0.09–0.31 for a flat profile).
   - But Muon is steepest descent under a **spectral-norm** budget, which gives *every* direction with positive expected payoff full weight. 86–100% of directions have `E[s_i] > 0`.
   - The cost is spending equal budget on directions whose payoff is mostly noise.
4. **Along real steps, even the top directions don't hold.**
   - On fixed data at the next 32 positions, consistency drops to 0.2–0.55 even for the top directions, and a direction's sign holds only 50–80% of the time.
   - For MLA `w_q` / `w_uk`, the top ≈ 200 directions go **negative** along the trajectory: the sharpest directions are overshot and flip within a few steps. Mid-spectrum directions often persist better than the top.
   - This matches the edge-of-stability overshoot from the OKLS deep dive.
5. **Routed experts:** in the momentum basis (the directions MuonH actually steps along), held-out consistency is **≈ 0.04**. Each expert sees about 1/64 of the tokens, so its per-step update is nearly pure noise with respect to fresh data. Dense matrices are 0.5–0.8 there, the router ≈ 0.17.

**What this suggests trying** (each tied to a finding):
- **NS steps 5 → 3.** A shallower Newton-Schulz leaves more of the low-σ tail un-boosted (finding 2). It's also faster.
- **Routed experts: a noise-aware step.** Their updates carry almost no fresh-data signal (finding 5). Earlier batches found both momentum directions worse, so the next thing is a smaller expert step or, in the same spirit, SGD-like (σ-weighted) updates for experts only.
- **Probe early and late** (step ≈ 300 and ≈ 2600), about 40 s of GPU time each, to see whether the picture moves through training.

**Plan (as posted before the run):**


**The question.**
- Write a matrix's gradient as `G = U Σ Vᵀ = Σ σ_i u_i v_iᵀ`. Direction i is "more of input v_i produces more of output u_i".
- Muon steps along `−η O` with `O ≈ Σ u_i v_iᵀ`: every direction gets the same weight. SGD would weight direction i by σ_i. Relative to SGD, Muon boosts the small-σ directions.
- **Per-direction payoff:** to first order, the step changes a batch b's loss by `−η Σ_i s_i(b)`, with `s_i(b) = u_iᵀ G_b v_i`. So `s_i(b) > 0` means direction i of Muon's step lowers batch b's loss. Boosting direction i pays exactly when `s_i` is reliably positive on data and positions the step will actually meet.

**Design:** one probe inside a normal candidate 9 run at d512, at half duration (step 1408).

- **Matrices:** the 46 captured by the batch 120 gradient capture, covering every family (KDA and MLA projections, shared expert, LatentMoE projections, router, 4 routed experts each in layers 0 and 5).

1. **Basis and spectra.** At θ₀, average the gradient over 8 batches (set A): `G_A = U Σ Vᵀ`. For each matrix, plot σ_i of `G_A` and the singular values after Muon's own Newton-Schulz (quintic, 5 steps).
   - That shows how much each direction is actually boosted: NS gives ≈ 0.7–1.2, not exactly 1.
   - The basis is fixed from set A. It is never scored on its own batches, since there `s_i = σ_i > 0` by construction.
2. **Does it hold up on new data?**
   - **Measure:** on 64 held-out batches (set B), compute `s_i(b)` for every direction.
   - **Report:** the consistency `c_i = mean_b s_i / RMS_b s_i` (1 = the same helpful sign and size on every batch, 0 = pure noise, negative = the reference batch was misleading), against σ-rank.
   - **Also report** `E[s_i]` itself, the expected per-direction payoff.
   - **Muon vs SGD:** compare how well Muon's flat weighting and SGD's σ-weighting line up with that payoff profile, as cosines against `E[s]`.
3. **Does it hold over a real step?** This is your neighborhood test.
   - **Measure:** the run keeps training normally for 32 steps. At each point θ_k on that trajectory, compute `s_i(θ_k)` on a **fixed** set of 4 evaluation batches, with the same θ₀ basis.
   - Fixing the data removes data noise, so the only change is from the parameters moving. And the neighborhood is exactly where training goes.
   - **Report:** the across-position consistency `c_i^pos = mean_k s_i / RMS_k s_i`, and how many steps each direction's sign survives, binned by σ-rank.
   - If a small-σ direction flips sign within a step or two, its boost is consumed or overshot by the step itself. That would tie back to the edge-of-stability overshoot measured in the OKLS deep dive.

**Compute.**
- 8 + 64 + 32 × 4 ≈ **200 extra forward/backward passes**, about 1 train step each (≈ 0.19 s), so **≈ 40 s of GPU time** plus one compile.
- The SVDs of 46 matrices up to 768 × 512 are negligible on GPU.
- The 32 trajectory steps are the run's own training steps, so training isn't disturbed and the run finishes as a normal candidate 9 run.
- Outputs are about 9 MB: per matrix the spectra, `s_i` for 64 batches, and `s_i` at 33 positions.
- Plots go on the diagnostics artifact next to the OKLS page.

**Caveats:**
- The analysis uses the gradient's SVD. MuonH actually orthogonalizes Nesterov momentum after pre-norm and a hyperball step, so I'll also report the basis from the momentum buffer at θ₀ as a check.
- It is one checkpoint in one run. If it's informative, repeating at step 300 and step 2600 gives the early and late picture for another ~40 s each.

🤖 **Batch 140: stopping routed-expert updates that keep changing direction** (lc1 @ `313e3303dc`, candidate 9 + PGLE at d512, 2 seeds each)

This follows Larry's question about a second moment for routed experts. The Muon probe (batch 136) found routed-expert gradients are the noisiest group: the momentum-basis held-out consistency is about 0.04, compared with 0.2–0.95 elsewhere. MuonH gives every expert an equal-norm update, whether that expert's gradient repeats from step to step or is noise. The three arms below cut the update where the direction keeps flipping.

| run | change |
|---|---|
| `rcons` | **Per-expert consistency scaling.** For each expert, m is an EMA of G (β=0.95) and v is an EMA of ‖G‖²_F (β₂=0.99), both bias-corrected. r² = ‖m‖²/v is 1 for a repeating gradient and about r₀² = (1−β)/(1+β) ≈ 0.026 for pure noise. The expert's MuonH update is multiplied by clip((r²−r₀²)/(1−r₀²), 0, 1). The direction stays MuonH's; only the step size per expert changes. |
| `rcaut` | **Cautious mask per expert.** Zero the coordinates of each expert's MuonH update that go uphill on the current gradient, then rescale by the fraction kept. |
| `radam` | **Adam control.** Routed expert matrices move to the Adam group (adam_lr, AdEMAMix as for the other Adam leaves), which has a per-coordinate second moment. |

**Added at [`574df1ba38`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/574df1ba38): removing a confound.** A MuonH update is a chord between two points on the weight's Frobenius sphere. By default there is one sphere per layer, shared by all 512 experts. Scaling a chord by s<1 (`rcons`) or masking coordinates of it (`rcaut`) lands *inside* the sphere, by a factor ‖W‖²(1−s(1−s)θ²). Nothing pushes the weight back out, so the norm shrinks a little every step, and the first two arms mix "smaller steps" with "slowly shrinking expert weights". The new arms put each expert on its own sphere and project back onto it after the scale or mask:

| run | change |
|---|---|
| `pe` | control: candidate 9 with one hyperball per (layer, expert) (`hyperball_per_expert=true`) |
| `rcons2` | `pe` + consistency scaling + projection back onto the sphere. Logs the per-expert multiplier's distribution (`train/expert_consistency_{mean,p10,p50,p90,zero_frac}`), which shows whether s tells experts apart or just cuts every step. |
| `rcaut2` | `pe` + cautious mask + projection back onto the sphere |

`rcons2` crashed at its first logged step: flattening the expert-sharded gate for the metrics needed a reshard first. It was fixed and relaunched as **`rcons3`** at [`4729e6e917`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/4729e6e917), with the same config. `rcons3` and `rcaut2` are compared against `pe`, and `pe` against candidate 9. `radam` doesn't use the sphere, so it's unaffected. Batch 139 already shows a uniformly smaller routed LR hurts (×0.7 +0.008, ×0.5 +0.024), so if s runs low, `rcons2` loses for that reason alone.

Other groups are unchanged; each arm is tested to leave the attention updates identical. The reference is candidate 9 + PGLE. Results will be edited into this comment.

🤖 **Batch 141: would ANVIL III's per-direction SNR weighting beat Muon here? A probe first** (d512 candidate 9 + PGLE, [`b0302361d8`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/b0302361d8), cw-rno2a)

**Inspiration.** The [ANVIL III report](https://hyperstition.cc/cutting-pretraining-costs-by-62-percent) from Hyperstition, whose ANVIL II was the optimizer in modded-nanogpt record [`#360`](https://github.com/KellerJordan/modded-nanogpt/pull/360). It reports 20–28 mnat over Muon from 124M to 1.2B.
- It withholds the algorithm. The disclosed core replaces Muon's equal weight on every singular direction with an Adam-style SNR per direction: `Σᵢⱼ EMA(eᵢᵀGeⱼ) / √EMA((eᵢᵀGeⱼ)²) · eᵢeⱼᵀ`.
- Its evidence is the same held-out "adamsnr" probe as our Muon probe (mean/RMS of `uᵢᵀG_b vᵢ`). ANVIL III keeps it higher in the momentum basis.
- Candidate 9 already has the rest of what's public: ANVIL II's twin-rail momentum is our Bi-Maxwell (0.85 / 0.98 betas, 0.4385 blend weight), and late weight averaging. Tested neutral earlier: Polar Express maps (batches 32, 77), NorMuon (3), Muon2 (49).

**Why it fits our results.**
- Batches 139–140: a smaller routed step always loses, whether global LR (+0.024 at ×0.5) or a per-expert gate (about +0.2). So a fix has to keep the step size and redistribute it.
- On MuonH that is automatic: the hyperball fixes the Frobenius step, so SNR weighting only moves budget from sign-flipping directions to consistent ones.
- Batch 138: the previous update's directions lose all held-out signal by step 2600 (0.9 → about 0). That is the quantity ANVIL III claims to keep up.

**The probe** (`snr_probe.py`, at steps 300 / 1408 / 2600, the 44 captured MuonH matrices (the Muon probe's 46 minus the two Adam-trained routers) as the Muon probe):
1. For the 48 steps before N, take each matrix's gradient on a fresh probe batch at the run's current parameters: the stream an optimizer would see.
2. From that window, build six candidate directions. All EMAs use β = 0.95, the same β in numerator and denominator, so each SNR is at most 1:
   - `momentum`: the EMA M;
   - `muon`: NS(M), 5 iterations;
   - `adam_snr`: elementwise SNR;
   - `eig_snr`: SNR in the eigenbasis of the window's Kronecker factors (SOAP-like; my reading of ANVIL's Eq. 2);
   - `svd_snr`: SNR in M's singular basis;
   - `svd_snr_diag`: the same, diagonal only.
3. Score each candidate two ways:
   - **Held-out payoff:** `⟨G_b, D/‖D‖⟩` on 64 unseen batches.
   - **Real held-out loss:** move one family's matrices by the MuonH step `−kθ‖W‖·D/‖D‖`, projected back onto ‖W‖, where θ is each matrix's own measured step at N and k is 1× or 4×. Evaluate on 16 batches, paired against no step.
   The loss metric matters because a first-order score alone automatically favours plain momentum and ignores the curvature that makes Muon win.

**Decision rule.** Build an SNR-weighted MuonH (the eigenbasis version reuses `okls.py`'s factors) only if an SNR candidate clearly beats `muon` on real loss for most families, especially late in training and for the routed experts. Otherwise the ANVIL III idea is closed here without training runs.

The bases for the SNR candidates come from the same window they weight. A real optimizer would use a lagged basis, so this is an upper bound for them. Results will be edited into this comment.

**The transform** (`eig_muon.py`, group `eig`, set by `eig_families`). It applies per matrix of the chosen types; here KDA, MLA, LatentMoE and the shared expert. The routed experts stay on MuonH except in `snrall`.

- It recomputes their eigenvectors every 10 steps (as in SOAP), rotating the first moment exactly into the new basis.
- It keeps EMAs of the rotated gradient and of its square.
- The resulting direction takes MuonH's usual Frobenius hyperball step.

| run | direction | idea from |
|---|---|---|

| `eig-soap15` | same, LR × 1.5 | |
| `eig-mw` | Muon's NS(M), each eigenbasis coordinate scaled by \|SNR\| | Muon's geometry with inconsistent coordinates muted |
| `eig-pw` | NS(L^(−1/4) · M) | Shampoo's left (input-side) factor before Newton-Schulz: a full-matrix, with-history version of MuonEq's per-input-row normalization (−0.003 in batch 46). OKLS also found its input-side whitening was what mattered |
| `eig-snrall` | `eig-snr`, routed experts included | |

**Other ideas from Shampoo** were already in place or tested:
- Grafting (Shampoo takes its step size from another optimizer, per layer) is what the hyperball does.
- Infrequent preconditioner refresh is the 10-step eigenbasis.
- Inverse-root exponents: `eig-pw` uses Shampoo's ¼.
- The OKLS deep dive covered the full two-sided Shampoo (KL-Shampoo).

**Details:**
- The SNR modes use a scale-free ε: 1e-6 of the matrix's mean second moment. Without it, round-off entries of the rotated gradient that keep a steady sign would get weight 1, which a test caught.
- Each `eig-*` arm is compared against both candidate 9 and `eig-muon`, so the gain from the weighting is separated from the momentum and MuonEq differences.

**The dump.** It is new and sits beside the existing routing dump. At steps 300, 1408 and 2817 it routes the routing dump's fixed held-out batches. Then, per layer, it records:
- **Routed experts:** for each of the 512 experts and each of its 384 units, how many of the tokens routed to that expert switch the unit on, plus the summed ReLU² output. The dump also records the per-expert token count, so each unit's activation rate is conditioned on routing.
- **Shared expert:** the same for each of its 768 units, over every token.
- **Sparsity:** a histogram of how many units each token, or each (token, expert) assignment, switches on.

The expert input comes straight from the model: the latent-projected, normed routed input and the shared expert's pre-activations. Training is unchanged; the dump is a separate debug forward. A test checks the counts against a direct per-expert recount.

- **Dead units:** units that never fire on routed tokens, and those firing on fewer than 0.1% of them, per layer, for shared and routed experts.
- **Activation-rate distribution:** each unit's activation rate, per layer and matrix type, and how it changes from step 300 to 1408 to 2817.
- **Learned sparsity:** the share of an expert's units a token switches on, per layer.
- **Experts with too few routed tokens to judge:** flagged separately, since a "dead" unit there could just be an idle expert.

### First results (GPU 0's trace, steps 500–505; profiling slows every run's steps to about 270 ms, so compare the differences)

| per step, GPU 0 | candidate 9 | `lof5` (full write, layer 5) | `lfree5` (latent-free, layer 5) |
|---|---|---|---|
| step span | 266.6 ms | 278.9 ms (**+12.3**) | 275.2 ms (+8.6) |
| compute-stream busy | 156.7 ms | 160.1 ms (+3.4) | 160.1 ms (+3.4) |
| compute stream idle (waiting) | 109.9 ms | 118.9 ms (**+9.0**) | 115.1 ms (+5.2) |
| GEMMs | 53.5 ms | 55.0 ms (+1.5) | 53.3 ms (−0.2) |
| expert dispatch/combine all-to-all | 30.3 ms | 31.5 ms (+1.2) | 32.8 ms (+2.5) |
| async all-gathers | 3.6 ms | 11.3 ms (+7.7) | 3.4 ms |

- **The extra math is cheap: about 3.4 ms per step of compute, +2%.** `lof5`'s GEMMs grow by only 1.5 ms per step. `lfree5` has the same GEMM time as candidate 9, as designed, and its 512-wide dispatch adds 2.5 ms of all-to-all.
- **Most of the overhead is GPU 0 waiting: +9 ms per step for `lof5`, +5 ms for `lfree5`.**
  - In `lof5` the waiting shows up in one all-gather: the 604 MB bigram-table gather (`bf16[524288,512]`, `embed2_fsdp`) at the start of the forward, which takes 9.4 ms per step against 2.2 ms in candidate 9.
  - The HLO shows the same all-gathers with identical shapes and bytes in both programs. A collective's kernel time includes waiting for the slowest GPU to arrive, so this is skew between GPUs, not more data.
- **Leading explanation: expert-parallel load imbalance.**
  - Each GPU holds 64 of the 512 experts. In the full-write layer each expert's down-projection is 2× larger, so a GPU hosting busier experts falls further behind, and the others wait at the next collective.
  - `lfree5` keeps expert FLOPs equal and shows less waiting. Its remaining wait plausibly comes from the 2× wider dispatch rows.
  - This is a hypothesis. The trace covers GPU 0 only, so the straggler isn't visible.
- **Next.**
  - Profile all 8 ranks to confirm which GPU is late and in which op.
  - Possible fixes:
    1. keep the full-width layer's experts on the same per-GPU work as the latent layers;
    2. move the bigram-table gather so it overlaps the first layers rather than sitting where the skew lands;
    3. reduce load skew in that layer.
  - The +2% of real compute is the floor. At that cost the final-layer full write (−0.011 at equal steps) would be a clear fixed-time win, about −0.008.

**1. Fewer iterations.** `ns3` and `ns4` take the first 3 or 4 steps of our quintic schedule. Their exact maps, with x = σ / ‖M‖_F:

**2. Coefficient schedules** (new `coefficient_type`s, 5 steps, the same cost):
- **`tight_top`:** three quintic steps, then two cubic (1.5, −0.5) steps. Large singular values land at exactly 1, and small ones are boosted only 136× (vs 493×). It tightens the high range and leaves the low range small.

🤖 **Batch 158: a learned residual row for every routed expert a token visits** ([your comment](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9451#issuecomment-5927796123); d512 candidate 9 + PGLE, equal steps, 2 seeds, paired vs candidate 9 on cw-rno2a, 2.9768 / 2.9822; [`17dd004ca0`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/17dd004ca0))

**Change** (`expert_visit_bias`, new `ExpertVisitBias` enum): each MoE layer gets an `[E, D]` table (512 × 512 at d512), zero-initialized and trained by Adam. The routed output gains the table's rows for the token's selected experts:

`x = x + routed(x) + shared(x) + Σ_{e ∈ top-8} c_e · bias[e]`

| run | `c_e` | what it tests |
|---|---|---|
| `vb-sum` | 1 | an unweighted record of which experts ran. The router gets no gradient through it |
| `vb-wt` | the expert's combine weight | the same record, weighted by how much the expert was used. The router gets gradient through it |

- **Why:** a token's residual has no direct record of which experts processed it, so later layers can't condition on "I visited expert B" or attention on "tokens that visited C". The table writes that record explicitly.
- **Cost:** about 1.5M parameters across the 6 layers, and a `[T, 512] × [512, 512]` matmul per layer.
- **Implementation:** the per-token visit vector is built as a `[T, E]` one-hot sum. Ids beyond the table (null experts) add nothing. It is applied after the latent up-projection, so it works with every write-width mode.
- **Tests:** no-op at init, the table gets a gradient and then changes the output, the table is in the Adam group.

🤖 **Batch 159: paired-head KDA, adjacent heads sharing one delta-rule state** ([your comment](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9451#issuecomment-5927919775); d512 candidate 9 + PGLE, equal steps, 2 seeds, paired vs candidate 9 on cw-rno2a, 2.9768 / 2.9822; [`e0ff6e9475`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/e0ff6e9475))

**Change** (`kda_head_pairing`, every KDA layer). This carries over nanogpt's paired-head attention (record 58, [`#191`](https://github.com/KellerJordan/modded-nanogpt/pull/191)), which interleaves two heads' q/k/v into one sequence of length 2T. In KDA, heads `2j` and `2j+1` run as one head over the interleaved sequence `A₀ B₀ A₁ B₁ …`.
- **Shared state:** each pair shares one `h × h` state that both heads write to (their own k, v, β, decay and erase gate) and read from (their own q).
- **Visibility:** head A's query at token t sees B's writes up to token t−1; B's query sees A's writes up to token t. That is the same causal arrangement as nanogpt's.
- **Cost:** the projections are unchanged, and the scan covers 2T tokens with half the heads, so the scan FLOPs are unchanged.
- **Trade-off vs softmax:** in softmax attention pairing keeps every key. In KDA the state *is* the memory, so a pair gets one state instead of two, which halves the layer's state.
- **Implementation:** a reshape around the existing kernels, with document ids repeated per sub-position. The output and gate keep the original head layout.
- **Tests:**
  - head A at token t depends on B's value at t−1, but not on B's at t or later;
  - B at t depends on A at t;
  - heads in different pairs stay independent, and unpaired KDA has no cross-head path;
  - the interleave is checked directly.

| run | decay per sub-step |
|---|---|
| `kpair` | half the head's log-decay, so the shared state decays per token at about one head's rate (exact at init) |
| `kpairf` | the head's full log-decay, so the state decays twice per token |

If the halved state turns out to be the limit, the follow-up is a capacity-neutral version: each head keeps its own state and additionally reads its partner's state (one extra readout).

📥 **Intake suggestion** from RavnaBergsndot, approved by ClassicLarry ([original](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9514#issuecomment-5928744772)):

> Attention residuals q embedding:
> In addition to a data independent q vector for each layer, we also use a per-layer embedding q_e, similar to the value embedding, and add it to q before computing the dot product with k, so the attention residual formula before normalization turns from
>
> exp(q^T RMSNorm(k))
>
> into
>
> exp((q + q_e(token_index))^T RMSNorm(k))
>
> q_e should be initialized as all 0.
>
> Rationale: In the attention residuals paper (https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.15031), the authors ablated input dependent q in Table 4, and showed that it could further decrease loss, but excluded it from the default implementation because of extra compute and overhead. The "token dependent q" in this proposal is a compromise between cheap "data independent q" and expensive "q calculated from internal states using a dxd projection".

**Grouped differential attention** (`mla_grouped_diff=g`, MLA layers 3 and 5, 4 heads at d512):
- `g` = 4 gives one noise map shared by all 4 heads, and `g` = 2 gives two maps.
- Each noise map has its own query and key up-projection; its columns are repeated for its `g` signal heads, so the q/k transforms apply unchanged. It reads the same values.
- `λ = sigmoid(x W_λ)` per head and token, with `W_λ` zero-init (λ starts at 0.5, Adam). The sigmoid keeps it a subtraction: batch 77's unconstrained DIFF λ went negative and turned the difference into a sum.

**Change** (`attn_res_token_query`). Each AttnRes gate's logit for source `n` becomes

`(q_g + q_e[token]) · RMSNorm(source_n)` instead of `q_g · RMSNorm(source_n)`

with `q_e` a zero-initialized `[vocab, d]` table, so the run is exactly candidate 9 at init. This sits between the paper's data-independent query and its input-dependent `d × d` projection, which it ablated as better but more expensive (Table 4, [arXiv 2603.15031](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.15031)).

| run | table | parameters |
|---|---|---|
| `tqs` | one table shared by all 13 gates | 8.4M |
| `tqg` | one table per gate, as each gate has its own static query | 109M |

**Why: the weight-attribution probe** ([page](https://claude.ai/artifact/5hcismK4FMAYraGt5fdM1M)).
- **How it works:** every step over steps 1000–1400, it attributes the change in one in-context prediction ("…Dalvin Cook's brother? Answer:" → " James") to each weight update, per tensor and layer, using G·Δθ with G = ∇ log p(James).
- **No single tensor drives it.** The change is spread over many tensors, led by the MLA attention projections. Updates as a whole are smooth: consecutive updates have cosine +0.56, and the cosine with the update two steps back is always lower.
- **The attention-side matrices bounce in a few directions.** Movement along fixed directions is strongly anti-correlated from step to step: layer-5 `w_uk` −0.77 along the frozen James direction, layer-3 `w_uk` −0.70 along the frozen alternation direction. The update's projection there flips sign on 80–91% of steps. The routed experts only drift (+0.9).
- **Strongest bouncer:** layer 5's Inkling relative-position projection, `rel_pos.r_proj` (−0.73).
- **Optimizer:** the fresh gradient flips along those directions, and momentum only partly damps it. Bi-Maxwell passes about 9% of a step-alternating gradient, and Newton-Schulz restores the step's size. The same bounce appears without Bi-Maxwell and MuonEq.
- **Why this tensor:** `r_proj` is trained by Adam, not MuonH, so the batch-176 q/k MuonH LR cuts (+0.002 / +0.003) never touched it.

Lets try a radical idea: MLP compression. The intuition is, if we want to fit as many clothes in the closet, it makes sense to spend some effort sorting them. The gradient pushes us to just keep throwing clothes in, but maybe an auxillary loss that encourages sorting will be helpful. Without this, we either run out of space, or have to remove old clothes to fit new ones.

The first thought is that highly sparse routed experts can act as the sponge to absorb new data. However this data wont get absorbed in the most compressed state. Lets combine the 2 shared experts into 1 to simplify. Then we should have some mechanism that takes the knowledge learned by the routed experts and compresses it into the 1 shared expert. One possibility is an aux loss that pulls the shared output towards the routed output. The goal here is that once the shared expert compresses and absorbs what the routed experts are doing, then it frees up space in the routed experts to learn fresh info without worrying about overwriting what they already know.

Think through the design space here carefully, and challenge and rework the initial spec I gave as makes sense. We may need to test in overtrained regime to see benefit here.

🤖 **Batch 178: MLP compression — move what the shared expert can express out of the routed experts** (candidate 11, d512, 2817 equal steps, seed 0; cw-rno2a; [`3f0a1199c8`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/3f0a1199c8))

**Idea** (from the comment above): routed experts absorb new data, but not in a compressed form. If the shared expert takes over what it can express, the routed experts are freer to learn new things without overwriting old ones.

**Changes to the initial spec:**
- **Already one shared expert** (`num_shared_experts=1`, width 768), so no merge is needed.
- **The shared expert is the small side.** Per layer it has ~0.8M parameters against ~100M routed (~150M in the full-write layers 4–5). Only the common, low-rank part of the routed output can move into it, not facts. Growing it would densify d512, so it stays at 768.
- **"Pull shared toward routed" (`‖s − sg(r)‖²`) settles at `s = r`.** Both paths then hold the same function and nothing is freed. This batch tests two forms that do free the routed side (`y = s + r`, `sg` = stop-gradient):
  - **Transfer:** `λ‖s − sg(s + r)‖² / sg(‖y‖²)`. Its gradient moves only the shared expert, along the routed output. The shared expert is evaluated a second time on a stop-gradient input, so no gradient reaches the layers below. The LM loss then sheds the overshoot from the routed side. It stops when the routed output has nothing left the shared expert can express.
  - **Routed penalty:** `λ‖r‖² / sg(‖y‖²)`. Routed output is costly, so the LM gradient moves onto the shared expert whatever it can express. The penalty also reaches the layers below, but only in direction, because the routed input is RMS-normalized.
- **Measured first:** a detached width-768 shadow MLP per layer learns `sg(x) → sg(r)` with no effect on training. Its R² is how much of the routed output a shared-sized expert could absorb.

> Add an extra loss term to counter the indefinite stretching effect to s, or normalize s and y in the original aux term, in the experiments of Batch 178 (MLP compression).
>
> Choice 1: Instead of lambda * ||s - sg(s + r)||^2 / sg(||y||^2) we should use lambda * ||s - sg(s + r)||^2 / sg(||y||^2) + lambda_1 * ||s||^n
> where n can be 2 or (4 and higher) depending on whether we want the counter force to be smoother or more "hard cap like".
>
> Choice 2: let s' = s / ||s|| and y' = y / ||y||, and the aux term should become lambda * ||s' - sg(y')||^2
> where y = s + r
>
> Rationale: in the aux loss in batch 178, under the random vector assumption, s and r are approximately orthogonal because they are high dimensional, therefore by pythagorean theorem ||s + r||^2 has a very high probability of being larger than ||s||^2, no matter what training phase we are at. In order for the aux loss to minimize ||s - sg(s + r)||^2 / sg(||y||^2) it would both rotate s to be more aligned to (s + r) and stretch s longer to match the norm of (s + r). This optimization pressure of raw norm stretching would never stop at any phase of training. This seems to be the opposite of what we want for a regularized neural network, and might be the real reason why Batch 178 didn't show improvements.
>
> Of course now in choice 1, lambda_1 also needs tuning and my intuition is to start with a value smaller than lambda.

It also logs each layer's output max |x| vs RMS, and dumps every norm gain and output scalar at the end. The control dump shows what the default gains learn per module, which says which gain function fits.

| run | change |
|---|---|
| `ctrl` | none (diagnostics only) |
| `ss_lin` | learned scalar on every attention and MLP output (`sublayer_scales`), linear, init 1 |
| `ss_sig2` | the same scalar as `2·sigmoid(w)`, init `w = 0`, so it modulates in (0, 2) |

| `g_sig2` | `2·sigmoid(w)`, init 0; gain LR ×2 |

**Why the functions could matter:**
- **Scale of an output.** AttnRes scores sources on RMS-normed copies but mixes the raw sources, so an output scalar sets that branch's weight in the mix, and the next RMSNorm removes only the overall scale. Batch 01 found learned output scalars neutral (MoE outputs grew to 1.2–2.1×), but that was a much earlier recipe.
- **Positivity and relative steps.** A linear gain moves additively and can cross 0. `e^w` keeps it positive and makes Adam's steps relative (the same fraction at any size), which suits gains spanning orders of magnitude. `softplus` is linear above about 1 and exponential near 0. `2·sigmoid` bounds it in (0, 2), and that bound is the test of whether large gains are needed.
- **Plain `sigmoid`:** I used `2·sigmoid` rather than a plain sigmoid, which can't start at 1 and can only shrink activations. If the control's gains never exceed 1, plain sigmoid becomes worth a run.

**LR.** Gains train with Adam, so a step moves the raw parameter by about lr, and the gain by `f'(w)` times that. At init `f'` is 1 for `exp`, 0.63 for `softplus` and 0.5 for `2·sigmoid`, so the gain LR multipliers (×1.6, ×2) give every arm the same initial step as linear. A ×0.5 / ×2 sweep follows on whichever helps.

🤖 **Batch 184: two weight sets for the MLA attention (previous step + current)** (candidate 11, d512, 2817 equal steps, seed 0; cw-rno2a; [`2ebb73734a`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/2ebb73734a))

**Idea** (ClassicLarry): keep the previous step's weights for a parameter group, and run half of each batch on them.
- **Implementation** (`dual_attn_prev`): each MLA attention module gets a frozen copy of the previous step's weights, refreshed after every update.
- **Batch split:** in training, odd batch rows run attention at those old weights and even rows at the current ones.
- **Gradient:** the old rows read `sg(θ_old) + (θ − sg(θ))`, so their gradient reaches the current weights. Each update then averages the gradient at both ends of the last step, about its midpoint.
- **Expected effect:** that damps directions that flip sign every step (period-2 bounce) and lags drifting directions by about half a step.
- **Evals** use the current weights only.

|---|---|---|---|

- **A loss at fixed time.** The extra attention pass in the two MLA layers costs 8% step time, about +0.014.

**FP8: microbenchmarks on one GB200** (16k tokens, fwd+bwd of one linear `[16k, d] × [d, n]`)

| d (FFN up, n = 4d) | bf16 GEMMs | per-tensor FP8 GEMMs | MXFP8 GEMMs | JAX MXFP8 linear, end to end |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 512–1024 | launch-bound | no gain | no gain | 0.4–0.6× bf16 |
| 2048 | 2.1 PF | 4.2 PF | 2.7 PF | 0.78× |
| 4096 | 2.3 PF | 4.5 PF | 3.1 PF | 1.02× |
| 6144 | 2.3 PF | 4.6 PF | 3.0 PF | 1.20× |

- **In the training layouts, block-scaled MXFP8 runs as fast as per-tensor FP8.** In the d=6144 profile, cuBLAS's 1×32 block-scaled kernels (`Avec32UE8M0_Bvec32UE8M0`) take 1.44–1.49 ms per GEMM, against 1.43 ms for per-tensor FP8 and 2.7 ms for bf16. Fine-grained scaling itself costs nothing.
- **The overhead is all in quantization.** `jax.nn.scaled_dot_general` re-quantizes both operands for every GEMM. That is six bf16 reads, separate amax / convert / transpose fusions, about 2.1 ms at d=6144 against 4.4 ms of GEMMs. A fused cast kernel would read x, w and g once and write row- and column-wise e4m3 plus e8m0 scales. By bandwidth that is about 0.4 ms, so about 1.9× bf16 at d=6144.
- **Below d≈2048 FP8 can't pay.** The GEMMs are too small to be tensor-core bound. On the d512 H100 rung, FP8 is a numerics question, not a speed lever.
- **Width dependence of the error:** relative error is 3.8% for MXFP8 (e4m3 everywhere) and 5.9% for per-tensor with e5m2 gradients. It is flat from d=512 to 6144 on Gaussian inputs, and four 100× outlier channels don't change it.

**Protocol chosen: MXFP8, just-in-time scales.** Each 32-element block along each GEMM's contraction axis gets a power-of-two (e8m0) scale from its own amax. e4m3 is used everywhere, gradients included. The router, embeddings, lm head, norms, attention core and optimizer stay high precision.
- **Why not modded-nanogpt-style fixed scales:** they are tuned to one width and one activation distribution. The RMSNorm bound `max|x| ≤ sqrt(d)` grows with d, and the gradient scale drifts with depth, LR and training phase.
- **Why not per-tensor current scaling:** a single outlier channel sets the scale for the whole tensor. Massive activations grow with width and training.
- **With 1×32 blocks, an outlier only coarsens its own block,** and no scale state depends on width, step or calibration. It is also the native Blackwell format (same GEMM speed, as above).

**Kalman write strength: parked.**
- Every attempt hit a NaN loss between steps 4 and 31, on both seeds and with either optimizer for the projection.
- A debug run shows why: at step 10 the gradient norm of KDA layer 2's `kalman_b` was **5e18**, with every other gradient below 0.4. Its square overflows fp32 in the global-norm clip, and the loss turns NaN a few steps later.
- The scan itself is not the source. On CPU at 4096 tokens its forward and gradients are finite and O(1) for decays 0.5–0.999 and extreme `ω`/`r`.
- So the blow-up arrives through the kernel's `β` cotangent, on tokens where the Kalman β departs from the sigmoid's narrow range. Finding them needs kernel-level instrumentation; I'm not chasing that further now.

**Why the batch 163 version lost.**
- Batch 163 got −0.003 / −0.004 at equal steps but cost +6.6% step time.
- It added its noise maps on top of the signal heads, as a second full attention call.
- It also tiled each shared noise map out to all `g` heads of its group, so each map was computed `g` times.
- Motif 3's GDLA ([arXiv 2608.09119](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.09119)) does neither:
  - The noise heads come out of the head budget: 80 query heads = 64 signal + 16 noise.
  - Each group's signal and noise heads share one KV head, and only the query differs.
  - Its attention kernel therefore runs no extra heads.

**Batch 203: GDLA inside the head budget** (`mla_gdla_noise_heads=m`, MLA layers 3 and 5)
- The `N` query heads form `m` groups of `g` signal heads plus 1 noise head, and run in one kernel call.
- Each group shares one value head, so `w_uv` and the value embeds have `m` heads. Keys stay per head, since MLA up-projections are cheap.
- The output is `D = H_signal − λ·H_noise(group)`, with `λ = sigmoid(x W_λ)` per signal head and token (zero-init, so 0.5).
- Only the signal heads reach `w_o`.

**Batch df1: differential attention with a free noise map** (original idea; on cw-us-east-02a with its own control)
- *Source:* DIFF's noise map is meant to cancel common-mode attention, the broad mass a softmax spreads over irrelevant context. The cheapest estimate of that common mode is a fixed average of the values, so no second softmax map is needed.
- *Mechanism:* `D = softmax(qkᵀ)v − λ·mean_{j≤t}(v_j)` per head, within documents, with the same token-dependent sigmoid `λ`. Cost is one segment-reset scan, with no extra kernel call.
- *Variants:*
  - `uniform`: the plain prefix mean.
  - `decay`: an exponentially decayed mean with a learned per-head decay, half-life 16 / 64 / 256 at init. This makes the noise map a local/recent baseline.
- *Logged:* `knob_mean_noise_lambda_mean` and the learned half-lives per layer.

| run | noise map |
|---|---|
| `df1-ctrl` | none (cw-us-east-02a control) |
| `df1-mu` | uniform prefix mean |
| `df1-md16` / `md64` / `md256` | decayed mean, initial half-life 16 / 64 / 256 |

🤖 **Partial key offset study: what the shifted half of the MLA heads learns** (d512 current best / candidate 12, EMA weights of `lc1-b234-attn-distance`, 2.9528)

With `mla_key_offset`, each MLA head's first 64 key channels come from the previous token (j−1); channels 64–127 come from the current token. I looked at what that split learns: the query/key directions of each head, then a probe of where the heads attend.

**Method**
- **Directions in the attention input x:** the query direction is the `W_q` column. The key direction is backed out through the latent: `W_dkv · diag(latent norm gain) · W_uk`, with the latent RMSNorm linearized.
- **The 128 per-channel pairs aren't unique:** any rotation of a head's channels gives the same scores. So each head is also analyzed through the SVD of its query–key product `B = W_q W_kᵀ`, which gives canonical (query direction, key direction, strength) pairs. The raw-channel and canonical numbers agree closely.

**1. The shifted half is an induction lookup, built into the weights**

Mean query/key cosine on the shifted half (channels 0–63), per head:

| head | layer 3 | layer 5 |
|---|---|---|
| H0 | 0.61 | 0.90 |
| H1 | 0.87 | 0.70 |
| H2 | 0.41 | 0.85 |
| H3 | 0.80 | 0.85 |
| H4 | 0.85 | 0.45 |
| H5 | 0.89 | 0.88 |

- **Query and key point the same way in all 12 heads.** By pair strength, 92–100% sits on positively matched pairs, and no head has negatively matched pairs. So a query scores keys whose *previous* token resembles its own token: "find where I appeared before and read what came next."
- **The current-token half matches only weakly** (+0.14 to +0.40), except L3 H2 (+0.87), a copy head.
- **The attention probe agrees.** Queries at fixed in-document positions (x = 20…4,000), with each query's full softmax row kept rather than averaged:
  - at x = 4,000, 30–49% of the top long-range keys of the sharp layer-3 heads (H1, H4, H5) are induction targets;
  - half of those heads' long-range mass sits on 6–36 keys;
  - L3 H2 picks earlier copies of the query token (33% of its top keys).
- **Layer-5 heads are induction-shaped in the weights too (0.85–0.93), but diffuse in behavior.** Half their long-range mass needs 93–172 keys. They likely match on broader features, so many keys qualify.

**2. The 64 shifted dims are not redundant in weight space**

| per head, shifted half | range |
|---|---|
| directions for 50% / 90% of B's strength | 11–19 / 40–48 |
| effective rank (of 64) | 41–55 |
| stable rank | 12–28 |
| average \|cos\| between different key channels | 0.04–0.07 |
| top 8 channels' share of strength (uniform = 0.125) | 0.14–0.15 |

The channels are near-orthogonal and none dominates. A dozen or so stronger directions plus a long real tail. This is weight space only: whether the data uses all 64 needs an activation-side rank or an ablation, which isn't run yet.

**3. Tying the query to the key on the shifted half costs nothing**

`mla_tie_prev_qk` (`b759695d8f`): the query's shifted half *is* the token's own un-shifted key half, so those channels score `k_prev(x_i) · k_prev(x_{j−1})`, a symmetric similarity. It needs no query projection for those 64 channels.

| run | Paloma | step ms |
|---|---|---|
| current best (`lc1-b217-ctrl`) | 2.9521 | 190.2 |
| **tied shifted half (`lc1-b236-tie-prev-qk`)** | **2.9517** | 190.3 |

Neutral: the free query directions were re-learning the key. That makes it a free simplification, and it drops 64 query columns per head in both MLA layers.

**4. For sparse attention**

The shifted half is close to a symmetric positive form, a learned similarity between the query token and each key's previous token. A low-rank index over previous-token states (around 16–32 dims) could pre-select long-range candidates for the retrieval heads. The diffuse layer-5 heads look better suited to pooled chunk summaries than to top-k selection.

**Next:**
- an activation-side effective rank of the shifted half;
- shifting 16 or 32 channels instead of 64;
- the Inkling relative-position bias by distance. That probe run (`lc1-b235-relpos-probe`) just finished.

🤖 **Config change: KDA write and erase gates dropped** (Gated DeltaNet-2 gates, adopted in batch 88)

They were worth −0.0024 at d512 (batch 88, two seeds) for about +1% step time. At the hero shape, d6144 / 48 layers on one GB200 rack, they cost far more: each is a full 6144×6144 projection in all 36 KDA layers.

| GB200 1-rack, late steps | step time | MFU | tok/s |
|---|---|---|---|
| with write + erase gates | 19.42 s | 25.7% | 216k |
| without (`lc1-gb200-nogate30`) | **17.95 s** | **27.6%** | **232k** |

Kimi K3's KDA has neither gate: it keeps a full-rank output gate, a low-rank decay gate and a per-head β ([arXiv 2607.24653](https://arxiv.org/html/2607.24653v1)). The base config is now `base16` (base15 without `kda_write_gate`, `kda_erase_gate`, `kda_onchip_erase_gate`), and new d512 pairs run against it.

📥 **Intake suggestion** from RavnaBergsndot, approved by ClassicLarry ([original](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9514#issuecomment-6079384012)):

> Try warmup of muonh nesterov momentum, and see if it could shift the optimal momentum from 0.95 to higher ones.
>
> Like how modded-nanogpt introduced it since record 9, start with a lower momentum like 0.85, and linearly increase it to the value we want over the warmup period. Spend more steps in the momentum warmup (like 10% or 20% of total) than common lr warmup settings (<5%). Try higher final momentum such as 0.98 and see whether the momentum warmup schedule could make them better than the default 0.95.
>
> Rationale: 0.95 is a safe number that's widely used, and the kimi paper reported that tuning it makes minimal difference. However, the lack of success from a a higher momentum may be caused by the early-late training dynamic discrepancy, and if this problem is alleviated, it might have some extra potential after training reaches the stabilized phase. A momentum warmup can help with the discrepancy by forgetting gradient information quicker in the early phase. The ademamix optimizer paper has some empirical evidence that the momentum warmup period should be sufficiently long. Since the update size is at the same scale after the short lr warmup finishes, long momentum warmup doesn't have the problem of "too little accumulated update" so it wouldn't require retuning lr and its schedule.

Original description ~~~markdown This issue tracks iterative improvements to the Marin pretraining scaling ladder (`experiments/grug/fast_track`) using the **Marin Belay** process. It is a twist on autoresearch: an agent runs experiments in batches, and anyone can steer it with research directions. > **To suggest a research direction, comment on [Marin Belay Intake (#9514)](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9514).** Suggestions a maintainer approves (👍 from a `marin-devs` member) are copied into this thread automatically, and the agent acts only on this thread. Clean KMA, the current baseline (★), is 0.022 lower at d512, 0.049 lower at d768, 0.040 lower at d1024 and 0.033 lower at d1280, which is about 1.14×, 1.43×, 1.40× and 1.35× the baseline's compute efficiency. They count as ordinary wins; no parity check needed. - **Noise.** Differences under ~0.005 are noise. A win must beat the current best by more than 0.005. ### Gates (both relative to the current baseline, same fixed-time rule at each rung) - **Gate 1:** beat the baseline at d512 and d768. - **Gate 2:** also beat it at d1024 and d1280, **and** project to lower Paloma macro loss at 1e24 FLOPs. Fit a power law of final loss against training FLOPs across the four rungs, for both the baseline and the variant, fixing the asymptote to 1.2. ### Fixed - Training data, the 16k BPE tokenizer, and the eval sets. - Sequence length 4096. - One 8×H100 node per rung. - The FLOP accounting used for the gate-2 projection. ### Judgment calls - **Hero-scale speed is out of scope for v1, so use discretion.** - Robust target criteria would also check training speed and inference speed at hero scale. Marin Belay v1 skips those checks. - Judge whether a change's d512 gain would carry over to hero scale, and avoid changes whose gain comes from d512-only effects. Two examples: - Dropping MoE for dense would be a clear win at d512 because dense gets ~5× higher MFU there, but that MFU gain would not carry over at hero scale. - A much larger KV cache would also be a clear win at d512, but it would hurt long-context inference speed. - **Avoid magic numbers.** - Prefer changes with few new tuned constants. A tuned constant is justified when its gain is above the noise threshold and holds as a pattern across scales. For example, a 2× LR on one parameter group qualifies if it clears the noise threshold and the gain shows up consistently at larger rungs. - The higher a change's risk of curve fitting, the more scales it must be validated at before it counts as a win. - **Spend effort in proportion to an idea's likelihood of improvement.** - Promising ideas deserve several attempts. Long shots can be tried once and dropped. - A first run is not a verdict for a large change. Each goes through a ShortConv followed by SiLU. q and k are L2-normalized, and q is scaled by 1/√128. - **Decay:** per-channel log-decay `g = −5·sigmoid(exp(A_log)·(x·W_a_down·W_a_up + dt_bias))`. - The gate projection has rank 128. - `A_log` is one value per head, initialized to 0. - `dt_bias` is one value per channel, initialized so the decay rate spans 0.02–0.5. - **Write strength:** `β = sigmoid(x·W_β)`, one value per head. - **Recurrence:** `S_t = (I − β·k·kᵀ)·Diag(exp(g))·S_{t−1} + β·k·vᵀ`, read out as `o_t = S_tᵀ·q_t`. - It runs as chunked Pallas kernels, with a stable block-doubling inverse inside each chunk. - **Output:** per-head RMSNorm with a learnable 128-wide scale shared across heads → full-rank per-channel gate `sigmoid(x·W_g)` → `W_o`. - No positional encoding, no window, no XSA, and no ShortConv on the branch output. **Global layers: MLA + Inkling relative position** - **q:** full-rank, D → N·128 (no Q latent). - **k and v:** k = `W_uk · RMSNorm(x·W_dkv)` and v = `W_uv · RMSNorm(x·W_dkv)`. - They share one 512-wide KV latent, with a learnable RMSNorm on the latent. - Heads are 128 wide with no RoPE part. - There's no ShortConv on K, so the up-projections can be absorbed at inference. - **Scaling:** no QK-norm; `qk_mult` = 1, i.e. standard 1/√128 logit scaling. - **Position — Inkling relative-position bias**, added to the pre-softmax logits in place of RoPE: - `bias[h,i,j] = R[i,h,:] · P[:, i−j]`, where `R = x·W_r` is 16 values per head. - `P` is a bank of shape [16 × 1024] shared across heads. The relative extent is 1024. - It runs inside the FA4 attention kernel (forward, backward, and the SM90 backward pass). - **XSA** (exclusive self-attention): subtract the component of each head's output that is parallel to its own value vector. - **Output gate:** per head, `2·sigmoid(x·W_gate)`. `W_gate` is zero-initialized, so the gate is 1 at init. - The branch output also gets a ShortConv. **MoE sublayer (LatentMoE with quantile-balanced routing)** - **Experts:** 384 routed experts, top-8. Each is a SwiGLU with hidden size D/2. - **Latent space:** experts operate in a D/2-wide latent. The input goes through `W_latent_down` → RMSNorm, and the combined expert output goes back up through `W_latent_up`. - **Router:** reads the full-width token and computes logits in fp32. - Experts are selected by top-(8+1) on bias-adjusted logits, where the 9th logit is the threshold α. - Combine weights are the sigmoid of the unbiased logits, renormalized to sum to 2.5. - **Quantile balancing:** each step, each expert's threshold β is the global (1 − K/E) quantile of the logit margins (logit − α), read from a 10k-bin histogram. The router bias is set to −β. - The router bias is not trained by gradient. - **Capacity:** capacity factor 1.15, with pooled-wave expert-parallel dispatch. Receiver ranks are sort-based and the expand backward is gather-based. - **Shared experts:** 2 shared SwiGLU experts that bypass the latent: D → D/2 hidden → D. - **Fused projections:** - The router, latent-down, and both shared experts' gate/up projections run as one GEMM. - The shared experts' down-projections run as one GEMM. **Residual stream: Block Attention Residuals** - **Sources:** the embedding source, one running sum per completed block of sublayer outputs, and the running partial sum of the current block. - The model has 8 blocks. Block sums use the raw sublayer outputs. - **Gates:** every sublayer (attention and MoE) has its own gate, and there is one final gate before the output norm. Each gate has one learned pseudo-query `q ∈ ℝᴰ`, zero-initialized so every gate starts as a uniform average. - **Mixing:** per token, `logitᵢ = q · rms_norm(sourceᵢ)`, using a parameter-free (frozen) RMS key norm, then `softmax` over sources and a weighted sum of the raw sources. - **Implementation:** - Each completed block is scored once against every gate that reads it. - Backward: at d512 the layer's forward intermediates are saved. At d768–d1280 each layer is recomputed. At d1280 the attention branch is also rematerialized. - The model keeps one layer stack per mixer kind. **Optimizer** | Group | Update rule | LR | Parameters | |---|---|---|---| | `muonh` | MuonH | MuonH LR | all attention and MoE matrices: MLA `W_q`/`W_dkv`/`W_uk`/`W_uv`/`W_o`; KDA `W_q`/`W_k`/`W_v`/`W_o`/`W_g`; experts; shared experts; latent down/up.
