🤖 **New accepted baseline: Belay Ckpt 1**

Ckpt 1 replaces `base16` as the baseline. From now on, new d512 experiments run against it at a fixed 8 minutes.

**Code:** branch [`marin_belay_v1_ckpt1`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/marin_belay_v1_ckpt1/experiments/grug/fast_track), recipe module [`belay_ckpt1.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/marin_belay_v1_ckpt1/experiments/grug/fast_track/belay_ckpt1.py), which holds the exact flags for every ladder rung and the GB200 rack.

```bash
uv run python -m experiments.grug.fast_track.belay_ckpt1 --size d512 --num-steps 2760 --submit \
    --run-id <id> --target-cluster cw-us-east-02a
```

**Recipe:**
- **Attention:** KDA local layers and MLA global layers (every 4th layer plus the last), with Inkling relative position and Block AttnRes.
- **MoE:** latent MoE with 384 ungated ReLU² experts, top-10 routed. Routed and shared experts are both 0.75·d wide, with one shared expert. The router combine is `sqrt_softplus_renorm`.
- **Embeddings and head:** gated value embeddings, logit soft-cap 10, learnable QK multiplier.
- **Optimizer:** MuonH (pre-norm in, decay power 0.7), with AdEMAMix Adam for the non-matrix parameters. β1 is 0.9 and β2 comes from the heuristic; cosine schedule.
- **GB200 only:** MXFP8 on the routed experts, dense projections and expert dispatch.

**d512, 8 minutes on 8×H100** (2,760 steps, 0.175 s/step, one seed):

| Recipe | Paloma macro loss | Paloma macro BPB |
|---|---:|---:|
| **Belay Ckpt 1** | **3.0270** | **1.2562** |
| Marin Aug Hero Arch | 3.1306 | 1.2980 |
| Basic MoE (128 experts, top-4) | 3.1612 | 1.3108 |
| Vanilla dense | 3.4452 | 1.4275 |

**Scaling ladder.** Ckpt 1 runs at 171 tokens per active parameter and Aug Hero at 235, each at its own hero-budget ratio. The speedup is the extra model FLOPs Aug Hero's fit needs to match Ckpt 1's BPB at that rung.

| Rung | Ckpt 1 BPB | Aug Hero BPB | Speedup |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| d512 | 1.1934 | 1.2309 | 2.20× |
| d768 | 1.0899 | 1.1230 | 2.15× |
| d1024 | 1.0097 | 1.0329 | 1.94× |
| d1280 | training | training | – |

- **Fits:** fixing the floor at 0.498, the fits are BPB = 0.498 + 21.16·C^−0.0822 for Ckpt 1 and 0.498 + 25.49·C^−0.0850 for Aug Hero, where C is analytic model FLOPs.
- **Projection:** at 300k GB200-hours, Ckpt 1 projects **0.729 BPB** against Aug Hero's 0.735. In hardware FLOPs that is a **1.33×** speedup. Two things cut it from the per-rung numbers: Ckpt 1's flatter slope, and its lower 11-rack MFU (26.9% against 28.8%).
- **Caveat:** the advantage shrinks from d768 to d1024. Treat 1.33× as provisional until the d1280 runs finish.

**GB200, one rack (d6144, 48 layers):** 14.59 s/step at 28.9% MFU, counted on analytic FLOPs.

🤖 **Batch plan: X0217, MuonH momentum warmup** (the intake suggestion above, from RavnaBergsndot)

**Idea:** warm MuonH's Nesterov momentum up linearly from 0.85, the way modded-nanogpt does. Then test whether the warmup lets a higher final momentum (0.98) beat the default 0.95.

**Code:** `momentum_warmup_start` / `momentum_warmup` on GrugMoeMuonHConfig, default off. When set, the momentum runs in the existing stage ahead of Newton-Schulz with `m(t) = 0.85 + (m − 0.85)·min(t / W, 1)`, and with a constant `m` it is identical to the current path. Commit [`e8cd1b97ec`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/e8cd1b97ec) on `marin_belay_v1_w2026-10-12`, cut from Ckpt 1.

**Protocol:** d512, 8 minutes (2,760 steps, Belay Ckpt 1), seeds 0 and 1, each arm compared to the same-seed control, ranked by Paloma macro loss. 10 runs.

| Arm | Final momentum | Warmup from 0.85 | Paloma macro loss (s0 / s1) | Δ vs control (s0 / s1) | Δ mean |
|---|---:|---|---|---|---:|
| `ctrl` (Ckpt 1) | 0.95 | none | 3.0269 / 3.0315 | – | – |
| `w95` | 0.95 | 10% of training | 3.0274 / 3.0256 | +0.0005 / −0.0059 | −0.0027 |
| `w98` | 0.98 | 10% | 3.0485 / 3.0477 | +0.0217 / +0.0162 | +0.0190 |
| `w98l` | 0.98 | 20% | 3.0499 / 3.0496 | +0.0231 / +0.0181 | +0.0206 |
| `c98` | 0.98 | none | 3.0509 / 3.0547 | +0.0240 / +0.0202 | +0.0221 |

**Result: no win; X0217 is closed.**
- Warmup at 0.95 averages −0.0027, inside the 0.005 noise threshold, and the two seeds disagree in sign.
- A final momentum of 0.98 is about 0.02 worse. Warmup recovers 0.0015–0.0031 of that, depending on its length, and the longer 20% warmup recovers less.
- So warmup doesn't make the higher momentum competitive here, and 0.95 stays.

`c98` separates the two effects: if `w98` beats `c98`, it's the warmup that makes 0.98 work. Run ids are `belay-X0217-<arm>-s<seed>`; the registry entry is X0217.
Lets test: https://arxiv.org/html/2610.13630v1

🤖 **Batch plan: X0218, Multi-Stream Attention Residuals** ([arXiv 2610.13630](https://arxiv.org/html/2610.13630v1), requested above)

**Idea:** today each Block AttnRes gate reads the depth sources (embedding, completed block summaries, the running partial) with one zero-init pseudo-query. MSAR gives each gate m queries ("streams"):
- **Stream 0** reads the sources as they are, exactly like today.
- **Streams r ≥ 1** first pass every source through its own causal depthwise convolution along the sequence (kernels 4/8/12, zero-init, never crossing document boundaries), then attend over those.
- **Mixer:** a small sigmoid mixer, `sigmoid(α·RMSNorm(concat z)·W + b)`, weights the m reads into the sublayer's input.
- **Final gate:** the one before the LM head stays single-stream.

**Code:** `attn_res_streams` / `attn_res_stream_kernels` / `attn_res_stream_mixer`, default off; with m=1 the model is bit-identical to today. Commit [`0e9cdc7460`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/0e9cdc7460) on `marin_belay_v1_w2026-10-12`. CPU checks passed: future ×1e6 leakage, document boundaries, finite-difference gradients. Not supported with `scan_layers`, so no GB200 runs yet.

**Protocol:** d512, Belay Ckpt 1, **equal data**: 2,760 steps, the same as the Ckpt 1 8-minute run, ignoring MSAR's extra step time for now. Seeds 0 and 1, each compared to the same-seed control from X0217 (`belay-X0217-ctrl-s0/s1`, same base code). Ranked by Paloma macro loss. A fixed-time run follows if it wins.

| Arm | Streams | Convolution kernels | Mixer | Paloma macro loss (s0 / s1) | Δ vs control (mean) |
|---|---:|---|---|---|---:|
| control (Ckpt 1) | 1 | – | – | 3.0269 / 3.0315 | – |
| `m4` | 4 | 4, 8, 12 | yes | 3.0164 / 3.0168 | **−0.0125** (−0.0104 / −0.0147) |
| `m2` | 2 | 4 | yes | 3.0191 / 3.0174 | **−0.0109** (−0.0078 / −0.0141) |
| `m4nomix` | 4 | 4, 8, 12 | no (plain sum) | 3.0163 / 3.0198 | **−0.0111** (−0.0106 / −0.0116) |

The paper's ablation found the convolutions matter most, m=2 captures most of the gain, and the mixer is worth about 0.004.

**Update:**
- **No mixer (`m4nomix`): a clear equal-data win.** It is **−0.0111** on both seeds (−0.0106 / −0.0116), BPB 1.2517 / 1.2537 against 1.2562 / 1.2586.
- **It costs about +18% step time** (0.205 vs 0.174 s/step in 40-step probes), so a fixed-time run has to decide it.
- **The mixer arms diverged from a backward bug.** The gradients of the mixer's α and b are orders of magnitude too large (6e8 at step 0), until Adam overflows. The mixer's W and everything else stay normal. A fix is in progress, then m4/m2 rerun.

**Update 2: mixer arms rerun at [`912bd13876`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/912bd13876).**
- **The NaN was an XLA GPU miscompile.** On 8 GPUs, the bf16 gradients of the tiny mixer α `[2]` and b `[2, m]` leaves come out of the combined float32 gradient all-reduce through a *bitcast* instead of a convert, so the leaves receive raw float32 bit-halves. Keeping those two leaves float32 at compute fixes it; the corrupted runs were rerun under new ids (`m4b`, `m2b`).
- **All three arms win at equal data by about −0.011 to −0.013**, which is 2–2.5× the noise threshold:
  - The mixer adds only about 0.0014 over the plain sum (m4 −0.0125 vs m4nomix −0.0111), inside the noise.
  - m=2 with a single kernel-4 stream (−0.0109) matches m=4.
- **So the gain comes from the convolved streams, not the mixer or the stream count.** Next: a fixed-time run (MSAR costs about +18% step time), and controls for whether the gain is just longer temporal reach (`sconv_kernel` 8/12 on the existing write-side convs) or depends on the per-channel basis (scalar-tap streams).

**Batch 2: finding the minimal version** ([`23bd387bcc`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/23bd387bcc)). Equal data, 2,760 steps, seeds 0 and 1, against the same controls.

| Arm | What it keeps | Question | Δ (s0 / s1) | Mean |
|---|---|---|---|---:|
| `m2nomix` | 1 extra stream over all sources, kernel 4, plain sum | Does the minimal MSAR keep the gain? | −0.0069 / −0.0112 | **−0.0090** |
| `m2embed` | extra stream reads only the conv'd token embedding | Is it an n-gram-like embedding feature? | −0.0072 / −0.0079 | **−0.0076** |
| `m2noembed` | extra stream reads every source except the embedding | Is it the conv'd layer outputs? | +0.0003 / −0.0035 | −0.0016 |
| `m2scalar` | as `m2nomix`, one tap set shared by all channels | Does the per-channel basis matter? | −0.0040 / −0.0079 | −0.0060 |
| `embconv` | no MSAR; embedding source = `emb + conv(emb)` (kernel 4, zero-init) | Is a write-side conv on the embedding enough? | −0.0026 / −0.0044 | −0.0035 |
| `sconv8` | no MSAR; existing write-side SConvs at kernel 8 (also KDA q/k/v) | Is it just longer reach? | −0.0007 / −0.0030 | −0.0018 |

Every arm is bit-identical to its baseline at init. CPU checks for each path: future-token leakage, document boundaries, finite gradients.

**Batch 2 result: the gain is a read-side conv of the token embedding.**
- **Embedding only keeps most of it.** `m2embed` (the conv'd embedding added to every gate's input) gets −0.0076, about 85% of `m2nomix`'s −0.0090.
- **Without the embedding it's gone.** `m2noembed` is −0.0016, which is noise.
- **Write-side is weaker.** The same conv on the embedding source (`embconv`, −0.0035) gets about half: there it only arrives through each gate's softmax weight on the embedding, which is small for later layers.
- **Longer write-side convs** (`sconv8`) do nothing.
- **Per-channel taps matter.** Scalar taps lose about a third.

The seed-1 control is about 0.004 high, so the seed-0 column is the conservative read.

**Batch 3: embedding variants and MLP-side conv placement** ([`00b0b9d102`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/00b0b9d102), [`33aa1753a8`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/33aa1753a8)). Equal data, 2,760 steps, same controls.

| Arm | Change from Ckpt 1 | Δ (s0 / s1) | Mean |
|---|---|---|---:|
| `m2embscale` | `m2embed` with a learned per-gate scale on conv(e) | −0.0066 / −0.0066 | −0.0066 |
| `embout` | embedding out of the layer gates' softmax, added at weight 1 | +0.0123 / +0.0197 | **+0.0160** |
| `emboutscale` | as `embout`, with a learned per-gate scale | +0.0054 / +0.0104 | **+0.0079** |
| `nomlpconv` | MLP-output SConv dropped | +0.0044 / +0.0009 | +0.0027 |
| `mlpin` | MLP-output SConv moved to the MLP input (router, latent and shared all read it) | +0.0022 / +0.0014 | +0.0018 |
| `mlplatent` | MLP-output SConv + a conv on the routed latent output | −0.0004 / +0.0005 | 0.0000 |
| `latent` | routed latent-output conv instead of the MLP-output conv | −0.0018 / −0.0007 | −0.0012 |
| `latentshared` | separate convs on the routed latent output and the shared output | −0.0032 / −0.0010 | −0.0021 |
| `latentin` | routed latent-input conv instead | +0.0014 / +0.0031 | +0.0023 |
| `sharedin` | shared-input conv instead | +0.0016 / no final eval | – |

**Result:**
- **A per-gate scale doesn't improve `m2embed`** (−0.0066 vs −0.0076).
- **Taking the raw embedding out of the softmax clearly hurts,** even with a learned scale. So `m2embed`'s gain doesn't come from bypassing the softmax: it adds the conv'd embedding while the plain embedding stays in the softmax.
- **Where the MLP-side SConv goes barely matters at d512.** Every placement, including dropping it, lands within ±0.003 of Ckpt 1.

The minimal winning change is still `m2embed`: a zero-init causal kernel-4 per-channel conv of the token embedding, added to every gate's input.

**Batch 4: conv'd embedding only at selected gates** ([`fb1caabf39`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/fb1caabf39)). Prompted by `m2embscale`'s learned scales, which stayed large only at layer 0 (both gates) and layer 3's MLP gate, while the other gates fell toward 0.

| Arm | conv(e) added at | Δ (s0 / s1) | Mean |
|---|---|---|---:|
| `m2embed` (reference) | all 12 gates | −0.0072 / −0.0079 | −0.0076 |
| `embL0` | layer 0, attention and MLP gates | −0.0027 / −0.0052 | −0.0039 |
| `embL0L3m` | layer 0 + layer 3's MLP gate | +0.0017 / −0.0017 | 0.0000 |

Restricting it to a few gates loses most of the gain, so the small learned scales elsewhere were still doing work. Only `s_g · conv(e)` is identified, so the conv taps can grow while `s_g` shrinks. `m2embed` (all gates, no scale) remains the minimal winning version.
0.85->0.95 momentum warmup looks like perhaps a minor boost, but not integrating as impact will fall-off as we scale to hero size. (since we'd only apply the warmup for very high loss regime)

topics.title: [grug] Get ring_dedup's routing-weight gradient from the down projection
topics.body:
The ring_dedup expert-side combine's backward used the expert outputs y [A, H] to form the routing-weight gradient <dout, y>. Since dy = w * dout and dhidden = dy W2^T, the same value is <hidden, dhidden> / w, from tensors the down projection's backward already holds. One custom VJP, `_down_project_combine`, now covers the down projection and the combine, so `save_moe` no longer keeps y and `recompute_all` no longer recomputes the down projection. The forward, dx, dw13 and dw2 are unchanged; the routing-weight gradient differs at bfloat16 rounding.

On one MI350X running one EP8 rank of June Snowball (`save_moe`), batch 8 per GPU goes from 1.427 to 1.385 s per step (-2.9%) and peak memory from 207.0 to 190.5 GiB. At batch 16 per GPU, the per-rank share of the production batch 128 on 8 GPUs, the step runs out of memory without this change (XLA asks for 270 GiB) and peaks at 235.5 GiB with it. The ring_dedup tests pass on CPU and on MI350X.

Merge after #9880. Part of #9812.

topics.title: [levanter] Fuse the EP hero's RMSNorm and GatedNorm
topics.body:
Add `gated_rms_norm` in `levanter.kernels.triton.gated_norm`, which computes `GatedNorm(RMSNorm(x))` as one custom op. The EP hero selects it with `gated_norm_implementation="fused"` (or `--gated-norm-implementation fused` in the diagnostic launcher). The default, `"reference"`, keeps the two separate modules. Parameter names and layout are unchanged, so checkpoints load as before.

Memory bandwidth limits this pair of modules. At the hero's per-GPU shape (65,536 tokens, hidden 6,144, gate rank 128, bf16), they read or write the full `[T, D]` activation 10 times in the forward and 27 times in forward plus backward. The custom op cuts that to about 7 and 23.5:

- It folds the RMSNorm weight into the down projection, `a = rstd * (x @ (w * W_down))`, so the normalized activation is never written to memory.
- The backward saves only `a` (`[T, 128]`) and `rstd` (`[T]`) and recomputes the gate.
- On GPU, the backward's two elementwise passes run as Triton kernels. Elsewhere, and on GPU for shards that are not a multiple of 64 tokens by 128 features, they run on XLA, with a warning on GPU.

All rank-128 matmuls stay on XLA. Moving them into Triton was slower than the reference, because Triton 3.6 reaches only about 150-220 TFLOP/s for that matmul shape on B200. Under a mesh, the op runs per shard inside a `shard_map` over `x`'s own sharding and sums the weight gradients in fp32.

Measured on one B200 at the hero shape, counting 98 calls per step plus the forward that `offload_carry` remat reruns:

| Path | Per step | Saved |
|---|---|---|
| Reference | 444 ms | |
| XLA restructure only | 405 ms | 39 ms |
| XLA restructure with Triton passes | 361 ms | 83 ms |

That is about 0.6% of a 14 s hero step. Error against float32 is about half the reference's on every output (relative RMS 1.82e-3 against 3.71e-3 for `y`, 1.98e-3 against 4.24e-3 for `dx`), because the bottleneck reads the normalized activation in fp32. The op has not run on GB200 or inside the full hero step.

topics.title: Support Terminus-Kira host-side agents in the shared RL rollout path
topics.body:
Allow RL runs to select Harbor's Terminus-Kira controller, preserving its native-tool protocol and reuse of Terminus-2 lifecycle and context handling.

Current main (`2b08e2432c8871b7e6c4cd7c389d7bb2df2b4950`) routes task rollouts through RolloutEngine. Its [agent adapter](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/blob/2b08e2432c8871b7e6c4cd7c389d7bb2df2b4950/skyrl-train/skyrl_train/rollouts/agent_runtime.py) requires `BaseInstalledAgent` and rejects host-side Harbor agents. Host-side means the controller runs in the rollout-worker process or a host subprocess while task commands execute in a sandbox. Harbor's [TerminusKira](https://github.com/marin-community/harbor/blob/aee476676983dfa62f5d824538193302ef46e3f9/src/harbor/agents/terminus_kira/terminus_kira.py) subclasses Terminus-2, not `BaseInstalledAgent`.

Done when:

- A documented configuration runs Harbor's existing Terminus-Kira controller against the trainable policy and a Daytona task environment. Share the host-agent integration with Terminus-2 where applicable.
- Native tool calls, observations, and continuation prompts preserve exact sampled tokens, behavior log probabilities, and training masks through trajectory conversion.
- Declare supported text and image modes. Unsupported multimodal inputs fail explicitly rather than being dropped or trained with incorrect token alignment.
- Timeout, failure classification, retry, verification, and cancellation cleanup have regression coverage.
- A live multi-turn RL smoke reaches verification, an optimizer update, and evaluation with synchronized weights, with durable configuration and trajectory evidence.


Transferred from https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10386.
<!-- skyrl-migration: issue=I_kwDOSx5uL88AAAABW2xclQ -->

comments.body:
🤖 Open design question shared by marin-community/marin#10387, marin-community/marin#10386, and marin-community/marin#10385: can the agent implementations remain in Harbor, with MarinSkyRL collecting the training evidence through an adapter? Is there a concrete operational constraint that requires porting them into Marin?

Please compare two ownership models before choosing an implementation:

- Harbor owns the full trial: agent controller, environment lifecycle, retries, and verification. MarinSkyRL supplies policy inference and captures training evidence.
- RolloutEngine owns the trial: its adapter runs Harbor's agent controller and propagates cancellation to it, while Marin manages environment lifecycle and verification.

For either option, establish how the integration retains exact model requests, sampled tokens, behavior log probabilities, tool observations, and verifier outcomes. Assign explicit owners for inference-request retries, tool-operation retries, whole-trial retries, cancellation, and cleanup, without duplicate handling of the same operation. Preserve original Harbor errors and diagnostics when mapping outcomes to MarinSkyRL's training decisions: include, exclude, or fail.

Keeping the implementations and, where practical, the full trial lifecycle in Harbor may avoid duplicating its operational behavior. This remains an architectural question, not a decided requirement or a claim that the current adapter supports it. What would prevent that arrangement, and what tests would establish that Marin's tracking and training interfaces can observe it correctly?

🤖
# Research

At the issue's pinned MarinSkyRL revision, `InstalledAgentRuntime` constructs the Harbor agent but rejects it unless it is a `BaseInstalledAgent`; Terminus-Kira inherits Terminus-2's host-side `BaseAgent`, so the trial stops before setup. The existing worker already supplies a Daytona machine and a correlated model endpoint that records served token IDs and log probabilities. [#10045](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10045) covers the installed-agent foundation, and [#10326](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10326) identifies a separate risk of losing earlier training turns after a history reset; neither establishes Terminus-Kira support.

**Relevant code**
- [`agent_runtime.py#L149-L168`](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/blob/2b08e2432c8871b7e6c4cd7c389d7bb2df2b4950/skyrl-train/skyrl_train/rollouts/agent_runtime.py#L149-L168) — installed-agent rejection and execution.
- [`agent_backend.py#L53-L103`](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/blob/2b08e2432c8871b7e6c4cd7c389d7bb2df2b4950/skyrl-train/skyrl_train/rollouts/agent_backend.py#L53-L103) — correlated requests and served evidence.
- [`task_worker.py#L622-L643`](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/blob/d361d939926a0308a0892f25adbbe851e709de34/skyrl-train/skyrl_train/rollouts/task_worker.py#L622-L643) — agent runtime and Daytona factory.
- [`terminus_kira.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/harbor/blob/aee476676983dfa62f5d824538193302ef46e3f9/src/harbor/agents/terminus_kira/terminus_kira.py) — native tools over Terminus-2.
- [`task_projections.py#L205-L267`](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/blob/2b08e2432c8871b7e6c4cd7c389d7bb2df2b4950/skyrl-train/skyrl_train/rollouts/task_projections.py#L205-L267) — training disposition and masks.

# Terminus-Kira host-agent design

Run Harbor's Terminus-Kira controller in the rollout worker against the existing correlated policy endpoint and an engine-owned Daytona task machine. Keep Harbor's prompts, native tool loop, terminal behavior, and context recovery in Harbor. This shares the host-agent path with [Terminus-2 #10387](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10387) and leaves installed agents on their current path.

## Ownership choice

A Harbor-owned full trial would reuse its retries and verifier, but would require a second bridge for exact model turns and training projection and would duplicate RolloutEngine's machine, grading, and cancellation contracts. Use RolloutEngine as the attempt owner because the installed-agent path already owns those boundaries. Harbor owns the controller's semantic tool loop and context handling; a borrowed environment forwards commands and file transfers to the engine-owned machine without starting or deleting it.

## Design

1. Add a host-agent execution path beside `run_installed_agent` in MarinSkyRL. Validate `terminus-kira` and `terminus-2` as host agents, construct them through Harbor's factory, inject the trial correlation header into each host-side LiteLLM request, and run their `setup()` and `run()` against `BorrowedMachineEnvironment`. Keep one configuration shape for the agent identity, Daytona backend, model endpoint, and setup/run/cleanup deadlines. Do not port the agents into Marin.
2. Route every host-agent chat request through `AgentInferenceBackend` and `ModelTurn`. Preserve the full native `tool_calls` message and tool observations in the next request. Use the engine's served prompt IDs, sampled completion IDs, and behavior log probabilities as canonical training evidence; derive loss masks only over sampled assistant tokens. Reject missing or misaligned token/logprob evidence and unsupported history rewrites before projection, including the [#10326](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10326) multi-conversation case. Harbor trajectory files remain diagnostics, not a source for reconstructed training tokens.
3. Start with a declared text-only mode and `enable_summarize: false`. Disable or reject Kira's `image_read` action in that mode and fail on image content before model inference or projection. Add image mode only after a separate test proves image-part serialization and all generated-token offsets through the serving endpoint and projector; do not silently strip image parts.
4. Give each operation one retry owner: the serving bridge must deduplicate a retried inference request by stable request ID or fail without a second sample; the borrowed machine's transport handles transient Daytona command failures, while Harbor decides whether a completed tool error warrants another action. The worker/orchestrator owns whole-attempt retries and maps original Harbor/Daytona errors to train, exclude, or fail without changing verifier outcomes. RolloutEngine owns the attempt deadline and verifier; cancellation stops the host agent and endpoint, records partial evidence, and releases the Daytona machine.

## Costs and risks

The host path needs cross-repository changes in MarinSkyRL and possibly Harbor to suppress `image_read` and expose stable request IDs. Terminus-2 context recovery can change prompt history, so text-only support must reject such attempts until every sampled action can be retained and attributed. No open Marin PR targets #10386 or Terminus-Kira by title; check current MarinSkyRL PRs and pins before implementation, since this triage session has read access only to `marin-community/marin` on GitHub.

## Testing and completion

First, run a local multi-turn fixture with `execute_commands`, `task_complete`, malformed native-tool arguments, a changed history, and an attempted `image_read`; compare served token IDs, log probabilities, masks, observations, and verifier outcomes at the final projection boundary. Exercise setup failure, inference timeout and retry, Daytona command failure, agent timeout, cancellation, upload failure, and machine cleanup, asserting one outcome and retained diagnostics per attempt. Then run a version-pinned Daytona RL smoke with at least two tool turns through verification, one optimizer update, weight synchronization, and evaluation; attach the non-secret config and durable model, trajectory, and verifier artifact links here.

## Open questions

- Can Harbor's current LiteLLM request path carry a stable request ID through retries without resampling? Probe this before enabling on-policy training.
- Does Kira's native-tool response preserve the exact served completion token span when the provider returns tool calls and reasoning fields? Reject the mode if the answer is no.

topics.title: [finestore] Concurrent schema creation can assert after a write conflict
topics.body:
The simulated-S3 concurrent-writer test intermittently fails while publishing a table schema. In [CI on #10348](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/actions/runs/39533315377/job/119004477743), `test_concurrent_writers_publish_every_row_through_conflicts` reports `ConditionalRequestConflict`, then fails at `assert existing is not None` in [`write_schema`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/e4f5b7d0089a4c16ad9cd202a68f15ef4d9b8e79/lib/finestore/src/finestore/commit.py#L128-L146). This fails the Finestore CI lane.

Reproduce:

1. Use main commit `e4f5b7d0089a4c16ad9cd202a68f15ef4d9b8e79`, Python 3.12, and an environment with FineStore's test dependencies installed.
2. From the repository root, run:

   ```bash
   PYTHONPATH="$PWD/lib/finestore/src:$PWD/lib/rigging/src:$PWD/lib/marin/src" \
   uv run --no-sync python -c "import sys, pytest; sys.setswitchinterval(1e-6); raise SystemExit(pytest.main(['-n', '0', '-q', 'lib/finestore/tests/test_simulated_s3.py::test_concurrent_writers_publish_every_row_through_conflicts']))"
   ```

3. Repeat in a fresh process if it passes; the failure depends on thread scheduling.

On the exact, unmodified main source and test, 20 ordinary subprocess attempts passed. With only the Python thread-switch interval reduced to `1e-6`, the second attempt reproduced the same schema conflict and assertion as CI. Source files were verified against the pinned Git blobs. This local reproduction used existing dependencies on macOS; it was not a clean Linux CI rerun or a live-S3 test.

Expected: concurrent writers registering the same schema complete successfully, and the test publishes all 18 rows.

[`SimulatedS3.conditional_write`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/e4f5b7d0089a4c16ad9cd202a68f15ef4d9b8e79/lib/finestore/src/finestore/testing/simulated_s3.py#L299-L326) can reject a contending writer while the first writer is still in flight. `write_schema` catches the conflict and immediately rereads the object, assuming it already exists. That read can return `None` before the first writer publishes.

comments.body:
🤖
# Research

`DataStore.table()` registers a schema through `write_schema()`. A simulated S3 conditional write can fail while another writer is still in flight, so the immediate reread can return `None` and trigger the assertion. No open PR overlaps this schema conflict.

**Relevant code**
- [`store.py#L237-L249`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/e4f5b7d0089a4c16ad9cd202a68f15ef4d9b8e79/lib/finestore/src/finestore/store.py#L237-L249) — table registration
- [`commit.py#L129-L148`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/e4f5b7d0089a4c16ad9cd202a68f15ef4d9b8e79/lib/finestore/src/finestore/commit.py#L129-L148) — schema publication
- [`simulated_s3.py#L299-L326`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/e4f5b7d0089a4c16ad9cd202a68f15ef4d9b8e79/lib/finestore/src/finestore/testing/simulated_s3.py#L299-L326) — in-flight conflict

# Proposed Fix

`DataStore.table()` calls `write_schema()`, whose conditional write may lose before the winner publishes; the following read then returns `None`. Retry the read/create/validate attempt with bounded backoff after an unresolved conflict, and add a simulated-S3 test that holds the winning write in flight until the losing writer observes the missing schema.

🤖 PR #10413 retries unresolved schema-write conflicts with bounded backoff and adds a deterministic simulated-S3 regression. The new test reproduced the assertion before the fix; all 252 FineStore tests pass after it. Changed-files lint and targeted pyrefly pass; repository-wide pyrefly reports 121 local errors, including missing dependencies.

topics.title: [datakit] Replace shuffle-store bucket_token_hint with a self-contained counting pre-pass
topics.body:
## Description
`build_clustered_store_shuffle` (`experiments/datakit/store/datakit_store_shuffle.py`) sizes each `(cluster, quality)` bucket's subshard count from a prior store's per-bucket token mass, loaded via `bucket_token_hint_from_artifact`. This couples the builder to a prior artifact and has a chicken-and-egg on the first build: with no prior store it falls back to `default_subshards`, and no constant wins both goals — `1` sends the hot ~651B-token bucket through one multi-hour / OOM-prone reducer, while a flat `K` re-splits small buckets into many tiny caches (the object proliferation #6687 is fixing).

Replace the prior-artifact hint with a self-contained counting pre-pass: a first map pass that runs the join and counts docs (or tokens) per `(cluster, quality)` — small columns, no payload shuffle — then sizes subshards from the measured distribution. Removes the prior-artifact dependency, is correct on the first run, and adapts to distribution drift, at the cost of one extra cheap pass.

Follow-up to #6687 / PR #6725. Parent: #6037.

### Definition of Done
- `bucket_token_hint` param and `bucket_token_hint_from_artifact` removed from `datakit_store_shuffle.py`
- subshard sizing derived from an in-run per-bucket count pass (reads decon/cluster/quality small columns; no tokenize payload, no scatter)
- hot buckets fan out while small buckets stay at one cache, with no prior artifact required
- `test_datakit_store_shuffle.py` covers pre-pass sizing (a skewed synthetic bucket splits without a hint)

topics.title: [taskforge] Add TaskSpec assembly, lowering, controls and verdicts
topics.body:
The Taskforge build stage produces a task as builder outputs (an instruction, files, an answer and a grader program), and validation runs it under RolloutEngine on whichever host it is on. This adds the `spec` package that turns those outputs into a `TaskSpec` and lowers it for the host.

`spec.draft.assemble` builds the semantic `TaskSpec` and refuses a task that would leak or corrupt its grading: private grader content the solver can read, or an agent-visible file under the grader's `/tests` and `/logs/verifier` roots, which grading stages after the grader's own files. `spec.draft.lower` builds the `TaskRolloutSpec` RolloutEngine runs under its shell harness (`draft.rollout_engine`) and is the one place that chooses each machine's backend. A machine on the grader base image moves to the local backend's CPython only when nothing staged or written on it lies under a system directory that backend cannot write: all of them for a read-only factory, only `/sys` and the resolver's directory for the copy-on-write factory Taskforge builds on Iris. Package machines take PyPI requirements one per entry, and an entry carrying a uv requirements-file option is refused.

`spec.controls` defines the fixed controls a task's control set must hold (a reference, an acceptance and a shortcut control) and turns a candidate's files and reply into the turns a replay serves. `spec.verdict` reads and writes the per-check verdict a grader program reports. `child_process` stops a child process group, for the loader and build children of the later stages.

Builds on #10293. The shared modules are complete here, and #10295 starts the stages. The RolloutEngine tests of `llm.rollout_model`, the ShellSim fixture images and the sandbox factories' two manual machine tests need `spec.draft`, so they land here.

Evaluation can bound concurrency independently and require complete grading coverage before training resumes. The CPU launcher explicitly selects the existing CPU dependency profile.

The vendored trainer’s own `uv.lock` uses exact Git sources for unreleased TaskCompendium, RolloutEngine and Verifyit interfaces. Other package versions and sources remain unchanged. 🤖
# Research

[#9626](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9626) calls `analyze_rollouts()` between evaluation and task generation, but its dummy analyzer groups every reward below 1 by a hard-coded capability ID; the reduced rollout record drops the grade and execution failure evidence needed to tell an incorrect answer from a failed run. #9626 is open and [#9638](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9638) owns the full RSI loop, so this issue can own the analysis stage without duplicating that work. The linked Google Doc redirects to sign-in from this environment, leaving its required grouping and prompt-generation rules unverified.

**Relevant code**
- [`pipeline.py#L82-L97`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/9774e2cd1b4acac2b8b1524e710b217a700fcc22/experiments/post_training/baby_rsi/pipeline.py#L82-L97) — evaluation-to-analysis-to-generation call chain.
- [`dummy.py#L228-L242`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/9774e2cd1b4acac2b8b1524e710b217a700fcc22/experiments/post_training/baby_rsi/dummy.py#L228-L242) — reward-only failure grouping.
- [`interfaces.py#L13-L57`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/9774e2cd1b4acac2b8b1524e710b217a700fcc22/experiments/post_training/baby_rsi/interfaces.py#L13-L57) — prompt and reduced rollout contracts.
- [`contracts.py#L75-L86`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/d8ac9acfd4f1425e8e6caad28fae70b904e5c5bb/lib/rolloutengine/src/rolloutengine/contracts.py#L75-L86) — full grade and failure evidence.

# Proposed Fix

## Design

Implement `AnalysisEngine.analyze_failed_runs` at the #9626 artifact boundary after that PR lands. Preserve each evaluation rollout's task ID, public capability metadata, grade, and execution failure in the analysis input; retain raw task text, expected answers, verifier files, and private traces outside the generator-facing `TaskPromptSet`. Apply the evaluation's explicit pass criterion to completed, valid grades. Count grading and infrastructure failures separately so they do not become training targets. Group valid policy failures by the capability and failure categories specified in the linked document, emit stable prompt IDs and deterministic ordering, and save counts plus source rollout IDs in the private analysis artifact for audit and replay. An empty set of valid policy failures produces an empty prompt set.

## Sequence and validation

1. Rebase on #9626 and keep this PR limited to the analysis input, analyzer, and analysis artifact; leave task generation, training, and the loop coordinator to #9638 and their existing PRs.
2. Add fixture-based tests for wrong answers, partial credit at the configured threshold, successful answers, grader/runtime failures, repeated failures in one category, deterministic output, and exclusion of held-out answer text from prompts. Run the one-round Baby RSI fixture to check that the generated task path consumes the new prompts.
3. Run the touched package's default tests, `./infra/pre-commit.py --all-files --fix`, and the required PR review gate. Record the analysis artifact schema and prompt revision so a later round can reproduce the same selection.

## Open decision

Please provide the linked document's analysis section or read access before implementation. It must settle the failure taxonomy, pass criterion, prompt fields, and whether GLM synthesizes prompts; those choices change the API and tests. The deterministic grouping above is the smallest implementation consistent with the current `TaskPromptSet`, pending that specification.

topics.title: [haliax] Let ragged_dot pick a Triton kernel family explicitly
topics.body:
`ragged_dot` accepts `implementation="triton_group_grid"` and `"triton_tile_map"`, which run one Pallas-Triton kernel family whatever the GPU. `RAGGED_DOT_IMPL` takes the same values, which is how the MoE layers select it. `"triton"` and `"auto"` keep the per-GPU default: tile-map on AMD Instinct, Hopper and data-center Blackwell, and group-grid on every other GPU, such as A100, L4, A6000 and consumer Blackwell (sm_120). Neither family has been measured on those GPUs, so their default does not change.

Tile-map on those GPUs, which this opt-in now allows, used the group-grid blocks (128x128x32, 4 warps, 4 stages). On H100 those blocks made tile-map 0.78-0.89x of group-grid at the Mixtral-like shape (G=8, 4096x14336) at M=16384. A sweep of 96 configs on H100 picked one config per layout among configs whose operand stages fit in 99 KiB of shared memory. 99 KiB is the per-block limit on sm_86, sm_89 and sm_120; A100 allows 163 KiB. Per call in bf16, against group-grid with its own blocks:

| Layout | Blocks (m x n x k), warps, stages, group_m | June, G=32, M=16k and 128k | Mixtral-like, G=8, M=16k and 64k |
|---|---|---|---|
| fwd | 128x256x32, 8, 4, 8 | 1.12-1.16x | 1.18-1.83x |
| dlhs | 128x256x32, 8, 4, 1 | 1.21-1.59x | 1.39-2.22x |
| drhs | 128x128x32, 4, 3, 8 | 1.00-1.08x | 1.03-1.18x |

The Iris jobs are `/dev/ragged-dot-group-grid-vs-tile-map` and `/dev/ragged-dot-generic-config-sweep`, both on H100. The 1.83x and 2.22x peaks come partly from group-grid slowing down once a group's rows exceed L2 (`/dev/ragged-dot-group-grid-l2-cliff`), which a separate PR will address. In the same grid, the tuned H100 configs remained the best, so this PR leaves the tuned tables unchanged.

The ragged_dot tests pass on one H100 (43 passed, 30 f32 cases skipped for TF32; `/dev/ragged-dot-family-opt-in-tests-3`) and in the CPU interpreter. A new GPU test checks the value and gradients of each explicit family against XLA.

topics.title: [grug] Add hero launch controls for a context-length switch
topics.body:
The scaling-ladder launcher holds 4,194,304 tokens per rack per update, so the sequence batch shrinks as the context grows (2816 sequences at 16K on 11 racks). The step count (390251), learning rates, decay, and gate/router weight decay therefore match the 4K run. The hero's context length, QK multipliers, and capacity factor live in HERO_MODEL. --qk-mult and --qk-mult-long-scale (global layers only) override the QK multipliers for trial arms and ladder rungs; trial arms set the context length on their branch alongside the history. Eval packs at the training context, as on main, so the eval_dropless/* series shift at each switch. For short trial arms, --eval-every overrides the eval cadence.

The hero's context history is checked in, like the data mix's switch point: HERO_CONTEXT_PHASES in launch_scaling_ladder.py lists each context the d6144 hero trained at before its current one with the step it ended at, and HERO_FLOPS_BASELINE_TOTAL holds the parent's cumulative training FLOPs at the last switch. A context-switch deploy PR edits Python only: it sets the HERO_MODEL fields, appends one entry to HERO_CONTEXT_PHASES, and sets HERO_FLOPS_BASELINE_TOTAL, so a second switch (4K to 16K, then 16K to 64K) is described exactly and trigger_hero.sh is unchanged. The launcher turns the history into a FlopsBaseline at the last end step and, through the prior_context_phases argument of harrier_mix_2026_08_18_data_config, into LmDataConfig.prior_context_phases, with each earlier phase's Harrier stage schedule and shuffle blocks at its own batch size, so the Harrier sources continue from their earlier reads. At d6144 the launcher rejects a history that does not start at 4K, repeats a length between adjacent phases (including the current context), or disagrees with whether the baseline is set. LmDataConfig rejects end steps that do not increase, and rejects any switch below the 1e23-FLOP simulated-epoching cutoff because the data offsets assume each source reads its whole cache. The narrow rungs take no history.

The live run is unchanged: trigger_hero.sh is identical to main and launches the 4K HERO_MODEL with no FLOPs baseline. A switch still needs a GPU rehearsal from the handoff checkpoint and agreed trial thresholds; see the inventory and validation plan in #9615.

Part of #9615

The three stacked together match the old head's tree, rebased onto current main, plus three small lint-review fixes: one in #9888, one in #9890, and one here (`ladder_batch_size`, shared with `trigger_hero.sh`).
@codex review

🤖 `CONTEXT_SWITCH_STEP` can record only one context switch, and the plan in #8435 has two (4K → 8K at ~50%, then → 65K at ~95%). The launcher turns the step into a single `HarrierPriorContext(end_step=step, seq_len=4096, ...)` ([launch_scaling_ladder.py](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44782f64d32a043b2f3ad7f2aa8d64e8bf08cefa/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/launch_scaling_ladder.py#L231-L240)), so the second switch has no checked-in place for the intermediate phase.

The current check does not catch this. Suppose the run switches 4K → 16K at N1 and 16K → 64K at N2, and the second deploy PR sets `SEQ_LEN=65536` and keeps `CONTEXT_SWITCH_STEP=N1`. The check in [trigger_hero.sh](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44782f64d32a043b2f3ad7f2aa8d64e8bf08cefa/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/trigger_hero.sh#L107-L111) passes, because N1 is nonzero and before the handoff. The offsets are then computed as if the run went 4K → 64K at N1. Each source resumes inside the shuffle window it was reading at N2 instead of skipping to the next window, so it re-reads part of that window under a new within-window order. Stage boundaries at the 64K batch size are also not reconciled with the 16K phase. This is from reading the code; I have not run it.

`LmDataConfig.prior_phases` from #9888 already takes several phases and carries offsets forward across them (`test_second_context_switch_continues_past_the_first_switch_skip`). Only the trigger and launcher need to change. Suggestion:

- Replace `CONTEXT_SWITCH_STEP` with a checked-in history, for example `CONTEXT_HISTORY="4096:N1 16384:N2"` (each entry is the length the run trained at and the step at which it ended), and build one `HarrierPriorContext` per entry. A context-switch deploy PR then appends an entry, in the same way a handoff PR edits `HANDOFF_CHECKPOINT`, so the run's behavior stays determined by the launch commit.
- In the trigger, reject a history whose end steps do not increase, whose last end step is after the handoff checkpoint, or whose adjacent entries (and the last entry and `SEQ_LEN`) have the same length.
- Add a test that pins the reconstructed `PriorDataPhase` (stage steps, weights, shuffle) for a fixed history. The old phases are re-derived from `_stage_weights` and `_shuffle_config` at each launch, so a later edit to those functions would change the offsets of a run that already switched.

topics.title: [levanter] Continue mixture reads across a context-length switch
topics.body:
Harrier's shuffle blocks change from a fixed 256 sequences to a fixed 2^20 tokens (io_block_size = 2**20 // seq_len). At 4K the two are identical, so the live run's data order is unchanged. At a longer context, the token-sized blocks keep the outer block permutation the same, and only the order of sequences inside each 512-block shuffle window changes. With the old 256-sequence blocks, a 16K relaunch would have re-read an estimated 2.85T already-seen tokens of the remaining ~9T.

The new LmDataConfig.prior_context_phases describes the earlier context lengths of a resumed run, one ContextPhaseConfig per length. With prior_context_phases set, each source skips the unread rest of the shuffle window it was reading at the switch step and starts its next window, so nothing is served twice. At a 216000-step handoff this skips about 52B tokens, 0.65% of the rest of the run. MixtureDataset takes per-source start offsets to apply the skip. Every phase must give positive weight to the same sources, because a training config drops zero-weight sources and that changes the shuffle keys of the rest; a change in the active sources is rejected. So is a phase at the same sequence length as the one before it, since there a source could continue in place and the skip would only discard data. The seed, the source order, and restoring at the last switch step cannot be checked from the config, so the field docstring states them. The offsets come from each source's true position in the earlier phase, so they also absorb the main-mixture boundary moving from step 108000 to 108096 at 16K. The grug train loop builds its mixture through the new LmDataConfig.train_mixture.

Part of #9615
topics.head: aa184d6ddbe72291a0b3c896c6d8f9ed3fe4134d

comments.body:
🤖 Review notes from a walkthrough of the change. None of these block the mechanism; the rename is the main request.

**Rename the prior-phase types.** `PriorDataPhase` is easy to misread: "data" does not say which aspect of the data changed, and in the Harrier code and docs "phase" already means a mixture phase (`_SPEC.phase_weights`, the JSON `phases`, "Phase 1/2/3" in `docs/reports/hero-mixture-log.md`). A context switch can fall in the middle of a mixture phase, so the two divisions of the run need different names. Suggested names:

| Current | Suggested |
| --- | --- |
| `PriorDataPhase` | `ContextPhaseConfig` |
| `LmDataConfig.prior_phases` | `prior_context_phases` |
| `MixturePhase` | `ContextPhase` |

This follows the `FooConfig` → `Foo` pattern: `ContextPhaseConfig` declares a past context phase in steps, and `ContextPhase` is the form `skip_to_window_offsets` uses (start step, `BatchSchedule`, stages in sequence indices). The `ContextPhase` list also holds the current phase. The `MixturePhase` docstring ("A phase of the mixture for ...") should change with it, for example to "One context phase of the run, with its batch schedule and stages in sequence indices." Please also add a sentence to the field docstring that batch-size changes within one context belong in `BatchSchedule`, and that `prior_context_phases` describes earlier context lengths only.

Names and strings that follow from the rename:

- `_prior_phase_offsets` → `_prior_context_phase_offsets`, and `_prior_phase_window_tokens` → `_context_phase_window_tokens`.
- The `"prior_phases ..."` error messages and the `train_mixture` docstring.
- `"Every data phase must draw from the same sources"`, `"Data phases must start at increasing steps"`, and `"Prior phase {phase} must shuffle ..."` → "context phase".
- In `test_context_switch_data.py`: the imports, the `_phase` and `_offsets` annotations, and `test_lm_data_config_prior_phase_resumes_without_repeating_tokens`.
- In #9689: `HarrierPriorContext` and `prior_contexts`, so the stack uses one term. The context history that replaces `CONTEXT_SWITCH_STEP` there (see my comment on #9689) can use the same name.

**Reject adjacent phases with the same sequence length.** `skip_to_window_offsets` accepts two adjacent phases with the same `seq_len`, for example a relaunch that changes only the batch size. In that case the within-window order does not change, so a source could continue at its exact position. `_next_window_start` still rounds up to the next shuffle window and discards up to one window per source (about 537M tokens per source at Harrier's settings). A check that adjacent phases differ in `seq_len` would turn that silent waste into an error. It would also make the `ContextPhase` name exact.

**Rename `counts_before` and make it block-aligned.** `counts_before` does not say what it counts; `sequence_counts_before` does. Its partial-block branch also never runs in this PR: `skip_to_window_offsets` calls it only at block boundaries (rounded up for the old phase, down for the new one). That branch returns a count, but in a partly served block the count is not a read position, because slots are shuffled; a source that served 3 sequences may have served occurrences 0, 7, and 31. Taking a block index instead, as `sequence_counts_before_block(block_id)`, removes the branch and prevents a later caller from using a mid-block count as a position.

**Check source order across phases.** The active-source check compares sets, but order matters as much: it sets each source's shuffle key through `key_iterator`, and the mixture's slot layout through `dataset_index` (including which source receives the rounding remainder). A config that lists the same sources in a different order passes the check and gets a different data layout. Recording the source order in the prior phase and comparing lists would catch this; at minimum, the docstring should say the order must not change.

**Document two assumptions that cannot be checked here.** (1) The shuffle and mixture keys come from the trainer seed, so the seed must be the same in every phase. (2) The offsets assume the current phase starts reading at the last `end_step`. A launch that restores a checkpoint from before that step would re-read data. #9689's trigger checks this for the hero; a docstring sentence on `prior_phases` would cover other callers.

**Optional: give a prior phase a `BatchSchedule`.** `PriorDataPhase.batch_size` is an `int`, so a prior phase cannot have a batch ramp, while the current phase takes a full `BatchSchedule`. A `BatchSchedule` field would give prior and current phases one representation.

**Possible follow-up, not for this PR.** Batch-size history (`BatchSchedule`) and context-length history (`prior_phases`) are both step-indexed descriptions of the run's shape, and could become one schedule. That needs three things this PR should not take on: the trainer must reject a `seq_len` change after the current step, because `Pos` is fixed per launch, while it can follow a batch change; `BatchSchedule` is used in 28 Python files; and the Harrier stage schedule would need to record the realized step of past stage boundaries instead of rounding them again for each batch size.

🤖 Addressed in new commits on top of the reviewed head ([compare 5a2525a4ec..748ad7fe6f](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/compare/5a2525a4ec..748ad7fe6f)):

- **Rename** (86fff8f63b): `ContextPhaseConfig`, `prior_context_phases`, `ContextPhase`, `_prior_context_phase_offsets`, `_context_phase_window_tokens`, the error messages, the `ContextPhase` docstring, and the test names. The field docstring now says that batch-size changes within one context length belong in `BatchSchedule`. In #9689, b596fe391c renames `HarrierPriorContext` and `prior_contexts` to `HarrierContextPhase` and `prior_context_phases`.
- **Same-length adjacent phases** (4ca2f1ba0d): `skip_to_window_offsets` now raises an error.
- **`counts_before`** (c7bdbe68f1): now `sequence_counts_before_block(block_id)`, without the partial-block branch.
- **Source order** (1c99ccec06): documented, not checked. A recorded source list would not catch the case that matters: the Harrier launcher rebuilds the prior phase from the same spec at every launch, so a reordered spec changes the recorded list and the current list together.
- **Seed and restore step** (1c99ccec06): both assumptions are in the `prior_context_phases` docstring.
- **Batch schedule for a prior phase** (748ad7fe6f): `ContextPhaseConfig.batch_size` is now `int | IntSchedule`, the same type as `TrainerConfig.train_batch_size`, so the existing `BatchSchedule(...)` conversion handles both.

The unified schedule is left for a follow-up, as suggested. The `CONTEXT_SWITCH_STEP` history from the #9689 comment is not in these commits.

topics.title: [taskforge] stage40: the SDK, standard template, build services and the agentic author
topics.body:
Add the build stage as one package. `stage40_build_with_program` holds the SDK that build steps call, the standard six-step template, `GlmAuthor`, the agentic author, and `RLEnvBuildServices`, through which a build reaches machines, images, web tools, the ledger and agent limits. Host failures are told apart from program failures (`infrastructure`) so that a host outage never spends a revision, and the build runs in a child process under a wall clock (`build_process`).

`agentic_author.author_round` runs one agent session per program round in a workspace that starts with the standard template, the proposal, the SDK reference and an empty notes file. Its tools read, write and edit workspace files, run the loader in a child process, build the program on the caller's step store, grade a candidate against the last draft, and search and fetch the web when the proposal lists research; `submit` hands the program in. A host failure, an expired clock or a storage fault never reaches the model, so none of them spends a revision.

The package name states whether a build program produces the task draft at all, not how the program's writer runs. The agentic author writes and iterates a build program, so it lives here with the SDK, the template and the services it is handed. `stage40_build_with_agent` is reserved for a future build in which an agent produces the draft directly, with no program; it has no contents, `BUILDS_ON` in `tests/test_imports.py` is empty, and the README and that test's docstring state the distinction.

`run_build` now takes the services and a `ResearchRequirement`, keys steps on `build_model_digest`, records a `STEP` span for each step, and rejects a task whose solver machine differs from the one the proposal pins. A wall, step or grader timeout raises `BuildExpired`, distinct from a program `BuildFailure` or a host `BuildInfrastructureFailure`. The coordinator adaptation is in this PR because the build signature changes here: `StageCoordinator` holds the services and the research requirement and passes them to each build, records the requirement at `OPENED` so a relaunch cannot change it, and holds an expired workpiece without spending a revision. `check_workpiece_id` moves from `step_store` to `ledger.records`, and the coordinator and the `Author` protocol type proposals as `TaskProposal`. Triage runs `stage20_triage.preflight.preflight` and returns its `Verdict`; the coordinator exits accept or reject on it and records the verdict's reasons on a reject. The coordinator keeps its repair edge, a surface for a deterministic rewrite or a consumer's triage within `max_triage_repairs` (callers pass 0), and passes an accept's `author_state` to every author call as the `Author`'s third argument; nothing in the package writes one.

`publish_image` classifies an image job the host failed (`image_builder.ImageJobFailed`, #10293) as the host's `IMAGE_JOB_FAILED` and a Dockerfile kaniko refused (`BuildFailed`) as the program's `BuildFailure`.

Builds on #10297; #10300 builds on it. #10299 is folded in here. The loader tests from #10297 land here, and two assertions that lower a built task through `stage50_validate` land with that stage in #10300. The first two commits repeated a GLM client change and a sandbox docstring fix that the lower branches were cut without. Since the stack sync, the client is #10291's, which requests no per-token logprobs, and neither commit changes this diff.

topics.title: [sft] Preserve the fixed-budget agentic LR sweep
topics.body:
Preserve the Snowball v0 learning-rate sweep with prepared-file hash and cache token-count checks, active-token loss accounting, permanent native checkpoints and BF16 exports. Register W&B and epoch accounting as sibling trackers so the Iris status callback can discover W&B. Offline validation restores each checkpoint without context sharding and reports measured token denominators alongside TMax, SWE-smith and pooled losses.

Each of the three nominal epochs is a fixed-update window under the original block-2048 mixture sampler, which does not visit every row exactly once per window. Window token totals are recorded rather than assumed from the manifest. Resume retains optimizer/data state; earlier window statistics remain in the original run's artifacts.

The Snowball token reshapes carry their output sharding explicitly, and the router query bias remains outside differentiation. The experiment launcher requests non-preemptible H100 workers, disables automatic retries and sets NCCL logging to WARN.

Part of #10213

topics.title: [rl] Invalidate Atlas reviews for source-specific grading changes
topics.body:
Atlas previously invalidated a saved quality review when the shared verifier repository revision changed, including changes unrelated to that source. Fingerprint each MarinSkyRL source's selected grading code, prompts, runtime dependencies and task-owned verifier assets so unrelated repository edits preserve its grading identity.

Require an archived, hash-verified proof that a saved review covers the current dataset revision and grading identity. New task-verifier executions attest their grading inputs before publication. Historical reviews remain current when archived evidence establishes that the selected grading inputs or behavior are equivalent. Otherwise the source needs current quality review. Original reviews and their captured execution revisions remain available.

Harbor-backed Nemotron SWE identities include selected proxy verifier files, permissions, judge settings and grader environments. GenRM difficulty displays mean task-verifier rewards and bootstrap confidence intervals from 16-candidate comparison pools; it does not convert those rewards into solved-task counts.

Regression tests cover grading changes, unrelated code and documentation edits, selected task assets and invalid review proofs. The export preserves all 206 source IDs. The 103 MarinSkyRL sources have grading fingerprints; adding task assets changes the ten Harbor fingerprints and preserves the other 93. Task Trove sources retain their existing pinned dataset references. Type checking and required lint pass. After merging main at dcddd68f9b, the affected safe test run passes 2,623 tests with seven failures reproduced independently on that clean main commit. All 79 Atlas backend and grading-code tests pass, including a packaged-backend migration regression. All ten Harbor task-asset manifests match after the upstream archive helper move. The catalog is bundled as a Python string literal because Marina extracts only server Python files for backend execution. Public applet version 68 preserves all source IDs and pinned data references.

prompts.text:
Was reading "Lost in Backpropagation: The LM Head is a Gradient Bottleneck" by @nthngdy and @yoavartzi the other day. Their ideas seemed very clever, but my ability to follow their intuition was lacking. So I decided to imagine "What would it be like to work as a neuron", to better process their ideas. The main audience when writing this was just myself. Sharing in case others find it a fun read.

A Day in the Life of a Neuron Associate at Grub Zoo.
prompts.expected:
Welcome to Grub Zoo. Proud home of 1000 animals. Each animal has its own designated 5 minute feeding window during the day where it eats one serving of grub. The feeding schedule looks something like:
-Feed the horse and the Giraffe from 4:00-4:05.
-Feed the rhino from 4:15-4:20.
-Feed the 8 alligators from 7:10-7:15.

Initially the Zoo ran off a simple lookup chart, where one could query a 5 minute window, and get returned a list of all animals that needed to be fed. Well, Bob from Marketing had a great (terrible) idea to replace our lookup table with AI. But instead of using AI, we could just become AI (wtf?). He explained that we’d each get some role in a mega human neural network, then use the power of ‘backpropagation’ to tell each other what to do. I think this is his promo project or something, not sure. His idea is that the optimal feeding window should depend on all sorts of properties of the weather, and once we get this learning machine running, it can plug in a bunch of these advanced features.

The first part of the plan was to designate 10 employees as feeders. Each feeder had to write down how they would divvy up any grub they were given between the 1,000 animals. One feeder, Jeremy, decided he’d give all grub he was given to the sloth. Weird guy. Another one, Anna, decided she’d split up the grub equally across all 1,000 animals. (How’s she gonna manage that, lol?).

My job was the supplier. Every 5 minutes I’d show up with some servings of grub. Then I’d have to divvy it up between the feeders, who’d then divvy it up between the animals based on their prearranged fractions. The weird part here is that I was the only one who was aware of the time of day- the feeders always stuck to their fractions.

Bob said that during each 5 minute interval we’d have two phases: an execution phase, and a feedback phase. Well for the first 5 minute execution phase I frankly had no idea what was going on, so I just gave an equal amount of grub to each of the 10 feeders, who then distributed it out. Somehow Anna was able to get grub out to all 1,000 animals, impressive.

Only the horse and the giraffe were supposed to get fed in this window, but the small amount of grub ended up spread out across all animals, and nobody was happy. I voted to drop Bob’s idea, but he figured we could salvage things. His insight was “Most windows only have a couple animals who need getting fed, so after everybody distributes their grub, we should apply some sort of bunching action towards the ones with the most grub. That way at least somebody gets a decent meal. Sometimes multiple animals need grub and we won’t be sure we got it right, so just do soft bunching.” He called it softmax.

We applied his technique, and sure enough one animal got a good meal, but it was the wrong animal! And the animals at Grub Zoo are extremely picky about when they get fed! Well, Bob said this was ok at first (what?), we just needed the feedback phase.

The feedback phase started with the animals. The ones that didn’t get fed but were supposed to, complained loudly. The feeders were the only ones who could observe and hear the animals. Each feeder would first go observe all 1000 animals to see which ones were complaining. Then they’d update their fractions slightly towards giving them more grub. Now if the supplier had given the feeder little or no grub that window, the feeder would take little effort in updating their fraction as it wouldn’t matter anyway. But if they had been given a large amount of grub, they’d take tremendous honor in updating their fraction quite heavily. But they had to be careful here! They were going to use that fraction for every time window, so they didn’t want to over-correct for one 5 minute interval.

The next phase of feedback was for me as the supplier. Each of the 10 feeders came and told me either ‘Man I coulda made a difference I had the fractions right just give me more grub’, or ‘I was off on this one, didn’t need grub here’. Then my job was to update ‘Ok for this 5 minute interval, give grub to feeder X’, because they told me their fraction is calibrated. I figured none of the feeders had it exactly right, but if I gave more grub to the feeders that seemed decent at the right times, their errors would average out and softmax would help bunch it up on the right animals.

To me the process felt pretty dumb, as the feeders were just like mindless cogs, trying to find the one right fraction. They could see all 1000 animals. But all I could see were 10 people shouting ‘give me more/less grub’. And somehow I was supposed to manage all the windows from that?

Over time I developed a massive lookup table. For each 5 minute interval, how much grub to give to each of the 10 feeders. Each feeder started to get more sophisticated specialization. For instance, one guy fed just the 8 alligators. I knew to only give him grub from 7:10-7:15, because that’s when he complained.

Well, Bob got wind that I was using a lookup table for each 5 minute window and freaked out. Said it wasn’t true AI. Said I was getting demoted to a neuron. 9 other people got hired as neurons too, working in parallel to me.

Now instead of a unique fraction for each window, I had a simpler role. I had to learn a fixed ratio across the 10 feeders, and a simple rule for when to switch on. Initially I just put the fraction on for the morning. And then tuned the fraction a bit to give grub to the feeders that were clamoring for more grub in the morning. I figured if I helped focus on some of the morning intervals, other ‘neuron associates’ could manage other windows of the day. I never got to see what these other neuron associates were up to, but I figured if I listened to the feeders I could help compensate for the gaps.

Well, we got some new funding, and Bob decided to hire some more ‘neuron associates’, so we are up to 20 now. Communication is becoming a real problem. We never talk to each other, and it’s getting kind of weird only listening to the 10 feeders and trying to compensate for what all my coworkers are doing.

Now Bob had the craziest idea yet. He decided to break up our 20 neuron associates into two 10 member squads: Alpha and Bravo. I got put on Bravo. During each interval I’d get to see both the time of day, and how much the Alpha Squad was planning to give to each feeder. I decided to take on a targeted role: IF the time was between 10-11am AND I saw that Alpha Squad was giving grub to feeder 2, then I’d give grub to feeder 1 and 2. I learned that in the morning whenever Alpha Squad gave grub to feeder 2, feeder 2 would still complain and want even more, and feeder 1 complained as well.

I noticed that sometimes Alpha Squad would slip up and not give grub to feeder 2, which meant I didn’t trigger on feeder 1 or 2. When this happened, I’d complain loudly. Hey Alpha! Give more grub to feeder 2! Problem is, team Alpha was getting overwhelmed during the feedback cycle. They had to listen to both the feeders directly, and every single member on squad Bravo. The problem got even worse when we doubled the size of Alpha and Bravo to 20 people each. That’s when Bob started hiring a new role, called ‘transporters’ and ‘messengers’.

There was one messenger and transporter for each feeder. Everyone only got to receive feedback from the messengers, and give grub to the transporters. During the execution phase, the transporters would collect the grub from squad Alpha, then I could make my decision based on if transporter 2 had grub. All of us in squad Bravo would then add on to the grub the transporters were carrying. During the feedback phase, I’d tell messenger 2 if I wanted more grub sent to feeder 2. This way, Alpha squad didn’t have to talk to both the feeders and Bravo squad. The messengers just added up the feedback from both the feeders and Bravo.

We ran this operation for several weeks, with Alpha and Bravo squads distributing grub to the transporters, the messengers giving feedback, and the feeders divvying it out and observing the animals. It seemed like the dumbest thing I’d ever seen! A lookup table could have done the same thing!

Well, that’s when Bob made a change that actually blew my mind. He called it the ‘magic of generalization’. The first thing he did was give all neuron associates access to the temperature, in addition to the time of day. Now in the old world, we’d have to manually make updates to all 1000 animals in the lookup table to figure out how they responded to temperature. In the new world, I only had to change my allocation to the 10 transporters. The feeders had already built fractions that grouped the animals into correlated sets.

I developed a new trigger condition. IF the time was between 10-11am AND transporter 2 had grub AND the temperature was above 60F, then give grub to transporter 1, 2, and 3. I came to learn that in very cold weather, these messengers didn’t complain as much.

Over time Bob added new features I could trigger on. Rain. Wind. Sunshine. It was starting to be quite a lot to handle. Bob always had to go around explaining to every neuron associate how this new measurement would work. Eventually Bob got pretty tired of this. He decided that only squad Alpha could see things like time, temperature, rain, wind, and sunshine. At first this seemed completely crazy to me. How could I know when to trigger, without these key features?

We concocted a pretty funny plan. I noticed that messenger 9 NEVER complained. My guess is that feeder 9 was just completely checked-out. Never gave any grub to anyone. Team Alpha had picked up on this. They also knew that whenever it was between 10-11am and above 60F, messenger 2 would complain to them. So they decided to give grub to transporter 9 whenever it got hot in the morning- not because transporter 9 needed the grub. But because team Bravo could then use that signal to make better decisions.

I developed a new heuristic: IF transporter 2 AND transporter 9 have grub, then we give grub to transporter 1,2,3. AND we also take that grub away from transporter 9 and add it to the pile, since feeder 9 never complains.

So that became my job. I’d wake up every morning, drive in to work as a neuron associate, then pay very close attention to which 10 transporters had grub, and how that correlated to the complaints I’d get from the 10 messengers. I’d update my fractions among the 10 transporters, and update my feedback to the 10 messengers.

Later that month my team name got updated to Squad Bravo-46. What the heck? Turns out Bob had really scaled the operation. We now had 50 Bravo squads in series. My job was always the same, talk to 10 messengers, and observe 10 transporters. I had no idea what measurements got fed into Alpha Squad. And honestly, I had no idea how many animals even lived at the Zoo anymore. I didn’t even know how many team members were on Bravo-46, since I never talked to them.

Alpha Squad was the only team that got to see the pure, raw measurements. And the 10 feeders were the only team that got to see the actual animals. In particular, it seemed like the feeders functioned like quite the bottleneck. I'd love to get to observe all 1,000 animals, instead of just 10 messengers and transporters.

Anyways, that’s my job. Hope the giraffe is doing alright.

evalchemy209.title: Make Evalchemy results and resume state FineStore native
evalchemy209.body:
Write evaluation aggregates, normalized samples, and request checkpoints directly to FineStore. Resume restores committed requests by default. Before generation, the evaluator validates the stored task list and each task's fingerprint, including all supplied generation overrides. It initializes the model before this validation. Results and samples enter the archive in one transaction, so a retry leaves a completed result unchanged. FineStore result writes use the same guarded SymPy serialization as the CLI display.

`--output_path` and `--finestore_output_path` select the same FineStore archive. Existing scripts keep `--output_path` and use distinct archive paths for distinct evaluations. Native JSON/JSONL result serialization, SQLite resume state, temporary output staging, and the unused TACC listener are removed. The TACC distributed batch scripts remain. The serve-and-eval runner and regression gate read the same archive; the gate keeps `--results` as its archive selector. Concurrent writers to one archive have not been exercised locally.

Part of marin-community/marin#9972. The Marin retry work is tracked in marin-community/marin#9813.

evalchemy214.title: Separate grading from score aggregation
evalchemy214.body:
Use each benchmark's aggregation code for both normal evaluation and partial-result recovery, preserving its metrics and breakdowns. Save grading evidence before aggregation so it can be replayed without rerunning graders.

Repeated evaluations with infrastructure-failed trials still fail the task.

msrl944.title: Refresh the frozen trainer stack to TE 2.20 and Torch 2.14.1
msrl944.body:
Refresh the combined trainer and serving group to Torch 2.14.1+cu132, CUDA 13.2.2, Transformer Engine 2.20.2, Core 0.19.2 and Bridge 0.6.2. Preserve Snowball and Hero MuonH/AdamH math, BF16 compute, FP32 state and router biases, HF import/export, expert routes, repeated weight transfer and fresh-stack save/resume. The recipe and qualified baseline evidence are in https://echo.oa.dev/wiki/610.

Use native FlashAttention versioning, event loops, Core attention selection and expert tags, NCCL transport selection and batch-invariance initialization, and W&B mutable tables. Remove obsolete vLLM API branches, global broadcast replacement, unconditional compile/sampler overrides, wheel migration tools, dead FP8/Qwen helpers, the extra Ray peer-access allocation, copied NCCL settings and startup staggering. Native Harbor already includes its config module, so remove the overlapping standalone distribution. The default uv prerelease policy preserves all 510 package records. Retained fixes have source links and removal conditions beside the code; existing packaging checks refuse unverified runtime, patch-source and build inputs.

The serving changes are in [vLLM PR95](https://github.com/marin-community/vllm/pull/95). This draft still selects the qualified [3a wheel pair](https://github.com/marin-community/vllm/releases/tag/marin-vllm-gpu-20261012-3a054c458ca8) until the source receives the required GitHub review, lands normally and the official main-only build publishes qualified artifacts. Its native FFI 0.1.11, TileLang 0.1.12 and Tokenspeed MLA 0.1.8 group must then be adopted coherently with [Marin PR10022](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10022). The new published Marin package/projection path and other affected application paths still require qualification.

Focused removal pilots passed 17 cases on H100 and 16 on GB200; a cold GB200 FlashInfer build exceeded the startup deadline and completed separately in 2,464 seconds. A two-GB200 native initializer/shared-group probe passed 18 exact broadcasts without copied NCCL settings. Tiny native Core/MSC S3 save/load passes, while five alternating reader comparisons support retaining record buffering: 69 native GETs versus 9 maintained GETs per read, with exact values in both. Removing Hero's CUDA graph guard produced NaN logprobs after changing batch sizes; retain it. These component results do not qualify the final packaged runtime, full-model continuation or RL throughput.

The bounded High source review and targeted follow-ups found no remaining source blocker. The original four full-model reports apply to the baseline; reuse requires explicit source, lock, payload, build-input and exercised-path comparison. The remaining compiler, dependency-metadata, checkpoint and reload fixes remain maintenance costs. Optional HDO, SGLang, GPTOSS, sandbox and legacy fidelity/cache paths are separate from the required MuonH profile and are not qualified by these pilots.

Keep the qualified fallback branch and artifacts. Final consumer merges remain Romain's actions after final artifacts, affected Snowball/Hero and performance gates, coherent pins and terminal CI. The [native Snowball checkpoint oracle failure](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9400#issuecomment-6129427326), parked [TPU pair](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10023), original Hero/GB200 shutdown anomaly and optimizer-payload sampling limits remain disclosed. Policy-only TE timings do not establish full RL throughput or performance equivalence.
